  • The API has no authentication on the LAN; firewall 9911 and 17000 to trusted hosts.

Scale

Transport is never the constraint: raw capture is 2 ms and 84 req/s on one phone, and phones are fully independent, up to 512 req/s aggregate across ten concurrent pollers with no contention from input traffic. The frame-driven settle sets the real pace instead, roughly 0.3-1.0 s per stop per phone, with the slowest-frame-rate device in the panel dominating the timing. If wheel scrolling turns out not to work and the design falls back to swipe, add ~300-500 ms of pointer-walk time per stop on top of the settle, which roughly halves throughput to an estimated 200-400 ad-stop captures per hour per phone across 19 phones — still far inside the kernel's own ceiling and gated by ad-serving cadence rather than the API. Storage is the real cost: raw BMP is 1.62 MB per stop (~920 MB for 19 phones x 30 stops), so archive as JPEG (~96 KB, capped ~21 req/s) or crop with rect and keep the raw frame only for stops that matched; never use JPEG on the loopback analysis path.

App Store ranking, rating and review monitoring

Needs plug-inWith caveats

Drives each phone to an App Store product page or the Search tab, lets the mirror settle, then reads star rating, review count and "What's New" text, or locates your icon among search results, from a cropped region of the frame. Every screenshot is kept as the dated record, so a rank change or a rating drop comes with an image of the page rather than a figure from a vendor's model. On this rig the navigation half works today; the reading half does not — /pic/ocr answers code 28 (plug-in not connected), so recognition has to run client-side on the raw BMP or wait on the vendor plug-ins.

How

  1. send_key (WIN+h) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<id1>,<id2>&fn_key=WIN+h, twice — normalise to a known home screen.
  2. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<id1>,<id2> — clear the stuck-click state on the whole target set.
  3. shortcut#13 Open URL GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<ids>&url=https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id<appid> — deep-link to the product page (needs the Shortcut).
  4. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y= — tap the App Store icon instead; works with no Shortcut at all.
  5. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — capture the rating / review-count / What's New block, one request per phone.
  6. ocr GET /api/pic/ocr?id=<id>&rect=[0,250,500,420] — read the block; blocked on this rig today (code 28).
  7. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y= — open the Search tab and focus the field; coordinates must be measured per phone and iOS build, never assumed.
  8. send_key (key=, ENTER) POST JSON {fun:"/key/sendkey", data:{id, key}} then GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<id>&fn_key=ENTER — type the keyword as POST JSON so spaces survive, then submit.
  9. find_image / find_image_ex POST /api/pic/find-image-cv {id, img_list, similarity:0.85, same:true} — locate your icon among results (plug-in gated).
  10. mouse_wheel (or swipe) GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=<id>&direction=down&len=30&number=1 — scroll the result list and repeat until found or exhausted.
  11. (client-side) none — logic over the frames from steps 5/9 — reconstruct rank; no endpoint returns a list index or scroll offset.
  12. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&jpg=true&save_path= — archive the dated evidence frame.

Needs

  • Vendor console running and logged in, with license capacity for the devices used.
  • Each phone mirroring (live air_pid, an ESTABLISHED socket on TCP 17000) and controllable (board state 2, non-empty location_crc).
  • iOS accessibility settings on every phone: AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock, vendor cable only.
  • Each phone signed into an Apple ID for the storefront being monitored — the API cannot set or read the storefront.
  • iMouse Shortcut installed and bound, for the deep-link route only.
  • OCR and image-search plug-ins connected, for the reading steps — currently absent, /pic/ocr returns code 28.
  • Per-phone, per-iOS-build calibration captured once: App Store icon, Search tab, search field and rating-block coordinates.
  • Competitor icon templates cropped from the same model at the same AirPlay compression ratio.

Watch out

  • Blocking today: /pic/ocr returns code 28; assume the image-search plug-in is in the same state until probed. Three ways out in order of cost: install the vendor plug-ins; run OCR and template matching client-side on the raw BMP; or the undocumented /shortcut/other/ocr-family fallbacks (Shortcut v1.3+) — probe before designing around them.
  • Every /pic/* call is single-device; only /mouse/*, /key/* and /shortcut/exec/url take a comma-separated id list.
  • Coordinates are mirror pixels (500x1080 here), never iOS points (414x896), and are per-phone and per-build — the two XRs on this rig have different home screens, so a shared coordinate hits a different app on each.
  • The storefront follows the Apple ID, not the phone's network or IP — monitoring N storefronts needs N phones signed into accounts for those regions; the API cannot change it.
  • outtime on Shortcut calls is milliseconds on XP (default 15000), not the seconds figure in the Phonefarm doc.
  • key= is ASCII only; non-Latin keywords need clipboard/set plus WIN+v, which reintroduces the Shortcut dependency. Send multi-word keywords as POST JSON, not a GET query string.
  • No endpoint returns a search-result index — rank is a client-side reconstruction over scrolled frames, and the paid slot at the top must be counted separately or every organic rank is off by one.
  • An ENTER press does not by itself prove the results page loaded: App Store shows live autocomplete suggestions while typing, and a frame taken right after ENTER can still show that dropdown. Settle detection needs a second, positive check, such as the ranked-card layout region, not just "the diff stopped moving".
  • Search ranking and suggestions are personalised to the signed-in Apple ID's install and search history — a farm account with an unusual history may not reproduce what a real prospective customer sees. State that scope limit next to any published rank number.
  • Nothing proves a page finished loading except pixels; use mean-absolute-pixel-diff, never MD5 or byte equality — an untouched mirrored phone never repeats a frame byte-for-byte.
  • Apple's terms prohibit automated scraping of listings and search results, and the account signed into a phone doing this at volume is exposed to search throttling or challenge interstitials. Treat any unexpected screen as a stop condition for that phone's run, not something to retry through, and keep cadence well below anything that would stress Apple's endpoints. The API has no authentication on the LAN.

Scale

Bounded by UI settle time and by each phone's own AirPlay frame rate, not by the API — raw capture is 2 ms and phones are fully independent, up to 512 req/s aggregate measured. Budget roughly 3-5 s for a rating read and 10-15 s per keyword end to end (open, tap, type, settle, one or two scroll-and-match rounds); the same panel spread applies here as elsewhere on this rig, roughly 29 fps versus 4.5 fps on otherwise-identical phones. Navigation and input fan out to N phones in one request, but screenshot and recognition are single-id, so the capture-and-read half runs as N concurrent requests — on this rig that is 2 phones actually mirroring, not the full 19 boards enumerated. With a full rack, tens of keyword checks per phone per hour is comfortable and the practical ceiling is what the store tolerates before throttling, not what the kernel delivers; at 2 live phones, expect on the order of 8-15 keyword-rank checks per hour per phone before that limit becomes the binding concern.

Network identity and provenance

Per-phone public IP truth table with carrier IP rotation

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Builds an auditable per-slot record of the network identity each phone presents to the internet: the kernel's own LAN IP, the phone's self-reported LAN and public IP via the Shortcut, and, on cellular-routed phones, a forced IP churn by cycling the cellular radio off and on. The vendor's static-IP-without-gateway Wi-Fi setting is what makes this possible — AirPlay mirroring stays on the LAN while all internet traffic leaves over the SIM, so a phone's public IP can change without its mirror ever dropping. The output is provenance, not evasion: a log of device, timestamp, LAN IP, public IP and egress path attached to every geo-sensitive measurement a phone produced, so a run can be replayed knowing exactly where it came from and aborted the moment a phone silently falls back to the wrong path.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get — inventory phones and their kernel-observed LAN address.
  2. (Shortcut health probe) GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 — ask the phone for its own LAN IP; a match against the kernel's value proves the board hotkey, the Shortcut and the LAN round trip all work.
  3. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1 — read the public (extranet) IP per phone.
  4. shortcut#21/#20 GET /api/shortcut/switch/cdpd?id=<ids>&state=0, wait ~5 s, then state=1 — cycle the cellular radio to force carrier IP churn; the only toggle that leaves Wi-Fi and the AirPlay mirror untouched.
  5. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1 — re-read and log the public IP against the pre-toggle value.
  6. (avoid) /api/shortcut/switch/flight and /api/shortcut/switch/wlan — documented but wrong for this job: both drop Wi-Fi and blind the phone, killing the mirror and the Shortcut's own return path together.
  7. get_usb_list / get_device_list GET /api/config/usb/get and /api/device/get — health gate: confirm board state 2 and a live air_pid before recording any Shortcut non-answer as a network fact.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed and bound on every phone (Advanced permissions, kernel IP edited in, an AssistiveTouch custom key) — not verified present on this rig; no /shortcut/* call has ever been probed here.
  • A SIM with an active data plan per phone — not verified on either live XR; without one, only the LAN round-trip health probe is exercisable.
  • Wi-Fi set to a static IPv4 address and subnet mask with the router/gateway field left empty, per phone.
  • Board bound and physically attached at state 2 — the Shortcut hotkey rides the board.
  • Phone unlocked, portrait, Auto-Lock Never, AssistiveTouch on, Full Keyboard Access on.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in.
  • Kernel reachable from the phone on TCP 9911 — restrict that port at the firewall to trusted hosts.

Watch out

  • Nothing in this chain has actually been probed on this rig — the 10 Sep live probe covered device/get, usb/get, group/get, ocr and screenshot only. Run one live /shortcut/device/ip?state=0 call and confirm code 0 before scheduling anything on top of it.
  • The id parameter shown in the shortcuts doc examples is a MAC address, not necessarily the same deviceid used by /device/get and /mouse/* — confirm which identifier this kernel actually expects before wiring deviceid straight through.
  • No SIM is confirmed on either live phone, so the headline capability, distinct per-phone public IP and carrier rotation, is currently a paper capability here: steps 4-5 are inert, and step 3 reports the same shared building address for both phones, exactly the "one vantage point wearing twenty hats" failure this chain exists to catch.
  • /shortcut/device/ip is single-id only, so a full audit is N sequential round trips of up to outtime (15 s default) each. The switch endpoints do fan out to a comma-separated list.
  • A radio re-attach is not guaranteed to obtain a new address, and CGNAT means several SIMs on one carrier can legitimately share one public IP — an unchanged reading is not by itself proof the toggle failed. Retry a small bounded number of times, then record the result rather than looping.
  • No carrier, ASN, country or geo field exists anywhere in the API; any such enrichment is an external lookup on the returned IP, run on the PC.
  • A mismatch between the kernel's ip field and the Shortcut's own reading is not by itself a fault — a DHCP lease renewal can legitimately change a LAN IP between two reads. Treat a mismatch as a prompt to re-read /device/get, not an automatic alarm.
  • outtime is milliseconds on XP (default 15000) and seconds in the Phonefarm doc — a value copied across editions is off by 1000x.
  • Repeated cellular re-attach cycling is externally visible to the carrier's network as anomalous device behaviour, independent of anything the API does; budget it as an infrequent provenance stamp, not a polling primitive.
  • Scope: this chain is for observing and recording egress identity for measurement provenance, logging which vantage point produced which data, not for concealing the relationship between accounts or evading platform limits. The API has no authentication on the LAN, so the resulting device/MAC/IP log is identifying data and should be kept out of version control.

Scale

The IP read is the bottleneck: single-id only, one round trip per phone bounded by a 15 s default outtime, realistically 1-3 s when healthy — a 19-slot audit is roughly 20-60 s issued concurrently, or 1-5 minutes serialised, since the kernel showed no shared bottleneck at up to ten concurrent pollers (512 req/s aggregate). Rotation itself is cheap and fans out: cdpd off then on for the whole cellular set is two calls plus a ~5 s settle, about 10-15 s regardless of rack size, so a full audit-rotate-reaudit cycle is dominated by the two single-id read passes. As documented today this rig can run zero verified carrier-rotation cycles per hour, since no SIM is confirmed; once a Shortcut and SIM are confirmed live, a sane cadence is a handful of rotations per hour per phone, an occasional provenance stamp rather than a streaming signal, both because re-attach cycling should stay low-rate and because none of this competes with screenshot polling or pointer input running on other macros.

Outside the box: the rack as a passive sensor

Notification Center sweep: harvest new alerts on every phone without opening an app

PartialWith caveats

One hotkey pulls down Notification Center on every listed phone at once, one screenshot per phone captures the stack, and a client-side pixel diff against the previous sweep says which phones have something new — no app-specific coordinate map, no foregrounding of any app, and because the whole loop uses only keyboard and screenshot calls, structural immunity to the stuck-click trap that silently kills /mouse/click. Notification Center is the one screen where iOS already aggregates every app's pushes, so detecting that something arrived is fully native on this rig; reading what a card says is not, since the OCR plug-in is absent (code 28) and needs either the plug-in, the Shortcut OCR fallback, or host-side OCR on the saved frame.

How

  1. send_key (WIN+h) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h, twice — normalise the whole target set to a static home screen.
  2. send_key (NoticeBar) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=NoticeBar — pull down Notification Center on every phone in one request; an XP-only hotkey with no Phonefarm equivalent.
  3. (client-side wait) none — settle ~400-600 ms for the pull-down animation, more on slow-frame-rate phones.
  4. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — capture one frame per phone.
  5. (client-side diff) none — mean-absolute-pixel diff of the stack region against the previous sweep; above roughly 5 means it changed.
  6. ocr / find-text GET /api/pic/ocr?id=<id>&rect= — read card text; optional, blocked today (code 28), host-side OCR on the saved BMP is the dependency-free route.
  7. find_multi_color POST /api/pic/find-multi-color — classify the source app by icon colour without OCR; plug-in status undocumented and unverified.
  8. mouse_wheel GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=<ids>&direction=down&len=60&number=3 — scroll a longer stack and re-capture; iOS honouring the wheel here is unverified.
  9. send_key (WIN+h) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h — dismiss and return home; notifications are not consumed by viewing, so the next sweep still sees them.
  10. mouse_reset + click (optional) GET /api/mouse/reset then GET /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y= — escalate by tapping the top card to deep-link into the originating app.

Needs

  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in; per-phone board bound at state 2, since NoticeBar is a HID hotkey through the board.
  • Per-phone video channel ready (state != 0, live air_pid) — the screenshot comes from the mirror, not the board.
  • Full Keyboard Access ON — without it iOS ignores fn_key combos entirely and the sweep silently does nothing.
  • AssistiveTouch, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock — none of these is queryable over the API.
  • Phones unlocked; a locked phone's Notification Center is unreadable and the API must not be used to enter a passcode.
  • iOS notification settings: previews shown, and grouping off per app if one card per event is needed.
  • For text reading only: the OCR plug-in connected, the Shortcut OCR fallback, or a host-side OCR library able to decode the bottom-up 500x1080 BMP.
  • Firewall 9911 and 17000 to trusted hosts before any sweep starts writing notification content to disk.

Watch out

  • Split the claim: "which phones have something new, and when" is fully native; "what it says" is not — OCR is blocked (code 28) on this rig today.
  • NoticeBar exists only in the XP edition; a Phonefarm-edition rig would need an undocumented top-edge drag instead.
  • Whether /mouse/wheel scrolls the Notification Center stack, and whether a second WIN+h reliably collapses it on iOS 18.7.10, are both unverified — fall back to a down/move/up drag or /mouse/swipe if the wheel does nothing.
  • The NoticeBar / WIN+h / re-diff sequence has never been run end to end on this rig, and unlike a stuck click there is no equivalent of /mouse/reset to independently prove a stuck hotkey — run one live cycle before scheduling anything.
  • Grouped notifications collapse many events into one card with a count; the pixel diff still fires but the count is unreadable without OCR.
  • Notification Center is a rolling window — a sweep interval longer than a busy app's retention loses events. This is a sampler, not a guaranteed-complete log.
  • /pic/screenshot is single-id, so captures scale with phone count even though the two hotkeys that open and close the panel are one request each regardless of rack size.
  • At full-rack scale, wall-clock time is dominated by the single slowest phone; a 19-phone rack could plausibly contain several units as slow as the ~4.5 fps XR measured here, stretching any sweep-time estimate.
  • Previews are among the most sensitive content a phone displays: names, order numbers, amounts, addresses, verification codes. Crop to the stack region rather than archiving whole screens, retain briefly and actually delete, keep the archive off shared or synced storage, exclude one-time codes from any log entirely, and sweep only phones and accounts you own or administer. The API has no authentication on the LAN, so anything on the subnet can pull the same content — firewall 9911 and 17000.

Scale

Two hotkey requests address the whole rack regardless of size, so opening and closing the panel is one request each; capture is one request per phone but cheap — 19 phones at ~2 ms raw BMP each is ~40 ms of API time, and phones measured fully independent, up to 512 req/s aggregate across ten concurrent pollers with no contention from input traffic. Wall-clock cost is dominated by the ~400-600 ms animation settle plus extra time on slow-frame-rate phones, landing a full-rack sweep at roughly 1-2 s and repeatable every 30-60 s indefinitely, on the order of 60-120 sweeps per hour per phone for the native change-detection signal alone. Adding OCR identification, once unblocked, adds a serialised single-id read of unknown latency per phone that fired, so budget several seconds per changed phone for the read-and-identify half rather than treating it as free.

Push-delivery latency measurement by high-rate banner-strip polling

PartialWith caveats

Turns the frame poller into a stopwatch: normalise to the home screen, then poll a narrow strip at the top of the mirror at 20-30 Hz per phone and flag the instant a banner slides in by a jump in mean-absolute-pixel difference against the phone's own idle floor. Differenced against your push provider's NTP-synced send timestamp, this yields an end-to-end delivery-observation time per phone, per SIM, per network path, with nothing installed on the phone and no taps at all, which makes it structurally immune to the stuck-click failure mode that affects every tap-based macro on this rig. Identifying which specific push arrived is a slower, separate step gated by the same absent OCR plug-in as the notification sweep.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get?id=<id> — confirm mirroring (air_pid) and read imgw/imgh for the strip's coordinate space.
  2. send_key (WIN+h) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h, twice — normalise every phone to a static home screen so the idle diff floor is real.
  3. get_device_screenshot (rect+binary) GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true&rect=[0,0,500,140] — poll the banner strip and timestamp each response; rect and binary together are undocumented and unmeasured on this rig.
  4. (client-side) none — mean-absolute-pixel diff detects arrival; never hash-compare, since an untouched mirror never repeats byte-for-byte.
  5. (external) none — record the push provider's own NTP-synced send timestamp; embedding a sequence id in the banner body lets step 6 confirm identity rather than infer it from send order.
  6. send_key (NoticeBar) then ocr GET /api/key/sendkey?fn_key=NoticeBar, screenshot, GET /api/pic/ocr — identify which push arrived; blocked today (code 28) and ends the measurement window when it runs.
  7. send_key (WIN+h) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<id>&fn_key=WIN+h — return the phone to baseline before arming the next send.
  8. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1 — attribute each phone to a network path; public IP only, carrier is an external lookup, and the Shortcut is unverified present on this rig.
  9. (phone-side configuration) none — vendor settings page section 4 — apply the static-IP-without-gateway Wi-Fi setting so the push actually traverses the carrier without killing the AirPlay mirror.

Needs

  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in; board bound at state 2 and Full Keyboard Access ON, or the two hotkeys are silently ignored.
  • Per-phone video channel live (state != 0, air_pid, an ESTABLISHED socket on 17000) — video is the entire measurement channel here.
  • Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock, StandBy off, brightness pinned — the idle pixel floor is only stable if nothing else on screen animates.
  • Banner-style alerts enabled with previews shown for the target app.
  • PC and push-provider clocks NTP-disciplined.
  • One SIM per phone plus the static-IP-without-gateway Wi-Fi setting, for per-carrier work.
  • OCR plug-in, Shortcut OCR fallback, or external client-side OCR, for the identification step only.
  • iMouse Shortcut installed and bound, for the network-attribution step only.
  • Poll from loopback — the 2 ms full-frame figure is a loopback number, not a LAN one.

Watch out

  • The measured quantity is not APNs delivery time; it is banner-render-visible-through-AirPlay latency, bundling phone-side render, AirPlay encode, Wi-Fi transit and PC decode into one unmeasured constant bias. Report it by that real name — only differential comparisons, same phone, condition A versus B, are defensible, not absolute figures.
  • Resolution is bounded by the phone's own frame production, not the poller: the two XRs on this rig deliver roughly 35 ms and 220 ms per new frame respectively under continuous motion, and that gap is the phone's own Wi-Fi link, not fixable in software. Publish a per-phone error bar, never a single rack figure.
  • Those fps numbers were measured under driven motion; a static idle screen is explicitly unmeasured and may resolve worse. Calibrate with a known stimulus at a known PC time before trusting any result.
  • rect and binary together are undocumented and unmeasured; the "~210 KB, ~2 ms" crop figures are arithmetic, not measurement. Smoke-test it, because if rect is silently ignored in binary mode the poller moves 1.62 MB per frame per phone instead, which changes the whole throughput budget.
  • /pic/screenshot is single-id, so N phones means N requests per tick; the comma-separated fan-out that makes /mouse and /key calls cheap does not apply here.
  • The identification step (NoticeBar plus OCR) destroys the measurement window it belongs to and is blocked today (code 28). Space test sends further apart than the worst plausible latency, or embed a visual marker decodable via /pic/find-multi-color instead, itself unverified on this rig.
  • A 6x fps spread between two otherwise-identical phones means no per-phone resolution figure should be assumed for a third phone — measure each phone before trusting its own latency numbers.
  • Scaling the measured "ten pollers give 512 req/s" ceiling to a 19-phone rack at 20-30 Hz (380-570 req/s) is extrapolation past the largest N actually tested. Treat the throughput figures as a plan to validate, step-tested at 12, 15 and 19 pollers, not a guaranteed ceiling.
  • A poll gives an interval, not an instant — record both request-issue and response-receipt clock and report arrival as a bracket. The measured p95 tail (142 ms on ten concurrent pollers) is measurement error, not a phone property.
  • This is legitimate QA on your own pushes to your own test accounts on devices you own; the risks are accuracy, privacy and network exposure, not platform abuse. Use dedicated test handsets signed out of personal accounts, crop the OCR region, retain crops only as long as the analysis needs them, and avoid calling an AirPlay-observed render time "APNs latency", which would itself be a false measurement claim. The API has no authentication on the LAN, and Auto-Lock Never plus a bright screen for long runs is a real battery and thermal load on the physical rack.

Scale

Per-phone, per-tick cost is one single-id screenshot request; measured ceilings on this rig are 84 req/s for one poller flat out, ~83-85 req/s per phone with two running concurrently and no shared bottleneck, and 512 req/s aggregate at ten concurrent pollers. A 19-phone rack at 20 Hz (380 req/s) sits inside that envelope; 30 Hz (570 req/s) exceeds the largest number ever measured here, so reserve 30 Hz for one or two phones under study and use 20 Hz rack-wide. The binding constraint may be bytes, not requests, if rect cropping does not work in binary mode: 19 pollers at 20 Hz would then move roughly 615 MB/s on loopback, untested at this rig, so pool one buffer per poller regardless. Polling faster than ~30 Hz buys nothing once a phone's own frame production tops out around 29 fps, since duplicate frames are discarded on the diff anyway. Practical throughput is bounded by test-send cadence rather than the API: spacing pushes seconds apart to keep identification unambiguous without OCR yields on the order of tens of timing measurements per hour per phone under a conservative, provider-rate-limit-respecting cadence, not the thousands per hour the raw polling rate alone would suggest.

Web and app content harvesting via the clipboard

Mobile web crawler: Safari page text harvested through the clipboard

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Feed a URL list to the rack: the Shortcut's URL opener loads each page in Safari on a real iPhone, a tap focuses the body, WIN+a / WIN+c select-all and copy the rendered text, and the clipboard read returns it verbatim. Because OCR is not connected on this rig (code 28), this is the only route to the mobile-rendered text of JS-heavy sites, and it returns exact characters rather than a recognition guess.

How

  1. shortcut#13 Open URL /shortcut/exec/url?id=<ids>&url=<page>&outtime=<ms> — dispatch the next queued URL to Safari; id takes a comma list but each phone still needs its own URL, so this is one call per phone per page.
  2. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — poll raw BMP frames (2 ms p50) until two consecutive frames differ by a mean pixel diff below ~1, so the tap lands after the page has actually loaded.
  3. click /mouse/reset?id=<id> then /mouse/click?id=<id>&x=250&y=700 — reset first, then tap a blank margin (mirror pixels, 500x1080 here) to focus the page body without navigating away.
  4. send_key fn_key /key/sendkey?id=<id>&fn_key=WIN+a then fn_key=WIN+c — select all, then copy; needs Full Keyboard Access on.
  5. shortcut#10 To the phone clipboard /shortcut/clipboard/set?id=<ids>&text=SENTINEL-<url-hash>-<ts>&sleep=<s> — poison the clipboard with a per-page sentinel before each cycle so a stale read is detectable.
  6. shortcut#11 Get phone clipboard /shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<id>&outtime=<ms> — read the copied text back into data.text; single-device, so this step is per phone.
  7. mouse_wheel /mouse/wheel?id=<ids>&direction=down&len=100&number=5 — scroll to force lazy-loaded content in before the next copy.
  8. none no endpoint — link discovery is not available from this chain: copied text carries no hrefs or structure, so drive the crawl from a known URL list or a conventionally fetched sitemap.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed on every phone, kernel IP edited in, run once with every permission granted, and bound to an AssistiveTouch key via Send Binding Key. Never verified on this rig; the cheapest proof is /shortcut/device/ip?state=0 returning the same address as /device/get.
  • USB board bound and connected (/config/usb/get state 2), since every /shortcut/* call and hotkey travels over it.
  • Full Keyboard Access on, AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity maxed, trackpad speed maxed, Auto-Lock Never, portrait locked. None of this is queryable over the API.
  • Phone on the same LAN as the kernel, reaching it on TCP 9911, with mirroring up.
  • Safari as the default handler for http/https; cookie and consent walls handled once per phone by a person, not the automation.
  • A per-phone clipboard round trip verified once: clipboard/set followed by clipboard/get returning the identical string.

Watch out

  • The whole chain is a paper design until /shortcut/device/ip?state=0 succeeds: a 15 s timeout (code 30) is indistinguishable from "Shortcut not installed" versus "page slow to load."
  • Only exec/url, clipboard/set, the mouse calls and the key calls take a comma list of ids. clipboard/get and /pic/screenshot are single-device, so the per-page work is per phone, not fanned out.
  • Whether WIN+a selects the whole document or only the visible viewport is unverified here; if it is viewport-scoped this becomes a slower scroll-and-deduplicate loop.
  • Copied text has no headings, hrefs or element boundaries: it is an undifferentiated text corpus, not anything resembling extracted "content," and the crawl cannot discover new URLs from it.
  • The focus tap is the fragile step: land it on a link and the page navigates before the copy runs. A blank-margin coordinate cannot always be precomputed from a URL list alone; some pages need a first-pass screenshot to find one at all.
  • The clipboard is shared state: a failed copy silently returns the previous page's text unless the per-page sentinel makes the failure visible.
  • robots.txt, site terms and applicable data-protection rules apply exactly as they would to any crawler; respect published rate limits and stop on an explicit block rather than working around it.
  • The slow XR's settle check needs a longer window, roughly 1.5-2 s rather than 500 ms, to reach the same confidence the fast phone gets, because it only delivers about 4.5 new frames a second.
  • The Shortcut round trip (hotkey to app launch to Safari automation to HTTP post back) has never been timed on this rig; a cold Shortcut launch can itself run 1-3 s, which is a large slice of any per-page budget.

Scale

This rig has two mirroring iPhone XRs, not 19 — 19 is the USB board count. At a realistic 8-15 s per page per phone, including an unmeasured Shortcut round trip, expect roughly 8-15 pages/minute combined, on the order of 12,000-20,000 pages/day running continuously with no stalls. That is below a 20-30k/day figure that ignores Shortcut latency, and far below a 150k/day projection that assumes 19 phones this rig does not have. This is orders of magnitude below a headless crawler, so spend it only where real-Safari fidelity is the point.

Clipboard harvest of your own native-app data: listings, orders and messages

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Native app content is not selectable on screen and OCR is unavailable on this rig, but the apps themselves expose an exact text channel: the share sheet's "Copy link," the long-press context menu's "Copy," and WIN+a / WIN+c in an editable field. Tap the affordance, then read the string back through the clipboard: a canonical URL, an order number, a buyer's message, verbatim and with zero recognition error. Applied to your own accounts this builds a live catalogue of your listing URLs, order IDs, tracking numbers and inbound messages with no transcription errors.

How

  1. send_key + mouse_reset_pos /key/sendkey fn_key=WIN+h (twice) then /mouse/reset?id=<comma list> — bring every target phone home and clear the stuck-click state before starting.
  2. shortcut#13 open URL /shortcut/exec/url?id=<comma list>&url=<https or custom scheme> — deep-link straight to your own account's profile, order list or thread without navigating the UI by hand.
  3. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — locate the share, order-number or message target from a stored per-app coordinate table, since neither OCR nor image search is available to re-anchor a drifted layout.
  4. click /mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y=&button=1 — tap the share control, then "Copy link" in the sheet; wait for the sheet animation before the second tap.
  5. click with time /mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y=&time=800 then Copy — long-press variant for captions, order numbers and message bubbles; time is documented as the press-to-popup delay, so no separate API is needed.
  6. shortcut#11 /shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<id>&outtime=<ms> — read the string off the phone into data.text; single-device.
  7. shortcut#10 /shortcut/clipboard/set?id=<comma list>&text=<sentinel>&sleep=<s> — clear the clipboard with a unique sentinel between items so a missed tap is detectable and no data lingers.
  8. mouse_wheel / swipe /mouse/wheel?id=<ids>&direction=down&len=90&number=2 — advance through your own order or listing history and confirm the next item is in position before the next copy.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut v1.3+ installed on each phone, IP-edited, run once with every permission granted, and bound to an AssistiveTouch key. Not installed on this rig; /shortcut/clipboard/get is the load-bearing call and nothing works without it.
  • Board bound and connected, since the Shortcut is triggered by a HID hotkey over it; a video-only phone cannot run this at all.
  • Full Keyboard Access on for the field-copy variant; AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity and trackpad speed maxed for the taps.
  • Your own accounts logged in on each phone.
  • A per-app, per-version coordinate table for the share icon, "Copy link" row and context-menu "Copy," re-measured after every app update.
  • Handoff / Universal Clipboard turned off on rack phones, or every copied string syncs to the owner's other Apple devices.

Watch out

  • /shortcut/clipboard/get is single-id, so the harvest step is strictly per-phone even though the tap, the clipboard write and the URL open fan out over a comma list.
  • The chain depends entirely on the iMouse Shortcut being installed and hotkey-bound, which it is not on this rig; a timeout surfaces as generic code 30, not as "not installed."
  • outtime is milliseconds on XP (default 15000), while sleep on clipboard/set is seconds; swapping them produces either instant timeouts or 15-second stalls per item.
  • No OCR and no image search on this rig, so every target must come from a stored coordinate table plus client-side pixel checks; an app update silently invalidates the table with no fallback to re-anchor it.
  • iOS shows a "pasted from" banner on every clipboard read, visible in captured frames and sometimes to the phone's own user; it does not block the read but does make the activity visible on-device.
  • The 15 s default outtime is a ceiling, not a target: if the bound hotkey misfires, each item silently costs up to 15 s instead of the assumed 2-5 s, which can drop realised throughput 3-5x.
  • Universal Clipboard syncs every copied string, including order numbers and buyer messages, to the account owner's other Apple devices unless Handoff is explicitly off on every rack phone.
  • Nothing in this chain can reliably distinguish an unexpected screen — a first-run permission prompt, a re-login, a 2FA/OTP screen triggered by a cold deep-link open — from normal content without OCR, so a run can stall or mis-tap into an unrelated field rather than failing loudly; a frame-diff-only heuristic can also false-flag an ordinary app-update dialog as a block.
  • High automated volumes against your own account can still trip a platform's own anti-automation detection independent of intent; treat any such signal as a stop condition. Nothing here is built to route around it, and this chain is scoped to your own accounts and your own data.

Scale

Each item is two or three taps plus one Shortcut round trip: the API costs are negligible (a click is one request, a raw screenshot 2 ms), so the 2-5 s per item is share-sheet animation plus the Shortcut's LAN round trip, roughly 10-20 strings a minute per phone if the Shortcut integration works as designed. Across the two phones mirroring here that is 20-40 items/minute combined, but it drops to roughly 4 items/minute per phone whenever the round trip stalls toward the 15 s ceiling, and the whole figure is aspirational until a single clipboard round trip is confirmed live on this rig.

Search and pricing intelligence from real handsets

Search-result monitoring from real iPhones on real carrier connections

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Dispatch the same search URL to every phone in one call, screenshot each first-result screen to a dated folder, and copy the page text through the clipboard so the order of domains can be logged as each device's own connection sees it, including the ad slots and local pack a rank-tracking API never returns. Each phone's egress IP is recorded alongside the sample so every result is labelled with the vantage point it came from.

How

  1. shortcut#13 Open URL with devlist /shortcut/exec/url?id=<id1>,<id2>,...&url=<search url>&outtime=<ms> — open the same query on every phone in a single request; the fan-out is genuine, but page load afterwards is per-phone network time.
  2. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&jpg=true&save_path=D:\serp\<date>\ — save a JPEG (40.5 ms p50, capped near 21 req/s kernel-wide) as the archival record; the directory must already exist or the call returns code 27.
  3. click + send_key + shortcut#11 /mouse/reset -> /mouse/click -> /key/sendkey fn_key=WIN+a -> fn_key=WIN+c -> /shortcut/clipboard/get — tap a blank margin, select all, copy, and read the text back to infer result ordering from copied domain order.
  4. mouse_wheel /mouse/wheel?id=<ids>&direction=down&len=80&number=3 — scroll to capture below-the-fold positions, then screenshot again per phone.
  5. shortcut#24 Get external network IP /shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1&outtime=<ms> — record the egress IP each sample actually came from; single-device only.
  6. n/a /pic/screenshot (archive) + stop the queue for that phone — if a CAPTCHA or interstitial appears, log it with a screenshot and stop querying from that device; there is no function for solving one and none should be built.

Needs

  • Everything the clipboard-crawl chain needs: Shortcut installed and bound, board bound, Full Keyboard Access on, phone on the LAN reaching 9911, mirroring up. Unverified on this rig.
  • The save_path directory must exist before the call, and the kernel process must be able to write it.
  • For genuinely different vantage points, a SIM per phone with cellular data carrying internet while Wi-Fi carries only the mirror, using the vendor's documented static-IP-without-gateway setup so mirroring survives.
  • Location Services on if local-pack results are wanted, or signed-out browsing for unpersonalised results.
  • Consent dialogs on any storefront handled once per phone by a person, not by the automation.

Watch out

  • The geo premise does not hold on this rig as built: both XRs sit on the same Wi-Fi behind one egress, so today every phone samples from a single vantage point. It becomes real only with a SIM per phone plus the gateway-less static-IP setup, verified by /shortcut/device/ip?state=1 returning genuinely different addresses.
  • An iPhone needs a physical SIM with an active data plan per phone to make this real, a procurement cost the plan does not otherwise surface, and carrier CGNAT can mean the reported IP still doesn't match what the destination server logs.
  • Automated querying of search results sits against the terms of service of Google and comparable engines. That is a legal and contractual constraint on the whole use case, not a technical one; where a first-party search API or licensed data source exists, it is the compliant route.
  • When a block or CAPTCHA appears, the only supported response is to record it and stop. Nothing in this API solves, bypasses or evades bot detection, and building that is out of scope.
  • Only the URL open and the wheel scroll fan out over a comma list; screenshot, clipboard read and IP lookup are all single-device, so per-phone work is serial.
  • Rank inferred from copied-text domain order is approximate: ads, the local pack and organic results are not distinguishable in plain text. The screenshot is the authoritative artefact; the text is an index into it.
  • "Same instant" describes the dispatch request, not a hardware-guaranteed simultaneous trigger: the kernel likely walks the id list within one HTTP call rather than firing every phone in true parallel.
  • Results from a signed-in account are personalised and not comparable across devices; use signed-out Safari for a clean comparison.
  • Only two phones are live today, so this is a two-sample pilot, not a monitoring fleet; scaling to a real panel needs more boards' phones brought online and the SIM/geo problem solved first.

Scale

Dispatch is one request regardless of fleet size; everything after it is per phone. With the two phones actually online, roughly 100 keyword queries per phone at 8-15 s each, including unmeasured Shortcut latency, works out to about 15-25 minutes wall clock — slower than a simple 7-10 minute estimate, and far short of a 20-30 minute, 19-phone, 19-geo projection; 19 is the board count, and only two XRs are mirroring here.

Simultaneous multi-geo render comparison of one URL

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Open one identical URL on every mirroring phone with a single call, then pull one raw BMP frame per phone back-to-back at ~2 ms each so the captures land within milliseconds of one another. Each phone's public IP is recorded first as the geo column, and a client-side pixel diff, plus an optional exact-text lift through the clipboard, shows where the same page differs: a different price, a blocked asset, a consent wall, a redirect.

How

  1. get_device_list /device/get — keep only phones with a live air_pid and identical imgw x imgh; different frame geometry makes a pairwise diff meaningless.
  2. shortcut#24 get external network IP /shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1 — record each phone's public IP as the geo label; single-device, roughly a 1 s Shortcut round trip each.
  3. shortcut#13 open URL /shortcut/exec/url?id=<id1,id2,...>&url=<target> — the only step that is genuinely simultaneous; page load afterwards is per-phone network time.
  4. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — grab one raw frame per phone in a loop; 2 ms p50 each, so the whole sweep is milliseconds even though it isn't batched.
  5. send_key + shortcut#11 /mouse/click -> /key/sendkey fn_key=WIN+a -> fn_key=WIN+c -> /shortcut/clipboard/get — optional: lift the exact rendered text (price string, banner copy) instead of guessing from pixels.
  6. get_device_screenshot (save) /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&jpg=true&save_path=D:\geo\<url hash>\ — archive the evidence frame with its IP and timestamp; the kernel writes the file and returns the path.
  7. mouse_reset_pos /mouse/reset?id=<id1,id2,...> — clear the silent stuck-click state before any tap-driven step, across the whole target set.
  8. none no endpoint, client-side — compare frames with mean absolute pixel difference, never MD5, and mask the status-bar band and the pointer dot before diffing.

Needs

  • Shortcut installed, IP-edited and bound on every phone; board bound and connected. Not verified on this rig, so /shortcut/device/ip?state=0 is the cheapest first proof.
  • Phones on the kernel's LAN reaching TCP 9911, with the static-IP-without-gateway setup keeping AirPlay on the LAN while the phone's internet rides cellular.
  • Each phone actually on the geo it is meant to represent, using accounts and SIMs you own or are authorised to test with, with Apple ID region, system language and login state held constant across phones.
  • All phones mirroring with identical imgw x imgh; Full Keyboard Access on for the optional text lift.

Watch out

  • The single biggest hole is the premise, not the chain: if both phones ride the same LAN/ISP uplink, /shortcut/device/ip?state=1 will often return the same public IP for every phone, or IPs that geolocate to the same city. Verify real IP diversity for every phone before trusting any diff, or the run produces N synchronised screenshots of one served variant that could be mistaken for "no personalisation detected."
  • This rig has two iPhone XRs, not 19; 19 is the USB board count. Every 19-phone throughput figure needs rescaling to what two phones can actually do.
  • Simultaneity is in the capture, not the render: the frame grabbed is the newest AirPlay frame, and the slow XR (~4.5 new frames/s) can be roughly 220 ms stale. Poll the slow phone until its frame stops changing rather than trusting a single grab after a fixed settle window.
  • No OCR on this rig (/pic/ocr returns code 28), so reading a price off the frame needs either the clipboard lift or client-side OCR against the raw BMP.
  • /pic/screenshot, /shortcut/device/ip and /shortcut/clipboard/get are all single-device, so the geo column and the text lift are serial per-phone Shortcut round trips at roughly a second each.
  • The exact-text lift (WIN+a then WIN+c) may need a preceding long-press to raise a Select All menu on native views; plain hotkeys reliably work only on selectable web/text content.
  • Evidence value depends on provenance you add yourself: store the IP, timestamp, device record and exact URL with every frame, since the API adds none of that.
  • Repeated automated loads of a commercial site are scraping under most terms of service regardless of intent; pace requests, honour rate limits, and stop on any block or challenge page rather than working around it.
  • Do not present a price difference as proof of geo discrimination without holding language, Apple ID region and login state constant — those confound geo far more often than IP does.

Scale

The URL open is one request regardless of phone count, and raw capture is trivial at 2 ms per phone. The expensive parts are the per-phone Shortcut round trips, roughly 1 s each for the IP and clipboard reads, plus a settle wait conditioned on the slowest phone. A full cycle on this two-phone rig is realistically 10-20 s end to end, or roughly 180-350 URL comparisons an hour for the whole panel, bounded by the serial single-id Shortcut calls rather than by screenshot cost. A larger rack adds mostly to that Shortcut-bound stage; concurrent dispatch keeps the cycle near the same length regardless of phone count, since the control and video channels showed no shared bottleneck up to ten concurrent pollers.

Passive telemetry: training data and health signals

Training-data collection: screen, action, next-screen tuples at rack scale

Native APIWith caveats

Instrument every input call so the raw frame immediately before it, the exact command and its mirror-pixel coordinates, and the settled frame after it are written as one dataset row. The action label comes from the request itself, not from perception, so it is exact and free, and the settle time comes from polling until consecutive frames stop differing. Raw BMP capture measured 2 ms on this rig, so before/after capture is essentially free, and the whole chain is native XP HTTP: no plug-in, no Shortcut, no professional edition.

How

  1. get_device_list /device/get — record imgw/imgh, model, iOS version and location_crc once per session as row metadata; a coordinate is meaningless without the frame size it was expressed in.
  2. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — capture frame_before; 2 ms p50, raw bottom-up BMP, single-device.
  3. click / swipe / mouse_wheel / send_key /mouse/click, /mouse/swipe, /mouse/wheel, /key/sendkey — perform the action and log the request verbatim as the ground-truth label.
  4. (poll) /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true on a fixed period — poll until the screen settles and record the settle time as a label; XP has no push frame stream, so polling is the only route (measured 84 req/s per phone flat out).
  5. mouse_reset_pos + pointer-box diff /mouse/reset?id=<comma list> — verify the action actually landed by diffing a small box around the commanded coordinate before keeping the row; there is no API call that reports "the tap landed."
  6. (callback) ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — error_push, dev_rotate, dev_connect, dev_disconnect — drop rows whose action failed at the board, and tag session and orientation boundaries.
  7. send_key + shortcut#2 /key/sendkey fn_key=shift+win+3 then /shortcut/album/get, /shortcut/album/down — optional high-resolution label pair for a subset of rows via a native iOS screenshot; Shortcut-gated, not available on this rig today.

Needs

  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in; each phone mirroring and bound to its board with a non-empty location_crc.
  • iOS accessibility prerequisites on every phone — AssistiveTouch, tracking sensitivity max, Full Keyboard Access, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock — none of which is readable over the API; verify with a per-phone input test.
  • A frame differ using mean absolute pixel difference on the decoded BMP, never MD5 or byte equality.
  • One reused buffer per poller: without reuse, this rig measured 488 MB/s allocation and 496 gen-2 GCs per 8 s; with reuse, 2.9 MB/s and 0-1.
  • Disk budget of roughly 1.6 MB per raw frame, or ~10 KB per JPEG-encoded before/after pair after client-side encoding.
  • Dedicated accounts on any app being driven, a review of that app's terms before recording its UI, and a scrubbing pass before any dataset leaves the machine.

Watch out

  • /pic/screenshot is single-id, so capture is one request per phone even though input calls fan out over a comma list; a mirrored action across N phones is one request but N capture requests.
  • Settle-time labels are quantised by each phone's own AirPlay source rate, which differs even between identical XR units (~29 vs ~4.5 new frames/s here); record measured fps as row metadata rather than treating settle time as a general iOS transition-timing signal.
  • An ignored tap still produces a well-formed "no change" row; without the pointer-box diff and /mouse/reset discipline, the silent stuck-click state contaminates the dataset with false negatives that look like legitimate no-op transitions.
  • The pointer dot is baked into every frame; either keep it deliberately or mask a small box around the commanded coordinate, consistently, or a model will learn to read the cursor instead of the screen.
  • The two XRs have different home screens, so mirroring one action for augmentation only produces a valid pair after normalising both phones to matching states; navigation fan-out to identical target screens is free, augmentation-by-mirroring generally is not.
  • This rig has 19 boards but only 2 phones mirroring, so "rack scale" throughput figures are a projection, not a measurement; video capacity, not board count, bounds a real run.
  • No text or element labels are available (OCR returns code 28), so the dataset out of this pipeline is (frame, action, frame) tuples only, not (screen_name, action, screen_name), unless a separate annotation pass adds those labels.
  • Recording third-party app UI at volume for a training set carries the same terms-of-service and copyright exposure as scraping; treat dedicated accounts and a scrubbing pass as mandatory before any dataset export, not optional.

Scale

Raw capture is not the bottleneck: 2 ms p50, 84 req/s per phone flat out, phones fully independent up to 512 req/s aggregate across ten pollers. The real cost is the action plus the settle wait: a realistic scripted or human-driven session yields roughly 600-2,000 labelled transitions an hour per phone, dominated by think time and in-app network waits rather than the near-free capture cost, so on the order of 1,200-4,000 rows an hour across the two phones mirroring today. That is an order of magnitude below a naive "one transition per second per phone" projection, and far below a 1.6M-row/day full-rack figure that assumes 19 mirroring phones this rig does not have.

Frame-rate as a signal: autoplay presence and app-hang detection

Native APIWith caveats

Poll raw BMP frames while sending no input, and count how many successive frames differ by more than a mean-pixel threshold. A still screen produces almost none, an autoplaying video or animated banner produces close to the phone's own frame ceiling, and an app that has stopped responding produces none after an action that should have changed the screen. The output is a number, not a picture, so it needs no OCR, no image-search plug-in and no template library, which matters because neither recognition plug-in is connected here.

How

  1. get_device_list /device/get?id=<id> — confirm a live air_pid and read imgw/imgh, the pixel space for frames and coordinates alike.
  2. mouse_reset_pos /mouse/reset?id=<comma list> — clear the stuck-click state before any input-driven step, or a "frozen app" verdict can actually be a stuck pointer.
  3. mouse_move + get_device_screenshot /mouse/move?id=<id>&x=&y= while polling /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — calibrate this phone's ceiling by driving continuous motion and counting new frames flat out; measured 28.9/s on one XR, 4.5/s on its identical twin, so the ceiling is a per-phone property that must be measured, never assumed.
  4. send_key (WIN+h) + get_device_screenshot /key/sendkey?id=<comma list>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) then poll /pic/screenshot — establish the idle floor on a known-static home screen; measured ~0.02-0.03 mean abs diff frame to frame.
  5. click / swipe / shortcut#13 /mouse/click, /mouse/swipe, or /shortcut/exec/url — navigate to the screen under test; the click/swipe route keeps the whole technique native, the Shortcut route is optional.
  6. get_device_screenshot (loop) poll /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true at a fixed period — send no input for a few seconds and count new frames as a fraction of the calibrated ceiling: near-ceiling means continuously animated content, near-zero means static.
  7. mouse_wheel /mouse/wheel?id=<id>&direction=down&len=40&number=1 — hang probe: act, then count new frames in the next second; zero after a scroll that should have moved the screen is the candidate signal.
  8. mouse_move + pointer-box diff; hotkey liveness /mouse/move then /pic/screenshot, plus /key/sendkey fn_key=WIN+h — disambiguate "app is frozen" from "control channel is dead" before reporting a hang; a working hotkey proves the channel but says nothing about taps.
  9. (callback) ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — error_push — optional: subscribe to asynchronous hardware failures that otherwise look identical to a frozen app.

Needs

  • Phone mirroring with Auto-Lock set to Never; a sleeping screen reads as a hang.
  • Per-phone ceiling calibration before any verdict, re-run periodically since the ceiling is a property of that phone's live Wi-Fi link and can degrade over a session.
  • A poller that reuses one ~1.6 MB buffer per phone and paces at a fixed period, recording frames on arrival rather than on a display tick.
  • Nothing else touching the screen during the measurement window; the pointer dot moving, a notification banner or an auto-dimming screen all register as a frame change.
  • Board bound and connected for the wheel/move/hotkey steps; the pure autoplay measurement needs only the video channel.

Watch out

  • On this rig the technique classifies autoplay reliably on only one of the two phones: the slower XR's ~4.5 new frames/s ceiling is well under the floor needed to separate "animated" from "slowly changing," so it must be excluded from autoplay classification and used only for the coarser hang probe.
  • This measures AirPlay mirror frame production, not the app's own render rate; a 60 fps app still can't deliver more than ~30 new frames/s over AirPlay, and a compressed stream can drop frames that did change. Treat it as a presence/absence classifier, never a performance metric.
  • Never use byte equality or MD5 to decide "new frame": an untouched phone measures ~0.02-0.03 mean absolute pixel difference every frame from clock and encoder noise, so MD5 would report every frame as new on a dead-still screen.
  • A zero-frame result after a wheel event has several causes beyond a hang: a stuck-click state, a screen that legitimately does not scroll (including one already fully scrolled), or a dropped mirror session. Rule those out with /mouse/reset, the pointer-box diff and /device/get state, and confirm the content actually has more to scroll before calling it a hang.
  • A rack-wide figure built on 19 phones is hypothetical; 19 is the board count, and the measured envelope (512 req/s aggregate across ten pollers) is close to the edge for a genuine 19-phone fleet at 30 Hz, so stagger pollers or drop to 20 Hz if that hardware is ever added.
  • The technique cannot distinguish "video paused deliberately by the app" from "app hang"; both look like a drop from near-ceiling to near-zero, so treat a rate drop as a hang candidate that still needs the independent liveness checks, not a hang signal on its own.
  • A 5 s calibration window is too short on the slow phone, yielding only ~22 samples; widen calibration to 15-20 s for any phone whose running ceiling estimate is under ~10 fps, and calibrate on a plain wallpaper page, since live widgets or wallpaper motion can inflate the idle floor.
  • AirPlay can buffer several frames under load, so a freeze under roughly one buffered frame interval on the fast phone may not register within a 1 s hang-probe window; treat the probe as reliable for freezes of at least a few hundred ms to a second, not instantaneous stutters.

Scale

Per phone: 84 req/s flat out, or 2.0 ms p50 when paced; phones are fully independent, with input traffic and frame polling shown not to interfere with each other. A full check cycle — calibration, autoplay measurement, hang probe — is roughly 11-26 s, on the order of 140-330 classification cycles an hour per phone run continuously and serially, and since phones share no bottleneck those per-phone rates hold simultaneously across the rack rather than being divided among phones. A steady-state monitor that skips full recalibration can classify a screen roughly every 5 s per phone, about 700 five-second verdicts an hour per phone, well inside the measured throughput envelope; this scales with phones actually mirroring, not with the 19 boards present.

Also worth knowing

Recognition against a supplied image instead of the live mirror

Needs plug-inWith caveats

Six recognition functions carry a target_img parameter: /pic/find-image, /pic/find-image-cv, /pic/ocr and /pic/ocr-ex, /pic/find-text and /pic/find-text-ex, and /pic/find-multi-color. The docs describe it the same way on every one of them: "big picture of goal, generally you don't need to fill it in, our internal screen image will be used by default." Leave it blank and the plug-in reads the live 500×1080 mirror frame, the same frame every other card in this section is stuck with. Fill it in and the plug-in reads whatever file or string you hand it instead, at that image's own resolution. That is the one lever in the entire API that separates recognition from the mirror, which matters because the mirror is the document's own recurring complaint: it is a re-encoded downscale of the XR's real panel, and small text sits at the edge of readable cap-height once it crosses that pipe. A native screenshot pulled back through the Shortcut's album chain and handed back in as target_img reads at full panel resolution instead. The same substitution also opens offline re-analysis of an already-archived frame corpus, and, since every call still needs a device id but that device's own screen is never touched once target_img is set, a queue of stored images run one at a time against whichever single bound phone is convenient.

How

  1. send_key (fn_key) /key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+SHIFT+3 — fire the native iOS screenshot chord (see the native-resolution capture card above for the full chain and its traps)
  2. shortcut#1 /shortcut/album/get?id=<single>&num=1&outtime=<ms> — confirm the shot landed, using its own create_time, not sort order
  3. shortcut#2 /shortcut/album/down?id=<single>&list=[{…}]&outtime=30000 — pull the native PNG to <install dir>\Shortcut\Media on the PC
  4. local (client-side) — point target_img at that file's path, or its contents, in place of leaving the parameter blank
  5. ocr / ocr_ex /pic/ocr?id=<id>&target_img=<file>&rect=[l,t,r,b] — recognize text against the supplied image; rect must be measured in that image's own pixel space, not the 500×1080 mirror space used everywhere else in this section
  6. find_image /pic/find-image?id=<id>&target_img=<file>&img_list=[…]&similarity=0.8 — the same substitution for template matching; find_image_ex (/pic/find-image-cv) and find_multi_color (/pic/find-multi-color) take target_img the same way
  7. local (client-side) — for offline re-analysis, skip steps 1-3 entirely and point target_img at any previously saved frame, e.g. one already written by /pic/screenshot?save_path=… or archived by an earlier sweep

Needs

  • OCR and/or image-search plug-in installed and connected; on this rig all six functions return data.code 28 today, and target_img changes what image the plug-in would read, not whether the plug-in is there to read it
  • A valid, hardware-connected device id on every call regardless of target_img — nothing in the parameter tables drops the id requirement, so there is no documented way to recognize an image with no phone in the request at all
  • For native-resolution sourcing: the full Shortcut install/IP-edit/AssistiveTouch-binding chain and Shortcuts > Advanced permissions, exactly as the native-resolution capture card above requires
  • rect recalculated per source image — a rectangle measured against the 500×1080 mirror is meaningless against a native screenshot; read that file's actual pixel dimensions rather than assuming a fixed size

Watch out

  • The parameter table lists target_img only as type String. img_list's own row on the same page spells out "base64 string image list or local path list"; target_img's row does not repeat that. Whether it wants a bare base64 string, a data URI, or a path on the PC running the kernel is unstated — test with one known-good file before building anything on it
  • Whether the id's device needs to be actively mirroring, or merely bound and hardware-connected, to accept a target_img call is untested on this rig. That answer decides whether "recognition on a phone whose video channel is down" actually works, or still fails with code 3 or 25 before target_img is ever read
  • The Shortcut-side fallbacks named in the docs, /shortcut/other/ocr, /shortcut/other/ocr-ex, /shortcut/other/find-image, /shortcut/other/find-image-cv, /shortcut/other/find-text, /shortcut/other/find-text-ex and /shortcut/other/find-multi-color, are listed as v1.3+ "special case" alternates with no parameter table at all; whether they accept target_img or only ever read the phone's own screen is unknown
  • None of this is a verified round trip on this rig: both plug-ins report code 28, so every claim above is a reading of the parameter table, not a call that has actually returned code 0 with a supplied image
  • All six functions are single-id, so feeding target_img fans out no better than live recognition would; a corpus of archived frames is worked one request at a time, same as a live sweep
  • Codes 31 ("OCR did not recognize the text") and 32 ("No text found") are the plug-in's own outcome codes, not evidence of a resolution cause; a low-resolution mirror crop is one plausible reason recognition comes back empty, but the docs do not attribute either code to image size specifically

Scale

target_img changes which image is read, not the cost of reading it: once a plug-in is connected, per-call latency should track whatever live-recognition latency turns out to be, which is undocumented on this rig either way. The only added cost is getting a native-resolution file onto the PC first, which is the same serial, single-id, per-phone album pipeline as the native-resolution capture card above (unmeasured; treat any per-shot figure there as a placeholder). Offline re-analysis of an already-archived corpus skips capture entirely and is bounded purely by plug-in throughput once one exists, so it is the cheapest of the three paths in this card once the plug-in gate is cleared.

Raising one phone's mirror resolution as a per-job lever, then dropping it back

Native APIWith caveats

The mirror's pixel size is not fixed to the model, it is a per-device runtime setting. air_ratio in /device/airplay/set takes one phone from its working resolution up to 720, 1080, 1400, 1920 or 2650 for as long as a vision pass needs the extra pixels, independent of every other phone on the rack, then back down when the pass is done. That is the fix for "screen too small at the current ratio," a real condition on this rig: the mirror is roughly 60% of the XR's linear panel resolution, and small captions sit at the edge of reliable OCR cap height once downscaled to 500x1080. The catch is that the pixel space every stored rect and click coordinate is keyed to moves with it, and the doc states the change disconnects the cast to apply.

How

  1. get_device_list /device/get — read the target phone's current imgw, imgh and air_ratio before touching anything; on this rig that is 500x1080 with air_ratio 0 (following the global default), so this is the baseline every stored coordinate assumes
  2. set_airplay /device/airplay/set?id=<one id>&air_ratio=1920 — raise just this phone's mirror height for the pass; air_refresh, air_fps and air_img_fps ride the same call, so a higher frame rate for the pass costs no extra reconnect
  3. local (poll) — the doc's own note under the parameter table says a non-zero value disconnects the cast immediately and the new geometry takes effect on the next screen projection; poll /device/get for that id until state is non-zero again and imgw/imgh reflect the requested ratio, never a fixed sleep
  4. get_device_screenshot / ocr / find-text /pic/screenshot, /pic/ocr?id=<id>&rect=[l,t,r,b], /pic/find-text?id=<id>&text=[…] — capture or recognize against the larger frame; the rect for this call must be measured at the new resolution, not carried over from the old one
  5. mouse_reset_pos + click /mouse/reset?id=<id> then /mouse/click?id=<id>&x=<x>&y=<y> — act on what was read, using coordinates measured at the raised resolution, not the working one
  6. set_airplay /device/airplay/set?id=<one id>&air_ratio=0 — drop the phone back to its working ratio once the pass is done; this is a second disconnect and reconnect, not a free undo
  7. local (poll) — poll /device/get again for state and imgw/imgh back at 500x1080 before resuming any job that assumed the working coordinate space

Needs

  • The phone already bound and mirroring, since air_ratio only changes the geometry of an existing or next cast, it does not start one
  • The coordinate registry keyed on (device id, resolution), not device id alone, so a rect or click measured at 500x1080 is never reused at 1920 or vice versa
  • A settle-and-poll routine on /device/get, the same pattern used for screenshot settle elsewhere in this section, applied to state and imgw/imgh instead of pixel diff
  • For the OCR half of the goal specifically: the kernel OCR plug-in actually connected. On this rig /pic/ocr and /pic/find-text answer data.code 28 at any resolution, so raising air_ratio here only removes the "too small" half of the problem; the vision pass this buys is client-side OCR on the fetched frame, not the kernel path

Watch out

  • Two different resolution knobs exist and are easy to conflate. air_play_ratio in /config/imserver/set is the server-wide default, applies to every phone whose own air_ratio is 0, and is not on the doc's short list of settings that skip a kernel restart, so changing it needs /imserver/restart and touches the whole rack. air_ratio in /device/airplay/set is per device and needs no kernel restart, only a re-cast of that one phone. Only the per-device knob is the single-job lever described here
  • air_ratio values (0, 720, 1080, 1400, 1920, 2650) are requested targets, not guaranteed output pixels. imgw/imgh in /device/get are the only confirmed result, read them back after the reconnect rather than computing them from the requested ratio
  • The disconnect is stated as unconditional for any non-zero value, not an occasional side effect, so a job that raises and restores resolution around every read pays two full reconnects, not one
  • Nothing in the docs gives a reconnect latency; anything mid-flight that assumed continuous mirroring, a diff-based watcher, an open Shortcut round trip, a queued click, breaks across the gap and needs to re-check state before resuming
  • This has not been exercised on this rig's two live phones, only read from the documented parameter table and the device-connect/disconnect callback schema; treat the reconnect timing and the exact post-change imgw/imgh as unverified until run once

Scale

/device/airplay/set accepts a comma id list, so raising resolution on several phones for the same pass is one call, but each listed phone pays its own independent disconnect and reconnect, there is no shared cast to break once for all of them. The lever is meant for one phone in one job at a time, not a rack-wide switch; a rack-wide change belongs on the global air_play_ratio instead, at the cost of a kernel restart and every phone's rects going stale together rather than one.

Server-side cropping as the default poll shape, not a special case

Every polling design earlier in this document, and elsewhere in this handoff, fetches the full mirror frame and crops on the PC: a wall thumbnail, a badge watcher, a banner-strip poll for push latency, the post-grid diff above all pull the complete binary=true payload (measured at 1.6 MB, 500x1080x3 plus a 54-byte header) and only then discard everything outside a few dozen pixels. /pic/screenshot does not require that. Its rect parameter, documented as a plain sibling of binary and jpg, crops on the kernel before the image leaves the process, so the reply body is the sub-rectangle, not the frame. save_path goes further and skips the transfer path entirely, writing the (optionally already-cropped) image straight to a file on the PC's own disk with no base64 field and no JSON image payload to build or parse. Neither costs anything extra to add to a call that already knows its target rectangle, and both are native, unauthenticated, plug-in-free XP behavior, no different in status from a call this document has already used elsewhere on this rig.

The same flat [left, top, right, bottom] array (never the Phonefarm four-corner form, see the coordinate-space note above) scopes the search area for /pic/find-multi-color, and for /pic/ocr where the OCR plug-in is connected, neither of which is this rig's case (data.code 28). For a badge watcher whose signal is a known color key rather than legible text, find-multi-color with a tight rect is the strongest version of this pattern: the response carries only {index, centre} pairs for a match, or an empty list, no image bytes at all, so the watcher's steady-state traffic is a few dozen bytes of JSON regardless of how large the full frame would have been. A banner strip that has to be read as pixels rather than matched by color (a diff strip, a piece of text once OCR is live) still goes through /pic/screenshot?rect=…, but the transferred image shrinks with the crop: a 500-pixel-wide, few-dozen-pixel-tall strip is on the order of tens of kilobytes rather than 1.6 MB, and a small badge glyph is a few kilobytes or less. Nothing in the docs or in HARDWARE.md benchmarks a cropped payload directly, so these are pixel-math estimates from the documented BMP layout, not measured figures; the one-call smoke test this section already recommends for the Shortcut chain has an equivalent here, run /pic/screenshot once with and once without rect on the same region and compare bytes and latency before sizing anything against it.

The reasoning connects directly to the GC pressure recorded in HARDWARE.md. That measurement (488 MB/s allocated, 496 gen-2 collections and a 96.9 ms GC pause in 8 seconds) is a direct consequence of a full 1.6 MB frame crossing .NET's 85 KB Large Object Heap threshold on every single poll, whether or not the poll needed more than a corner of it. A badge or banner-strip crop sized in kilobytes, not megabytes, most likely never reaches that threshold at all, which is a stronger fix than the buffer-reuse mitigation HARDWARE.md measured (2.9 MB/s allocated, 1 collection, 8.5 ms pause): reuse still allocates and refills a 1.6 MB buffer per pump, while a genuine server-side crop for a narrow job has no reason to touch an object that size in the first place. That distinction has not been measured on this rig either; the direction is well supported by the documented allocation mechanics, the magnitude is not.

This changes the arithmetic behind the throughput budget card, which currently prices every observation at the full-frame numbers (84 req/s flat out, 12.7 ms p50, 1.6 MB per call). A badge or banner watcher that adds rect to the same call is not bound by that ceiling; it is bound by whatever the kernel's own crop and encode cost turns out to be for a much smaller output, which nothing in the current documentation or measurements isolates. Until that is measured, the honest position is that per-phone poll rate for a narrow rect job is very likely higher than the full-frame figure implies, not lower, and any card that reuses 84 req/s or 1.6 MB as the per-observation cost for a badge or banner watcher should be flagged as pricing the wrong payload rather than treated as a conservative floor.

MARK-QA-MARK

Section 8 · Testing, QA and research

Testing, QA and research

The rack's most defensible use is as a bank of real iOS devices you can drive and observe programmatically: real link routing, real push rendering, real mail-client layout, and a frame-diff oracle cheap enough to run on every screen of every build. Everything below runs on the XP kernel at 127.0.0.1:9911 with path-style calls; the two-phone rig here proves the pipeline, not full 19-board throughput.

Campaign link, push and email QA

Deep-link and universal-link verification matrix

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Fire every campaign URL, custom-scheme link and https universal link at the whole phone group in one request, then capture a raw-BMP frame per phone before and after and classify where each link actually landed: app opened to the right screen, Safari fallback, App Store page, "Open in app" banner, or error. App state is varied per phone first (cold, warm, and one phone deliberately without the app) so routing, fallback and not-installed branches are all covered, and each verdict is backed by a stored frame rather than a log line.

How

  1. get_device_list + get_usb_list GET /api/device/get, GET /api/config/usb/get — inventory geometry, online state and board binding; exclude any phone whose imgw/imgh, state, vid/pid or location_crc doesn't match the set.
  2. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> — clear the silent stuck-click state across the whole target set before any tap-critical run.
  3. send_key WIN+h GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h — two presses, normalize every phone to home page one.
  4. send_key AppSwitch + swipe GET /api/key/sendkey?fn_key=AppSwitch, GET /api/mouse/swipe — set the row's app state: warm (WIN+h), cold (AppSwitch plus a dismiss swipe), or reserve one phone with the app absent.
  5. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — capture the "before" frame, one request per phone.
  6. shortcut#13 Open URL GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<ids>&url=<link>&outtime=<ms> — fire the link at the whole group in one request; the only documented XP way to open an arbitrary URL from the PC.
  7. get_device_screenshot, polled GET /api/pic/screenshot?binary=true — poll on a fixed period until consecutive frames stop differing, then capture the "after" frame.
  8. get_device_screenshot with rect GET /api/pic/screenshot?rect=[l,t,r,b] — classify the landing by mean absolute pixel diff against the before frame and a per-phone golden of the expected destination.
  9. find_image / ocr (optional) POST /api/pic/find-image-cv, GET /api/pic/ocr — assert a specific artifact (banner, badge, title text) instead of a whole-screen diff; not available on this rig, code 28.
  10. find_multi_color (optional) POST /api/pic/find-multi-color — colour-signature classification of the fallback route without OCR; plug-in status unprobed, treat as unproven.
  11. send_key TAB+b / WIN+h GET /api/key/sendkey?fn_key=TAB+b|WIN+h — return home and advance to the next URL; TAB+b is best-effort, WIN+h is the reliable reset.
  12. get_device_screenshot, saved GET /api/pic/screenshot?save_path=<dir>&jpg=true — persist the classifying frame to disk, named by device, URL and app state.
  13. send_key + click (fallback) GET /api/key/sendkey?key=<url>, GET /api/mouse/click — fully native fallback when the Shortcut is absent: type the URL into a note and tap the auto-linked text so the link is followed from a real in-app tap.

Needs
