Two identical iPhone XRs on the same iOS build and the same LAN measured 28.9 and 4.5 new frames per second under continuous motion; nothing in either API edition reports RSSI, link rate or retransmits, so delivered frame rate is the only observable the rack has for radio health, and every endpoint in this chain already answers on this rig.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get — enumerate the rack; only score phones with state non-0 and a live air_pid.
  2. none GET /api/config/imserver/get — read the global cast configuration before attributing a low score to the radio; a throttled air_play_fps would explain it instead.
  3. get_usb_list GET /api/config/usb/get — confirm the control channel (board state 2) so a dead board is never mistaken for a dead radio.
  4. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> — clear the stuck-pointer state across the whole target set before the swipe stimulus.
  5. send_key (fn_key) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) — normalise every phone to the home screen so the stimulus produces comparable motion.
  6. swipe GET /api/mouse/swipe?id=<ids>&direction=left&len=0.8 — fire one synthetic motion stimulus at every phone in a single request; two live doc traps in the parameter spelling and typing.
  7. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — poll raw frames, one concurrent poller per phone; single-id only, no server push on XP.
  8. none none — client-side — count genuinely new frames by mean absolute pixel difference above ~1; never MD5, which produced a documented false conclusion earlier in this project.
  9. none none — client-side — validate the run before publishing a score: if the largest single-frame difference never exceeds ~20, the swipe never landed and the cause is unbound hardware, not a bad radio.
  10. set_airplay_mode GET /api/device/airplay/set?id=<ids>&air_ratio=720 (or air_fps / air_refresh / air_img_fps / air_audio) — optional remediation: lower cast cost for a weak phone and re-measure; disconnects and re-casts, and changes imgw/imgh.
  11. get_device_list (ip, mac) GET /api/device/get — optional correlation with AP association tables or DHCP leases outside the API; neither edition reports RSSI, channel or PHY rate.

Needs

  • XP kernel reachable at 9911 with path-style calls; IMConsole.exe running and logged in.
  • Each phone mirroring (state non-0, live air_pid) with an established AirPlay socket, since video delivery is what is being measured.
  • Board bound at /config/usb/get state 2 with a non-empty location_crc, or the stimulus cannot be delivered.
  • Invisible iOS prerequisites (AssistiveTouch on at maximum sensitivity, tracking speed at maximum, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock) — none queryable over the API, and any one being off makes the stimulus silently do nothing.
  • Phones parked on content where the swipe produces full-screen motion, such as a multi-page home screen; a still screen scores every phone near zero.
  • One HTTP client per phone able to sustain ~1.6 MB per poll with buffer reuse; no plug-in, Shortcut or edition gate involved anywhere in this chain.

Watch out

  • The metric is delivered frame rate, not Wi-Fi link quality — no function in either edition reports RSSI, link rate or retransmits; earn the "Wi-Fi" label by re-running a phone alone and together, which is exactly how the 28.9-versus-4.5 fps gap on this rig was shown to be the phone's own link rather than kernel contention.
  • Cross-phone ranking is only fair when phones show the same content, since source frame rate is content-dependent and the two XRs here have different home screens; treat per-phone trend against its own baseline as the defensible use, the league table as indicative only.
  • The stimulus is real input on a real phone — run it only on a normalised, disposable screen, never mid-task.
  • AirPlay tops out around 30 fps; treat anything above ~27 as "full rate" and do not chase the difference — the score has little headroom among healthy phones and is much better at catching a phone that has fallen far.
  • Use a fixed poll period, never one derived from observed frame gaps — adaptive pacing fed by measured gaps decayed a 23 fps stream to 16.5 fps through positive feedback.
  • Two live doc traps in the swipe call: the parameter table says "stepping," every JSON example spells it "steping," and direction is typed Integer in the table but passed as strings in every example.
  • The remediation step is not free: /device/airplay/set drops the cast and changes imgw/imgh, invalidating every cached coordinate and template for that phone.
  • /config/imserver/get was not exercised in the 10 Sep probe — confirmed as a real documented path, but treat that read as "should work," not "proven," until one live GET is run.
  • Pin the stimulus to a single normalised state (home screen page 2 or later), since a vertical scrollable list under a horizontal swipe may not move at all and would falsely read as a dead link.

Scale

Frame pollers are independent with no shared kernel bottleneck: two phones polled flat out gave 83 and 85 req/s at p50 3 ms, identical to either alone, and ten concurrent pollers sustained 512 req/s aggregate at p50 3 ms; input and video traffic do not interfere in either direction. The stimulus itself is a single request regardless of fleet size, since /mouse/swipe fans out on a comma list and the boards walk in parallel, costing roughly 300 ms of pointer travel whether one phone or twenty are listed. A 5 s measurement window plus normalisation puts a full-rack pass well under a minute, and each phone's full cycle (two Home presses, swipe settle, 5 s window) is on the order of 6-7 seconds even though the calls fan out in parallel — comfortable for a nightly or per-shift cadence, not a continuous poll. The remediation path is the slow part, since each air_ratio change forces a disconnect and re-cast per phone.

Remote diagnostics and hands-on control

Remote-hands desk for one phone in a closet

Native APIWith caveats

A support engineer picks one phone anywhere on the rack and operates it as if it were in hand: a polled raw-BMP mirror from /pic/screenshot, real pointer control via /mouse/move plus down/up (or /mouse/click and /mouse/swipe), and the full ASCII-plus-hotkey set through /key/sendkey. Because control and video are separate channels, the same session catches the failure the vendor console cannot tell apart from a working phone: a perfect picture that ignores every tap. A four-rung recovery ladder, pointer reset, board restart, mirror reconnect, phone restart, sits behind it for when the phone itself is stuck.

How

  1. get_device_list + get_usb_list GET /device/get?id=<id> and GET /config/usb/get — read both channel states first: video-ready is device state non-0 with a live air_pid, control-ready is that phone's board at state 2 with vid/pid/uid and location_crc populated. Also record imgw/imgh (500 x 1080 here), the coordinate space for everything that follows.
  2. get_device_screenshot GET /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — single-id polled mirror. Raw BMP measured p50 2 ms at 1.62 MB (84 req/s); jpg=true trades that for ~96 KB at a hard ~21 req/s cap. There is no server-push video stream on XP.
  3. mouse_reset_pos GET /mouse/reset?id=<id> — open every session with this. It is the only call that clears the measured stuck-click state, where /mouse/click silently does nothing while moves and hardware keys keep working.
  4. mouse_move / down / up / click / swipe / wheel /mouse/move?id&x&y · /mouse/down?id[&button] · /mouse/up?id · /mouse/click?id&x&y · /mouse/swipe?id&direction&len · /mouse/wheel?id&direction&len&number — a real drag is down, streamed moves, up, not a canned swipe. button is numeric (1 left, 2 right, 3 middle). The board walks the pointer at ~0.6 ms/px, so coalesce to the latest position rather than streaming every intermediate point.
  5. send_key / key_down / key_up / key_release_all /key/sendkey?id&key=<ASCII> or &fn_key=<hotkey> · /key/down · /key/up · /key/upall — the documented hotkey table covers Home, Back, App Switch, Control/Notice bar, Lock, screenshot, pass-through mode, clipboard and volume/media keys. key is ASCII only in both editions.
  6. Unicode text — POST /shortcut/clipboard/set?id&text=<unicode>[&sleep] then GET /key/sendkey?id&fn_key=WIN+v — XP has no direct Unicode send; paste via the iMouse Shortcut's clipboard is the documented route, and it needs the Shortcut installed and bound.
  7. Recovery ladder — mouse_reset_pos / key_release_all /mouse/reset · /key/upall, then restart_usb /device/usb/restart?id=<vid>|<pid>, then discon_airplay / auto_connect_screen /device/airplay/disconnect then /connect, then restart_device /device/restart or /shortcut/switch/device?state=1 or fn_key=CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r — four rungs of escalating disruption, cheapest first.
  8. Session feed — ws://<host>:9911/api — hold a socket for im_connect (the only place the kernel version is exposed on XP), error_push (the only async signal an input call failed at the board), and airplay_connect_log/restart_log during the session.

Needs

  • A network path to the kernel on TCP 9911 restricted to a VPN or a firewalled management segment, never an open LAN — the API has no authentication of any kind.
  • Target phone bound to its board (state 2) with mouse parameters present, and mirroring live (state non-0, matching air_pid).
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in; IMService.exe alone leaves the phone at state 0 and the board list empty.
  • iOS settings no API call can read: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity maxed, Full Keyboard Access on, Trackpad & Mouse tracking speed maxed, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock.
  • iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited, run once with permissions granted, and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key — only for Unicode typing and the Shortcut restart route.
  • Board firmware generation read once from the phone's own AssistiveTouch → Devices screen; the API's ver/uver field is unusable on this build.

Watch out

  • No server-push video on XP: the live view is fixed-period polling, one request per phone. Over a WAN, prefer jpg=true with a rect crop of the working area.
  • Bandwidth is the real remote-link constraint: raw BMP is 1.6 MB per frame at 2 ms, JPEG is ~96 KB but 40 ms with a hard ~21 req/s ceiling.
  • Pointer feel degrades with distance, not load (~0.6 ms/px, ~600 ms edge-to-edge); coalesce operator input rather than sending every intermediate point.
  • Each phone's own AirPlay link caps what "live" means regardless of the API — one XR here delivered ~29 new frames/s and its twin ~4.5 on the same network. A fixed poll period on the slow phone mostly re-fetches the same frame; verify with a pixel-diff wait, not a 30 fps assumption.
  • /device/restart is expected to fail on this rig until the OCR plug-in is installed (code 15/28); use the Shortcut route or the CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r hotkey instead. That dependency is specific to the UI-driven restart and to any script that drives Control Center's mirroring picker by coordinates — /device/airplay/connect itself is a direct call and does not require OCR.
  • Restarting the phone (rung 5) is not actually remote-hands: it returns the phone to the Lock Screen and nothing in the API can type a passcode, so this rung converts the session into "needs a human at the rack afterward" rather than a same-tier recovery step.
  • Verify a gesture landed by mean pixel difference in a small box around the target (1.4-9.8 against a ~0.02 idle floor) — /mouse/click and /mouse/move return only a status code, and MD5 or byte comparison of the whole frame is unusable because of encoder noise and live UI elements.
  • The session is, functionally, unaudited remote access to whatever the phone is signed into, with no log beyond what your own tooling keeps.

Scale

One operator per phone by design, since /pic/screenshot refuses multiple ids, but that single session is cheap: raw frames sustain 84 req/s at p50 2 ms, and input and polling measurably do not contend (streaming moves while polling raised throughput to 98.8 req/s). Several engineers can run independent sessions on different phones without scheduling, ten concurrent pollers sustained 512 req/s total, but on this rig only two phones currently show state non-0, so the real concurrency ceiling today is two simultaneous sessions, not the API's request budget. Per-session pace is bounded by pointer-walk physics and operator think time: a full-screen traversal costs ~600 ms, and a realistic move-click-verify cycle runs one to three actions every two to four seconds, on the order of 900-1,800 verified UI actions per hour per phone.

Rack-wide controllability matrix and cross-wired board detection

Native APIWith caveats

A state-independent optical self-test that proves, per phone, that the board bound to its device record actually drives that screen. Pass A sends one mirrored /mouse/move to the whole id list and diffs a small pixel box per phone to separate controllable from mirroring-but-deaf. Pass B is the part that actually catches cross-wiring: it sends every phone its own distinct coordinate via N single-id calls and checks which coordinate showed up on which screen, because a mirrored move to a swapped pair looks identical from pass A alone. It runs natively today on this rig: no OCR, no image-search plug-in, no Shortcut, no WebSocket required.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /device/get (no id = all) — imgw/imgh per phone is the coordinate space for the whole test; live-probed on this rig at 500 x 1080 for both XRs.
  2. get_usb_list GET /config/usb/get — 19 boards, state 1 = on PC unbound, state 2 = phone attached; this is the denominator of control-ready slots. Never parse or display the ver field, it is mojibake on this build.
  3. send_key GET /key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice, ~1 s apart) — normalizes every phone to a known screen before probing; optional for the pointer test itself.
  4. mouse_reset_pos GET /mouse/reset?id=<list> — clears the stuck-click state and gives the walk a known 0,0 origin so its duration is predictable.
  5. get_device_screenshot GET /pic/screenshot?id=<one id>&binary=true — one baseline frame per phone; single-id only, no batching.
  6. Pass A liveness — mouse_move GET /mouse/move?id=<list>&x=470&y=1050 — one mirrored request drives every board in parallel; from 0,0 a ~1150 px diagonal is ~600-700 ms of walk.
  7. Verify pass A client-side: re-screenshot and take the mean absolute pixel difference in a ~40 px box around the target — 1.4-9.8 means controlled, ~0.02-0.03 means no control; never MD5-compare whole frames.
  8. Pass B cross-wire permutation — mouse_move N x GET /mouse/move?id=<one id>&x=<Xi>&y=<Yi> — a distinct coordinate per phone, issued concurrently, then box-diff every assigned coordinate on every screen. This is the step that actually reveals a swapped board, and it must cover every phone on every run, not just "suspect" ones.
  9. set_dev GET /device/set?id=<deviceid>&vid=720A&pid=<correct pid> — remediate a confirmed swap, one device per call, vid and pid together, then a second call to rewrite the slot name. Re-read /device/get to confirm, since the response only echoes the ids that were set.
  10. mouse_reset_pos GET /mouse/reset?id=<list> — park pointers and re-clear the stuck-click state before whatever runs next.
  11. Optional — subscribe to ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api for error_push and usb_change during the run, so a board that disconnected mid-run is attributed correctly instead of read as a wiring fault.
  12. Publish the matrix (phone x control-ok, video-ok, bound-to, actually-drives, hub/port) — entirely outside the API; there is no notification or webhook endpoint in either edition.

Needs

  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in — with only IMService.exe up, /device/get reported both phones state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list.
  • Every probed phone mirroring (state non-0, live air_pid, ESTABLISHED socket on TCP 17000); an offline phone cannot be optically proved at all.
  • Each phone bound to a board (vid/pid/uid non-empty) and that board at state 2, or /mouse/move returns code 2 or 3.
  • location_crc non-empty per phone, or every mouse call returns code 11 "No mouse parameters".
  • iOS side, unqueryable over the API: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity maxed, Full Keyboard Access on, Trackpad & Mouse speed maxed, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock.
  • imgw/imgh read per device record, not assumed, so the probe grid matches each phone's own mirror geometry.
  • A client-side BMP decoder (bottom-up, 54-byte header, 500x1080x3) and a mean-absolute-difference function. No OCR or image-search plug-in required, and none is installed here.

Watch out

  • A single mirrored move to the whole id list cannot detect cross-wiring: if A's record is bound to B's board and vice versa, the mirrored request moves both to the same coordinate and both screens show a dot, so both phones look healthy. Distinct per-phone coordinates (pass B) are the only mechanism that finds the swap, and it must run every time, not only against phones already under suspicion.
  • Offline phones are invisible to this test: the proof is optical over the AirPlay channel, so a state-0 slot has no observation channel. Report such slots as unproven, never as ok, and never rely on a code-0 /mouse/move return as proof of anything, since that is exactly the condition under which the measured stuck-click state hides.
  • The probe is blind to the stuck-click state by design: moves and hotkeys kept working on the stuck phone while /mouse/click silently failed. This matrix proves the pointer channel only; the tap channel needs a separate runbook.
  • Signal margin is real but not huge (1.4-9.8 against a 0.02-0.03 idle floor). Place probe coordinates away from the clock, live widgets and high-contrast wallpaper edges, and diff against a same-run idle control rather than a stored baseline.
  • Phones with different imgw/imgh must get their own grid rather than a shared coordinate; this rig's two XRs match at 500x1080, but the doc's own examples show 750x1334 and 460x818, so a mixed rack is the normal case.
  • Remediation is manual-ish and destructive: /device/set is one device per call and rewrites persistent fleet state (DeviceList.json). Require two consecutive agreeing runs plus an operator confirmation before any rebind, and log the before/after vid/pid/uid — a false positive from a stalled Wi-Fi frame would swap a working binding into a broken one.
  • Home-screen normalization changes what is on every screen; capture the baseline after both WIN+h presses settle, and give the slow phone (~4.5 new frames/s) several hundred ms rather than waiting for a frame to change.
  • Pass B's "N concurrent single-id calls run in one ~600 ms walk, not N times" is a reasonable inference from board-independence data measured for two phones, but concurrent dispatch to N separate boards as N separate HTTP requests was not directly measured — treat it as inferred, not confirmed, at larger N.
  • This test and stuck-click detection are two separate runbooks that happen to share the same reset/normalize steps; do not conflate a clean cross-wire matrix with a clean tap channel.

Scale

Pass A is cheap and sublinear in requests: for 50 phones, about three fan-out calls plus 2N screenshots and one ~600-700 ms pointer walk, well under two seconds of wall time. Pass B is the expensive half and is now mandatory: N concurrent single-id moves (still one ~600 ms walk, not N times) plus another N screenshots, then an N x N box-diff that is trivial client-side CPU — a full 50-phone matrix including cross-wire recovery is a few seconds end to end. On this 2-phone rig a full pass is dominated by one diagonal walk plus four screenshot round trips, well under two seconds, so hundreds of passes per hour are technically possible; scaled to a 19-board rack, on the order of 100-300 full-rack passes per hour is achievable before the grid-capacity ceiling (~56 distinguishable probe points at >=60 px spacing on a 500x1080 mirror) forces pass B into batches for larger racks. The real limits are bandwidth and memory, not the kernel: 1.62 MB per raw frame means 3N frames is ~240 MB of loopback traffic for 50 phones, so reuse one buffer per poller. Realistic cadence, given that both passes move every visible pointer and press Home twice, is nightly or per-shift, not continuous, and it is mutually exclusive with running automation on the same phones.

Guarding fleet configuration

Config-drift guard on an unauthenticated kernel

Native APIWith caveats

Anything on the LAN can rewrite the kernel config, rebind a board, move a phone between groups, delete a device record or log the kernel out, the XP API has no authentication of any kind. Hold one WebSocket, keep a hashed baseline of the config, device, group and USB lists, and treat the broadcast callbacks as a free change feed: diff each callback against the baseline, auto-revert the fields that apply live, and alert-only on the fields that need a kernel restart. One attribution shortcut helps: im_config_change is documented as going to other connected clients only, so any copy you receive is by definition not your own write.

How

  1. Open the feed — ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — held for the controller's whole life. Callbacks are WS-only with no HTTP polling equivalent; the envelope is {fun, status, message, msgid:0, data}, and msgid is 0 on every broadcast, so it carries no correlation value.
  2. Baseline the kernel config — GET /config/imserver/get — air_play_name, mdns_type, allow_ip_list, thread_mode, mouse_mode, air_play_ratio/fps and the rest, in one payload.
  3. Baseline every device record — GET /device/get (optional id list) — hash only the policy fields: deviceid, name, gid, vid, pid, uid, location_crc. Exclude state, air_pid, air_handle, ip and rotate, which change legitimately every session.
  4. Baseline groups and the board inventory — GET /device/group/get and GET /config/usb/get — hash vid|pid|uid only; exclude ver, which is mojibake on this build and would read as phantom drift on every poll.
  5. Log your own writes (path, field, value, time) so an incoming callback can be matched by value within a short window — there is no client id or origin field anywhere in the API, and msgid is always 0.
  6. On im_config_change: diff the pushed config against the baseline — the callback carries the full object, so no re-GET is needed, and any copy you receive is by definition someone else's write.
  7. Revert live-apply fields immediately — POST /config/imserver/set — the nine fields that apply with no restart are lang, mdns_type, connect_failed_retry, allow_ip_list, auto_connect, auto_updata, thread_mode, mouse_mode, flip_right.
  8. Alert, never auto-revert, on restart-required fields — GET /imserver/restart — air_play_name/port/ratio/fps/img_fps/refresh_rate/audio, opencv_num, ocr_num and enable_hardware_acceleration all need a restart, which drops every mirroring session on the PC.
  9. On dev_change: diff the pushed device record, then revert an unauthorized binding, group or calibration change with GET or POST /device/set — name/gid/location_crc can be batched across phones in one call, but a board rebind (vid+pid) is one call per phone, and there is no documented way to clear a binding.
  10. On group_change / group_delete / dev_delete: restore structure with /device/group/set and /device/set — a deleted device record is only partly repairable; the record itself does not return until the phone next casts, and online devices cannot be deleted at all (code 7).
  11. Watch the licence/session channel — WS logout, im_log, user_info; baseline with GET /config/user/info — anyone can log the kernel out over the LAN, which then refuses to bring devices online. Alert only; never auto-relogin.
  12. Network layer, the only actual control — a Windows Firewall rule restricting inbound TCP 9911 and 17000 to the controller host and phone VLAN. mdns_type/allow_ip_list gate only AirPlay discovery, never the HTTP/WS API itself.

Needs

  • XP-edition kernel on TCP 9911; Phonefarm-style POSTs return HTTP 500 and 9912 is closed, so the whole guard must use XP path style.
  • A persistent WebSocket client with automatic reconnect and an immediate full re-baseline on reconnect — every observation channel here is a broadcast callback with no polling fallback, so a dropped socket is a blind spot.
  • Your controller as the only intended writer, with a durable write log for self-echo filtering.
  • IMConsole.exe running — a baseline taken with only IMService.exe up is garbage; gate baselining on a non-empty board list and at least one device record.
  • Operator agreement on which host may write, since the vendor console is itself a legitimate writer and will otherwise trip the guard on every manual action.
  • Local admin on the rack PC for the firewall rule (hardening, not required for detection itself).

Watch out

  • The entire detection half rests on WebSocket broadcast callbacks that were never live-probed on this rig, only documented. This is a materially bigger unverified leap than most other entries in this section, which are built on live-probed request/response endpoints; treat the mechanism's confidence accordingly until a callback is actually observed firing.
  • /config/imserver/get and /set are documented but not probed here; the 10 Sep probe used /config/get, which 404s. Confirm the documented path answers before building on it.
  • Partial-set semantics of /config/imserver/set are undocumented — every example sends the full field set, and nothing says omitted fields are preserved. Re-send the complete baseline object on revert until measured otherwise, but note that a stale baseline plus a full-object revert can clobber a concurrent legitimate change; tie baseline refresh to the write log, not to a fixed schedule.
  • enable_hardware_acceleration is settable but appears in neither the GET response nor the im_config_change payload, so drift in that one field is invisible with no workaround.
  • Attribution is best-effort everywhere except im_config_change: dev_change is documented as going to all clients, so self-echo must be filtered by value-compare, and two writers setting the same value in the same window are indistinguishable.
  • A deleted device record is only partly repairable, and there is no documented call to clear a binding once set.
  • This is detection and repair, not a security control — a hostile LAN caller can rewrite faster than you can revert. The firewall rule is the only thing that actually prevents anything, and a compromised guard host itself gets unauthenticated write access to every phone's binding, exactly like everything else on the LAN.
  • The user_info push is described as "every 30 seconds," but nothing establishes that cadence as a guaranteed heartbeat rather than an on-change push; verify it before wiring liveness alerting to its absence.

Scale

Effectively free at any rack size: the steady state is one open WebSocket and zero polling, since the kernel pushes change callbacks only when something actually changes, plus a user_info heartbeat roughly every 30 seconds. Baseline re-reads are four small GETs taken at startup, after reconnect and after each accepted change, not on a timer, and payloads scale linearly with the rack while staying far below the 1.6 MB of a single screenshot frame. Input and screenshot traffic measurably do not interfere with each other, so a guard loop costs the video and control pipelines nothing. Revert writes are batchable for name/gid/location_crc across a comma-separated id list; only board rebinds are one call per phone. Revert-action rate, not request rate, is the only throughput question that matters, and it should stay low by design: rate-limit reverts and escalate to a human after a small number of flaps rather than fighting a persistent second writer.

Scaling beyond one rack

Multi-PC scale-out: one XP kernel per receiver, mDNS-pinned phones, and an external federating coordinator

Plus external toolingWith caveats

Nothing in either API edition spans PCs, so scaling past one rack means one IMService/IMConsole per PC, each with its own AirPlay receiver name and its own 9911 API, plus an external coordinator holding one WebSocket per kernel and presenting the union as one rack under <pc>/<deviceid> keys. Two verified per-kernel levers make it workable: mdns_type plus allow_ip_list pins which phone IPs may discover a given PC's receiver, applied live with no restart, and air_play_ratio/fps/img_fps/refresh_rate (global, needs restart) or /device/airplay/set (per device, needs a reconnect) tune capacity. Recovery per kernel is /device/airplay/connect/all plus /imserver/regmdns. The coordinator itself is entirely your own code; XP has no cross-PC function, no cross-PC id namespace and no multi-receiver concept.

How

  1. Give each PC a unique receiver identity, then restart — /config/imserver/set?air_play_name=...&air_play_port=17000 then /imserver/restart — both fields need a restart since neither is in the documented no-restart list.
  2. Pin discovery so only this PC's phones see this PC's receiver — /config/imserver/set?mdns_type=1&allow_ip_list=[...] — applies live; the doc's own wording for rule 1 vs 2 is self-contradictory, so validate on a spare phone before relying on it.
  3. Give each phone a static IP with the router/gateway field left empty, so allow_ip_list, which is keyed by IP, has a stable target — a phone-side iOS setting, not an API call.
  4. Set the capacity profile per kernel or per phone — /config/imserver/set (air_play_ratio, air_play_fps, air_play_img_fps, air_play_refresh_rate, air_play_audio) + /imserver/restart; or per device /device/airplay/set?id=<ids>&air_ratio=&air_refresh=&air_fps=&air_img_fps=&air_audio= — XP has no mode preset; the Phonefarm sibling's ~5/10/20 Mbps figures do not apply here.
  5. Coordinator: one event-bus socket per kernel — ws://<pc>:9911/api — the same JSON envelope works over HTTP and WS, so poll over HTTP and keep the socket only for pushes.
  6. Key every device as <kernel host>/<deviceid> — GET /device/get (optional id list) — deviceid is phone-derived and distinct from mac, so it likely survives a re-cast to a different kernel; namespace by host anyway, since the host is the routing address.
  7. Cross-PC fan-out is N parallel requests, one per kernel — /mouse/*, /key/sendkey, /device/set, /device/airplay/connect|disconnect, /device/usb/restart — the comma-id list only collapses fan-out within a single kernel.
  8. Per-kernel health — /config/usb/get, /device/get, /config/user/info; WS user_info, im_log, im_connect(data.ver), error_push — control-ready is board state 2 plus a bound uid; video-ready is device state non-0 with a live air_pid; im_connect is the only place the kernel version is exposed on XP.
  9. Licence each kernel, but do not assume a utag partitions the pool — /config/user/login (phone, password, utag 1-10), /config/user/switch (id 1-10) — nothing in the docs states each utag carries its own licence headroom.
  10. Move a phone between PCs — /device/airplay/disconnect on the old kernel → edit allow_ip_list on both → /imserver/regmdns on the new PC → /device/airplay/connect (or auto_connect) on the new PC — the board moves physically with the phone; XP has no force flag, so disconnect explicitly first.
  11. Rack recovery after a PC reboot — /device/airplay/connect/all (no parameters), per kernel; /config/imserver/set?auto_connect=true&connect_failed_retry=<n> — progress arrives on the airplay_connect_log callback.

Needs

  • One licensed XP kernel and a running, logged-in IMConsole.exe per PC — the coordinator cannot bring a rack up by itself.
  • Phones and their rack PC on the same L2 segment, since mDNS/Bonjour does not cross subnets, with AirPlay's port reachable.
  • Static IPs on every phone with the gateway field left empty.
  • Each phone's control board physically cabled to the same PC that hosts its receiver — a board cannot be reached across machines.
  • An external coordinator process you write; there is no federated id space or cross-PC addressing in the API.
  • Firewall discipline on every rack PC: 9911 and 17000 restricted to trusted hosts.
  • For programmatic re-casting, the OCR and image-search plug-ins installed and connected on each kernel — not satisfied on this rig, /pic/ocr returns code 28.
  • Per-PC USB hub topology recorded from Windows PnP, since PIDs are opaque and slot labels do not survive a phone moving to another PC.

Watch out

  • The federation layer is entirely your own software, which is why this is "needs external tooling," not native.
  • XP has exactly one AirPlay receiver per kernel; the Phonefarm sibling's N-receivers-per-PC concept has no XP equivalent, confirmed by an HTTP 500 on the bare function name. You add PCs, not receivers.
  • allow_ip_list gates AirPlay discovery only, never authentication — any LAN host can still drive every phone on any rack PC's 9911, and each added PC multiplies that surface.
  • Treat the ~50-100 phones-per-PC and Mbps figures as Phonefarm-edition planning estimates for "one landscape game," never measured on an XP build; XP has no mode preset, and this rig's own two identical XRs already show a 6x frame-rate spread on the same AP. Derive per-PC phone count empirically from measured new-frames/s per phone after placement, and expect the shared Wi-Fi AP's aggregate throughput, not USB hub slots, to be the true per-PC ceiling.
  • Automated re-cast (steps 10-11) depends on /device/airplay/connect driving Control Centre via the OCR/image-search plug-ins; those are not connected on this rig, so expect phone-to-PC moves and post-reboot recovery to need a human at each rack until they are installed.
  • Changing air_play_name or air_play_port needs a restart that drops every mirroring session on that PC; only the nine documented fields apply live.
  • The kernel version is only readable from the im_connect WS callback; a coordinator that never opens the socket cannot tell which kernels are on which build.
  • The coordinator, not the API, must enforce the one real invariant: a phone's control target (its board, cabled to one PC) and its video source (AirPlay, routable to any receiver it can see) must terminate on the same machine. A discovery misconfiguration silently violates this and produces exactly the split-channel failure this whole design exists to prevent.
  • Scale-out is bounded by human onboarding speed: each new PC needs IMConsole.exe manually started and logged in, so a coordinator cannot auto-provision a new kernel unattended.

Scale

The kernel API is not the constraint: ten concurrent pollers on one PC sustained 512 req/s, and input and screenshot traffic measurably do not interfere. The real per-PC ceilings are USB hub ports (21 slots, 19 populated on this rig) and shared Wi-Fi/AirPlay bandwidth, and frame size dictates the topology: a raw BMP is 1.62 MB at 2 ms on loopback, so a coordinator that pulls frames across the LAN should never do so, keep vision pipelines on the PC that decodes the frames and ship only results. Orchestration overhead across K kernels is just K simultaneous HTTP calls, no coordination cost beyond that; the comma-id list only collapses fan-out within one kernel. Start per-PC phone count from the vendor's unverified ~50-100 planning figures, then correct downward using measured per-phone new-frames-per-second, since this rig's own identical twins already differ 6x on the same AP; a defensible starting plan is 15-20 phones per PC at normal quality, validated post-deployment.

Readiness and resource tuning

App pre-warming across the rack before a traffic spike

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Foreground and pre-load a set of apps on every phone ahead of a demo, sale or load test by pushing a deep link to the whole rack in one /shortcut/exec/url call, clearing any interstitial with a mirrored tap, and confirming the warm state on a sampled phone. Deep linking skips UI navigation entirely, so warming is layout-independent, no per-phone icon coordinates to hand-map, and the call accepts a comma-separated id list, making the whole rack one request.

How

  1. Confirm control- and video-readiness — GET /device/get (optionally id list) and GET /config/usb/get — control-ready is board state 2 plus a bound uid, video-ready is device state non-0 with a live air_pid; the two channels are independent.
  2. Normalize the target set — GET /key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+h (x2), GET /mouse/reset?id=<list> — reset clears the stuck-click state that would otherwise make the interstitial-dismiss tap a silent no-op.
  3. Deep-link the whole rack in one call — GET /shortcut/exec/url?id=<id1,id2,...>&url=<scheme://path>&outtime=<ms> — response carries only data.code/id/message: success means the URL was handed to the phone, not that the app reached the intended screen.
  4. Clear any interstitial in the way — GET /mouse/click?id=<list>&x=<x>&y=<y> — only valid mirrored if every listed phone shows the same dialog in the same place; read what it says on a sampled frame first, never blind-tap.
  5. Confirm the feed loaded on a sampled phone — GET /pic/screenshot?id=<single id>&binary=true — judge "loaded" by mean absolute pixel difference against the pre-launch frame, not byte equality; allow ~220 ms+ per new frame on the slow XR.
  6. Keep the rack mirrored and re-cast anything that drops — GET /config/imserver/set?auto_connect=true (global) and GET /device/airplay/connect?id=<list> or /device/airplay/connect/all — auto_connect is a single global flag with no per-device override; turning it on affects the whole rack, not just the warmed phones.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed on every phone with the kernel's LAN IP edited in, run once with every permission granted, and Shortcuts > Advanced set to allow running scripts — not verified present on this rig.
  • The Shortcut bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, since /shortcut/* is triggered by a HID hotkey from the board even though the payload travels over Wi-Fi.
  • Each phone able to reach the kernel on TCP 9911 so the Shortcut can post its result back.
  • Phones unlocked, Auto-Lock Never, portrait locked — a locked phone leaves the Shortcut unlaunched and the call times out at outtime with code 30.
  • Apps installed and signed in, and a known URL scheme or universal link that lands on the exact screen you want warm.

Watch out

  • /shortcut/exec/url is unusable until the Shortcut is installed and bound on each phone; on this rig that is unverified, and the failure signature is a silent code-30 timeout after the outtime window, or code 2/3 if the board is unbound.
  • Success only means the URL was dispatched, not that the app reached the target screen; "is the app warm" must come from the separate single-id screenshot diff, never from the exec/url response code alone. Not every app exposes a deep link to the exact screen you want, and universal links can bounce through Safari first, reintroducing the layout dependency the deep link was meant to avoid.
  • Warming is not durable: a notification, a mirroring drop or auto-lock can silently un-warm a phone, and there is no API push for eviction — the only way to know warming held is to re-poll each phone right before the spike.
  • A rack-wide call returns only when the slowest phone answers or times out, so one bad Shortcut binding taxes the whole call's wall-clock time even though the HTTP request itself is O(1); raise outtime for a large rack rather than splitting the call.
  • Any bandwidth-lowering figure quoted for /device/airplay/set (the ~5/10/20 Mbps range) is the Phonefarm-edition's own vendor estimate, not measured on this XP rig; label it as a ballpark from the wrong product's docs.
  • Do not blind-tap the interstitial-dismissal step: a consent sheet or purchase confirmation dismissed sight-unseen across a whole rack is the single most expensive failure mode in this cluster, since it can trigger a real transaction.

Scale

Warming dispatch is O(1) for the whole rack, effectively instantaneous request cost, but wall-clock is bounded by the slowest phone's Shortcut round trip up to the outtime ceiling (default 15 s; raise to 30-60 s for a large rack to tolerate a slow-Wi-Fi phone). Verification is O(N) single-id screenshot diffs at ~2-3 ms server-side each, so confirming warm state across 20 phones costs well under a second of API time, though actually waiting for a fresh frame on the slow phone adds ~220 ms+ per phone. A full warm-and-confirm cycle across a rack of ~20 phones should complete in well under a minute if all phones respond promptly, and any pre-spike schedule should still budget up to the full outtime ceiling per attempt to avoid false negatives on the slow phone.

Brightness and cast-quality knobs as a rack power/heat lever

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Hold idle phones at low screen brightness and a downgraded per-device AirPlay profile (low air_ratio/air_fps/air_img_fps, audio off), then restore full quality only on the phone an operator is actually watching. Brightness goes through the iMouse Shortcut (/shortcut/switch/bril, one request for a comma-separated id list); cast quality goes through /device/airplay/set, which is per device but disconnects that phone's cast and only applies on the next connect, so this is a batched mode switch, not a live dimmer.

How

  1. Read current cast settings and mirror geometry — GET /device/get?id=<deviceid> — the record carries air_ratio/refresh/fps/img_fps/audio (0 = use global) plus imgw/imgh, which is the coordinate space for every /mouse call and can move when air_ratio changes.
  2. Dim every idle phone in one request — GET /shortcut/switch/bril?id=<id1>,<id2>&state=0.05 — state must be strictly greater than 0 and less than 1; use ~0.05 to dim and ~0.9 to restore, never 0.0 or 1.
  3. Downgrade the idle set's mirroring profile — GET /device/airplay/set?id=<id1>,<id2>&air_ratio=720&air_fps=5&air_img_fps=5&air_audio=1 — XP has no 0/1/2 preset, so the profile must be expressed as explicit numbers; the change disconnects the cast immediately and takes effect on the next connect.
  4. Re-establish the dropped casts — GET /device/airplay/connect?id=<id1>,<id2> (or /connect/all) — XP has no force flag, so disconnect first if a session is stuck; progress arrives on the airplay_connect_log WS callback, not in the HTTP reply.
  5. Restore the operator-selected phone — GET /shortcut/switch/bril?id=<that>&state=0.9 then GET /device/airplay/set?id=<that>&air_ratio=0&air_fps=30&air_img_fps=30 then /device/airplay/connect?id=<that> — air_ratio=0 returns that phone to the global adaptive setting, budget a full disconnect/reconnect round trip.
  6. Verify the change took — GET /device/get?id=<id> then GET /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — confirm state non-0, a live air_pid, and the echoed air_* values; if imgw/imgh moved, every cached coordinate and colour table for that phone is invalid until re-read.
  7. Optional global fallback — GET /config/imserver/get then /config/imserver/set?air_play_ratio=..&air_play_fps=..&air_play_refresh_rate=.. then /imserver/restart — these fields are not in the no-restart list, so a global change drops every mirroring session on the rack; the per-device call is the cheaper lever.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed on every phone, its kernel IP edited in, run once with permissions allowed, and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key — brightness is a Shortcut function needing both the board hotkey trigger and the phone's LAN path to 9911. Not verified on this rig; the 10 Sep probe never called any /shortcut/* path.
  • Board bound and connected (state 2) for the hotkey that launches the Shortcut.
  • Phone unlocked, Auto-Lock Never — a locked phone cannot run the Shortcut.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in — IMService.exe alone leaves the rig at state 0 with an empty board list.
  • A per-phone record of imgw/imgh and any colour/template tables, so a later air_ratio change can be detected as invalidating them.

Watch out

  • The "power/heat" framing is not physics-checked anywhere in the source material: nothing in the measured hardware facts contains a watt, milliamp or thermal reading for board, hub, PC or phone. A phone screen at minimum brightness plausibly saves on the order of 0.3-1 W, a real but modest amount, while the dominant heat sources named for this rig, 19 USB HID boards, three hubs, a PC decoding up to 19 AirPlay streams, sit entirely outside the API and are unaffected by air_ratio or brightness. Present this as an unverified, plausible, low-magnitude side effect of a real bandwidth-reduction lever, not as validated thermal management.
  • There is no airplay_mode on XP at all; the Phonefarm 0/1/2 presets and their Mbps/phone-count figures are that edition's vendor claims, not measurements of this rack, and there is no substitute Mbps table for XP's raw knobs.
  • /device/airplay/set disconnects the target phones' casts immediately and applies only on the next cast, so it is strictly a batch, shift-level mode switch, never call it on a phone with an in-flight tap-critical sequence.
  • Auto-cast recovery after the drop is uncertain on this rig: the OCR plug-in is confirmed not connected (code 28), and the XP code table lists 15 and 28 as cast failure modes, so run one real disconnect/reconnect cycle on a spare phone as a go/no-go gate before building any workflow that assumes automatic re-cast — a rig where re-cast silently fails turns every idle-dim into a one-way trip needing a human to re-cast by hand.
  • Lowering air_ratio changes imgw/imgh, the coordinate space for every /mouse call and the scale for any colour table; re-reading /device/get after every /device/airplay/set should be automatic, not an optional check.
  • Brightness via the Shortcut has a 15 s default timeout per phone, and a rack with even one broken binding turns a one-request brightness call into a 15+ second block, silently, unless code 30 is checked per id.
  • This lever covers screen and radio only; board, hub and USB heat, and the PC's own decode load, are outside the API entirely.

Scale

Both levers fan out, so dimming or re-profiling the whole rack is one request each, not N, but every /device/airplay/set drops and re-establishes the listed phones' casts, so batch the idle-set change once per shift rather than per operator focus change, and consider upgrading only the focused phone while leaving the rest at the global profile. Brightness has no cast side effect and can be toggled freely, but a rack-wide call is bounded by the slowest phone's Shortcut round trip, worst case the full 15 s timeout per stalled phone, so budget a handful of rack-wide brightness toggles per hour rather than continuous use. Quality-profile switching, since each call drops and re-establishes casts, should be treated as a per-shift operation, on the order of 1-4 switches per hour across the whole rack, and if auto-reconnect fails, plausible given this rig's code 28/15, effective throughput for that phone drops to zero until a human re-casts it by hand.

MARK-OUTSIDE-MARK

Section 10 · Outside the box

Outside the box

Every entry below rides the same load-bearing fact: an XP input endpoint that takes a comma-separated id list costs the same board time whether it addresses one phone or the whole rack, because the board walks the list in parallel rather than looping over it. That single property turns a phone farm into a synchronized display wall, a camera array, a Unicode input bus and a UI-driving harness for apps with no API of their own. None of it needs anything the vendor doesn't already ship, and all of it inherits the rig's two hardest lessons: control and video are separate channels, so "looks right in the mirror" is never proof a phone obeyed, and the API has no authentication, so anything built here is only as safe as the LAN it runs on.

Fleet-wide synchronized actuation

Mirrored tap/swipe loops: the mechanical core of a rack

Native APIWith caveats

Every XP input call, /mouse/click, /mouse/move, /mouse/swipe, /mouse/wheel, /mouse/reset, /key/sendkey, accepts a comma-separated id list, and the board walks every listed phone in parallel. That is the primitive every other entry in this section builds on: normalize to a known screen, run a canned tap-swipe-wheel sequence, sample one phone to confirm progress. No emulator, no jailbreak, nothing installed on the phone.

How

  1. send_key (fn_key WIN+h), then mouse_reset_pos GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+h (send twice) then GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<list> — leave the app, return to home page one, then clear the silent stuck-click state before any tap is trusted.
  2. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<list>&x=&y=[&button=][&time=] — open the target app at one mirror-pixel coordinate shared by every phone on the list.
  3. click / swipe / mouse_wheel GET /api/mouse/swipe?id=<list>&direction=&len=0.9[&stepping=&step_sleep=&brake=&sx=&sy=&ex=&ey=] and GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=<list>&direction=&len=1..127&number= — run the actual gesture loop, still one request per step for the whole set.
  4. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<one id>&binary=true — sample a representative phone's raw BMP and threshold a mean absolute pixel difference against the idle floor; round-robin which phone you sample.
  5. find_multi_color (optional gate) POST /api/pic/find-multi-color — branch on a colour-table match instead of a fixed delay; unverified on this rig, see the colour-detector card below.

Needs

  • Per phone: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity maxed, Full Keyboard Access on, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock, StandBy off — none of this is queryable over the API.
  • Board bound and at /config/usb/get state 2, and location_crc non-empty in /device/get (shared library CRC B0DBD800 for iPhone11,8 on this rig), or every /mouse call returns code 11.
  • Video up for verification (state non-0, live air_pid) — needs IMConsole.exe running, not just IMService.exe.
  • Identical screen geometry and identical on-screen layout for any phone sharing a coordinate; the two XRs here have different home screens, so a shared tap opens a different app on each.

Watch out

  • A phone can silently stop honouring /mouse/click while /mouse/move and hardware keys keep working: measured 0.09 mean pixel diff on a click (idle floor 0.02-0.03) versus 141.96 after /mouse/reset. Moving and pressing Home prove nothing about taps.
  • Phonefarm's documented swipe-jitter randomization does not exist on the XP kernel, no Phonefarm function name is even accepted (HTTP 500), and the XP swipe table has no randomization parameter at all: assume every gesture lands exactly where sent.
  • A loop that never re-checks state will tap into a dialog, login prompt or rate-limit screen for hours. Gate on an observed state and stop on any unexpected screen, rather than trusting a fixed delay.
  • Verification is single-id and sampled, not exhaustive, so a phone can drift into a stuck-click state or a wrong screen for many cycles before a sampled check happens to land on it.
  • The slower of the two XRs on this rig delivers ~4.5 new AirPlay frames/s under motion against ~29 for its twin; any screen check on it must tolerate roughly 220 ms per new frame.
  • /mouse/wheel's latency and whether iOS honours a synthetic HID scroll on a touchscreen app are both unmeasured here; treat it as an unverified alternative to swipe, not an equivalent.

Trap One reply code, no per-phone result

A mirrored call returns a single data.code and echoes the id list back. There is no per-phone success flag anywhere in the response, so a partial failure across the set is invisible until a screenshot or error_push says otherwise.

Scale

Input is O(1) per action regardless of rack size: a 100 px move measured 78 ms whether it targeted one phone or two, and a full 1000 px move ~592-594 ms either way. Latency tracks pointer distance at roughly 0.6 ms/px, not fleet size. Verification is O(N): one raw-BMP poller per phone at up to 84 req/s each (ten concurrent pollers sustained 512 req/s aggregate at p50 3 ms), and input traffic measurably does not slow polling. A short-gesture loop could run on the order of 3,000-6,000 rack-wide gestures/hour if verification is sparse, dropping to roughly 500-1,500 verified actions/hour/phone once every cycle waits on the slow XR's ~4.5 fps ceiling.

Lockstep demo wall: one request drives every phone

Native APIWith caveats

Apply the mirrored-input primitive to a showroom or retail fixture: a wall of identical phones scrolling the same feed or demoing the same app in visible unison, driven by one HTTP request per gesture instead of N. It is the single workload this API is unusually good at, and the clearest way to show a customer what the rack can do.

How

  1. Batch hardware operation, once, optional GET /api/config/imserver/set?thread_mode=true&mouse_mode=true — one of the few live-apply config fields (no kernel restart needed); not probed on this rig, verify with /api/config/imserver/get first.
  2. get_device_list GET /api/device/get — enumerate the wall and admit only phones with state non-0, non-empty vid/pid/uid, non-empty location_crc, and matching imgw/imgh.
  3. get_usb_list GET /api/config/usb/get — confirm every board reads state 2 (enumerated and phone attached); 19 boards at VID 720A on this rig.
  4. send_key GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) then mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<list> — normalize every phone to home page one and clear the stuck-click state across the whole set.
  5. click / shortcut#13 GET /api/mouse/click?id=<list>&x=&y= or GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<list>&url= — launch the demo app on every phone at once.
  6. swipe / mouse_wheel GET /api/mouse/swipe?id=<list>&direction=up&len=0.9 and GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=<list>&direction=down&len=30&number=3 — run the demo loop in lockstep.
  7. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<one id>&binary=true — one request per phone, run pollers concurrently (measured 512 req/s aggregate across ten).
  8. Callbacks ws://<host>:9911/api → error_push, usb_change, dev_disconnect, dev_change — the only asynchronous per-call failure signal there is.

Needs

  • Every wall phone bound to its own board (state 2), identical mirror geometry (500x1080 on this rig), and identical app/home-screen layout across the set — the two XRs here already differ.
  • The same per-phone iOS accessibility settings the mirrored-loop card lists, none of it API-visible.
  • IMConsole.exe running and signed in; with only IMService.exe up, both phones read state 0 and the board list comes back empty.
  • Only for the optional brightness/open-URL steps: the iMouse Shortcut installed and bound on each phone, unverified on this rig.

Watch out

  • Groups exist (/device/group/set, /device/group/get-dev) but no input endpoint accepts a group id: expand a group to a comma-separated id list client-side before every call.
  • The documented brightness state range is "greater than 0 and less than 1" — state=1 is out of range; use 0.99, and note this also contradicts the vendor's own rack checklist of keeping brightness lowest.
  • Swipes are not instantaneous: a mirrored full-height swipe is ~580 ms of pointer walk before /mouse/up can follow, and velocity-dependent iOS gestures may not fire at that speed.
  • Because /pic/screenshot is single-id, confirming N phones all advanced needs N reads; one phone's poller stalling (the slow XR, or one that dropped Wi-Fi) will make the wall look behind schedule when only the observation channel is lagging.
  • Only the vendor console can bring the rack up in the first place; automation cannot bootstrap mirroring or board enumeration through the API alone.

Trap Video bandwidth, not the kernel, is the real ceiling

Fan-out on the actuation side is free at any fleet size, but mirroring is a genuine Wi-Fi/AirPlay load per phone (roughly 5-20 Mbps depending on content), so 19 phones mirroring at once can need on the order of 100-380 Mbps just for video, well past what a typical access point sustains cleanly with that many clients. That, not the board, is the likely reason two identical XRs on this rig deliver such different frame rates.

Scale

Actuation is fleet-size-independent, measured identically at 2, 10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 700 and 1000 px jumps for one phone and for two: a demo loop of short gestures can run roughly 2,000-5,000 lockstep actions/hour for the whole wall regardless of phone count, provided per-phone video bandwidth holds up, a real risk past roughly 10-15 simultaneously-mirroring phones on one access point. Verification scales per phone at up to 84 req/s each and does not bottleneck actuation. Beyond two phones this rig is untested.

Turning the rack into other hardware

Phones as network-addressable cameras with torch illumination

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

A rack of iPhones is also a rack of calibrated cameras with flashes, all addressable from one HTTP endpoint. Fan the torch on across phones, fire the shutter on every phone with a single mirrored /mouse/click, then pull full-resolution captures off one phone at a time. That makes synchronized multi-angle capture, time-lapse arrays and always-on visual sensors one-request operations, with the non-capturing phones' torches acting as controllable lighting for the one that shoots.

How

  1. send_key (WIN+h), mouse_reset_pos GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice), GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<list> — normalize and clear the pointer on every capture phone.
  2. shortcut#16 /api/shortcut/switch/torch {id: <list>, state:1} — turn on LED illumination for the whole rack in one request.
  3. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<list>&x=&y= — open Camera on every phone sharing that coordinate.
  4. click (shutter) GET /api/mouse/click?id=<list>&x=&y=, unverified alternative GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=VolumeUp — fire the shutter; the coordinate tap is the documented, stable path.
  5. shortcut#17 /api/shortcut/switch/torch {id: <list>, state:0} — torch back off.
  6. shortcut#1 /api/shortcut/album/get {id: <single>, album_name, num} — list new captures on one phone; snapshot before capture and diff on create_time, since XP has no date filter.
  7. shortcut#2 /api/shortcut/album/down {id: <single>, list:[{album_name,name,ext}], zip} — transfer captures to the PC, into <install dir>\Shortcut\Media.
  8. shortcut#3 (optional) /api/shortcut/album/del or /api/shortcut/album/clear — irreversible; confirm with the operator before wiring to a button.
  9. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single>&binary=true — checks the viewfinder chrome only, never the sensor image.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited, run once with every permission, bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key on every phone — torch and album transfer both ride this channel.
  • Camera permission granted and the app left in Photo mode; mode is sticky and there is no API to read or set it.
  • Board bound and at state 2 for the shutter tap; mirroring only needed if viewfinder confirmation is wanted.
  • Per-phone coordinate map for the Camera icon and shutter, identical across phones for the fan-out to work.

Watch out

  • Opening Camera almost always releases any torch already lit on that same phone, because iOS gives the foreground camera session exclusive ownership of the flash unit. Treat "light this phone with its own torch, then shoot with it" as not possible; design lighting from idle phones onto the one that's shooting.
  • fn_key=VolumeUp as a shutter is unverified: the hotkey exists and returns code 0, but whether iOS treats a HID volume key the way it treats a physical button is undocumented here.
  • The mirror shows the Camera app's UI, not the sensor feed; the real image exists only after album/down, and retrieval, not capture, is the bottleneck by two to three orders of magnitude.
  • Camera UI shifts a few pixels between iOS point releases and isn't queryable, so a coordinate map calibrated on 18.7.10 isn't guaranteed to survive a silent update on one rack phone.
  • album/get and album/down both need an exact name+ext pair per file, and album/get's own list is the only source of those names, so the pipeline must serialize get-then-down per phone.
  • No API signal exists for iOS's thermal throttling of the flash; a hot, enclosed rack can silently produce dim or absent illumination with a code-0 success reply.

Scale

Capture fans out cleanly (torch, click and hotkey all take comma-list ids, measured identical board time for 1 and 2 phones), so synchronized N-phone capture completes in well under a second. Retrieval does not fan out at all: album/get and album/down are single-id, so pulling frames is N sequential Shortcut round trips, each bounded by outtime (milliseconds on XP, raise it well past the 15 s default for full-resolution media) and by that phone's own Wi-Fi link. A 20-phone capture-and-retrieve cycle should be budgeted in the 1-2 minute range serialized, or pipelined per phone for roughly 500-1,000 capture+download cycles/hour/phone.

Phone rack as a pixel wall and stage-light array

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Push each phone to a full-screen solid-colour page served from a LAN host, drive brightness, and pulse the camera LEDs, each addressed to a comma-separated id list so a whole colour region updates in one request. Device groups act as the region map, expanded client-side into id lists. It turns a rack that already exists into a reusable pixel wall, countdown board, tally display or audience-light effect, and is the clearest demonstration that the Shortcut channel is a general-purpose actuator, not just a file-transfer helper.

How

  1. set_group GET /api/device/group/set?id=0&name=Region-A — create one group per physical region; id=0 creates, any other id renames.
  2. set_dev GET /api/device/set?id=<list>&gid=&name=R2C4 — assign phones to regions and give them grid labels; comma-list id, but the vid+pid hardware binding stays single-device.
  3. shortcut#13 GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<region id list>&url=http://<host>/red — paint a region by opening a colour page on every phone in it.
  4. shortcut#15 GET /api/shortcut/switch/bril?id=<list>&state=0.99 — drive brightness for the region; no readback exists anywhere.
  5. shortcut#16 / #17 GET /api/shortcut/switch/torch?id=<list>&state=1 then state=0 — flash the camera LEDs across a region; invisible in the mirror.
  6. shortcut#13 once GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<all>&url=http://<host>/wall?slot=R2C4 — for animation, open one self-animating page and let it drive itself over its own WebSocket/SSE instead of re-issuing URLs per frame.
  7. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single>&binary=true — sample raw BMP pixels against the commanded colour; solid colour is the easy verification case.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited, run once with all permissions, bound to an AssistiveTouch key on every phone — this entire use case is gated on it and it has never been probed on this rig.
  • Phones unlocked with Auto-Lock Never so Safari stays foreground, and a LAN web host serving the colour/pattern pages.
  • Phones physically arranged as a grid with positions recorded (name/hub/port), which the API does not expose on its own.

Watch out

  • Opening a URL launches Safari with its normal chrome (address bar, tab strip, home indicator) unless the page has already been added to that phone's Home Screen as a standalone web app, a step the API cannot perform. Without it every "pixel" tile shows a colour rectangle with visible Safari UI at the edges.
  • No state readback exists for torch or brightness; the switch endpoints return data.code and nothing else.
  • Frame rate for URL-swap animation is well under 1 fps (a Safari load plus a Shortcut round trip bounded by outtime); usable for cues and countdowns, useless for motion unless the page animates itself.
  • No API call reports thermal state; iOS dims the display and disables the torch on its own when a phone gets hot, with nothing in the kernel to say so.
  • Turning Wi-Fi or Airplane Mode on via the same /shortcut/switch/* family kills both the AirPlay picture and the Shortcut's own return path to the kernel — never mix them into a light cue.
  • Even with Auto-Lock off, iOS can evict a backgrounded Safari tab under memory pressure, silently reloading the page and losing any client-side animation state with no API-visible signal.

Trap One integration test gates all three effects

Screen colour, brightness and torch all depend on the same per-phone Shortcut bound to a HID-triggered AssistiveTouch key via the vendor console's Send Binding Key feature, a mechanism never probed on this rig. If that binding doesn't reliably trigger the Shortcut, the whole use case, not just one step, drops to not achievable as configured. Confirm with a cheap round trip on /shortcut/device/ip before building anything on top.

Scale

exec/url, bril and torch all accept a comma-separated id list, so one colour region of any size is one request, the limit is round-trip latency (bounded by outtime, default 15 s), not width. Torch pulses are fastest since nothing renders. For discrete cue changes, expect on the order of 12-30 changes/hour per region if polled conservatively, effectively unusable for anything resembling motion. Once a self-animating page is loaded, frame rate is decoupled from the iMouse API entirely and limited only by that phone's own Wi-Fi and rendering, the only path to a usable pixel wall rather than a slow cue board. Nothing about Shortcut fan-out has been measured beyond the two phones on this rig.

Driving real consumer apps end-to-end

iMessage and FaceTime automation by driving the UI

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Blue-bubble iMessage and FaceTime have no on-device API any script can call. Driving the genuine app from a real Apple ID and SIM, with taps and hardware-keyboard input, is the only route to automating them on accounts you own, useful for end-to-end testing of message-dependent flows and reproducing customer-reported bugs on real hardware. ASCII bodies go straight through /key/sendkey; anything non-ASCII needs the clipboard bus below, because the XP kernel has no send_text function at all.

How

  1. send_key (WIN+h), mouse_reset_pos /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) then /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> — normalize the phone before any coordinate is trusted.
  2. click /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=&y= — open Messages or FaceTime and the compose/recipient field; per-phone coordinates, the two XRs have different home screens.
  3. send_key /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&key=<ascii text> — type an ASCII recipient or body directly; needs Full Keyboard Access on.
  4. shortcut#10 /api/shortcut/clipboard/set {id, text, sleep, outtime} — for non-ASCII/emoji, put the text on the phone clipboard as a POST JSON body, not a query string.
  5. send_key /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+v — paste into the focused field; XP's paste key, not Phonefarm's combo.
  6. click /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y=, or /key/sendkey?fn_key=ENTER — tap Send, or the FaceTime call control; FaceTime needs no dedicated endpoint.
  7. get_device_screenshot /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — verify by mean absolute pixel diff over the bubble region, never MD5.
  8. (Wanted, not available) ocr / find_image /api/pic/ocr, /pic/find-text, /pic/find-image — plug-in gated; on this rig /api/pic/ocr answers code 28, so reading the sent bubble text back has no server-side path here.

Needs

  • Apple ID signed in and iMessage enabled on each phone; automate only accounts you own or administer, and only to recipients who have consented.
  • iMouse Shortcut bound (clipboard path only), Full Keyboard Access on, AssistiveTouch on, Auto-Lock Never, portrait locked — none of this is queryable over the API.
  • A per-phone coordinate map captured from that phone's own screenshots; the two XRs here have different home screens and wallpapers.
  • The phone unlocked — nothing in the API can type a passcode.

Watch out

  • No server-side vision exists on this rig (/pic/ocr code 28); any adaptive step, like reading a contact suggestion or locating the Send arrow, must be client-side template matching on the raw BMP.
  • Recipient-suggestion rows reorder by recency, so blind-tapping a suggestion can address the wrong person; prefer typing the full number or Apple ID and pressing Enter.
  • Paste timing is a real failure mode: fire the paste hotkey too early and a stale or empty clipboard lands. Use the sleep parameter and read back with /shortcut/clipboard/get when correctness matters.
  • The stuck-click trap applies at full force here too; send /mouse/reset to the target before any send sequence.
  • Apple-side security challenges, a "verify it's you" prompt, a 2FA code, an account lock, look identical to a stuck UI to this pipeline, and the automation has no way to complete one (it cannot read an SMS OTP).
  • A fixed bubble region for verification breaks as a thread scrolls and bubble heights change; diff the whole visible transcript area, not a small fixed box.
  • Full Keyboard Access can silently drop after an OS update or restart with no API-visible flag; verify it once per session with a canary keypress rather than assuming it stayed on.

Scale

Clipboard set and key send both take comma-list ids, so seeding N phones with the same body is one request each, but navigation is not shareable in practice: each conversation sits at a different scroll position and the two XRs have different layouts, so the tap sequence is effectively per phone. Screenshot verification is one poller per phone (measured 83-85 req/s each, 512 req/s aggregate across ten). Counting navigation, the ~0.6 ms/px pointer walk, clipboard settle time and frame-gated verification, a realistic ceiling is roughly 4-12 messages per minute per phone, an order of magnitude below any "per second" assumption, and further reduced by Apple's own anti-abuse throttling on the account, which this pipeline cannot see or negotiate.

AirDrop transfers between phones on the same rack

PartialWith caveats

Move a photo or file phone-to-phone by driving the iOS share sheet and AirDrop picker on the sender and the Accept sheet on the receiver, coordinating two control sessions from one controller. AirDrop is peer-to-peer over BLE discovery and a direct Wi-Fi link, leaving no copy on the PC, which makes it the only way to test AirDrop-dependent app flows and move an asset between two phones without routing it through the controller's filesystem.

How

  1. send_key (WIN+h), mouse_reset_pos /api/key/sendkey?id=<sender>,<receiver>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) then /api/mouse/reset?id=<sender>,<receiver> — bring both phones to a known state.
  2. send_key /api/key/sendkey?id=<receiver>&fn_key=ControlBar — receiver opens Control Center; an XP-only hotkey, use it instead of an edge swipe.
  3. click (long press) /api/mouse/click?id=<receiver>&x=&y=&time=800 — long-press the connectivity tile and set AirDrop receiving; time is the XP long-press mechanism, no separate endpoint.
  4. click /api/mouse/click?id=<sender>&x=&y= — sender opens the asset and taps Share.
  5. get_device_screenshot + find_image / ocr /api/pic/screenshot?id=<sender>&binary=true, then client-side matching (/pic/find-image, /pic/ocr exist as XP paths but are plug-in gated here) — locate the receiver's AirDrop tile; this step decides the whole design.
  6. click /api/mouse/click?id=<sender>&x=&y= — tap the located tile.
  7. get_device_screenshot then click /api/pic/screenshot?id=<receiver>&binary=true in a poll loop, then /api/mouse/click?id=<receiver>&x=&y= — catch and accept the incoming sheet; if sender and receiver share one Apple ID, iOS auto-accepts and no sheet ever appears.
  8. shortcut#1 /api/shortcut/album/get {id: <single>, album_name, num} or /api/shortcut/file/get — confirm arrival by snapshotting the list before the transfer and diffing on create_time; XP has no date filter.

Needs

  • Both phones close together, on Wi-Fi with Bluetooth on by hand — there is no Bluetooth toggle anywhere in the XP API.
  • Both phones bound (state 2) and mirroring (state non-0, live air_pid) — both sheets are only observable through their own mirror.
  • Per-phone, per-model coordinate maps for the connectivity tile, AirDrop sheet, share glyph and Accept button.
  • Client-side template matching, or the OCR/OpenCV plug-in installed and connected, to locate the dynamic AirDrop target tile.

Watch out

  • The AirDrop target tile's position depends on which devices have been discovered and in what order; without matching or a plug-in this step is a coin flip, and a wrong tap sends the asset to the wrong device.
  • AirDrop receiving set to Everyone reverts to Contacts Only after 10 minutes on this iOS version; a long batch has to re-arm the receiver mid-run, and there is no API signal telling you it reverted.
  • Only 2 phones on this 19-board rig are actually mirroring today, so on the current rig this is a single pair, not a fan-out scenario; the comma-list fan-out for setup steps is real but has nothing to fan out to yet.
  • A realistic verified transfer runs 15-40 seconds once pointer-walk distance, the 800 ms long press (itself unmeasured, a guess pending per-iOS-version verification) and receiver-side confirmation polling are counted, not "several seconds."
  • Reaching the AirDrop toggle needs the Control Center two-row icon layout so the connectivity tile sits at a queryable coordinate; without it the long-press coordinate is invalid.

Scale

Inherently pairwise and sequential. Setup fans out (ControlBar, WIN+h, /mouse/reset all take comma-list ids), but the transfer itself needs a screenshot-decide-tap loop on both sides, and /pic/screenshot is single-id, so N pairs means 2N pollers, not the bottleneck since ten concurrent pollers measured 512 req/s. On the present rig's one possible pair, expect roughly 90-240 verified transfers/hour, bound by UI navigation and verification latency. For bulk staging, route around AirDrop entirely: /shortcut/album/upload and /shortcut/file/upload both take a comma-list id and push the same file to N phones in one request.

Filling API gaps: text and vision

Phone clipboard as a bidirectional Unicode data bus

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Use the phone clipboard as a two-way channel: push arbitrary Unicode, emoji or URLs to many phones in one request with /shortcut/clipboard/set, paste with WIN+v mirrored to the same list, and harvest what a phone copied with /shortcut/clipboard/get. It is the only documented way to get non-ASCII text onto an iPhone on this rig, since /key/sendkey is explicitly English/digits/ASCII-punctuation only and Phonefarm's send_text does not exist on the XP kernel.

How

  1. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 — prove the Shortcut path works at all before trusting anything else; not yet run on this rig.
  2. shortcut#10 /api/shortcut/clipboard/set {id: <list>, text, sleep, outtime} — push text to the whole target set in one request, as POST JSON UTF-8, not a query string.
  3. click / send_key /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> then /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=&y= (or fn_key=OPENKeyboard) — focus a text field; reset first, the stuck-click trap applies.
  4. send_key GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+v — paste, mirrored to the same set; XP's own paste key, not Phonefarm's combo.
  5. shortcut#11 GET /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<id> — harvest what a phone copied; single id only, so harvesting a rack is N requests.
  6. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — verify the paste landed by mean absolute pixel diff; no OCR available here to assert the text directly.
  7. shortcut#10 then shortcut#11 /api/shortcut/clipboard/set?id=<id>&text=imouse-<timestamp> then /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<id> — a state-independent round-trip self-test, run once per phone before relying on paste.
  8. shortcut#13 GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<list>&url= — adjacent use of the same channel for deep links.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited, run once with every permission, bound to an AssistiveTouch key — not verified on this rig, the probe in step 1 never ran.
  • Full Keyboard Access on with 1 s auto-hide, AssistiveTouch on, phone unlocked with Auto-Lock Never.
  • Phone reachable to the kernel on TCP 9911, since the Shortcut posts its result back over the LAN.

Watch out

  • This rig's own probe already found /api/shortcut/get returns 404 inside the same /shortcut/* namespace the whole chain depends on. Treat the design as unverified-and-suspect, not just unverified, until the IP round trip actually returns data.
  • A phone whose Shortcut binding is missing does not fail fast; it returns code 30 (call timeout) after the full 15 s outtime.
  • Asymmetric fan-out: clipboard/set, exec/url and the paste hotkey all take comma-list ids, but clipboard/get is single-id only. Seeding is O(1) requests, harvesting is O(N).
  • outtime is milliseconds on XP while sleep on clipboard/set is seconds; getting this backwards produces instant timeouts or 15-second stalls.
  • Since iOS 16, a cross-app paste can raise an "Allow Paste" system sheet that is invisible to the API and blocks the paste until dismissed; a verification step must distinguish that from "paste hasn't landed yet," since both look the same in a pixel diff unless the sheet is captured in the crop.
  • The clipboard is global on the phone and clobbers whatever a human operator had copied; a scripted read can also return stale data if something else wrote the clipboard between set and get.
  • Displaying a QR via a rendered page is supported; reading one back from a neighbour's camera is not, there is no camera API and no OCR here, so treat that half of any QR-relay idea as not achievable on this rig.

Tip Round-trip self-test before you rely on it

Push a timestamped string and read it straight back per phone (clipboard/set then clipboard/get) before wiring the clipboard bus into any real flow. It is the only state-independent proof that Unicode survives the Shortcut path end to end, and it costs two requests per phone.

Scale

Seeding the rack is two requests regardless of phone count (comma-list clipboard/set then comma-list paste), each fan-out request bounded by the slowest phone's Shortcut round trip, so send per-group rather than rack-wide if any phone is unhealthy. Harvesting is one request per phone since clipboard/get rejects multiple ids. A single push-paste-verify cycle chains a POST, a phone-side Shortcuts run (roughly 0.5-2 s including app-switch overhead), the paste hotkey, and a frame-gated verify, call it 1-3 s per phone end to end, or roughly 20-40 cycles per phone per hour run conservatively, well below the kernel's own 512 req/s ceiling because the bottleneck is iOS-side Shortcut execution and permission UI, not the API.

find-multi-color as a plug-in-free state detector

PartialWith caveats

Gate automation on multi-point colour matches instead of OCR: sample a handful of pixels that uniquely identify a button or screen state, pass them as a colour table to /pic/find-multi-color, and branch on whether a match comes back with a centre to tap. No template image and no text recognition needed, but whether it runs without the vendor plug-in is unverified on this rig, and the docs' own placement of it argues against optimism.

How
