  1. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single>&binary=true[&rect=] — grab a raw reference frame and read the pixels to key on; the BMP is bottom-up, flip y before converting an offset to mirror-pixel coordinates.
  2. find_multi_color first_color + offset_color + dir (client-side) — build a colour table of 5-10 anchor pixels; XP's first_color format is a comma-separated list of absolute points x|y|RRGGBB-tolerance, there is no offset_color or dir on XP, those are Phonefarm-only.
  3. find_multi_color / find_multi_color_ex POST /api/pic/find-multi-color {id: <single>, list:[{first_color, rect, similarity}], same, all} — run the search; returns data.list[{index, centre}] on code 0.
  4. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<id or list>&x=centre[0]&y=centre[1] — branch: tap the returned centre directly, no coordinate conversion needed.
  5. (no XP equivalent to loop_device_screenshot) — repeat /pic/find-multi-color on a fixed period to implement "wait until this state appears"; XP has no server-push frame stream.

Needs

  • Probe first, with a negative control: call once with a known-present table, then invert one anchor and call again. A code-28 reply on either call means it is plug-in-gated like OCR and this approach is unavailable until the plug-in is installed.
  • Device online with a live air_pid, since the search runs against the kernel's internal mirror frame.
  • Colour tables rebuilt whenever air_ratio or the device's imgw/imgh changes, since tables are resolution-specific, and fixed display settings (True Tone off, Night Shift off, constant brightness).

Watch out

  • The XP documentation does not describe this as kernel-internal or plug-in-free: it sits on the same "Picture Text Recognition" page as /pic/ocr and /pic/find-image, both plug-in-gated, and carries the same Shortcut-fallback footnote those carry. Given OCR already returns code 28 on this exact rig, the realistic default assumption is that this is gated too, not merely unknown.
  • Single-id like every /pic/* endpoint, so state checks never fan out; detecting once on a "representative" phone is only safe for truly identical UI, like a system dialog, not app content, given the two XRs here already have different home screens.
  • Brittle compared with real OCR: a theme change, dark mode, a badge count or a localisation change silently breaks the table, and the failure mode is a confident wrong branch, not an error.
  • The vendor's own example tolerance of 000000 will not hold against a live AirPlay stream; expect to tune tolerance and similarity per element.
  • The pointer itself is visible in the frame as a small grey dot and moves with in-flight /mouse/move calls; anchors placed near where the pointer idles can pick up the pointer as a false match.
  • If gated, the client-side fallback, matching the same colour table against the raw BMP you already fetch at 2 ms, works today with no server dependency; plan around it from day one rather than treating the server call as the default path.

Trap Silent misdetection, not a clean failure

A colour table that matches the wrong element, or a control test that was never run, produces an automation that taps confidently in the wrong place, and on a mirrored fan-out it does so on every phone at once. Fail closed on codes 28, 29, 33 or 36 rather than falling through to the tap, and re-verify after any app update.

Scale

Per phone, not fleet-wide, and cheap relative to any external vision path if it works at all: one call replaces a 1.6 MB frame transfer plus a round trip to a matcher, but its own cost is unmeasured on this rig. In the likely case it is gated, throughput collapses to the client-side path, raw BMP grabs sustain 84 req/s/phone flat out, with the real cost shifting to client-side pixel comparison time, which still needs benchmarking before quoting a number. Either way, a sane production polling loop runs at 1-5 Hz rather than the theoretical ceiling, since most polls see an unchanged frame.

Also worth knowing

Counting and enumeration without OCR: same/all as a quantity primitive

PartialWith caveats

The state-detector framing above treats find-multi-color as a boolean: does this one pattern appear or not. The same and all flags turn it, and find-image-cv, into a counter and an indexer instead. same asks the search to return every occurrence of a match, not just the first; all asks it to evaluate every entry in the colour-table or template list, not stop at the first hit. Together they answer "how many" and "which one" for anything with a repeatable visual signature: unread badges, loaded grid tiles, toggled rows, the third of N identical icons, all without a coordinate map and without OCR.

How

  1. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single>&binary=true&rect= — pull a scoped reference frame over just the region holding the repeated items, to build the colour table or crop the template image from.
  2. find_multi_color POST /api/pic/find-multi-color {id: <single>, list:[{first_color, rect, similarity}], same:true, all:false} — count every on-screen occurrence of one anchor pattern; returns data.list[{index, centre}], one entry per match, length of the list is the count.
  3. find_image_cv POST /api/pic/find-image-cv {id: <single>, img_list:[<template>], same:true, all:false, rect, similarity} — same idea with a template crop instead of a colour table; returns data.list[{index, centre, rect, similarity}], which also sizes each match via rect.
  4. Either function, all:true with N distinct list entries (one colour table or template per control) — checks every entry instead of stopping at the first, so a list of per-row anchors comes back as exactly the rows currently in the "on" state.
  5. Client-side, sort data.list by centre (row-major: y ascending, then x) before treating any index as an ordinal — the doc does not document the scan order the match list comes back in.
  6. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<single>&x=<centre[0]>&y=<centre[1]> — tap the Nth sorted centre directly; no coordinate map, no separate lookup step.

Needs

  • The same plug-in this rig has not confirmed: /pic/ocr answers code 28 here, find-image and find-multi-color sit on the same doc page and are "assume the same" per the rig notes. Run the negative-control probe from the state-detector card before trusting any count.
  • A tightly scoped rect or anchor pixel set per item, since a loosely bounded pattern can match chrome elsewhere on screen and inflate the count.
  • For find-image-cv, a template as base64 or a local path resolved on the PC running IMConsole, not on the phone; a template built from step 1's screenshot has to be saved to a path the kernel host can read, or embedded as base64 inline.
  • Device online with a live air_pid, same as any /pic/* call.

Watch out

  • Both endpoints are single-id, "multiple is not allowed" per the doc, same as every /pic/* function: counting is per phone, not fleet-wide. Enumerating badges across 19 boards is 19 sequential calls, each returning its own list.
  • find-multi-color's match entries carry only index and centre, nothing for size or confidence; find-image-cv additionally returns rect and similarity per hit, useful for confirming every matched tile is actually the same size before trusting the count.
  • An off count is a quieter bug than a flipped boolean: a badge template that also half-matches a status-bar glyph, or a tolerance set too loose, silently returns one extra centre with no error and nothing distinguishes it from a real hit.
  • No dedup or overlap rule is documented for adjacent or overlapping matches; a large tolerance value against a busy background can plausibly double-count a single item, unverified either way on this rig.
  • If the plug-in turns out gated, this specific capability, an indexed list of all matches, has no equivalent client-side fallback: hand-rolled pixel diffing against the raw BMP can answer a yes/no state check but not cleanly enumerate and index N separate on-screen instances the way data.list does.

Scale

Per phone, same as any /pic/* call: no fan-out, so counting across the rack is N sequential requests, one per phone, each returning its own indexed list in one round trip rather than one request per item. Cost scales with the number of distinct patterns searched under all:true, not with how many phones share the same layout. Whether the underlying search is plug-in-gated on this rig is unverified, so no throughput number for the server-side path exists yet; if gated, this specific quantitative capability is unavailable, not merely slower, since the client-side pixel-diff fallback proves state but does not enumerate.

MARK-INTEGRATION-MARK

Section 11 · Architecture and integration

Building on it: architecture and integration

Everything so far has been about single calls. This section is about the shape of the program you wrap around them. The XP kernel is a local HTTP and WebSocket server on 127.0.0.1:9911 with no authentication, no outbound notification of any kind, no job queue, no locking, and, on this rig, no server-side recognition at all. That means the interesting architecture lives in your process, not in the vendor's: a scheduler that serializes the right resource, a socket that turns broadcast callbacks into events, a bridge that carries those events to a human, a perception step that substitutes for the missing plug-ins, and, at the far end, an on-phone Shortcut channel that can reach parts of iOS the API never touches.

The two things worth building first

A scheduler and an event socket. Between them they answer the two questions every later component asks: which phone is safe to drive right now, and what just changed. Both are pure XP, need no plug-in, and need nothing installed on the phone.

Per-phone job queue with board-serialized leases

Native APIVerified

Model the rack as N independent workers, one per phone and board pair, and hold exactly one lease per board uid so two jobs never interleave HID traffic on the same pointer. Jobs are declarative step lists, tap, drag, wheel, key, wait-for-screen-change, compiled to XP calls on 9911, with every coordinate expressed in that device's imgw x imgh mirror pixel space and every step carrying a mean-pixel-difference verification rule. The measurements say the kernel itself has no shared bottleneck, so the board is the only resource that must be serialized. Getting that boundary right is the difference between a rack that runs many jobs concurrently and one that mysteriously drops taps because two scripts fought over one pointer.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get — inventory state, imgw/imgh, uid, vid/pid, gid, location_crc, air_pid. Probed live here: two iPhone XR, imgw 500 x imgh 1080, width 414 x height 896, location_crc B0DBD800.
  2. get_usb_list GET /api/config/usb/get — control-channel readiness per board, data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}]. Eligibility is the two-channel AND: device state != 0 with a live air_pid, board state 2, location_crc non-empty.
  3. none none (client-side) — acquire an exclusive lease keyed by board uid (C241BFBD, C214BEBD here), not by deviceid. No API-side locking exists in either edition.
  4. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> — clear the silent stuck-click state once at lease acquisition, not once per step.
  5. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=&y=&button=1&time=<ms> — tap at an absolute mirror pixel, or long-press via time. XP's button is numeric, Phonefarm's is the string "left"/"right".
  6. swipe / mouse_wheel GET /api/mouse/swipe?id=&direction=up&len=0.9 | GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=&direction=up&len=1-127&number= — flick or scroll. XP adds left/right to the wheel, which Phonefarm does not have.
  7. mouse_down / mouse_move / mouse_up /api/mouse/down → /api/mouse/move?x=&y= → /api/mouse/up — arbitrary-path drag. Coalescing intermediate points to the newest position is free: 14 steps, 7 steps and 2 jumps produced the same 26.2 / 22.9 mean pixel change.
  8. send_key GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&key=<ascii> or &fn_key=WIN+h — ASCII only on key; fn_key for the documented hotkey table, and the two are mutually exclusive.
  9. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<one id>&binary=true — capture before and after. Single id, "Multiple is not allowed". XP defaults to BMP, the opposite of Phonefarm's JPEG default.
  10. none none (client-side) — decide "did it land" on mean absolute pixel difference, never on MD5 or byte equality.
  11. none GET /api/device/get + GET /api/config/usb/get — release the lease, and re-prime from these two GETs after a connection refusal. There is no session or heartbeat endpoint on the HTTP side.

Needs

  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. Measured: with only IMService.exe up, /device/get showed both phones state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list. Automation cannot bring the rack up through the API alone from that state.
  • Every phone bound to its board with /device/set?id=<deviceid>&vid=720A&pid=<pid>. vid and pid must be set together, and hardware binding is single-device only, while name, gid and location_crc accept comma lists.
  • Non-empty location_crc per phone (shared library B0DBD800 here), or every /mouse call returns data.code 11, "No mouse parameters".
  • The iOS accessibility checklist on every phone: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity max, Full Keyboard Access on, Trackpad & Mouse tracking speed max, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock. None of it is queryable over the API.
  • Job coordinates authored per device in that device's own imgw x imgh space, read from its /device/get record, not a global constant and not iOS points.
  • No plug-ins. This design touches only /device/*, /config/usb/get, /mouse/*, /key/* and /pic/screenshot, all of which answered on this rig.

Watch out

  • status 200 only means the request was accepted. The result is in data.code: 0 success, 2 not bound to hardware, 3 hardware not connected, 11 no mouse parameters, 25 offline, 26 screenshot failed, 36 parameter error. Match on the code, never on the message, which is Chinese on this build.
  • The lease is advisory only. The API authenticates nobody and accepts commands from every LAN client, so another console or script can drive the same board while your lease is held. Treat a verification mismatch with no corresponding queued action as evidence of a lease collision and log it distinctly.
  • A "screen changed" assertion can pass on the wrong screen. The two XRs here have different home screens and wallpapers, so the same coordinate is Clock on one and Reminders on the other. Normalize with two Home presses, the first leaves the app and the second returns to page one, and confirm the layouts match before replaying a job across phones.
  • If the jobs are identical across phones this design is the wrong tool. Every mouse and key endpoint takes a comma-separated id list and the board walks all listed phones in parallel, so a mirrored action is one request, not N.
  • Correction to the capacity claim: board state 2 only proves a phone is USB-attached. A usable worker also needs live mirroring and a non-empty location_crc, which on this rig is 2 phones, not 19. The other slots need someone to seat a phone, pair it with /device/set, and walk the full non-queryable accessibility checklist by hand, minutes per phone, none of it provisionable by the scheduler.
  • Correction to the reset assumption: /mouse/reset is confirmed to clear the stuck-click state, but it is unverified whether it also corrects a drifted or offset pointer. The queue has no detection step that distinguishes "taps are landing progressively off-target" from "clicks stopped registering", because both currently rely on the same box diff. Also note that reset returns the pointer to the origin, so the first action after it pays a full-distance pointer walk.
  • Verification latency is per phone, not per rack. The healthy XR delivers roughly 29 new frames/s under motion while its twin delivers roughly 4.5, so a wait-for-change step on the slow phone needs a 220 ms per frame budget and must not time out on a 30 fps assumption. A still screen produces almost no new frames, so most polls legitimately return an identical frame.
  • Report worker count as a live computed value, not as the static 19-board inventory number. 19 is hub topology capacity.
  • Automating third-party apps at scale can breach those apps' terms and can get the accounts or devices involved restricted. Confine this to accounts and apps you own or are authorized to operate, and stop a job when an app signals a block rather than retrying through it.

Scale

Workers equal the number of eligible phones, currently 2. Per worker a tap-verify cycle is about 2 ms capture twice, plus 0 to 650 ms of pointer walk at the measured 0.6 ms/px, plus one to seven frames of settle (35 ms/frame on the fast XR, about 220 ms on the slow one). The fast phone sustains roughly 450 to 1,200 ten-step jobs per hour, about 4,500 to 12,000 discrete actions; the slow phone roughly 240 to 450 jobs per hour, because settle time dominates. Jobs run fully in parallel, so the rig total today is on the order of 700 to 1,650 ten-step jobs per hour. Quote capacity per phone class, never as an average: throughput here is bimodal. Cross-phone scaling is linear in principle, ten concurrent pollers measured 512 req/s at p50 3 ms with worst p95 142 ms and input traffic did not interfere with frame polling in either direction, but it is gated by the manual per-phone setup, not by the kernel. Reuse one 1.6 MB buffer per poller: without reuse the frame pump allocated 488 MB/s and forced 496 gen-2 collections in 8 s, with reuse 2.9 MB/s and 0 to 1.

Trap Your lock is a suggestion

There is no locking, session, or ownership concept anywhere in either edition. A lease protects your own processes from each other and nothing else. On an open subnet the correct mental model is that the rack has no owner, which is why the firewall rule on 9911 and 17000 is part of the architecture rather than a hardening afterthought.

Kernel WebSocket callbacks as the rack's event bus

Native APIWith caveats

Hold one WebSocket to ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api and treat the kernel's broadcast callbacks as first-class triggers. dev_connect and dev_disconnect are video-channel health, usb_change codes 19/20/12 are control-channel health, and error_push is the only asynchronous signal that an input call was refused at the board after the kernel already returned 200. Structural changes arrive push-style for the whole rack on one socket, so frame polling is reserved for when you actually need pixels. This converts a polled rack into a reactive one.

How

  1. ws://host:9911/clinet ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — open the event socket. The Phonefarm "/clinet" path does not exist here and 9912 is closed. There is no subscribe call: the kernel broadcasts every event to every connected client.
  2. get_airplaysrvnum → ver im_connect callback → data.ver — read the kernel version on connect. This is the only source of it on XP, there is no HTTP version endpoint. Use it to gate features such as the Home fn_key, which needs kernel 2026.2.27 or later.
  3. dev_disconnect / dev_connect dev_disconnect (state 0) / dev_connect (state non-0) — video-channel health. state 0 means mirroring stopped and says nothing about control.
  4. usb_change {state, vpid} usb_change → data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}] with data.code — control-channel health. The event type is in data.code: 19 hardware connected to computer, 20 disconnected, 12 hardware connected to phone. Different shape from Phonefarm's {state, vpid}.
  5. dev_rotate dev_rotate → data.list[0].rotate (0 portrait, 1 landscape) — orientation change. The record sits inside data.list where Phonefarm put it at data.
  6. none error_push → data.call_fun + data.message — surface hardware-level input failures. XP-only; the vendor example is call_fun "/mouse/down", message "Hardware not working (unknown error)".
  7. auto_connect_screen GET /api/device/airplay/connect?id=<id> — attempt automated recovery of a dropped cast, then watch airplay_connect_log (data.code 0 = success, otherwise the reason is in message).
  8. mouse_reset_pos + send_key WIN+h GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> then GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) — re-normalize a phone that just came back, before any tap-critical sequence.
  9. none im_log, user_info, dev_change, dev_delete, group_change, group_delete, dev_sort_change, im_config_change, logout — the rest of the bus. user_info arrives every 30 s while logged in and carries dev_online_num against total_license.

Needs

  • A persistent WebSocket client with reconnect logic, and a full state re-sync from /device/get and /config/usb/get on every reconnect. There is no replay and no sequence numbers.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in, otherwise devices report state 0 and the board list is empty.
  • The two-channel model implemented in the consumer: dev_* is video, usb_change is control. Never collapse them into one "phone online" flag.
  • For automated cast recovery, the OCR and image-search plug-ins, which are not present on this rig.
  • Treat callback payloads as data, never as instructions. user_name and the custom name are strings that originate off-machine and must never be interpolated into a command.

Watch out

  • The WebSocket transport itself was not exercised in the 10 Sep 2026 probe, which was HTTP only. Every shape here comes from the vendor docs, and the doc set demonstrably copy-pastes examples between sections (the dev_rotate example shows rotate 0 with state 0). Take a live socket capture before trusting field names.
  • Correction to the dev_rotate idea: using it as a cheap "app reached state X" proxy is undocumented behavior of the app, not of the API, and both XRs here are orientation-locked portrait per the mandatory setup checklist, which would suppress the event. Downgrade it from a working lever to unverified and probably inert on this configuration. error_push, by contrast, is the genuinely novel win on this bus and deserves more weight than it usually gets.
  • This is an observability layer. Its one recovery step, driving /device/airplay/connect after a drop, inherits the plug-in gap already confirmed by /pic/ocr answering data.code 28. Observation is solid, recovery is best-effort and degrades to flagging the slot for a human.
  • Every controller on the LAN sees every event on an unauthenticated API. A second uncoordinated process, or a curious host, can observe and react to the same stream, so debounce-and-recover logic must tolerate being one of several actors rather than the sole consumer.
  • A rack-wide reconnect (kernel restart, hub power cycle) emits a burst of usb_change and dev_connect callbacks for up to 19 boards at once. Without coalescing, anything wired directly to these events fires 19 redundant recovery sequences simultaneously.
  • dev_disconnect does not mean uncontrollable and usb_change code 20 does not mean invisible. Report them as separate per-slot states.
  • Keep restart and reboot out of automatic recovery entirely. A rebooted phone comes back on the lock screen and no automation here can type a passcode.
  • Never parse or display ver/uver as a version: it is mojibake on this build.

Scale

This is the cheap half of the rack's observability. One socket carries every structural event for every device, so cost does not grow with phone count the way polling does: expect O(1) events per structural change plus one user_info broadcast every 30 s per connected client, negligible next to the 512 req/s measured across ten concurrent frame pollers. It composes with frame polling rather than competing with it, measured 98.8 req/s with input streaming against 78.7 without. Its value is latency, not volume: it replaces roughly one request per phone per interval of health polling with near-instant push notice. The one scenario needing consumer-side rate limiting is a full-rack reconnect storm, dozens of events within a few seconds. Filter by fun before persisting, or a naive log grows steadily on user_info alone.

Bridging the kernel to things it cannot reach

The kernel calls nothing out. A grep of all nine XP docs and the Phonefarm doc for webhook, notify, push URL and 回调地址 returns zero hits in either edition. It also cannot see anything on this rig beyond raw pixels, because the recognition plug-ins are not connected. Both gaps are filled the same way, by a process of yours sitting next to the kernel.

Alert bridge: kernel callbacks to Slack and email pages

Plus external toolingWith caveats

A small out-of-process daemon holds one WebSocket and turns the kernel's callbacks into human pages. It splits every event along the two-channel model, enriches each with the device record's name, gname, ip and uid from a cached /device/get plus the hub and port slot label from Windows PnP, debounces and rolls up per phone, runs a self-healing rung and reports its outcome, then posts outbound. A page that reads "Hub#0010-P02 (Slot-01, 192.168.4.68) lost CONTROL, usb_change code 20; USB restart 720A|C241 attempted, board did not return to state 2; cable suspect" is what turns a phone farm into something you can leave running overnight.

How

  1. WebSocket ws://{host}:9911/clinet ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — one socket, kept open. On connect XP pushes im_connect with data.ver, for example "2024.12.21.910".
  2. §3 server-initiated callbacks, {fun, data, message} envelope {fun, status:200, message, msgid:0, data:{...}} — understand the delivery model first. No subscribe or filter call exists, so the daemon and IMConsole.exe coexist without contending. status is always 200; meaning lives in data.code and data.list[].
  3. get_device_list GET /api/device/get → data.list[] — cache the device inventory for alert enrichment, refreshed on the dev_change callback that any client's /device/set triggers.
  4. get_usb_list GET /api/config/usb/get → data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}] — cache the board inventory for the control-channel side. Verified live: 19 boards, VID 720A, states 1 and 2.
  5. dev_connect / dev_disconnect record inside data.list[], state non-0 / 0 — classify video-channel events. Page them as "VIDEO down", never as "phone dead".
  6. usb_change {state, vpid} usb_change, data.list[] with the event type in data.code — classify control-channel events, codes 19, 20 and 12.
  7. none error_push, data.call_fun + data.message — catch input-path failures at the board, the signal nothing else gives you. No Phonefarm equivalent exists.
  8. none im_log (data.message) and user_info (user_state, total_license, dev_num, dev_online_num, overdue_time) — catch license, login and kernel notices. The Phonefarm API has no user or account concept at all.
  9. n/a dev_change, dev_delete, group_change, group_delete, dev_sort_change, im_config_change, collection_mouse, airplay_connect_log, restart_log — suppress planned and cosmetic churn instead of paging on it, correlated against your own outstanding jobs.
  10. mouse_reset_pos / restart_usb / discon_airplay + auto_connect_screen GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> ; /api/device/usb/restart?id=720A|C241 ; /api/device/airplay/disconnect then /api/device/airplay/connect — run the self-healing rung before paging and say which rung was tried. Note usb/restart takes VID|PID, not the deviceid and not the 8-hex uid. XP has no force flag on connect, so disconnect first.
  11. none none, nothing in the XP doc set — deliver the page. Slack incoming webhook or SMTP, done by your daemon, which is the whole reason this is external rather than native.
  12. none user_info, pushed automatically every 30 s while logged in — heartbeat the bridge itself. A 90 s silence is a reasonable "socket dead" trigger, but only while logged in.

Needs

  • IMService.exe reachable on 9911 and IMConsole.exe running and logged in.
  • A WebSocket client that reconnects with backoff and re-snapshots /device/get and /config/usb/get on every reconnect, because callbacks missed while disconnected are not replayed.
  • An outbound Slack incoming-webhook URL or an SMTP relay reachable from the rack PC, with its secret stored outside the repo.
  • A slot table mapping deviceid to board uid to hub and port, built from Windows PnP. Three 7-port hubs, VID 1A40 PID 0201; the two live XRs sit on Hub #0010 ports 2 and 3. Physical topology is not in the API.
  • A maintenance-window and job-correlation list, so the daemon suppresses disconnects it or an operator caused.
  • Windows firewall rules restricting who may reach 9911 and 17000.

Watch out

  • Elevate the WebSocket check from caveat to blocking pre-flight. The 10 Sep 2026 probe was read-only HTTP, so if ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api behaves differently from the HTTP surface, none of the classification logic can be trusted yet. Connect and confirm an im_connect frame with data.ver before building on it.
  • The highest-value bug this daemon could ship with: alerting keyed on "code != 0 means alert" silently misses error_push, whose own vendor example carries data.code 0 for a genuine hardware error. Gate that one on the presence of the callback and on call_fun/message.
  • Match on data.code, never on message text. This build returns 成功, 插件未连接, 未登录，不允许上线 and 接口不存在.
  • error_push, im_log, user_info and im_connect are XP-only. On the Phonefarm edition the bridge degrades to dev_connect, dev_disconnect, dev_rotate and usb_change, with no input-failure and no license signal at all.
  • usb_change has no documented code for a phone being unplugged from its board; 12 only covers attach. Detect it from data.list[].state dropping 2 to 1, or re-poll /config/usb/get on every usb_change. Note also that state appears in the vendor example but not in its field table, so the 1 and 2 meanings are measured, not documented.
  • False rack-wide outage: if IMConsole.exe exits, every phone reads state 0 and the board list empties while IMService.exe is healthy. Detect that combination and page it as "console down", not as 19 board failures.
  • The self-healing rung is an unauthenticated write path fired automatically off a broadcast the daemon did not cause. Two bridge instances, or the daemon plus a human at the console, can race on the same /device/usb/restart with no documented idempotency. Add a per-slot in-flight lock and cooldown before letting it fire automatically.
  • Keep the Slack integration strictly outbound. A slash-command or email-reply path that sends commands back into the rack hands rack control to anyone who can post in the channel.
  • Never include the contents of C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json in an alert: it holds the vendor-account password as reversible hex obfuscation. Alert bodies also leak topology, phone names, LAN IPs and MACs into a third-party service, so alias them if the channel is broadly visible.
  • Attaching a screenshot works only for a phone whose video is still up, which by definition excludes a dev_disconnect page. If you want a video signal independent of the kernel, check ESTABLISHED sockets on TCP 17000 per phone IP.
  • A bridge that pages on every dev_disconnect without maintenance-window suppression trains its audience to ignore it. That is the real failure mode.

Scale

One WebSocket per kernel regardless of phone count, since the kernel broadcasts rather than being polled: 2 phones or 100, it is the same socket, and it does not contend with the vendor console. Payloads are small JSON; the 1.62 MB screenshot path is not involved unless you deliberately attach an image, and user_info every 30 s doubles as a free keepalive. The load driver is alert volume, not kernel load. A flapping board can emit a usb_change every few hundred milliseconds, so the debounce and rollup window, roughly 30 s, is the actual rate limiter, capping pages at about 120 per hour per slot before rollup and at whatever the target Slack app's own webhook limit allows in aggregate. Measure that limit against your workspace rather than assuming it.

Vision-model computer-use loop: raw frame in, tap out

Plus external toolingWith caveats

Close a full see-think-act loop against a physical iPhone: pull the raw mirror frame as a bottom-up BMP, downscale it, hand it to an external multimodal model with the task and the allowed primitive set, take back one action in a normalized 0 to 1000 grid, map that grid to this device's imgw x imgh (500 x 1080 here, not the 414 x 896 logical points), and execute it. The external model substitutes for the OCR and image-search plug-ins that are not installed, so the loop reads arbitrary UI instead of matching fixed coordinates, which matters here because the two XRs have entirely different home screens. Perception costs 2 ms and input traffic does not slow frame polling, so the only expensive part of the loop is the model call. The phone sees nothing but a HID pointer and keyboard on the Lightning port.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get?id=<deviceid> — preflight the record and learn the coordinate space. Use imgw/imgh only; location_crc must be non-empty or every /mouse/* call returns code 11. Phonefarm's record has no imgw/imgh at all.
  2. get_usb_list GET /api/config/usb/get — preflight the control channel. Video-ready and control-ready are independent; check both.
  3. send_key (fn_key WIN+h) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h — normalize the screen, twice. "Home" as an fn_key name also exists but needs kernel 2026.2.27 and targets iOS 26.1+; these XRs run iOS 18.7.10, so WIN+h is the right call.
  4. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<comma list> — clear the stuck-click state before any tap-critical step. A responsive keyboard proves nothing about taps.
  5. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — perceive. The body is the image bytes with no JSON envelope: 1,620,054 bytes = 500 x 1080 x 3 plus a 54-byte bottom-up header, p50 2 ms, against 40 ms and a 21 req/s cap for jpg=true and 26 ms for the base64 JSON default.
  6. none none — think. Decode and row-flip the BMP, downscale, prompt with the task plus the primitive list, and ask for coordinates in a normalized 0 to 1000 grid. Map back with x*imgw/1000, y*imgh/1000 and clamp.
  7. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=&y=&button=1&time=<ms> — act, tap. time is the press-to-release delay, so time=800 is a long press.
  8. swipe / mouse_wheel GET /api/mouse/swipe?id=&direction=up&len=0.9 | GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=&direction=up&len=30&number=3 — act, scroll. A 1080 px stroke is about 580 ms of pointer walk and iOS may read it as a drag, so prefer the 500 px short axis or the wheel, which scrolls without moving the pointer.
  9. send_key GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&key=<ascii> — act, type ASCII. English letters, digits and English punctuation only, no CJK and no emoji.
  10. send_text / shortcut#10 + paste POST /api/shortcut/clipboard/set {id, text, sleep} then GET /api/key/sendkey?id=&fn_key=WIN+v — act, type Unicode. XP has no send_text and no send_text_ok callback, so this two-call path is the documented route. sleep is in seconds while outtime is in milliseconds.
  11. shortcut#13 POST /api/shortcut/exec/url {id, url, outtime} — optionally jump straight into an app screen, skipping UI navigation for anything with a URL scheme.
  12. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true (optionally rect=[l,t,r,b]) — verify, then loop. Threshold a mean absolute pixel difference: idle floor 0.02 to 0.03, a real reaction 20 to 160, a landed pointer dot inside a 40 px box 1.4 to 9.8.
  13. none ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api → error_push — listen for board-level failures the HTTP reply hides.

Needs

  • An external multimodal model endpoint plus network egress from the rack PC or a bridge host. There is no on-rig recognition: /api/pic/ocr returned data.code 28, 插件未连接, on 10 Sep 2026, and the image-search plug-in is presumed absent too.
  • The kernel on 9911 with IMConsole.exe running and logged in.
  • Per phone: state non-0 with a live air_pid, board state 2 with vid/pid/uid bound, and a non-empty location_crc.
  • The full iOS accessibility checklist on every phone, none of it readable over the API.
  • A per-device coordinate mapper from the model's output space into that device's imgw x imgh, with clamping.
  • The iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited and bound only if the loop needs Unicode text or /shortcut/exec/url. Taps and ASCII typing need no Shortcut.

Watch out

  • Correction, and it is a hard limit on the action space: there is exactly one HID pointer per phone and no multi-touch. Pinch to zoom, two-finger scroll and any simultaneous multi-point input are categorically impossible on this rig, not merely slow. The primitive list handed to the model must exclude them, because a hallucinated multi-touch instruction is not a retryable failure, it is a request the hardware cannot service.
  • Correction to the downscale step: at 250 x 540 a standard 44 pt iOS touch target is about 25 px, and denser UI, list rows, keyboard keys, small icon grids, falls below what a vision model can reliably discriminate. Expect a materially higher misclick rate on dense screens, and note that clamping to the frame does not fix a coordinate that is confidently wrong rather than out of bounds.
  • The perception step is entirely off-rig. With no OCR and no image search there is no slower-but-working fallback: a transient model outage stops the loop dead rather than degrading.
  • /pic/screenshot is single id, so one poller per phone; only the act step fans out over a comma list. Fan-out is safe only across phones with identical layout and identical imgw/imgh, since the same coordinate is Clock on one XR and Reminders on the other.
  • binary=true returns raw bytes with no envelope, so error codes 25 (offline) and 26 (screenshot failed) arrive as a JSON body where an image was expected. Sniff the "BM" magic and handle both shapes.
  • Each frame is 1.6 MB, over the .NET Large Object Heap threshold. Without buffer reuse a poller measured 488 MB/s allocation and 496 gen-2 GCs per 8 s; with one reused buffer per poller, 2.9 MB/s and 0 to 1.
  • Use a fixed poll period. Deriving it from observed frame gaps decayed a 23 fps stream to 16.5 fps through positive feedback.
  • Phonefarm's loop_device_screenshot server-push stream does not exist in XP. There are no binary WebSocket frames, so poll.
  • The pointer-box verification trick assumes AssistiveTouch's on-screen pointer dot is enabled and visible on every target phone. It is one more setting the API cannot query, and its absence makes every "did the tap land" check read as a false negative even when the tap worked.
  • Sending frames of signed-in sessions to a third-party model is a data-egress decision each deployment makes explicitly, not an implementation detail, and it is easy to lose track of once the loop is wrapped in tooling. Frames and model transcripts are also a retention decision.
  • Operating consumer apps with an autonomous agent conflicts with most platforms' terms of service, and the account-level consequence lands on accounts you own. There is no sandbox: a hallucinated coordinate acts on a live phone, so clamp, verify with a pixel diff before chaining anything destructive, and cap the step count. Never let the loop type credentials or complete a purchase; put those behind a human.

Scale

Perception is per phone and cheap: p50 2 ms paced, 84 req/s flat out per phone, and phones are independent (two pollers 83 and 85 req/s at p50 3 ms each; ten pollers 512 req/s aggregate, worst p95 142 ms). Input and frame traffic do not contend, measured /mouse/move p50 0.5 ms while both phones were polled flat out. Per loop step: about 2 ms capture, a few ms downscale, 1 to 5 s of model latency, 0 to 600 ms of pointer walk at 0.6 ms/px, and a settle wait bounded by the phone's own source rate, about 35 ms on the .68 XR and about 220 ms on the .27 XR. That is 2 to 7 s per action per phone, roughly 500 to 1,800 actions per hour per phone as a kernel-and-hardware ceiling. Across the rack it scales close to linearly, but at 19 phones the bottleneck is entirely the model provider's concurrency and cost, not IMService or the boards.

Reaching into iOS through the Shortcut channel

Every /shortcut/* endpoint works the same way underneath: the board sends a HID key combination, iOS runs the Shortcut bound to that AssistiveTouch custom button, and the Shortcut talks back to the kernel over Wi-Fi. Naming that mechanism is useful, because it is the only path on this rig to structured, non-pixel data from inside iOS. It is also where the documented API ends, and the three cards below map that edge, from what the vendor ships to what is merely plausible.

Hotkey-to-Shortcut as an extension point, and its ceiling

PartialWith caveats

The vendor half of this mechanism is fully supported and covers album, file, clipboard, URL, brightness, torch, airplane, cellular, WLAN, shutdown and restart, plus LAN and external IP, with comma-separated id fan-out. The tempting extrapolation is that anything Shortcuts can reach is therefore triggerable from the PC. The honest finding is narrower: the XP API exposes no way to bind, name, list or invoke a custom Shortcut, the binding is a console-only manual step, and XP's fn_key vocabulary is a closed documented list with no arbitrary-combination entry. Extending the rack means driving UI with the pointer or getting a custom Shortcut onto an AssistiveTouch button by hand.

How

  1. §5.1 setup none (no API) — phone-side permissions, once, by hand. Settings > Shortcuts > Advanced: allow running scripts, allow sharing large amounts of data, allow deleting without confirmation. Documented only in the Phonefarm doc; the XP docs assume it.
  2. §5.2 setup none (no API) — install the vendor iMouse Shortcut: console QR code, get the Shortcut, edit the kernel IP inside it (192.168.4.29 here), run once, allow everything. If the PC's LAN IP changes, it must be edited again on every phone.
  3. §5.3 setup none (no API) — bind the trigger. Accessibility > AssistiveTouch > Devices > "iMouse4.x" > Customize More Buttons, then "Send Binding Key" in the console. This is the only documented binding step in either edition, and no endpoint performs it.
  4. shortcut (id 1-24 dispatcher) /shortcut/album/get|upload|down|del|clear, /shortcut/file/get|upload|down|del, /shortcut/clipboard/set|get, /shortcut/exec/url, /shortcut/switch/device|bril|torch|flight|cdpd|wlan, /shortcut/device/ip — trigger the documented vendor functions. XP has no generic dispatcher: each is its own path with typed parameters and outtime in milliseconds, where Phonefarm's outtime was seconds and its parameter a double-encoded JSON string.
  5. click (button left/right only) GET /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&button=<4..8> — candidate route A to a custom Shortcut, a spare pointer button. The API side is documented; whether iOS routes an extra button to a Shortcut assigned under Customize More Buttons appears in neither the XP docs nor the vendor setup pages.
  6. send_key fn_key (CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+v) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=<name> — candidate route B, an arbitrary combination. Refuted as written: the XP table is a closed vocabulary of named actions and the Phonefarm combo is absent from it. Nothing documents fn_key as a general combination encoding.
  7. shortcut#11 GET /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<id>&outtime=<ms> — return path 1. Single id, returns data.text, and works regardless of what put the text on the clipboard, which makes it the cleanest confirmation channel available.
  8. send_text none — return path 2, corrected: the kernel exposes no endpoint that accepts arbitrary posted data, so a custom Shortcut must call your own listener, not "the kernel's HTTP port".
  9. none (send_text_ok, Phonefarm only) none — confirmation. /key/sendkey and /mouse/click return code 0 when the board accepted the input, which says nothing about whether a Shortcut ran. A vendor /shortcut/* call that never fires returns data.code 30, "Call timeout", after outtime.

Needs

  • The iMouse Shortcut installed on each phone with the kernel's LAN IP edited in, run once with every permission granted, and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom button. None of this has an API.
  • The board bound to the phone with vid and pid set together, and physically connected at board state 2. The trigger travels over USB HID, so a phone that is mirroring but unbound cannot be triggered at all.
  • Full Keyboard Access on for any fn_key path; phone unlocked, portrait, Auto-Lock Never.
  • Phone and kernel on the same LAN with the phone able to reach 9911, since the Shortcut's return leg is Wi-Fi and that port is unauthenticated.
  • iOS 15+ for /shortcut/file/* and /shortcut/switch/device; iMouse Shortcut v1.3 or higher for the /shortcut/other/* recognition fallbacks.
  • For a custom Shortcut: a spare trigger that does not displace the vendor binding, plus your own HTTP listener if it needs to report back.

Watch out

  • Correction to the framing: every documented working path here is the vendor's own pre-bound Shortcut occupying the single available trigger button. Reaching a genuinely custom Shortcut has not been verified end to end anywhere. Route A is an untested hypothesis about iOS behavior and route B is refuted by the fn_key table, so the only end-to-end-confirmed capability is triggering the vendor's own functions.
  • Only one trigger binding is documented and the vendor's Shortcut occupies it. Rebinding it would plausibly break every /shortcut/* endpoint on that phone at once, so try it only on a phone you can fully re-provision, never on one in active use.
  • Nothing in the /shortcut/* family has been probed on this rig; the live probe covered /device/get, /config/usb/get, /device/group/get and /pic/ocr only. Whether the iMouse Shortcut is even installed on either XR is unknown. The cheapest single proof is GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 returning code 0 with data.text equal to the ip field in /device/get, and it should be run before anything else in this group.
  • The binding step has no API and must be repeated by hand on every phone added, and redone after a board or phone swap. That is O(phones) manual work that does not compose with the comma-separated fan-out model the rest of the rack uses.
  • Trigger fan-out is one request for many phones, but every return channel, clipboard/get, device/ip, album/get, file/get, is single id.
  • Turning WLAN or airplane mode on via /shortcut/switch/wlan|flight kills the AirPlay video channel and the Shortcut's own return path while leaving USB control alive, so the call may time out even when it succeeded.
  • Return path 2 means standing up another inbound service on the same LAN that already carries an unauthenticated kernel. Scope and access-control it independently rather than treating it as a free extension of an already open design.
  • Only 2 of the 19 boards currently carry a mirroring, bound phone, so even the fully supported vendor half is exercisable on 2 phones today.
  • /shortcut/album/clear and /shortcut/file/del are destructive with no undo, on a phone where "delete without confirmation" is explicitly enabled. Do not wire them to anything automatic.

Scale

Triggering is cheap and parallel: /key/sendkey, /mouse/click and the set, switch, upload and exec paths all take a comma-separated id list, and the board walks every listed phone at the same cost as one. Reading back is serial: the single-id paths are each bounded by outtime (default 15000 ms) plus the phone's actual execution time, so confirmed round trips run roughly 1 to 16 s each and must be run one connection per phone to parallelize. Across a fully provisioned 19-phone rack that is on the order of a few hundred to low thousands of confirmed trigger-and-read cycles per hour, run concurrently. A phone also has only a handful of AssistiveTouch custom buttons, so a large Shortcut library has to be multiplexed behind one dispatcher Shortcut that reads its instruction from the clipboard, not one button each. For the custom-Shortcut idea no throughput number can be given in good faith: none of the required binding steps has been exercised on this hardware.

Open One cheap call decides this whole group

GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 returning data.code 0 with data.text equal to that device's ip proves the vendor Shortcut is installed, the trigger fires, and the phone can reach the kernel. A data.code 30, "Call timeout", after 15 seconds means the chain is broken somewhere you cannot see. Run it on one XR before designing anything on top of the next two cards.

Phone-initiated reverse channel to your own gateway

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

The vendor's Unicode-text and album features work only because iOS runs a Shortcut on the phone and that Shortcut talks back over Wi-Fi. The same architecture can carry your own payload: author a second Shortcut that gathers what the API is blind to, battery level, Wi-Fi SSID, free storage, whether an app is installed, App Intents output from apps that publish actions, and have it POST JSON to an endpoint you run or write to the clipboard where /shortcut/clipboard/get reads it back. This matters because the API has no visibility into battery, thermal state, SSID or storage, yet those explain the rig's real failure modes: one XR delivers about 29 new frames/s while its twin delivers about 4.5, which is a Wi-Fi or AirPlay problem rather than a kernel one, and a phone that stops mirroring may simply be flat. On an OCR-less rig it is also the only structured-data path: results arrive as JSON rather than pixels you cannot read.

How

  1. get_device_list /device/get (optional id, comma list) — enumerate targets and get correlation keys, ip, user_name, mac, state, imgw/imgh, so gateway posts can be joined to device records. Confirmed live: two iPhone XR at 192.168.4.68 and 192.168.4.27.
  2. shortcut#13 (Open URL) /shortcut/exec/url (id comma list, url, outtime ms) — trigger path A, preferred and fully documented on the XP side. shortcuts://run-shortcut?name=<name> is an Apple URL scheme that the vendor doc neither documents nor forbids, so it must be probed on one phone.
  3. send_key (fn_key) /key/sendkey (id comma list, fn_key, key left blank) — trigger path B, the AssistiveTouch chord. The endpoint and parameter are verified, but the published fn_key table is closed, so an arbitrary user chord has no documented syntax.
  4. none (Shortcut "Get Contents of URL") none, external tooling — return path A: the Shortcut POSTs its JSON to a listener you run. The network path is proven, since that is how the vendor Shortcut returns data, but the listener is yours to build and must not be co-hosted on 9911.
  5. shortcut#11 (Get phone clipboard) /shortcut/clipboard/get (id, multiple not allowed, outtime ms) — return path B, no listener needed. Returns data.text; a data.code 30 means the Shortcut never ran.
  6. shortcut#24 (external IP) /shortcut/device/ip (id single only, state 0 LAN / 1 external, outtime ms) — the cheapest end-to-end proof that the Shortcut channel is alive, before you debug your own Shortcut. state=1 is a legitimate egress check on infrastructure you own.
  7. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot (id single only, binary=true) — visual confirmation the first time, because a stuck iOS "Allow" prompt is invisible to every other call. You must read the prompt yourself: /pic/ocr answers data.code 28, 插件未连接, here.

Needs

  • The vendor iMouse Shortcut installed on each phone with the kernel IP edited in, run once with every permission allowed, and bound via the console's "Send Binding Key". Neither HANDOFF.md nor HARDWARE.md records this being done on either XR, so treat it as unproven.
  • Your own Shortcut authored on each phone, and for trigger path B bound to a spare chord under AssistiveTouch > Devices > Customize More Buttons.
  • Board bound and connected at state 2, since both trigger paths travel over the board. Full Keyboard Access on, rack-wide, for any hotkey path.
  • Phone unlocked, Auto-Lock Never, and on the same LAN as the kernel.
  • An HTTP endpoint you control for return path A, with a per-phone token, since the LAN carrying this traffic also carries the entirely unauthenticated 9911 API.
  • iMouse Shortcut v1.3 or later if you also want the /shortcut/other/* recognition fallbacks.

Watch out

  • Correction: nothing on this rig exercises /shortcut/exec/url, /shortcut/clipboard/get, /shortcut/clipboard/set or /shortcut/device/ip. Every measured number here is for /pic/screenshot, /mouse/*, /key/sendkey and /device/get, so treat the whole chain as unverified in practice, not just trigger path B.
  • Correction to the verdict: because every step depends on the single unverified vendor-Shortcut install, the realistic status today is "blocked on a manual one-time setup step per phone" rather than "achievable". That install is a single point of failure for the entire use case.
  • Correction: the first time shortcuts://run-shortcut runs on a phone it will very plausibly raise an iOS confirmation banner. Treat that as an expected one-time step per phone, cleared with a screenshot and a manual tap, since no API call can dismiss a system dialog.
  • No rig evidence exists for what /shortcut/exec/url or /key/sendkey with an unrecognized fn_key actually returns, whether silently ignored, an HTTP error, or a 500 like the Phonefarm function names. Probe that before building retry or alerting logic around it.
  • Return path B is single id, as are /pic/screenshot and /shortcut/device/ip. Only the trigger fans out. The measured lack of a shared bottleneck, 512 req/s across ten pollers, says to issue those 19 reads concurrently rather than serially.
  • The Phonefarm sibling marks its whole shortcut dispatcher professional-version-only. The XP docs state no edition gate, but licensing here is per device through /config/user/info and has not been checked against shortcut use.
  • A user Shortcut runs in the foreground with the phone owner's full app permissions and may show a banner, so it can interrupt whatever job is running, with no API signal that it did.
  • Trigger failure and the stuck-click failure are independent: a phone mid-way through a stuck-click episode tells you nothing about whether its Shortcut trigger will fire, and /mouse/reset does nothing for a Shortcut trigger failure. Check both.
  • App Intents coverage varies enormously by app and version. An action present in one app's Shortcuts pane may simply not exist in another.
  • Firing a chord by mistake against a comma-separated id list runs it on every phone in the list, and two chords in the documented table are destructive (restart, pass-through toggle). A Shortcut that POSTs is a data path off the phone with the phone owner's permissions: scope it to facts you need, give each phone its own token, and point it only at an endpoint from your own configuration. Reading account or order data through App Intents is legitimate only on accounts and devices you own, and the app's own terms govern automated use.

Scale

The trigger is O(1) per report cycle regardless of fleet size, one comma-separated fan-out request, and the board lease is held only for the keystroke or URL hand-off. Zero screenshot and zero OCR cost. A 19-phone sweep is therefore 1 trigger request plus up to 19 single-id return requests, which the measured concurrency ceiling says can be issued in parallel, so a full-rack report cycle likely completes in 15 to 20 s bounded by the slowest phone's Shortcut execution plus outtime, not by the API. Because each run interrupts the foreground app and may show a banner, a 5 to 15 minute cadence is the right ceiling, roughly 4 to 12 cycles per hour per phone, far below the API's raw capacity.

Fire your own Shortcut from a spare mouse button

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

The XP mouse endpoints expose buttons 1 to 8, not just left and right: /mouse/click, /mouse/down and /mouse/up all document "1 left button, 2 right button, 3 middle button, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 button". iOS AssistiveTouch lets any button on a connected pointer device be taught an action, and the action list includes running a Shortcut. That is the same channel the vendor's own text-entry feature uses, except the vendor teaches a key combination rather than a mouse button. So: author a Shortcut on the phone, teach iOS that button 5 on the board runs it, and fire it from the PC with one down-and-up pair carrying a comma-separated id list. Buttons 3 to 8 are the only input primitives on this board with no pre-assigned iOS meaning, which makes them the natural place to hang a custom trigger, and unlike the vendor's Unicode path this needs neither plug-in nor a send_text endpoint that XP does not have.

How

  1. none (phone-side; the vendor equivalent is the §5.3 "Send Binding Key" console button) none — one-time per phone: author the Shortcut, then Settings > Accessibility > Touch > AssistiveTouch > Devices > the board entry > Customize Additional Buttons, press the button when iOS asks, pick the Shortcut. No endpoint in either edition reads or writes iOS accessory-button mappings.
  2. mouse_move, click /api/mouse/move?id=<id>&x=&y= then /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&button=1&x=&y=, then /api/mouse/down?id=<id>&button=5 + /api/mouse/up?id=<id>&button=5 — optionally drive the teaching screen remotely, and use it as the test: if iOS never registers the press, the board does not transmit that button and the idea stops here.
  3. get_device_list, get_usb_list GET /api/device/get?id=<ids> and GET /api/config/usb/get — pre-flight the control channel. Require state != 0 with a live air_pid, vid/pid/uid non-empty, location_crc non-empty, and the board at state 2.
  4. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<id1>,<id2>,... — clear the silent stuck-click state on the whole target set. Whether that state also swallows down and up on button 5 was never measured, so reset anyway.
  5. mouse_down + mouse_up GET /api/mouse/down?id=<id1>,<id2>&button=5 then GET /api/mouse/up?id=<id1>,<id2>&button=5 — fire on every phone in one round trip. Neither call takes x or y, so the pointer never moves and there is no 0.6 ms/px walk and no risk of a stray tap. Prefer this over /mouse/click, which requires coordinates.
  6. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — confirm it visibly ran. Compare by mean absolute pixel difference, idle floor 0.02 to 0.03 against a real reaction of 20 to 160.
  7. shortcut#11 (professional version only on Phonefarm) GET /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<id>&outtime=15000 — read a result back, route A: the Shortcut ends with "Copy to Clipboard". Catch: this endpoint is served by the vendor's own Shortcut, so it needs a second, separate binding alongside your button 5.
  8. none none (the Shortcut's "Get Contents of URL", aimed at a collector you run) — route B. Point it at your own endpoint; the kernel has no "store a result for me" path, and /shortcut/clipboard/set writes to a phone.

Needs

  • Board bound and cabled per phone, showing state 2, with mouse parameters present (location_crc, the B0DBD800 shared library on this rig).
  • AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity max, Trackpad & Mouse tracking speed max, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock. None of this is queryable: a phone can mirror perfectly and ignore every input.
  • iOS 13.4+ for pointer-device support and button customization, with the Shortcuts app present. The vendor's own shortcut features want iOS 15+, and the file endpoints are explicitly iOS 15+.
  • The Shortcut authored on each phone and run once manually with every permission granted. An unanswered "Allow" prompt blocks the run silently and permanently.
  • The unverified prerequisite: that this board actually transmits HID buttons 4 to 8 as distinct buttons and that iOS records one. The XP API documents 8 buttons, but the board's 9-byte vendor HID output report layout is an open unknown and nothing here has been exercised beyond button 1.
  • For the clipboard readback only: the vendor iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited, and bound to its own separate trigger key.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in.

Watch out

  • Correction, and it gates everything else: a 200 with data.code 0 from /mouse/down?button=5 proves the HTTP layer accepted the parameter, not that a HID report with a nonzero button-5 bit left the PC. Test step 2 on one phone before treating any of this as achievable. If the board implements only left, right and middle, the mechanism collapses.
  • The keyboard fallback is not a clean substitute on XP. The fn_key list is fixed, the Phonefarm "send Chinese" combo does not appear in it, no XP endpoint sends an arbitrary custom combination, and every combo XP does expose already carries an iOS meaning, so hanging your own Shortcut on one steals that function. That is what makes the spare button the better XP route rather than the exotic one.
  • Correction to the framing: only 2 of the 19 boards currently have a phone attached and mirroring, so this is a 2-phone capability today. Each additional phone needs a fully manual AssistiveTouch binding that nothing in the API can set, verify or audit.
  • Nothing about the binding is visible over the API on either edition. Your only evidence a phone is armed is a screen diff after firing, so budget one screenshot round trip per phone and keep a per-phone checklist. The mapping survives nothing but the phone itself: a restore, an iOS update or a cable swap to a different board can lose it.
  • Silent failure modes cluster. An unanswered permission prompt, a Shortcut waiting on a dialog, a locked screen and a phone whose AssistiveTouch was turned off all look identical from the PC, because data.code 0 only reports that the button event reached the board.
  • Verification cannot use MD5 or byte equality: the AirPlay encoder never repeats a frame. Use mean absolute pixel difference against an idle control, and remember a still screen produces almost no new frames at all.
  • There is no operator-facing way to tell which physical board maps to which iOS button assignment once bound. LED color semantics are unconfirmed and ver/uver is known-unreliable mojibake, so a board swapped after a cable fault will silently fire the wrong phone's Shortcut, or none, with identical code-0 responses either way.
  • A phone doing both the vendor text path and this one needs two independent bindings, the spare button for your Shortcut plus whatever binds the vendor Shortcut for clipboard reads. The AssistiveTouch button budget is not unlimited.
  • A stray press of the mapped button later runs the automation unintentionally, including from any other host on the LAN, since the API authenticates nobody. Pick a button you will not use otherwise, firewall 9911, and do not bind anything destructive. A Shortcut that reaches the network is an egress path off the phone independent of the vendor stack.
  • Anything the Shortcut drives inside a third-party app is governed by that app's terms. Use only accounts you own, keep to actions the app publicly exposes as Shortcuts actions, and stop on a rate limit or a block response rather than retrying into it.
  • Edition split: Phonefarm's click, mouse_down and mouse_up document only "left" and "right", so buttons 3 to 8 are an XP-edition capability, and Phonefarm's generic shortcut dispatcher, including clipboard read, is professional-version only.

Scale

Firing is one round trip regardless of fleet size: down and up both accept a comma-separated id list, the board walks all listed phones in parallel, and because neither carries coordinates there is no pointer-walk cost at all, against up to about 592 ms for a 1000 px walk on /mouse/click. Two requests, a few milliseconds, N phones. Everything after that is per phone: /pic/screenshot is single id at p50 2 ms, and /shortcut/clipboard/get is single id with a 15 s default outtime. The real ceiling is the Shortcut's own run time, roughly 3 s end to end for the vendor's comparable Shortcut and slower for anything touching Photos, Files or a third-party app, plus a confirmation bounded by the phone's AirPlay source rate, about 29 new frames/s on one XR here and about 4.5 on its twin. On the 2 live phones, budget on the order of 15 to 25 fire-and-confirm cycles per hour per phone. It does not extrapolate to 19, because the core HID-button assumption is untested at any N.

Addressing: groups, fan-out and coordinate spaces

Before anything else in a console, two questions have to have hard answers: which phones does this step go to, and what coordinate space is the step written in. The XP kernel answers the first with groups plus comma-separated id lists, which the Phonefarm edition does not have at all. It answers the second only through imgw and imgh on the device record, and it will never tell you that you got it wrong.

Group targeting and comma-id fan-out as the addressing layer

Native APIWith caveats

Use kernel groups as the rack's addressing layer, one per client, per campaign, per model, plus a quarantine group, and drive each group through the comma-separated id list that every /mouse/*, every /key/* and most /shortcut/* endpoints accept. One HTTP request steps the whole group and the boards walk their pointers at the same time. Capture cannot follow the same pattern, because /pic/screenshot refuses multiple ids, so verification is N concurrent raw-BMP polls with a mean pixel difference check, and any phone that reads no reaction drops out of the next step's id list.

Measured on this rack, a mirrored move to two phones costs exactly what a move to one costs (2 px = 1.0 ms, 1000 px = 592 ms, identical either way), and frame polling does not contend with input. That makes one input request per step plus N parallel capture verifications the cheapest correct batch architecture the kernel offers.

How

  1. set_group /device/group/set — create the group with id=0 (0 means add), read the new group id out of data.list[{id,name}]; a group_change callback goes to every connected client
  2. set_dev /device/set — assign members with id=<id1,id2,...>&gid=<gid>; only the hardware binding is single-device, since pid and hardware id must be set together, and the response data.list names the ids that actually took
  3. none /device/group/get-dev — resolve members (id=0 lists ungrouped), keep records with state != 0 and imgw/imgh/rotate equal to the master's, then join on uid against /config/usb/get and keep only boards at state 2
  4. mouse_reset_pos /mouse/reset — reset the whole target set whenever its membership changes and before any tap-critical sequence; comma id list supported
  5. send_key /key/sendkey — normalize with fn_key=WIN+h twice, the first press leaving the app and the second returning to page one
  6. click / swipe / mouse_wheel /mouse/click, /mouse/swipe, /mouse/wheel — step the group; button is numeric on XP (1 left, 2 right, 3 middle, up to 8), time=<ms> makes a long press, swipe len is a fraction of the screen, and wheel scrolls without moving the pointer at all
  7. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot — verify per phone, one poller each, binary=true, mean absolute pixel difference against the pre-step frame
  8. send_key / send_text /key/sendkey, /shortcut/clipboard/set — type ASCII with key=, or push Unicode to the clipboard and paste it with fn_key=WIN+v
  9. del_group /device/group/del — tear down, but move members back to gid 0 first, because a populated group returns data.code 34

Needs

  • Every member bound to its board (/device/set with vid and pid together, one device per binding call) and that board reading state 2 in /config/usb/get.
  • Every member carrying a non-empty location_crc, or mouse calls return data.code 11, no mouse parameters.
  • Members sharing imgw x imgh and rotate, and sharing the UI layout being targeted: same page, same app version, same icon at that coordinate.
  • Phone-side accessibility satisfied on every member (AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access for hotkeys, tracking speed at maximum, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock). None of it is queryable over the API.
  • For the Unicode branch only, the iMouse Shortcut installed on each phone, the kernel IP edited in, bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, and the phone able to reach 9911 on the LAN.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. With IMService.exe alone the probe saw both phones at state 0 and an empty board list.

Watch out

  • A comma-list input call returns one data.code, one data.id and one message for the whole list. There is no per-device result, so a request can report success while one board did nothing. Per-phone screenshot verification is not defense in depth here, it is the only failure detection that exists today.
  • The only asynchronous per-device failure signal is the error_push callback (data.call_fun plus message, for example /mouse/down and "Hardware not working (unknown error)"), and that requires an open WebSocket, which was never opened during the 10 September probe.
  • Fan-out amplifies the silent stuck-click state rather than mitigating it. A comma-list click against N phones, one of which is stuck, returns the same success code as a fully successful call, so spot-checking a subset under-detects stuck phones in proportion to N.
  • /pic/screenshot, /pic/find-image and /pic/ocr all refuse multiple ids, so verification is inherently N requests while input is one.
  • The parallel-walk claim is measured on two phones. The "10 phones costs the same as one" line is a vendor-side inference. The ten-way numbers in the measurements are concurrent frame pollers, a read path, not simultaneous multi-phone pointer walks, which are a write path through shared USB HID bandwidth across three chained 7-port hubs. Do not use 512 req/s as evidence that a 19-phone click fans out for free.
  • Groups are kernel-global and unauthenticated. Any LAN host, including the vendor console's own operator, can move a phone in or out of the target group between your resolve step and your click step, and there is no locking primitive. Re-resolve per job and react to group_change and group_delete rather than caching membership.
  • Destructive adjacency: /device/group/del and /device/del are one path element away from /device/group/get-dev, and they refuse only the specific guarded cases (code 34, code 7).
  • Prefer /mouse/wheel for scrolls. It moves no pointer, so it skips the roughly 0.6 ms per pixel walk entirely, which swipe and click sequences cannot.
  • The Unicode branch is not merely unverified, it is a separate manual prerequisite chain: a companion app installed per phone, the kernel IP typed in, an AssistiveTouch key bound. None of that is exposed by any API call in this document, so it cannot be provisioned by automation.
  • On a Phonefarm-edition kernel this whole design collapses. Phonefarm has no multi-id addressing, its only fan-out being the shortcut dispatcher's devlist array, so every step becomes N requests.
  • Driving the same account or session across many phones from one controller is visible to the destination service as coordinated automated behavior from a single operator. That is a terms-of-service and fraud-detection exposure to weigh before scaling group size, and the correct response to a rate limit or an "action blocked" interstitial is to stop the job.

Scale

Input costs exactly one request per step regardless of N, with latency set by the longest pointer walk in that step: about 592 ms for a 1000 px move, about 580 ms of travel for a full-height 1080 px swipe (which iOS may read as a slow drag rather than a flick, so prefer the 500 px short axis or the wheel), plus 1 to 12 ms of HTTP. Verification is the real bottleneck, because it needs N independent captures and a fresh AirPlay frame: on this rack one XR delivers about 28.9 new frames per second and its identical twin only about 4.5, so a mixed fleet's cycle time is set by its slowest phone, roughly 0.8 to 1.5 s per step for a short move plus settle and verify. That is on the order of 2,000 to 4,000 group-level steps per hour for the rack as a whole, not per phone, and it is only trustworthy at the measured scale of two phones. Consider thread_mode in /config/imserver/set ("use thread mode to batch operate hardware", applies live with no restart) before scaling the id list. The hard ceiling on phones per PC is the hub topology, 21 physical slots with 19 populated, not the API.

Coordinate-space registry keyed by model, iOS and mirror geometry

Native APIWith caveats

A client-side template store in which every named UI target ("Settings icon", "Safari address bar") is keyed by model, iOS version, imgw x imgh and rotate, and stored in mirror-image pixels. A resolver reads each phone's live geometry from /device/get and refuses to fan a coordinate out to any phone whose space differs from the master's. Templates are authored by cropping raw BMP frames from /pic/screenshot, so the author's pixel is literally the pixel /mouse/click receives.

This encodes the single most expensive trap measured in the project: using iOS logical points (414 x 896) where the kernel wants mirror pixels (500 x 1080 on these XRs). Only /device/get exposes imgw and imgh at all, and the Phonefarm device record does not carry them, so making the space an explicit registry key is the difference between a script that ports across models and one that silently mistaps.

How

  1. get_device_list /device/get — read imgw, imgh, width, height, model, version, rotate, state, gid and location_crc per record; live-probed here as two iPhone11,8 on iOS 18.7.10, imgw 500 x imgh 1080, physical 414 x 896
  2. dev_rotate ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — invalidate a cached space entry on dev_rotate (orientation changed) and on dev_change (name, group, binding or calibration changed by any client); Phonefarm has dev_rotate but no dev_change
  3. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot — author a template from a full raw frame (binary=true), or add rect=[l,t,r,b] to crop and save_path=<dir> to have the kernel write the crop and return its path in data.image; record name, model, version, imgw, imgh, rotate, x, y and the crop file
  4. none none (client-side) — resolve at run time as registry[model, iOS major, imgw x imgh, rotate], and on a miss fail the job rather than falling back to another entry; there is no kernel-side check that a coordinate belongs to the device it is sent to
  5. none /device/get + /config/usb/get — fan-out guard: build the comma id list only from phones whose geometry equals the master's, whose state != 0, whose location_crc is non-empty, and whose board reads state 2
  6. send_key /key/sendkey — normalize with fn_key=WIN+h twice before applying a page-one template; the newer fn_key=Home exists only for iOS 26.1 and later and needs kernel 2026.2.27, so WIN+h is correct on these XRs
  7. mouse_reset_pos, mouse_move /mouse/reset, /mouse/move, /pic/screenshot — drift probe: reset, move to the template point, then take the mean absolute pixel difference in a roughly 40 px box around it; log offsets over about 5 px as needing calibration
  8. mouse_collection_* /device/collection/mouse, /device/collection/mouse/save, /device/set — remediate a drifted phone with cmd=1 (0 query, 2 stop), watch the collection_mouse callback, save with a describe remark, then write location_crc back
  9. set_airplay_mode /config/imserver/get, /device/airplay/set — freeze the space the templates were authored in: keep air_play_ratio fixed globally and leave per-device air_ratio at 0

Needs

  • XP kernel reachable on 127.0.0.1:9911 with IMConsole.exe running; with IMService alone both phones read state 0 and the board list was empty.
  • air_play_ratio fixed globally and per-device air_ratio left at 0, or the whole template set rebuilt whenever either changes.
  • Templates authored per phone wherever home-screen layouts differ. The two XRs on this rack have different home screens and wallpapers, so a shared page-one coordinate is not a shared target.
  • Phone-side input settings for the drift probe to mean anything: AssistiveTouch on at maximum tracking sensitivity, Trackpad and Mouse tracking speed at maximum, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock. None is queryable.
  • A client-side decoder for bottom-up 24-bit BMP and a mean absolute difference routine. There is no server-side compare.

Watch out

  • Three of the nine steps rest on things never exercised on this rig. The WebSocket bus and its dev_rotate and dev_change callbacks were never opened, so cache invalidation on rotate is a paper design; ship a periodic /device/get poll every 30 to 60 s as a fallback in case a dead socket silently freezes the cache.
  • rect and save_path on /pic/screenshot are documented but were never live-probed. Only the plain full-frame binary=true capture was measured (2 ms, 1,620,054 bytes). Verify them before building the authoring tool on them; the fallback of full frame plus client-side crop works but pays the full 1.6 MB transfer.
  • Whether imgw and imgh swap when rotate flips to 1 is stated nowhere in the XP docs. Re-read /device/get after a rotation instead of transposing the cached pair, which means the registry key cannot be computed offline from one portrait pair.
  • Landscape behavior is also affected by the kernel-wide flip_right ("horizontal screen flip right mode"). If it is ever changed it belongs in the registry key, and it applies live with no restart.
  • A phone with an empty or uncollected location_crc returns data.code 11, no mouse parameters. The resolver should check that field before adding a phone to any fan-out list, not only geometry equality.
  • Calibration remediation is a hard human-in-the-loop step, not an API gap a retry fixes: the XP docs never publish the phone-side collection URL, so starting a collection needs the vendor console's QR code and a person holding the phone. Budget a manual queue; drift correction cannot run unattended overnight.
  • The pointer-dot box diff is only valid once the phone's AirPlay stream has produced a new frame. On the slow twin at 4.5 fps the probe must wait about 220 ms or more, or it reads the pre-move frame and reports a false "needs calibration".
  • There is no OCR or image-search fallback on this rig to re-find a moved element: /api/pic/ocr answers data.code 28, plug-in not connected, and image search is presumed equally absent. A stale template fails blind. Keep the crop so a client-side matcher can be added later.
  • Because /mouse/click returns code 0 for a coordinate that lands nowhere useful, a bug in the registry itself (wrong crop, stale cache) is indistinguishable from a genuinely drifted phone until the box-diff check runs. The registry's correctness rests entirely on its own client-side test coverage.
  • The kernel returns BMP by default or JPEG, nothing else, so a PNG template store re-encodes client-side.
  • Templates are per model, per iOS major, per ratio. An iOS update can move elements without changing any other component of the key, so re-author after updates.
  • The API has no authentication, so any LAN host can move the same phone's pointer while a probe is running and corrupt the measurement. Single-flight the probe per phone.

Scale

Resolution is an O(1) dictionary lookup with no kernel round trip. The only kernel cost is one /device/get at start plus invalidations. Authoring is a one-time cost per combination of model, iOS major, geometry and rotation, one capture of roughly 2 to 40 ms plus a human placing the crop, and this two-XR rig needs one combination since both phones share model, iOS and ratio.
