The recurring cost is the drift probe: reset plus move (worst case about 600 ms for a full 1080 px jump, usually far less because template points are local) plus a 2 ms capture plus the diff, roughly 0.7 to 1.3 s per phone end to end. Phones are independent, ten concurrent pollers having measured 512 req/s at p50 3 ms, so a full-rack drift sweep across all 19 boards run in parallel finishes in under two seconds of wall time rather than 19 times that. The practical ceiling is hub capacity, not this feature's software cost.

The control plane: events, and actions that prove themselves

Two components sit under everything else in a console built on this kernel. One owns the single WebSocket and the rack's cached state. The other owns the rule that no input is believed until a frame proves it landed. Both are buildable today on documented XP calls, and both carry the same honest gap: the socket itself was never opened during the 10 September probe.

WebSocket event bus: msgid-correlated RPC plus broadcast state cache

Native APIWith caveats

One long-lived client on ws://<pc>:9911/api doing two jobs. As an RPC channel it sends the identical {"fun":"/path","msgid":n,"data":{...}} envelope the HTTP POST form uses, keeps a pending map from msgid to promise, and resolves on the reply whose msgid matches. As a state cache it consumes the kernel's unsolicited broadcasts into an in-memory rack model that every other component reads instead of polling on a timer.

Two signals exist only on this socket. error_push carries {call_fun, message} and is the single asynchronous notice that an input call failed at the board. im_connect's data.ver is the only kernel-version readout in the entire XP API, since there is no HTTP version endpoint. user_info's dev_online_num against total_license is likewise the only way to see a license cap before phones start being refused.

How

  1. connect ws://host:9911/clinet ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — open the socket and record data.ver from the im_connect callback; Phonefarm's path is literally /clinet and its HTTP lives on 9912, neither of which applies here, and 9912 is closed on this rig
  2. get_device_list / get_group_list / get_usb_list /device/get, /device/group/get, /config/usb/get, /config/imserver/get — subscribe first, buffer what arrives, then prime the cache with these four and apply the buffer over the snapshot
  3. same envelope, different fun names {"fun":"/mouse/click","msgid":17,"data":{...}} — send any request over the socket with a monotonic msgid; every XP endpoint page states that the WebSocket accepts the same JSON, and bare Phonefarm-style names are rejected with HTTP 500
  4. dev_connect / dev_disconnect / dev_rotate dev_connect, dev_disconnect, dev_rotate, dev_change, dev_delete — patch device state; XP nests the record in data.list[] where Phonefarm sent a bare record, renames fields (air_handle, air_pid, srv_name, user_name, plus imgw/imgh, uid, gname, uver, integer gid), and sends dev_delete as an array of deviceid strings
  5. usb_change {state, vpid} usb_change — patch control-channel state from data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}] with the event type in data.code: 19 hardware connected to computer, 20 disconnected, 12 hardware connected to phone
  6. set_group / del_group group_change, group_delete — patch groups, noting that group_change carries data.id and data.name at the top level of data and not a list (the /device/group/set response is the one returning data.list), while group_delete does carry a list of deleted gids
  7. none error_push, im_log, user_info, logout, im_config_change, dev_sort_change — route operational signals; error_push has no Phonefarm counterpart, im_log carries notices such as "not logged in, going online not allowed", and user_info arrives at login and every 30 s with pass, license counts, device counts, overdue time and user state
  8. mouse_collection_cfg_ret collection_mouse, airplay_connect_log, restart_log — track long-running operations; collection_mouse folds Phonefarm's two callbacks into one code space (0 success, 4 failed, 5 a device is collecting, 6 this id is not, 8 scan code opened, 9 entered the collection page, 14 start working, 21 at work)
  9. loop_device_screenshot none, poll GET /api/pic/screenshot — keep frames off this socket; XP documents no push frame stream and no binary frame protocol, and binary=true returns raw bytes instead of a JSON envelope, so its behavior over a JSON-framed socket is undefined
  10. none reopen ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — reconnect and re-prime on close; /imserver/restart drops the socket by design, and no resume token or replay buffer is documented

Needs

  • XP path style on 9911 only. Phonefarm's /clinet path and bare fun names are rejected by this kernel with HTTP 500 and a Delphi-flavored "List index out of bounds (1)" message, and 9912 is closed.
  • A client that ignores message strings and branches on data.code. This build returns Chinese text.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in, or the primed cache is empty.
  • Only documented paths. Guessed ones return 404 with a JSON-shaped body you might otherwise parse as a real error; /config/get, /user/get, /shortcut/get and /device/model/get all 404'd here.

Watch out

  • Documented, unprobed. Every callback shape above comes from the vendor doc's examples, not from this rig; only the four HTTP priming endpoints were actually hit on 10 September. Require a live capture (open the socket, trigger one connect and disconnect, one usb_change via /device/usb/restart, one deliberate /mouse/down failure) before any component trusts the cache in production.
  • msgid correlation is assumed to allow arbitrary concurrent requests, but nothing in the doc or the probe confirms the kernel replies out of order under load. A single-threaded kernel, which the TStringList error on the HTTP side is consistent with, may simply serialize and echo the msgid. Treat msgid matching as correct but possibly serialized until a burst test proves otherwise, and do not architect for socket-level parallelism.
  • No heartbeat or keepalive interval is documented. user_info every 30 s is a message-level heartbeat only while the client is logged in and healthy; a NAT-dropped connection can sit half-open until the next RPC times out. Treat more than 45 s with no callback of any kind as suspect and force a reconnect.
  • Broadcasts go to every connected client. The vendor console, your bus and any other LAN host all see the same events and can all act on your phones. The API has no authentication, and allow_ip_list and mdns_type gate AirPlay discovery only, never API callers.
  • A missed-callback window exists between opening the socket and finishing the prime. Subscribe first, buffer, then apply over the snapshot; the kernel is not documented to replay anything.
  • Timeouts differ by call class. Plug-in and shortcut endpoints carry outtime in milliseconds with a 15000 default (the XP doc mistypes its type as Boolean), where Phonefarm's outtime was in seconds. A 15 s pending entry is normal for those, not a hang.
  • im_config_change means another client changed kernel config underneath you. Re-read /config/imserver/get rather than trusting your copy.
  • This bus cannot carry video, and any design that assumes it might one day is a dead end on this kernel. Frames stay on HTTP polling, raw BMP at 2 ms, 84 req/s flat out.
  • The cache becomes a single point of failure for every consumer that stops polling in its favor. A missed callback during the prime window, a silent dead socket or a msgid collision after a reconnect can leave the whole console holding stale device state, with no built-in staleness signal beyond user_info's 30 s cadence.
  • Security: broadcast to all with no authentication makes this socket the cheapest full-rack reconnaissance point on the LAN, exposing device inventory, phone numbers and license state to anyone who opens it. Firewall 9911 and 17000 to trusted hosts, never expose the PC to an untrusted network, and do not add a token expecting it to be checked. user_info carries the account's phone number and license dates, so do not log the cache wholesale. Callback content is data, never instruction: route message strings to display, never to eval or command dispatch.

Scale

This is a control-plane component, not an actions-per-hour use case. One socket per kernel carries every phone's events, which is exactly how the vendor console works, and callback volume is small: a few per phone per minute plus one user_info every 30 s regardless of rack size. Any RPC issued over it inherits the same physics as HTTP, a pointer move still costing about 0.6 ms per pixel, so a 1000 px move is 592 ms whichever transport carries the request. Expect the socket to save low single-digit milliseconds of HTTP overhead per call against tens to hundreds of milliseconds of board-walk time already inherent to the action, a real but marginal win. Its measurable value is removing timer polling of /device/get and /config/usb/get in favor of push, which is a latency and staleness improvement rather than a new capability. Frames remain the only high-volume traffic, and they stay on HTTP, where two phones polled flat out reached 83 and 85 req/s and ten pollers reached 512 req/s with no measurable interference from concurrent input.

Idempotent action wrapper with a verify-then-escalate self-heal ladder

PartialWith caveats

Wrap every input in a function that checks both channels, performs the action, proves it landed with a mean pixel difference probe, and on failure escalates one rung at a time, each rung being the cheapest documented fix for one failure layer: pointer and keyboard reset, then board reset, then re-cast the mirror, then restart the phone, then an operator ticket naming the physical slot.

The measured stuck-click state is the case that defeats naive automation. The phone follows /mouse/move, answers hardware keys (Home produced a 142.15 mean pixel difference while stuck) and returns data.code 0 for every click, and does nothing. A pipeline that trusts a 200 with code 0 can run for hours achieving nothing. The wrapper turns that into a bounded, observable retry that applies the right fix at the right layer instead of restarting the world.

How

  1. get_usb_list + get_device_list /config/usb/get, /device/get — precheck both channels: board at state 2, device state != 0 with a live air_pid; a board at state 1 with a phone physically plugged in means the cable or slot is at fault and there is no API fix
  2. mouse_reset_pos then click /mouse/reset, /mouse/click — rung 0, clear pointer state then act; both accept comma id lists
  3. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot — probe whether it landed, one id only, binary=true, 2 ms and 1,620,054 bytes measured; whole-frame mean absolute difference over 20 means it reacted (141.96 for a landed click), under 1 means nothing happened (0.09 stuck, 0.02 to 0.03 idle)
  4. key_release_all + mouse_up + mouse_reset_pos /key/upall, /mouse/up, /mouse/reset — rung 1, release stuck keys and buttons and retry once; this targets an interrupted chord or an abandoned drag and will not fix the stuck-click state on its own
  5. restart_usb /device/usb/restart — rung 2, reset the control board at both ends; the id is vid|pid (doc example 720D|F735), not the deviceid and not the 8-character uid, and the pipe must be URL-encoded on GET
  6. discon_airplay then auto_connect_screen /device/airplay/disconnect, /device/airplay/connect — rung 3, rebuild the video channel; XP has no force flag, so an explicit disconnect first is the documented substitute, and /device/airplay/connect/all exists for whole-rack recovery
  7. restart_device /device/restart | /shortcut/switch/device | /key/sendkey — rung 4 by three routes: the kernel restart with restart_log progress, the Shortcut route (state=0 shutdown, state=1 restart, iOS 15 and later, comma id list), or the CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r hotkey
  8. none none (Windows PnP, not the API) — rung 5, open a ticket with the physical slot; hub plus port is the only stable label, three 7-port hubs (VID 1A40 PID 0201), 19 of 21 slots populated, the two live phones on hub 0010 ports 2 and 3, and the API exposes no topology at all

Needs

  • The WebSocket event bus for usb_change, airplay_connect_log, restart_log and error_push. Rungs 2 to 4 have no synchronous completion signal, so without the socket you are guessing.
  • A repair queue separate from the work queue, because rungs 2 to 4 take a phone out of the pool for seconds up to roughly 90 s.
  • For rung 4 via Shortcut: iMouse Shortcut installed with the kernel IP edited in, run once with every permission allowed, bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, iOS 15 or later. Via hotkey: Full Keyboard Access on.
  • A decision about what happens after a restart. The phone boots to the lock screen, mirroring drops, and a passcode-locked phone cannot be unlocked by this automation. Set auto_connect in /config/imserver/set or call /device/airplay/connect explicitly, and expect to strand passcode phones for a human.
  • A probe of the plug-in state. This rig has no OCR plug-in (/api/pic/ocr answers data.code 28) and image-search status is unknown; assume absent.

Watch out

  • Rungs 0 to 2 are documented XP calls with no plug-in dependency and are usable today. Rungs 3 and 4 are documented but unverified here: the XP doc never states a plug-in requirement for /device/airplay/connect or /device/restart, yet its code table carries 15 "no coordinates" and 28 "plug-in not connected", and the Phonefarm sibling explicitly required OCR plus image search for the equivalent calls. That is inferred from doc silence, not confirmed absence of a dependency, so treat both rungs as expected to fail until probed and make the ladder fall through to a human rather than loop.
  • Rungs 3 and 4 depend architecturally on the WebSocket bus for their completion signals, and that bus is itself unverified on this rig. Today, over HTTP alone, those rungs are fire and hope exactly like the Phonefarm predecessor, because /device/airplay/connect returns before the cast completes and there is no synchronous alternative.
  • The "over 20 means it reacted" threshold is generalized from two data points, both large high-contrast transitions. A tap that only toggles a checkbox, a keyboard key or a low-contrast control can produce a whole-frame mean under 20 and be misclassified as stuck, triggering a destructive escalation for an action that actually succeeded. Calibrate per action class with a box diff around the expected change, not one global whole-frame constant.
  • The probe cannot catch a tap that landed 30 px off target, and whether /mouse/reset corrects a drifted pointer is explicitly unverified; it is confirmed only to clear the stuck-click state. Drift needs a positional check.
  • /device/usb/restart is addressed by VID and PID, not deviceid. Passing a deviceid is a silent no-op class of bug.
  • Rung 2's precheck, and the whole state-2 gate, rest on the state field of /config/usb/get, which is absent from the documented field table and whose meaning is reconstructed from the usb_change code table and this rig's measurements. A kernel update could change it silently, producing wrong routing decisions with no error. Monitor it rather than treating it as a contract.
  • The 20 then 19 then 12 usb_change sequence after a board reset is inferred from the documented code meanings, not stated. Treat any of the three arriving as progress rather than requiring that order.
  • Restarting a passcode-locked phone strands it on the lock screen, and screenshot verification is useless during the reboot because the mirror is gone. Use the callback plus a reachability check plus /device/get state instead, and give the queue a terminal "needs human" state distinct from "retry eligible", or the ladder will re-strand the same locked phone forever and consume repair slots.
  • Give the ladder an explicit numeric backoff and circuit breaker. Without a cap on escalations per phone per hour, a flapping fault such as a marginal cable can cycle a phone through rungs 2 to 4 repeatedly at 60 to 90 s of downtime each, degrading a healthy-looking rack far more than the original fault would have.
  • Rung 0's reset forces a full-distance walk on the next move, up to about 650 ms. That is a per-phone latency budgeting concern for the calling code, not a rack-wide throughput limit, since the boards walk phones in parallel with no shared kernel bottleneck measured.
  • Every rung above 1 is destructive to some degree and should be rate-limited and logged. Do not use the restart rung to work around an app that is deliberately blocking automation; if the app signals a block, stop that job and surface it rather than escalating hardware. The kernel is unauthenticated, so these same destructive calls are available to anything on the subnet. Keep /device/del and /shortcut/album/clear out of any automatic ladder.

Scale

Rung 0, the steady-state guarded path, adds two roughly 2 ms raw-BMP captures per guarded action plus an occasional full-distance reset walk of up to about 650 ms, paid only when the target set changes or before a tap-critical sequence rather than per call. For typical UI taps 100 to 500 px apart, 78 to 300 ms each, one phone can sustain roughly 3,000 to 6,000 guarded actions per hour before verification overhead, and because /mouse/reset, /key/upall and /mouse/up all take comma-separated id lists, resetting an entire target set before a batch is one request that the board walks in parallel. There is no shared kernel bottleneck to contend for, ten concurrent pollers having reached 512 req/s at p50 3 ms with input traffic not slowing frame polling, so rungs 0 and 1 scale close to linearly with rack size. Escalations are the rare and expensive path: rung 2 costs seconds, rung 3 seconds to tens of seconds, rung 4 roughly 60 to 90 s plus a re-cast. At even a 2 percent fault rate needing rung 4, a 19-phone rack loses on the order of 0.4 phone-equivalents of throughput per restart cycle, which is why the separate repair queue is load-bearing rather than optional.

Boundaries: an authenticated gateway and a measured rack

The kernel has no authentication, no outbound calls, no audit trail and no metrics. Those four gaps are the same gap seen from four angles, and both components here exist to close it: one is the boundary anything outside the LAN must cross, the other is the instrument that tells you whether the rack is actually working.

Authenticated HTTP gateway so n8n, Zapier or Make can drive the rack

Plus external toolingWith caveats

A small reverse proxy in front of 9911 that requires a bearer token, exposes a handful of high-level verbs (health, tap-group, open-url-on, type-on, screenshot-of), translates each into XP path calls with the reset-and-verify wrapper, and returns re-encoded screenshots as URLs. It also holds the one WebSocket session and turns dev_disconnect, usb_change code 20, error_push and im_log into outbound webhooks, because the kernel can only push to connected clients and cannot call out on its own.

This is simultaneously the only safe integration surface and the authentication boundary the product lacks. The kernel's error model is also unusable by no-code tools: HTTP status is 200 for a failed operation, the real result is data.code against a 41-entry table, and messages come back in Chinese.

How

  1. none none (network layer) — run the gateway on the rack PC or a jump host on its own port, and restrict 9911 in the Windows firewall to localhost, the gateway host and the phone subnet, since the phones need 9911 for the Shortcut return path and 17000 plus mDNS for AirPlay
  2. get_device_list, get_usb_list /device/get, /config/usb/get — verb "health", merged per slot into control (board state 2 and a bound uid), video (device state non-zero with a live air_pid) and an observedFps the gateway computes itself
  3. shortcut (id 13) /shortcut/exec/url, /device/group/get-dev, /pic/screenshot — verb "open-url-on": resolve members, call the Shortcut with outtime=15000, then one capture per phone, re-encoded and uploaded, replying with the URLs
  4. mouse_reset_pos, click, get_device_screenshot /mouse/reset, /mouse/click, /pic/screenshot — verb "tap-group": registry resolves the coordinate in that group's space, reset the id list, click the id list, then diff per phone and reply {ok:[ids], failed:[ids]}, which is the whole reason the gateway is worth building
  5. send_key, send_text /key/sendkey, /shortcut/clipboard/set — verb "type-on": ASCII through key=, non-ASCII through the clipboard then fn_key=WIN+v
  6. dev_disconnect, usb_change ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — outbound: hold one socket and POST dev_disconnect, usb_change, error_push and im_log to the n8n webhook URL, since there is no outbound webhook facility anywhere in the API
  7. none msgid echoed on every request — audit: log every inbound call with token id, verb, resolved id list, msgid and before and after frame fingerprints, because the kernel keeps no audit trail of its own

Needs

  • A gateway process to write and run. This is external tooling, not an API feature.
  • n8n, Zapier or Make reachable from the gateway over outbound HTTPS. The rack PC must never be reachable from the internet.
  • Firewall rules that restrict 9911 and 17000 to localhost, the gateway host and the phone subnet.
  • Object storage or a static file host for screenshots, plus a BMP decoder and a PNG or JPEG encoder on the gateway.
  • For the open-url-on and Unicode type-on verbs: iMouse Shortcut installed on each phone, kernel IP edited in, bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in, or /device/get reports state 0 and no boards enumerate.
  • Per-group coordinate templates in the mirror-pixel space of those phones.

Watch out

  • The "health" verb as specified cannot detect the stuck-click state. A phone can be board state 2, bound, mirroring with a live air_pid, while /mouse/click produces a 0.09 mean pixel difference no-op and moves and hardware keys still work. Document control-ready and tap-verified as two different guarantees, or the gateway will report a broken phone as healthy.
  • observedFps computed by counting frames whose mean difference exceeds about 1 reads near zero on an idle screen, because a still screen produces almost no new frames. That is a property of content, not a health signal. Either drive a trivial 2 px move before sampling, or label an idle reading "not measured" rather than "slow phone".
  • air_fps in the device record is a configuration override where 0 means use the global value. It is not a measured rate, and reporting it as fps would be wrong.
  • The reset-and-verify wrapper only protects the click it immediately precedes. A multi-step verb can enter the stuck-click state between two of its own taps, so re-verify mid-sequence rather than resetting once at the top.
  • The kernel cannot initiate an outbound call, so the event-to-webhook bridge is a hard requirement for any "notify me when a phone drops" flow, and the gateway's single socket becomes an unmonitored single point of failure for all of it. Its reconnect and backoff behavior is unaddressed and was never live-tested.
  • Do not wire /config/user/login into any verb. It takes the vendor account phone and password, and this rig already stores that credential as reversible hex obfuscation in C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json, so a gateway that proxies it turns a token leak into an account compromise. Leave account login to the vendor console and the user.
  • Exclude destructive endpoints from the verb surface or gate them behind explicit human confirmation: /shortcut/album/clear, /shortcut/album/del, /shortcut/file/del, /device/del, /device/group/del, /device/restart, /shortcut/switch/device with state=0, /imserver/restart. An automation platform's retry can fire any of them twice.
  • Make every verb idempotent by requiring a client-supplied job id and deduplicating on it. The kernel offers no idempotency of its own; msgid is only a response-correlation token.
  • Diff with mean absolute pixel difference thresholded around 1, never byte or MD5 equality. Clock ticks, encoder noise and wallpaper parallax make an MD5 check report a false positive on every idle phone.
  • Verified actions are bounded by the phone's own AirPlay rate, about 28.9 new frames per second on one XR here and about 4.5 on its twin, so do not use a fixed timeout tuned to the fast phone.
  • /pic/screenshot takes a single id, so screenshot-of a group of N costs N concurrent requests.
  • Shortcut-dependent verbs are unverified on this rig and will fail with data.code 30, call timeout, if the Shortcut is not installed or its binding does not fire.
  • There is one HID pointer per phone, so multi-touch gestures such as pinch and rotate cannot be added to this design without a different mechanism.
  • A leaked gateway token is a full rack takeover, because the thing behind it authenticates nobody. Scope tokens per group, rate-limit them, rotate them and log every call. Over-firewalling is its own outage: blocking 9911 from the phone subnet silently breaks every Shortcut-backed verb, and blocking 17000 or UDP 5353 breaks mirroring. Verbs that type into third-party apps carry whatever terms-of-service exposure the underlying activity carries, amplified by a webhook that can fire a job thousands of times, so cap job rates at the gateway and stop a job when a platform returns a rate limit or an "action blocked" response. Finally, map data.code to HTTP status yourself (0 success, 2 not bound, 3 hardware not connected, 11 no mouse parameters, 25 offline, 26 screenshot failed, 28 plug-in not connected, 30 call timeout, 36 parameter error, 41 incompatible command) and never match on message text.

Scale

Per-verb latency is the right unit, not throughput. Gateway overhead on loopback is roughly 1 ms, and unverified control calls (health, reset, click, sendkey) are sub-10 ms at the kernel, scaling to something over 500 req/s aggregate across phones on the measured evidence. Verified verbs are bounded by the phone's own AirPlay source rate: a confident before-and-after diff needs roughly two fresh frames, about 70 to 140 ms on a 29 fps phone against about 450 to 700 ms on a 4.5 fps phone, on top of real iOS settle time the API cannot shorten. Practically, expect hundreds to low thousands of verified taps per hour per phone for real UI navigation, not the thousands the raw click latency alone would suggest. A URL open through the Shortcut is typically seconds and bounded by outtime. Screenshots are 1,620,054 bytes raw at 2 ms each; re-encode on the gateway rather than paying the kernel's 40.5 ms JPEG path and its roughly 21 req/s cap. One WebSocket session carries every callback for the whole rack.

Observability stack: frame archive, per-phone metrics and a rack SLO

Plus external toolingWith caveats

A collector process that holds one WebSocket and turns broadcasts into events, polls each phone's raw BMP, keeps only frames whose mean difference from the last kept frame exceeds a threshold, re-encodes client-side and uploads keyed by deviceid and time, and exports metrics: video state and air_pid from /device/get, control state from the board, new frames per second from the diff meter, a pointer probe result, error_push counts labeled by call_fun, license headroom from user_info, and kernel version and liveness from im_connect. The SLO is the fraction of phones simultaneously control-ready, video-ready and pointer-probe-good.

Every real trap in this project was found by measuring, and none of them is exposed as a kernel metric: that one XR delivers about 29 new frames per second while its identical twin delivers about 4.5, that a phone can accept moves and hardware keys while silently swallowing every tap, that board state and mirroring state are two independent channels. Without a diff-based frame meter and a scheduled pointer probe, a half-dead rack looks healthy in the vendor console.

How

  1. dev_* / usb_change callbacks ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — one socket for all broadcasts; the XP envelope is {fun, status:200, message, msgid, data:{list:[...], code, id, message}} with device records inside data.list, and callbacks are WebSocket-only, with no HTTP long-poll or event feed
  2. get_device_list /device/get — video-state gauge from state (0 not online, non-zero online) plus air_pid, measured here as the AirplayMirroring.exe PID and the most reliable live proof that mirroring is up
  3. get_usb_list /config/usb/get — control-state gauge from data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}], where 1 is a board on the PC with no phone and 2 is a board with a phone attached
  4. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot — frame meter at a fixed period, since deriving the interval from observed frame gaps was measured to decay 23 fps to 16.5 fps through positive feedback
  5. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot with rect and save_path — archive with dedupe: keep a frame only when its mean difference against the last kept frame exceeds about 5, then re-encode client-side; rect crops server-side for a cheap detector and save_path writes to disk, two XP-only options the Phonefarm edition lacks
  6. mouse_reset_pos + mouse_move /mouse/reset, /mouse/move — scheduled control probe, reading a box diff of 1.4 to 9.8 around the commanded coordinate against an idle floor of 0.02, which a whole-frame diff cannot see
  7. none error_push, im_log, user_info, /config/user/info — error and license telemetry; a counter labeled by call_fun is genuinely new information, and user_info arrives at login and every 30 s with license and device counts
  8. get_airplaysrvnum im_connect (data.ver) — kernel identity and liveness; this is the only source of the kernel version in XP, so export it as an info metric and set kernel_up=0 on socket close
  9. derived /config/usb/get + /device/get + the probe — the SLO: phones with control state (board at 2 and the phone bound to that board's uid) and video state (device state non-zero with a live air_pid) and a good pointer probe, over total enrolled; the rack has been observed with 13 boards carrying phones while only one phone was mirroring

Needs

  • A metrics scraper and an object-storage endpoint, both external. The scraper must reach the collector, never the kernel, so 9911 stays closed to everything but the collector host.
  • Buffer reuse in the poller. Each raw frame exceeds the 85 KB .NET Large Object Heap threshold; without reuse this measured 488 MB/s of allocation and 496 gen-2 collections per 8 s, against 2.9 MB/s and zero to one with reuse.
  • A board lease shared with the job queue, so a probe never moves the pointer during a human-driven or scripted session.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in, or every gauge reads zero for the wrong reason.
  • A WebSocket client that reconnects. All event telemetry is socket-only.

Watch out

  • The 19-phone extrapolation (190 req/s, roughly 300 MB/s) is bandwidth-only math that ignores client-side cost: diffing nineteen concurrent 1.6 MB BMPs at 10 Hz is 300 MB/s of decode and compare work inside the collector. The only measured concurrency point is ten pollers against the same two devices, not 19 distinct AirPlay sources feeding 19 diff buffers. Pilot at four to six phones and measure CPU and GC before committing.
  • A uniform 10 Hz poll is partly self-defeating. On the 4.5 fps phone roughly 55 percent of polls return the identical previous frame. Make the rect-cropped cheap detector the default poll and reserve full frames for archive-on-trigger, or the fast and slow phones share one period tuned for neither.
  • state in /config/usb/get, and air_pid and air_handle in /device/get, are present in live responses but absent from the vendor's field tables. They are safe as liveness evidence and unsafe as a stable contract, so alarm loudly if they ever vanish from a response, since that would zero both readiness gauges at once.
  • The pointer probe mutates the rig: /mouse/reset snaps the pointer to 0,0 and /mouse/move walks it. Gate it on the lease, keep hops short, and when the lease is held for a whole scrape interval report unknown rather than not-ready, or every busy phone fails the SLO purely from lease contention.
  • The box-diff signal was validated on two XRs with one particular pointer rendering. A different model or iOS build could render the cursor differently, or not at all if AssistiveTouch is off, and silently break the probe. Calibrate the threshold per device model.
  • new_frames_per_second is a property of the phone's own Wi-Fi and AirPlay link as much as of the kernel, and the vendor console hits the same wall. Alert on a drop relative to each phone's own baseline, never on a single global threshold.
  • Never compare frames by MD5 or byte equality. An untouched mirrored phone changes every frame; threshold the mean absolute difference instead, under about 1 being nothing and a real reaction 20 to 160.
  • License headroom must read both total_license and local_total_license, and user_state 1 against anything else distinguishes a formal license from a trial.
  • Size archive storage from the kept-frame rate after dedupe, not the raw poll rate. An idle rack approaches zero, but a rack under active automation can sustain close to each phone's native rate, up to about 29 kept frames per second on a fast phone, times however many phones are active at once. Budget for the worst case.
  • Archived frames contain whatever is on the phone, including signed-in accounts, message previews and one-time codes, so the bucket is as sensitive as the devices. Encrypt it, restrict it, set retention. Exposing metrics means exposing a process that can drive the rack, so scrape the collector and never open 9911 to a remote scraper. A probe firing during an operator's session will visibly move their pointer. And do not read C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json for inventory: it holds the account password under trivially reversible obfuscation.

Scale

Measured headroom: raw BMP capture at p50 2.0 ms when paced at 50 ms, 84 req/s flat out at p50 12.7 ms per phone, 1,620,054 bytes per frame. Phones are independent, two concurrent pollers reaching 83 and 85 req/s at p50 3 ms each, identical to either alone, and ten reaching 512 req/s aggregate at p50 3 ms with a worst p95 of 142 ms. A 30 fps thumbnail wall cost the master poller nothing (17.7 fps at p50 31.9 ms with the wall off against 17.6 fps at p50 32.3 ms with it on), and input and screenshot traffic do not interfere in either direction. The probe costs one reset, one short move (about 1 ms for a 2 px hop) and two 2 ms captures per phone per interval. Today's two phones sit comfortably inside that envelope. Scaling to all 19 boards at a uniform 10 Hz raw poll is an untested extrapolation; a safer default is adaptive rect-cropped polling per phone at 3 to 5 Hz with full frames only on a detected change or a slow archive cadence, which at 19 phones is about 95 req/s for the cheap check plus one 1.6 MB frame only when something actually changed. Archive volume after dedupe is near zero on idle phones and bounded by the source rate under motion, so cap the kept-frame rate per phone.

Further out: the rack as a render lab

The last entry in this part is the one that uses the rack for something other than driving accounts. It is worth reading even if you never build it, because it is the clearest case where the hardware's real advantage, genuine iOS devices with a live video channel, is the product rather than a means to one.

Campaign send to on-device render proof to CRM event loop

Plus external toolingWith caveats

A webhook from the marketing platform reaches an n8n or gateway bridge, which drives a small QA group of real iPhones: open the tracked link in Safari through the Shortcut, or open Mail and Messages by tapping registry coordinates, capture the rendered screen as raw BMP, scroll below the fold, then upload the frames and post a "rendered on iPhone XR, iOS 18.7.10" event with image URLs back to the CRM profile or a Slack channel.

Emulator-based inbox previews do not reproduce iOS Mail dark mode, Messages link-preview rendering or Safari landing-page behavior on a real 414 x 896 XR. The rack already owns the two things such a service sells. Every rack-side call is a documented XP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:9911; the CRM, the bridge and the object store are entirely outside the kernel, which never holds a CRM credential.

How

  1. get_group_list / get_device_list /device/group/get-dev — ingest the send event and resolve the QA target set, reading imgw and imgh per phone, because every later coordinate is a mirror pixel (500 x 1080) and not the 414 x 896 in width and height
  2. mouse_reset_pos /mouse/reset — clear the stuck-click state across the whole target set before any tap; measured, /mouse/up does not clear it and reset does, and it stays cleared
  3. send_key fn_key=WIN+h /key/sendkey — normalize every phone to home page one with two presses; requires Full Keyboard Access on the phone, which is invisible to the API
  4. shortcut#13 /shortcut/exec/url — web channel: open the tracked landing page, with outtime in milliseconds (default 15000) rather than the seconds Phonefarm used; the only step that depends on the iMouse Shortcut being installed and bound
  5. click /mouse/click — email and SMS channel: open Mail or Messages and the top message row from registry coordinates, button numeric, time=<ms> for a long press
  6. mouse_wheel / swipe /mouse/wheel, /mouse/swipe — scroll below the fold; the wheel takes direction, len 1 to 127 and number, and moves no pointer, so prefer it, while swipe takes len as a fraction plus stepping (spelled "steping" in the doc's JSON), step_sleep and brake
  7. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot — capture the rendered frame, one request per phone run concurrently, binary=true giving raw bytes with no JSON at 2.0 ms and exactly 1,620,054 bytes, with rect, jpg and save_path available
  8. send_key fn_key + click /key/sendkey fn_key=ControlBar, /mouse/click — dark and light variants; there is no API for the iOS appearance setting, so reaching dark mode still means a long press on the brightness slider then a tap on the tile, both from the registry
  9. get_device_screenshot (x2) /pic/screenshot before and after — verify something actually rendered using mean absolute pixel difference, never MD5, and budget for the source frame rate before claiming proof
  10. send_key fn_key=WIN+h /key/sendkey, /shortcut/clipboard/set — clean up and post the CRM event; uploads and the CRM write are entirely external, and credentials live in the bridge because the kernel has no auth and no secret store

Needs

  • A webhook bridge plus a token-scoped gateway in front of 9911. The kernel has no authentication of its own, so the bridge is also the access control.
  • Object storage for the frames and CRM API credentials, both held by the bridge and never by IMService.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in.
  • Per phone: the board bound with vid and pid set together, one device per binding call, board state 2, a non-empty location_crc (B0DBD800 here, a shared-library profile), and device state non-zero with a live air_pid.
  • Phone-side accessibility settings, none of them queryable: AssistiveTouch at maximum tracking sensitivity, Full Keyboard Access on, tracking speed at maximum, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock.
  • For the URL channel only: the iMouse Shortcut installed, kernel IP edited in, run once with all permissions granted, bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, and the phone able to reach 9911.
  • A test mailbox and number on the QA phones, enrolled in the CRM's own test segment, on accounts the operator owns.
  • A per-model, per-iOS coordinate registry for Mail and Messages, maintained by hand, because no server-side OCR or template matching is available here.

Watch out

  • The rack-side half is fully native XP. The loop only closes with external pieces the kernel cannot provide.
  • The Safari channel depends on the Shortcut, which is not confirmed installed here. The cheapest single probe is /shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0, which should return data.code 0 with data.text equal to the device record's IP; data.code 30 means the hotkey never launched the Shortcut.
  • The Mail and Messages channels have no element lookup at all on this rig. Locating the top message row means fixed registry coordinates or template matching written into your own client. Installing the vendor OCR and OpenCV plug-ins, and setting ocr_num and opencv_num, which need a kernel restart, would move this to /pic/find-text or /pic/find-image-cv.
  • Mail's inbox row position shifts with unread state, and opening a message marks it read, so the "top row" template drifts between runs. Prefer the tracked-URL channel where the campaign offers one.
  • One reset at job start is not enough. The stuck-click state can occur at any point, so a later tap, the Mail or Messages tap or the long press on the brightness slider, can silently no-op and be misreported as "rendered". Reset, or at minimum diff, immediately before every tap-critical step.
  • Verification inherits the AirPlay asymmetry: on the 4.5 fps XR a before-and-after pair needs about 450 ms or more just for a second fresh frame to exist, before any real render time. A short timeout tuned to the fast phone produces false "nothing rendered" verdicts on the slow one.
  • The wheel avoids the pointer walk, but the taps and the long press do not, so chaining several 400 px or longer moves inside one job adds hundreds of milliseconds of board time on top of the settle wait.
  • Dark-mode toggling has no API and depends on a long press then a tap on a slider whose position can shift with iOS version and layout. Treat dedicated per-mode phones, one permanently light and one permanently dark, as the default design rather than the fallback.
  • /pic/screenshot accepts one id, there is no multi-device capture, and there is no push frame stream in XP; the Phonefarm loop_device_screenshot binary protocol has no equivalent here.
  • Screenshots of a rendered marketing email or SMS contain real recipient data: subject lines, personalization, numbers in Messages threads. Treat the bucket as sensitive, set retention, and do not reuse a shared test mailbox or number, or prior test data leaks into new captures.
  • Repeatedly hitting the same tracked link from the same LAN address on a fixed cadence can trip the destination's own bot and rate-limit heuristics even though the devices are genuine. That is a real detection risk distinct from the terms-of-service argument for using owned devices and accounts, and the correct response to a rate limit or a block page is to stop the job and surface it.
  • Never use jpg=true in the loop. It costs 40.5 ms and caps at roughly 21 req/s; encode client-side.
  • The two failure modes that masquerade as "the campaign broke" are the silent stuck-click state, fixed only by /mouse/reset, and a phone-side accessibility setting being off. Neither is visible over the API, so a per-phone input self-test belongs in the job's preflight.

Scale

Per phone the wall-clock cost is app launch and render settle measured in seconds, not API time: clicks and key presses are sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds, a raw capture is 2 ms, and a wheel scroll is trivial. A realistic light-plus-dark render-proof cycle, normalize, open the channel, scroll, capture, verify, toggle appearance, capture, verify, clean up, is roughly 10 to 20 s on the fast phone and 20 to 40 s or more on the slow one once verification waits are budgeted honestly, giving on the order of 100 to 300 render jobs per hour per phone. Frame capture does not contend: two pollers flat out gave 83 and 85 req/s each, ten gave 512 req/s aggregate at p50 3 ms, and input and screenshot traffic were measured not to interfere. Concurrency across phones is not kernel-limited, but concurrent AirPlay video for more than two phones is unverified on this rig, so treat phones per PC for this workflow as unproven above two until it is tested. Mirroring a click to N phones is one request that the board walks in parallel, but only where the layout is genuinely identical.

Hardening the control plane

Everything else in this section assumes something is standing between the world and port 9911. Nothing in the kernel provides that, so it is the first thing to build and the last thing to skip.

Security posture for an unauthenticated control plane, with emergency stop

Plus external toolingWith caveats

The XP kernel accepts any HTTP or WebSocket caller on 9911 with no authentication of any kind. There is no auth setting to turn on and no vendor fix, so every control lives at the network and gateway layer: phones and rack PC on a dedicated VLAN, Windows Firewall allowing 9911 only from localhost and one gateway host, and every human or machine call routed through a token-scoped gateway that keeps an append-only audit ledger and denies destructive endpoints by default. Bolted on top is a one-verb emergency stop that releases held keys, releases held mouse buttons, resets every pointer, and optionally blinds remote viewers, each as a single comma-list request for the whole rack. The mdns_type and allow_ip_list settings gate AirPlay discovery only, not the API, so they are defence in depth and nothing more.

How

  1. none no API involved. Network isolation. Phones and rack PC on their own VLAN or SSID with no route from the office network, with the gateway host the only peer permitted to reach 9911. This is the only control the kernel cannot ignore.
  2. none host firewall, ports confirmed from the docs and the live probe. Inbound 9911/TCP from 127.0.0.1 and the gateway IP only. That single rule covers both the HTTP API and the WebSocket, because XP serves /api for both on the same port. Allow 17000/TCP (air_play_port, default 17000 in /config/imserver/get, matching the live AirplayMirroring.exe listener) and 5353/UDP mDNS from the phone subnet only.
  3. none /config/imserver/set?mdns_type=1&allow_ip_list=["192.168.4.68","192.168.4.27"]. Narrow screencast discovery. Documented as "Screencast Discovery Rules" with allow_ip_list taking effect only when the rule is 1. Both are in the no-restart set, so they apply live and broadcast im_config_change to other clients.
  4. (policy layer, no kernel support) deny by default: /device/del, /device/group/del, /shortcut/album/clear, /shortcut/album/del, /shortcut/file/del, /config/user/logout, /imserver/restart, /device/restart, /shortcut/switch/device, /device/usb/restart. All of these exist, which is exactly why they need a gate. /shortcut/album/clear accepts a comma id list, so one request can wipe an album on every phone in the rack. /shortcut/switch/device?state=0 shuts a phone down on iOS 15 and later. The kernel offers no scopes, roles or rate limits at all.
  5. dev_delete / group_delete WS callbacks dev_delete, group_delete, dev_change, im_config_change, logout, im_log, error_push, dev_sort_change on ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api. Audit ledger. The kernel broadcasts these to every connected client when any client deletes a device, changes settings or takes one offline, which is what makes a second vendor console on the LAN visible to the ledger even though it bypasses the gateway entirely. Record token, verb, ids, msgid, args, resulting data.code and before and after frame hashes for gateway calls, plus every broadcast for everything else.
  6. key_release_all /key/upall?id=<every id, comma separated>. Emergency stop, keyboard. Releases all held keys, comma id list, no other parameters. One request for the whole rack.
  7. mouse_up /mouse/up?id=<all>&button=1. Emergency stop, mouse buttons. button is documented as "1 left button, 2 right button, 3 middle button, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 button", defaulting to left when empty. There is no /mouse/upall counterpart to /key/upall, so plan for one call per button your automation presses until the list behaviour is tested (see Watch out).
  8. mouse_reset_pos /mouse/reset?id=<all>. Emergency stop, pointer state. Comma id list. Measured on this rig, this is the only call that clears the silent stuck-click state, and /mouse/up does not, so reset is the load-bearing step of the stop rather than an afterthought. It also returns the pointer to 0,0.
  9. discon_airplay /device/airplay/disconnect?id=<all>. Optional: cut the video channel. Comma id list. Blinds anyone watching a mirror without touching the USB control channel, because the two channels are independent. Recovery is /device/airplay/connect?id=<ids> or /device/airplay/connect/all, with progress on the airplay_connect_log callback. If phones cannot see the receiver afterwards, /imserver/regmdns re-broadcasts it.
  10. restart_usb /device/usb/restart?id=720A|C241[,720A|C214]. Harder stop for a board that will not behave. Note the addressing difference from the Phonefarm edition: XP takes vid|pid, not the phone's deviceid and not the 8-character uid. Read vid and pid from /device/get or /config/usb/get. Expect usb_change callbacks with code 20, then 19, then 12.
  11. none /config/user/login, do NOT call from an integration. Secrets stay with the operator. This endpoint takes phone, password and utag in plaintext over an unauthenticated local API. Licence login belongs to the operator at the console over an operator-only path, never to a gateway or a script.

Needs

  • Administrative control of the LAN or VLAN and of Windows Firewall on the rack PC.
  • The token-scoped gateway process, the same one fronting the other integrations, with an append-only ledger store.
  • A WebSocket client inside the gateway holding ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api, so out-of-band kernel broadcasts land in the ledger.
  • An operator-only path, console or RDP, for licence login, kernel restarts and anything on the deny-list.
  • An inventory of every host that legitimately needs 9911, ideally exactly one.

Watch out

  • The emergency stop is three or four requests, not three. /key/upall, then /mouse/up once per button held, then /mouse/reset, plus /device/airplay/disconnect if you want to blind viewers.
  • The one-call-per-button reading is conservative but not confirmed either way. The button field says "up to 8 keys are supported", the same wording the id field uses for comma-list semantics elsewhere in the same document, and no example shows whether button accepts a list. Test /mouse/up?id=<all>&button=1,2 against a phone with both buttons held before finalising the script. If it releases both, the stop is one call shorter and you avoid maintaining an open-ended list of every button the automation might ever press.
  • Order the stop as key/upall, then mouse/up per button, then mouse/reset. That order is correct because /mouse/up does not clear the stuck-click state and /mouse/reset does. State plainly in the design that /mouse/reset's effect on a currently held-down button is unverified: the rig data confirms reset clears the silent stuck-click state and returns the pointer to 0,0, not that it releases a physically held mouse-down. Up before reset is the safe sequence for exactly that reason.
  • Nothing cancels an in-flight gesture. The board walks the pointer at roughly 0.6 ms per pixel, so a swipe or long move already dispatched keeps consuming board time for up to about 592 ms on a 1000 px stroke after the stop calls return 200. The emergency stop has a soft tail latency, not an instant cutoff, on whichever phone had a gesture in flight. This applies to any in-flight /mouse/move, not only to /mouse/swipe.
  • /device/usb/restart is not part of the fast stop path. Each restart triggers a full re-enumeration through usb_change codes 20, 19 and 12 before the board is control-ready, which takes seconds. Keep it in a separate "hard reset a misbehaving board" runbook.
  • mdns_type and allow_ip_list are screencast discovery rules, not API access control. The document's own description of values 1 and 2 is self-contradictory, so verify the behaviour on this build before relying on either.
  • Any use of /shortcut/* requires the phones themselves to reach 9911, which re-exposes the unauthenticated API to the phone subnet. Either accept that with a tightly scoped per-IP rule, or forgo the shortcut functions.
  • A second vendor console anywhere on the reachable subnet bypasses the gateway completely. The firewall rule is the only real control. The broadcast callbacks merely make the bypass visible after the fact.
  • Match every response on data.code, never on message text. The kernel replies in Chinese, guessed paths return a 404 with 接口不存在 rather than a structured error, and Phonefarm-style function names return HTTP 500 "List index out of bounds".
  • /imserver/restart and /config/user/logout are each one unauthenticated GET away from taking the whole rack offline. Keep both admin-scoped and expect the WebSocket to drop and every phone to need re-casting after a restart.
  • A VLAN posture assumes physical and network control the automation layer cannot verify. No endpoint confirms the rack is actually isolated, so the ledger can prove what happened through the gateway but never that no other path to 9911 exists. That is inherent to an API with no authentication, not a gap in the design.
  • Screenshots expose logged-in accounts and message contents. /shortcut/album/clear and the file and album delete calls are irreversible from the API's side. Several deny-list calls destroy data, so require an explicit admin scope plus an operator confirmation and never put them behind a single-click button. C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json stores the account password under reversible hex obfuscation: no tool should read it, print it, copy the scheme, or let a build carry it forward.

Scale

Firewall rules and a loopback gateway hop add no measurable latency, roughly 1 ms on loopback against a 2 ms raw capture and sub-millisecond input calls. The emergency stop is a fixed three to four comma-list requests regardless of phone count, because every input endpoint accepts an id list and the board walks all listed phones in parallel, so resetting 19 phones costs what resetting one costs. Each request is sub-10 ms on loopback given the measured input latencies of 0.5 to 11.7 ms p50 for small moves, so the request layer completes in well under 100 ms for the whole rack. The real bound is the uncancellable gesture tail of up to about 592 ms, and seconds more if a board restart is invoked. The exception to the flat cost is /device/usb/restart, which is addressed per board as vid|pid. Ledger volume is a few hundred rows per job plus the broadcast stream, which is low-rate except for user_info every 30 s.

Pricing the work before you run it

The rig's timing is dominated by two things that are invisible to an HTTP latency histogram: pointer distance and per-phone AirPlay frame production. A planning model that knows both is worth more than a faster client.

Throughput budget calculator built from the rig's measured constants

Native APIWith caveats

A client-side planning function that turns a job description, meaning step count, pointer distance per step, target phone set and verification policy, into a wall-clock estimate plus a kernel-load figure. It uses only constants measured on this rig: raw BMP capture at p50 2.0 ms when paced (12.7 ms and 84 req/s flat out, 1,620,054 bytes per frame), the JPEG variant at p50 40.5 ms with a hard cap near 21 req/s, the board's roughly 0.6 ms per pixel pointer walk, per-phone new-frame rate (28.9 fps on 192.168.4.68 against 4.5 fps on 192.168.4.27), and the fact that a comma-separated id list costs the longest single move rather than the sum. The model emits wall-clock per phone, rack wall-clock, requests per second, MB/s of frame traffic, and names the slowest phone from the device record's name and user_name fields.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get (optional id=a,b comma list). Returns data.list[] with imgw/imgh (500 x 1080 on these XRs, the space every distance in the model must use), width/height (414 x 896 logical points, not the input space), state (0 means offline), air_pid (a live AirplayMirroring PID is proof of mirroring), and the two name fields for the slow-phone callout.
  2. mouse_move GET /api/mouse/move?id=<ids>&x=&y=. Drive continuous motion so the frame-rate calibration measures something. Alternate two points 200 px apart, measured at 133 ms per move and identical for one phone or both. A still screen produces almost no new frames, so calibrating an idle phone measures nothing.
  3. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true. Poll raw frames for 5 s per phone to derive that phone's fps. The document states id "Multiple is not allowed", so this is one request per phone. Run one poller per phone concurrently: measured 83 and 85 req/s for two, 512 req/s total for ten. Do not add jpg=true, which costs p50 40.5 ms and caps near 21 req/s because the kernel re-encodes.
  4. none (client-side analysis) none, the XP kernel exposes no frame-change or fps field. Count new frames by mean absolute pixel difference, not byte equality. Threshold above 1 on the 0 to 255 scale: idle measures 0.02 to 0.03, a real reaction 20 to 160. MD5 or byte comparison reports "changed" on an untouched phone and has already produced one wrong conclusion in this project.
  5. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=&y=&button=1&time=<ms>. Price one step. time is the delay between pressing and popping up, in milliseconds, handled internally if omitted, and that is the hold term. t_step = 0.6 ms x distance_px + hold + settle + captures. Use 2.0 ms per capture when the poller is paced near 50 ms and 12.7 ms when it is saturating.
  6. click / swipe / mouse_move with devlist same endpoints with id=<id1>,<id2>,.... Price the fan-out as a maximum, not a sum. Measured, a 1000 px move costs 592 ms for one phone and 594 ms for both. Frame capture is the exception, single id only, so N phones means N concurrent pollers.
  7. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids>. Add a pointer-reset allowance whenever the target set changes. One request, comma list accepted. A phone can silently stop honouring /mouse/click while /mouse/move and hotkeys still work; /mouse/up does not clear it and /mouse/reset does, and it stays cleared. Budget one reset per target-set change and before any tap-critical sequence.
  8. loop_device_screenshot (Phonefarm push stream) none, XP documents no server-push frame stream. Sum kernel load and frame bandwidth. This absence is why requests per second is a real budget line on this rig: there is no push channel to amortise, every frame is a poll. Load is the sum over pollers of 1 divided by poll period, with a measured ceiling of 512 req/s at ten pollers (p50 3 ms, worst p95 142 ms). Bandwidth is req/s multiplied by 1.62 MB.

Needs

  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. With only IMService.exe up, /device/get reported both phones in state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list.
  • A per-phone fps calibration run, or a live frame-rate meter, before any estimate is trusted. The two XRs differ by about six times.
  • Per-step pointer distances known in the target phone's imgw x imgh space, measured from the previous step's end point, not from iOS logical points.
  • One reusable 1.62 MB buffer per poller. Without reuse the measured cost was 488 MB/s of allocation and 496 gen-2 collections in 8 s.

Watch out

  • The "fan-out costs max, not sum" rule only holds when every listed phone receives the same x,y in its own imgw x imgh space, meaning a genuinely mirrored action. It does not generalise to the common pattern where each phone runs its own script against its own screen content: on this rig the same coordinate is Clock on one XR and Reminders on the other. For that pattern the model must cost N separate requests, one id each, because the coordinates differ. Expose both modes explicitly, mirrored fan-out and independent per-phone, rather than defaulting to the cheap max formula.
  • The time parameter on /mouse/click is documented only as handled internally if omitted, with no stated default duration. The t_step formula treats hold as a small known constant, so until the internal default is measured, which could be tens or hundreds of milliseconds, any estimate that omits an explicit time= value is assumed rather than verified. Call that out in the output.
  • Frame-count settle rules are heuristics, not measured constants. Nothing in the XP docs or the rig measurements defines a settle time. Every settle wait needs a hard wall-clock ceiling, because a step that does not change the screen produces no new frames and the wait would never terminate.
  • AirPlay frame delivery is motion and content dependent, so inter-frame gaps on the 4.5 fps phone are not a steady 222 ms. They cluster and stall. Treat "3 frames, roughly 660 ms" as a best-case average, not a bound; real settle time on the slow phone can run into seconds in the tail.
  • Frame capture cannot be fanned out. /pic/screenshot documents "Multiple is not allowed", so verification cost scales linearly with phone count even though input cost does not. Any verification-heavy plan across more than a couple of phones is bandwidth-bound on raw BMP well before it is CPU or board bound, so surface MB/s alongside req/s rather than letting a 19-board plan silently assume loopback bandwidth a remote client will not have.
  • Per-phone fps is recalibrated daily in this design, so a phone that degrades mid-session through Wi-Fi interference or thermal throttling silently invalidates the estimate until the next pass. Flag calibration age in the output, not only at input time. The worked example already shows one slow link tripling a verified job's wall clock against its identical twin.
  • The rig has 19 boards but only 2 phones mirroring. Any example sized at 19 pollers is hypothetical; the aggregate poller floor beyond ten concurrent pollers is listed as unverified in the project handoff.
  • Every constant is from this rig: two iPhone XRs on iOS 18.7.10, one board generation, loopback HTTP. The 0.6 ms per pixel walk is a property of this board and firmware and must be re-measured on other hardware. The 84 req/s and 512 req/s ceilings are loopback figures and will not hold over a LAN link.
  • The model estimates time, not success. It cannot predict a stuck pointer, an unsatisfied iOS accessibility setting (none are queryable over the API), or a licence cap. Those appear as repair-queue allowances against an assumed failure rate, which is an input, not a measurement. Publishing an estimate as a commitment is the business risk: the numbers are honest about the rig and silent about the app being driven.
  • Calibration frames are live screenshots and may contain account content. Do not archive them by default, and remember that with no authentication on 9911 any LAN host can read the same frames this tool polls.

Scale

Worked example on this rig, a 12-step verified job averaging 400 px of pointer travel per step: fast XR, 12 x (240 ms walk plus about 104 ms settle at 28.9 fps plus 4 ms capture), roughly 4.2 s; slow XR, 12 x (240 plus about 667 plus 4), roughly 10.9 s; mirrored to both in one comma-separated id list, the rack wall clock is the slower phone's 10.9 s, not the sum. In actions per hour that is about 350 ms per verified step on the fast XR, roughly 10,300 verified actions per hour per phone, against about 911 ms and roughly 3,950 per hour on the slow twin, with a mirrored pair bounded by the slow phone at about 3,950. Open-loop, with no screen verification, a 400 px step costs 240 ms, roughly 15,000 actions per hour per phone, and N mirrored phones cost the same as one. That parallelism does not extend to independently scripted phones, where wall clock across phones is limited by the client's concurrent request capacity and the 512 req/s poller ceiling rather than by the board. Frame load: each raw poll is 1,620,054 bytes, so ten pollers at 10 Hz is 100 req/s and about 162 MB/s on loopback, inside the measured 512 req/s ceiling; the same ten on JPEG would hit the 21 req/s per-stream cap at 40.5 ms each. Input traffic and frame polling were measured not to interfere, 98.8 req/s with /mouse/move streaming against 78.7 without, so the two budgets add independently.

Capturing operator work and replaying it

With no OCR or image-search plug-in connected on this rig, a recorded pixel signature is the only screen-side verification available without adding software. That constraint turns out to shape the whole design.

Record-and-replay macro compiler with per-step pixel signatures

Native APIWith caveats

Record an operator's session on the master phone, meaning real /mouse/down, streamed and coalesced /mouse/move, /mouse/up, discrete /mouse/click and /key/sendkey hotkeys, capturing a raw BMP frame immediately before and after each step. Compile that into a job in which every step carries its primitive, its arguments already in the master's imgw x imgh mirror-pixel space, its pointer distance from the previous end point, the expected whole-frame mean absolute pixel difference, the bounding box of the region that actually changed, and a reference crop of that box. Replay onto phones whose imgw, imgh and rotate match the master, addressed as one comma-separated id list per step, then verify each step per phone against the recorded signature rather than a generic "something changed". Recording also solves the classic coordinate trap for free, because iOS logical points (414 x 896) are not the input space (500 x 1080 mirror pixels) and a recorded session is in the right space by construction.

How

  1. get_device_list / get_group_list GET /api/device/get, GET /api/device/group/get, GET /api/device/group/get-dev?id=<gid> (0 = ungrouped). Resolve the replay set and confirm it is geometrically comparable. get-dev is XP-only and returns full device records. Filter on identical imgw/imgh and rotate: a coordinate on a different-sized screen is a different place. On this rig /device/group/get is empty and both XRs are gname 未分组, so group-based targeting needs groups created first with /device/group/set?id=0&name=..., and until then get-dev?id=0 is the only populated list.
  2. mouse_reset_pos + send_key fn_key WIN+h GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids> then GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h twice. Normalise every phone before recording and before replay. WIN+h is the documented Home hotkey for these phones; the distinct Home fn_key exists but needs kernel 2026.2.27 or later and targets iOS 26.1 or later, and these XRs are on 18.7.10. Two presses: the first leaves the app, the second returns to page one. The reset is not optional, being the only measured cure for the silent stuck-click state.
  3. click / mouse_down / mouse_move / mouse_up / send_key /mouse/click (button 1-8, x, y, time ms), /mouse/down, /mouse/move, /mouse/up, /key/sendkey (key ASCII only, or fn_key). Record the primitives as the operator performs them. Hook the console's existing gesture stages, BeginGesture, TrackGesture and EndGestureAsync, which already take plain points, plus InputTargetIds(). Record a real down, move, up stroke rather than a canned /mouse/swipe, so the path is reproduced instead of approximated.
  4. get_device_screenshot (binary) GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true (optionally &rect=[l,t,r,b]). Capture before and after frames for the signature. Single id only, 1,620,054-byte bottom-up BMP, p50 2 ms paced. XP's rect is a flat left, top, right, bottom array, not Phonefarm's four corner points, and can crop the reference region server-side; save_path can write the crop straight to disk.
  5. none (client-side compiler) none, no XP endpoint stores or executes a macro. Compile each step into primitive, arguments, distance, expected diff, bbox and crop. The kernel has no macro, schedule or job concept in either edition, so the compiler, the store and the runner are all the console's responsibility.
  6. devlist fan-out same mouse and key endpoints with id=<id1>,<id2>,.... Replay each step to the whole set in one request. The board walks all listed phones in parallel, a 1000 px move measured 592 ms for one phone and 594 ms for two. Coalescing intermediate move points is free: the same stroke sent as 14, 7 or 2 points produced identical reactions.
  7. none (client-side comparison); ocr / find_image would be the alternative /pic/ocr and /pic/find-image exist but return data.code 28 插件未连接 on this rig. Verify per phone against the recorded signature. Two-part test: whole-frame mean absolute difference within a tolerance band of the recorded value, for example 141.96, and crop diff inside the recorded bbox below a calibrated threshold. Idle floor is 0.02 to 0.03, a real reaction 20 to 160. Exclude the status-bar band from every bbox, because the clock changes on its own.
  8. mouse_reset_pos / restart_usb / auto_connect_screen /mouse/reset?id=, /device/usb/restart?id=720A|C241, /device/airplay/connect?id= (progress on the airplay_connect_log callback). Handle divergence without stalling the rest of the set. Retry the single failed step in place first, meaning reset, re-issue that exact step, re-verify, since reset is the documented cure for this failure mode. Only then drop the phone from the id list, archive its frame, and escalate to the board (addressed vid|pid, not deviceid) and then the mirror session. Watch error_push{call_fun} on the WebSocket bus for board-level failures the synchronous reply does not report.

Needs

  • The 2.0 console's gesture path (BeginGesture, TrackGesture, EndGestureAsync) as the recording source, and InputTargetIds() for the fan-out list.
  • A homogeneous replay set: same model, same iOS, same imgw/imgh, same rotate, and genuinely the same on-screen layout. The two XRs in this rack have different home screens and wallpapers, so the same coordinate is Clock on one and Reminders on the other.
  • Recording performed on a normalised phone (/mouse/reset then two WIN+h presses) with Auto-Lock Never and portrait orientation locked.
  • Each phone's iOS accessibility prerequisites satisfied: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity max, Full Keyboard Access on, Trackpad and Mouse tracking speed max. None of these is queryable over the API, and a phone can mirror perfectly while ignoring every input.
  • A per-follower calibration check. A board with an empty or mismatched mouse-parameter library returns data.code 11 "No mouse parameters" on every mouse call, not a diff divergence. Add a /device/get location_crc check, or an explicit /device/collection/mouse capture, to the pre-flight, or a code 11 reply will be misread as "the tap did not land" and trigger the wrong recovery.
  • IMConsole.exe running. With only IMService.exe up, both phones read state 0 and the board list was empty.

Watch out

  • The recording step is inherently a manual operator session. The value comes from a human performing the task once, so this is a human-in-the-loop tool, not an unattended one.
  • Two raw captures per step undercounts verification cost. Because a still screen yields almost no new AirPlay frames, a single post-action poll can return bytes identical to the pre-action frame even though the tap landed, especially on the 4.5 fps twin. The compiler needs a bounded retry-poll loop sized to each phone's measured fps, polling at roughly one over fps with a timeout of a small multiple of that, not a single grab and diff.
  • Resetting once at the start of a run is not enough. The stuck-click state was observed appearing mid-session with no known trigger, and /mouse/up does not clear it.
  • Carry the 0.6 ms per pixel pointer-walk time as a scheduling constraint, not just as metadata. If the runner fires the next step before pointer walk plus settle plus verify window has elapsed, queued moves coalesce to the newest position, which was measured to happen silently and can merge a recorded double tap or a deliberate two-step drag into a single motion on replay.
  • Any step that types non-ASCII text cannot be recorded as /key/sendkey, which is documented ASCII-only in both editions. The XP route is /shortcut/clipboard/set with text, sleep and outtime, followed by /key/sendkey fn_key=WIN+v, and that requires the iMouse iOS Shortcut installed, IP-edited and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key on every phone, which is not verified present on this rig. A macro containing Unicode typing is therefore not natively replayable here.
  • The verification thresholds are unvalidated. "Within plus or minus 50 percent of the expected whole-frame diff" and "crop diff below about 10" are proposals, not measurements. The only measured anchors are an idle floor of 0.02 to 0.03 and real reactions of 20 to 160. Calibrate per macro against an idle control, or the tool will manufacture both false divergences and false passes.
  • Signatures encode the recording phone's wallpaper and theme. Keep bounding boxes tight around the element that actually changed and exclude the status-bar band; a whole-frame signature will not transfer between the two XRs at all.
  • Screen-side verification on the slow phone is expensive: 4.5 new frames per second against 28.9 on its twin, so any settle-by-frames wait needs a wall-clock ceiling.
  • A near full-height 1080 px stroke is about 580 ms of pointer travel before /mouse/up can even be sent, which iOS may read as a slow drag rather than a flick. Velocity-dependent gestures recorded by hand may simply not fire on replay, and replay timing for such steps will not match the human gesture's real duration. Prefer short-axis strokes.
  • App updates invalidate a macro silently: the coordinates still land, the signature diverges, and nothing explains why. Store the app version and the recording date with every macro.
  • No server-side recognition is available as a fallback. /pic/ocr answered data.code 28 on this rig and the image-search plug-in is presumed absent too, so if pixel signatures prove too brittle for a given app there is no documented alternative short of installing the vendor plug-in.
  • Verification does not fan out the way input does. N phones need N concurrent HTTP pollers against /pic/screenshot, measured comfortable to ten pollers at about 512 req/s aggregate and p50 3 ms. Scaling the replay set well past that needs the poller pool explicitly sized and paced, even though the mouse and key relay stays one request per step.
  • Recorded frames and reference crops are screenshots of live, possibly logged-in sessions, and the 9911 API has no authentication protecting the files or the console that stores them. Local-only storage and scrubbing before any sharing is a hard requirement, and never publish a macro bundle that still contains full frames.
  • Replaying the same recorded interaction across many phones against a third-party app is exactly the kind of automated use many consumer app terms of service restrict, and platforms detect and may action it. Whether a given macro is permissible depends on that app's terms, and that judgement belongs to the operator before the macro is built, not to the tool.

Scale

Recording adds two raw captures per step, about 2 ms each when paced and 1.62 MB each, so keep only the diff bbox crop, which is kilobytes. Replay costs one request per step regardless of set size, with per-step wall clock equal to the longest single pointer walk plus hold plus settle. On the fast phone that is roughly 30 to 150 ms of walk for typical short taps and drags, plus about 35 ms of settle and one to three verify polls, so 100 to 300 ms per step: a ceiling near 12,000 to 36,000 steps per hour and realistically 3,000 to 8,000 actions per hour per phone once retries and periodic resets are budgeted. On the 4.5 fps twin the verify wait alone is about 220 ms per new frame and often needs two or three polls to escape a still-screen run, 440 to 660 ms, capping practical throughput near 1,000 to 2,000 actions per hour per phone. A macro dominated by full-height swipes at 580 ms of travel each caps even the fast phone near 4,000 to 6,000 such gestures per hour. Verification does not fan out, so N phones means N concurrent pollers, measured comfortable at ten. A compiled job is portable to another PC running the same phone model, because the coordinates are in that model's mirror-pixel space, but not to a different imgw/imgh.

Past the boundary of one PC

The comma-id fan-out that makes mirroring cheap stops at the PC boundary. This is the one pattern that carries it across, and it is also the one with the least measurement behind it.

Cross-PC follow-the-master input relay over XP kernel WebSockets

Native APIWith caveats

The XP kernel accepts the identical JSON envelope {"fun":"/mouse/click","msgid":n,"data":{...}} over HTTP POST and over ws://<host>:9911/api, because every endpoint page in the XP docs prints the same body with the note that WebSocket can also send the same JSON request. A relay process can therefore hold one WebSocket per kernel PC, take each input the master console emits, rewrite data.id to that kernel's eligible follower list, assign a fresh msgid per socket, and fan one operator gesture out to phones on several racks. Followers are eligible only when their device record matches the master on imgw, imgh and rotate, state is not 0, and their board reports state 2 in /config/usb/get. Frames for verification are polled per phone over HTTP on each kernel, because XP has no server-push frame stream, so the WebSocket carries input and callbacks only.

How

  1. (ws connect to ws://host:9911/clinet) ws://<pc>:9911/api. Open one WebSocket per kernel and wait for the im_connect callback, which carries data.ver, the only kernel-version readout in XP since there is no HTTP version endpoint. Note the XP WS path is /api, not the Phonefarm /clinet typo. msgid is echoed verbatim on every reply, which is what makes many in-flight requests on one socket matchable.
  2. get_device_list /device/get (optional id=a,b filter). Prime each kernel's inventory. Returns data.list[] with imgw, imgh, rotate, state, vid/pid/uid, location_crc and gid. imgw/imgh is the coordinate space for every mouse call, 500 x 1080 on this rig's XRs against logical 414 x 896, and a follower whose geometry differs from the master must be excluded because the same coordinate is a different place. Phonefarm has no imgw/imgh field at all.
  3. get_usb_list /config/usb/get. Check the control channel per follower. Returns data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}], where state 2 means the board is enumerated and a phone is attached. State semantics come from the usb_change code table (19 board to PC, 20 disconnected, 12 board to phone) and the measured rig. Do not parse ver or uver, which are mojibake on this build. /device/get state only proves video.
  4. mouse_reset_pos /mouse/reset?id=<comma list>. Re-sync the pointer whenever the follower set changes. This is the only call that clears the silent stuck-click state, where a phone obeys /mouse/move and hotkeys but produces a 0.03 mean pixel difference on a click. /mouse/up does not clear it, and it stays cleared after reset.
  5. click /mouse/click {id: comma list, x, y, button, time}. Relay a tap. button is numeric, "1" left, "2" right, "3" middle, up to "8", not the Phonefarm "left"/"right" strings. time is the press-to-release delay in milliseconds, so a long press is a click with time near 800. Coordinates are mirror-image pixels.
