  6. mouse_down / mouse_move / mouse_up /mouse/down, then repeated /mouse/move {x,y}, then /mouse/up, each with the comma id list. Relay a real drag. Coalesce queued moves to the newest position per kernel: the board traverses the path regardless, measured with 14 steps, 7 steps and 2 jumps producing identical 26.2 and 22.9 mean pixel change, and latency is roughly 0.6 ms per pixel of distance rather than jitter.
  7. swipe / mouse_wheel /mouse/swipe {direction up|down|left|right, len (0.9 = 10% to 90%), stepping (spelled steping in the doc's JSON examples), step_sleep ms, brake, sx/sy/ex/ey} and /mouse/wheel {direction, len 1-127, number}. Relay canned gestures and scrolling. XP adds left and right wheel plus step_sleep and brake over Phonefarm. Trust the parameter table, not the examples. A full-height 1080 px swipe is about 580 ms of pointer walk, so prefer the 500 px short axis.
  8. send_key /key/sendkey {id: comma list, key (ASCII only) | fn_key}; /key/down, /key/up, /key/upall for held chords. Relay keystrokes and system hotkeys. XP's fn_key vocabulary is larger than Phonefarm's: WIN+h, Home (needs kernel 2026.2.27 or later, for iOS 26.1 or later), TAB+b, AppSwitch, ControlBar, NoticeBar, TAB+l, OPENKeyboard, shift+win+3 and +4, CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r, CTRL+ALT+WIN+p, WIN+c/v/a/x, SwitchIme, VolumeUp and Down, Play/Pause. Two WIN+h presses normalise every phone to home page one before a mirrored sequence.
  9. none error_push WS callback, data.call_fun plus data.message. Catch per-kernel input failures the synchronous reply hides. XP-only, and the only asynchronous signal that an input actually failed at a board, which matters because a comma-list reply carries one data.code for the whole list.
  10. dev_connect / dev_disconnect / dev_rotate / usb_change same callback names on XP but a different envelope: {fun, status:200, message, msgid:0, data:{list:[record], code, id, message}}. Track membership changes without polling. Records live inside data.list, and usb_change carries the event type in data.code. XP adds dev_change, dev_delete, im_log, user_info every 30 s, and im_config_change. Rebuild the follower list on dev_disconnect, dev_rotate (which swaps the meaning of imgw/imgh) and usb_change code 20, then re-send /mouse/reset to the new set.
  11. get_device_screenshot HTTP GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single id>&binary=true. Verify per phone on each kernel. The document says id "Multiple is not allowed", and with binary=true no JSON is returned at all. XP documents no binary WebSocket frame protocol, and Phonefarm's loop_device_screenshot push stream has no XP equivalent, so frames must be polled over HTTP, one request per phone. Measured: raw BMP p50 2 ms, 1,620,054 bytes, 84 req/s; JPEG p50 40 ms capped near 21 req/s.

Needs

  • Each kernel PC running the XP kernel with its vendor console (IMConsole.exe) started and logged in. Measured here, with only IMService.exe running, both phones reported state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list.
  • Each kernel's account licensed, checked via /config/user/info for pass true and dev_online_num under total_license. Unlicensed devices are refused with the im_log push 未登录，不允许上线. Re-check this after every WebSocket reconnect, because a kernel that drops below its licensed count after a restart refuses new devices with no HTTP-visible error and surfaces it only as an im_log push.
  • Followers bound to a board, with vid and pid set together via /device/set, one device per binding call, and a non-empty location_crc. Verify that location_crc at the same pre-flight step as geometry, or every mouse call returns data.code 11 "No mouse parameters" regardless of network health and gets misdiagnosed as a relay or WebSocket fault.
  • Follower device records matching the master on imgw, imgh and rotate, with phones normalised to the same screen state first. The two XRs on this rig have different home screens and wallpapers, so the same coordinate is a different app on each.
  • Per-phone iOS settings, none of which are queryable over the API: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity max, Full Keyboard Access on, Trackpad and Mouse tracking speed max, Auto-Lock Never, portrait orientation lock.
  • A network path from the relay host to each kernel's TCP 9911, opened deliberately at the firewall. The API authenticates nobody, so every kernel the relay can reach is also reachable by anything else on that path.

Watch out

  • No XP function publishes the master console's outgoing input stream. The relay works only if you own or instrument the master, meaning your own console emitting a copy of each envelope. There is no API to subscribe to another client's requests, and the WS callbacks broadcast state changes, not other clients' input calls. This is a lawful relay of the operator's own console, not a mechanism to observe or intercept anyone else's session.
  • "One gesture becomes one request per kernel" holds only for a discrete /mouse/click. A drag is down plus N moves plus up, so one drag becomes 2 plus N relay messages per kernel, and cross-kernel jitter compounds per move message, not once per gesture. Coalesce intermediate moves to the newest position per kernel, which is verified safe on a single kernel, both to bound WAN traffic and because the 0.6 ms per pixel board walk already dominates fine-grained sampling.
  • A comma-separated id list returns one data.code, data.id and data.message for the whole list. There is no per-phone acknowledgement anywhere in the XP response shape, so per-phone verification by frame diff stays mandatory and error_push is the only asynchronous per-call failure signal.
  • Verification gains nothing from the relay. Control and video stay independent per kernel exactly as on one PC, so confirming a tap landed rather than merely sent still requires one HTTP poller per phone against that phone's own kernel. Input traffic scales as total kernels; verification traffic scales as total phones.
  • Latency skew is real but unmeasured for this pattern. The 1 to 5 ms per-kernel relay cost is an estimate. What is measured is loopback: /mouse/move p50 0.5 to 11.7 ms depending on concurrency, and a distance-proportional board walk of roughly 0.6 ms per pixel that dominates anything longer than a tap. Taps will look simultaneous; a fast drag on a remote kernel will visibly trail the master.
  • Cross-PC operation is untested on this rig, which has exactly one kernel and two phones. The "10 kernels by 50 phones" figure is arithmetic from the comma-list fan-out, not an observation.
  • Per-kernel phone count is also gated by Wi-Fi airtime, not only by licence count. The 28.9 against 4.5 fps figures were measured with two phones total on one access point, and per-AP phone density has not been measured in this project, so the real per-kernel ceiling from Wi-Fi contention alone is unproven.
  • A dropped WebSocket silently orphans that kernel's followers. Alarm on close and, on reconnect, re-prime /device/get and /config/usb/get, re-check the licence, and re-send /mouse/reset before resuming. A stale follower list sends taps into the wrong coordinate space.
  • A WebSocket dropped mid-drag leaves that kernel's phones pointer-down with no /mouse/up ever sent. Track outstanding down-state per kernel and issue /mouse/reset on reconnect, since /mouse/up alone is documented not to clear the related stuck state.
  • Kernel restarts via /imserver/restart and per-device changes via /device/airplay/set drop mirroring sessions. Followers return only after re-casting through /device/airplay/connect or the global auto_connect flag.
  • The stuck-click trap is per phone and invisible: moves and hotkeys keep working while taps do nothing. Send /mouse/reset to the whole target set before any tap-critical relayed sequence.
  • A relay makes one operator's mistake land on every rack at once, with no undo and no per-phone confirmation. A mis-mapped coordinate taps whatever sits at that spot on each follower. Relayed input also inherits each follower's own session, so verify which accounts are logged in before broadcasting anything that posts, messages or purchases.
  • Reaching kernels across PCs means exposing an unauthenticated control port. Anything that can reach the relay's path can drive the phones directly, read frames of logged-in sessions, or restart the kernel. Restrict TCP 9911 to the relay host at the Windows firewall and keep phones on their own VLAN.
  • Mirroring identical actions across many accounts can violate a destination platform's terms even when every account is legitimately yours. Pause on any "Action Blocked" or rate-limit screen rather than retrying.

Scale

Inside one kernel, mirroring to N phones is one request and the board walks all listed phones in parallel: a 1000 px move costs about 592 ms whether it drives one phone or the whole list. Across kernels the relay issues one request per kernel, so ten kernels is ten requests regardless of phones per kernel. One drag gesture becomes roughly (2 plus N_moves) times K WAN messages, so a typical 7 to 14 point drag across ten kernels is about 100 to 160 relay messages; at a 50 to 100 gesture per minute operating pace that is roughly 5,000 to 16,000 relay messages per minute, well inside what loopback measurements suggest a kernel absorbs (512 req/s aggregate across ten concurrent HTTP pollers, with WS framing cheaper still). Verification is the bottleneck, scaling as total phones rather than kernels, with the slowest AirPlay link on any kernel setting that kernel's confirmation floor. Input and frame traffic do not contend: streaming /mouse/move to both phones while polling flat out gave 98.8 req/s against 78.7 with no input. A 50-phone, 10-kernel fleet with even one 4.5 fps class phone per kernel is gated at 220 ms or more per settle per phone, so serialised fleet-wide confirmation runs at only about 3 to 4 confirmed gestures per second, while confirmation pipelined per phone and asynchronously is bounded only by each kernel's own board-walk time, not by the relay.

Also worth knowing

x-callback parameters and Personal Automations: the two halves the ceiling analysis missed

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

The hotkey-to-Shortcut card above concludes the channel cannot be parameterised and can only be triggered from the PC. Both conclusions are about the vendor's own pre-bound Shortcut, not about the mechanism underneath. iOS exposes two documented ways past both limits: the shortcuts://x-callback-url/run-shortcut scheme, which carries a per-call input value into a Shortcut and can chain a result back out, and Personal Automations, which bind a Shortcut to a phone-side trigger, time of day, charger state, battery level, an NFC tag, so iOS runs it with no board, no kernel, and no PC involved at all. Both ride entirely on top of the already-documented /shortcut/exec/url, clipboard and album endpoints; neither adds a new XP endpoint.

How

  1. shortcut#13 (Open URL) GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<ids>&url=<encoded shortcuts:// URL>&outtime=<ms> — the parameterised trigger. url is documented only as a String with no format check, and the same action already used to jump into an app screen can equally hold shortcuts://x-callback-url/run-shortcut?name=<Shortcut>&input=<text>&x-success=<callback>. The GET form needs the whole scheme URL-encoded as one query value; the JSON POST form documented alongside it avoids that by sending url as a plain string.
  2. none (Shortcut "Shortcut Input" action) none, on-device — the target Shortcut reads input as its starting value, so a fan-out over a comma id list can no longer carry one shared payload: each phone needs its own exec/url call if the input differs per phone.
  3. shortcut#10 (clipboard/set) POST /api/shortcut/clipboard/set {id, text, sleep} — an alternative way to seed input when the payload is long or has characters that would not survive two layers of URL-encoding cleanly; the Shortcut reads "Clipboard" instead of "Shortcut Input".
  4. none (Shortcut "Output" / "Stop and Output") none, on-device — the callback half. x-success reopens on the phone, it does not reach the PC or the kernel by itself. In practice it is a second shortcuts://x-callback-url/run-shortcut?name=<Reporter>&input={result} call, chaining the result into a Shortcut that actually reports out.
  5. shortcut#11 (clipboard/get) GET /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<single id>&outtime=<ms> — read the chained result once the reporter Shortcut's last action is "Copy to Clipboard". data.code 30 means the chain stalled before that action ran, not that the input never arrived.
  6. none (Take Photo, Record Audio, and other built-in or App Intent actions) none, on-device — once a Shortcut is running, any action installed on the phone is available to it, not just the vendor's list. Take Photo saves straight to an album without a single tap coordinate, which is the direct fix for a camera card built on UI taps that break on any Camera app layout change. Record Audio, HomeKit scene control, a Health category read, setting a Focus mode, and showing or adding a Wallet pass are the same story: real actions, reachable only by authoring a Shortcut, with no XP endpoint of their own.
  7. shortcut#1 (album/get) then shortcut#3 (album/down) GET /api/shortcut/album/get?id=<single id>&album_name=&num= then GET /api/shortcut/album/down?id=<single id>&list=[{album_name,name,ext}] — retrieve what Take Photo produced, both already-documented and unrelated to the pixel-tap chain they replace.
  8. none (Shortcuts app, Automation tab, Create Personal Automation) none, no API, phone-side only — the autonomous half. Bind the same kind of Shortcut to Time of Day, Charger Connected or Disconnected, Low Battery, or an NFC tag, with "Ask Before Running" turned off. iOS runs it on its own schedule; nothing on 9911 is called, so it fires whether the kernel is up, the board is unplugged, or the video channel is showing dev_disconnect.
  9. none (automation's own "Get Contents of URL" action) none, external tooling — point the automation straight at your own listener, the same gateway built for the reverse-channel card, so a phone can report battery, storage, or "still alive" on its own schedule. Anything it cannot push out this way still lands on the clipboard for /shortcut/clipboard/get once the control channel is back.

Needs

  • The vendor iMouse Shortcut already bound as described in the hotkey card, since /shortcut/exec/url and every clipboard and album call still travel over that same HID-triggered channel.
  • A second, custom Shortcut authored by hand on each phone. Both x-callback-url and Personal Automations target Shortcuts you write, never the vendor's own.
  • The phone-side Shortcuts permissions from the setup checklist: allow running scripts, allow sharing large amounts of data.
  • Per action: a configured Home app and the phone signed into it for HomeKit, a one-time Health permission grant for Health reads, and the pass already sitting in Wallet for a Wallet action. None of this is settable or queryable over the API.
  • For the autonomous half, the automation created directly in the Shortcuts app on the phone. There is no remote call to create, list, edit, or delete a Personal Automation.
  • A listener endpoint if an automation reports over the network rather than the clipboard, scoped and tokened the same way as the reverse-channel gateway.

Watch out

  • shortcuts://x-callback-url is Apple's own scheme, documented by Apple, not by the vendor or by either edition of this API. Nothing in this card has been probed on this rig. Confirm on one phone that /shortcut/exec/url passes such a URL through unmodified before designing anything on top of it.
  • x-success is an on-device relay, not a network return path. It only becomes PC-readable data once the shortcut it reopens takes a further action, Copy to Clipboard or Get Contents of URL. Calling this "a structured callback to the PC" without that second hop overstates what Apple's mechanism actually does.
  • Turning off "Ask Before Running" removes the automation's own confirmation, not iOS's. The first time an automation touches Health, HomeKit, or the camera it can still raise a one-time system permission prompt, and an unattended phone with an unanswered prompt blocks silently, the same failure mode as an unanswered AssistiveTouch prompt elsewhere in this group.
  • Nothing in /device/get or /config/usb/get reports whether a Personal Automation exists, is enabled, or last fired. It is phone state the rack cannot see; the only evidence is whatever the automation itself chooses to report.
  • Take Photo captures whatever the camera is actually pointed at in the rack, not the mirrored screen. It produces a photo, not a screenshot, so check its content by hand at least once before trusting an unattended capture.
  • HomeKit, Health, and Wallet actions carry real-world and account-level side effects on the phone owner's own accounts: a HomeKit scene changes something in a physical home. Confine every one of these to accounts, homes, and health records you are authorized to operate, and stop rather than retry if an app signals a block, consistent with the automated-use caveat on every other Shortcut card in this section.
  • Fan-out changes shape here: the vendor's own /shortcut/* calls take one comma id list for identical work on every phone, but a personalised input value makes that one call per phone again, not one call for many.

Scale

The triggered half costs what /shortcut/exec/url already costs, one request per distinct input, so a shared payload is still O(1) but a personalised fan-out is O(phones). Reading a result back stays governed by whichever documented endpoint the reporter Shortcut ends on: clipboard/get, album/get, and album/down are each single id at their usual outtime ceiling. The autonomous half costs the kernel nothing until an automation chooses to call in: zero polling, zero HID, and it runs on 19 phones or 2 with identical marginal cost to the API, since iOS is the one doing the scheduling. That makes it the cheapest possible source of a self-report from a phone whose video and control channels are both down, at the price of being entirely unverified on this hardware and invisible to every rack-facing endpoint until it speaks.

Device-as-a-service: partition boards per client with groups, not with sub-accounts

Plus external toolingWith caveats

19 boards and 2 mirroring phones is exactly the shape of a rentable device farm, and every piece needed to sell it that way is already in this doc set: name a group of boards after a client, gate the gateway with a key, log who touched what. The one primitive that looks purpose-built for multi-tenancy, /config/user/switch with its utag 1 to 10 sub-accounts, is not that primitive. It switches which vendor licensing account the whole kernel process is logged in as. It is global process state, not a per-request or per-connection scope, and nothing in the API lets a caller attach a utag to an individual call the way id scopes a device. Build tenancy on gid groups and your own gateway instead, and never wire client onboarding to /config/user/switch.

How

  1. none GET /api/config/user/login?phone=&password=&utag= — log IMConsole into the vendor account once, at rack setup, not per client. utag here just selects which of that account's own 1-10 licensing buckets is active; it is not a tenant id you hand out. Phonefarm has no equivalent call at all, no user concept in that edition's API.
  2. set_group GET /api/device/group/set?id=0&name=<client> — create one group per client. id=0 means "new group"; the response returns the generated numeric gid. This is the real partition boundary: it lives under the one logged-in account and needs no utag switching to use.
  3. set_dev GET /api/device/set?id=<deviceid list>&gid=<gid> — assign that client's boards to the group. id takes a comma list so a whole allotment moves in one call; gid is independent of vid/pid hardware binding, so grouping and USB pairing are two separate steps.
  4. none GET /api/device/group/get-dev?id=<gid> — the gateway's source of truth for "which device ids may this client's key touch." id=0 means ungrouped, not wildcard, so a board left unassigned is invisible to every client's allow-list, which is the safe default while onboarding.
  5. none none (client-side, your gateway) — front 9911 with your own authenticated reverse proxy. Every /mouse/*, /key/*, /pic/* and /device/* call gets rewritten to check the caller's key against the current /device/group/get-dev snapshot for their gid before it is allowed through, because the kernel itself checks nothing.
  6. none none (client-side, your gateway) — per-client frame retention. Tag every /pic/screenshot capture with client id, device id and timestamp before writing it to storage; the kernel's response carries none of that, only raw bytes or a JSON error shape.
  7. none none (client-side, your gateway) — per-client audit trail. Log caller key, resolved client id, fun, device id list and data.code for every call at the gateway, because the kernel's envelope carries no caller identity anywhere, and two clients' traffic is otherwise indistinguishable on the wire.
  8. none GET /api/config/user/info / user_info callback — treat this as an operator canary, not a tenant API. It carries utag, dev_num and dev_online_num for whichever account is currently active and repeats every 30 s while logged in; a value that does not match what you expect means someone called /config/user/switch underneath you.

Needs

  • One IMConsole login for the whole rig, holding the licensing account that authorizes all 19 boards. Devices cannot come online unlicensed under that account (the kernel pushes im_log "未登录，不允许上线" otherwise), which is one more reason not to be logging in and out of different utag buckets on a live rack.
  • A gateway process you write and run, since neither edition authenticates callers on 9911. This is the same shape as the alert-bridge daemon described earlier in this section, extended to also authorize and log, not just observe.
  • A provisioned gid per client, created and populated with /device/group/set and /device/set before that client's key goes live, plus a cached /device/group/get-dev snapshot the gateway refreshes on its own schedule, since gid membership changes are not pushed as callbacks.
  • Storage outside the kernel for the audit log and the retained frames, keyed by client id, since C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json and the kernel's own state hold none of it.
  • A decision made once, in the design, not discovered after the second client signs up: either one kernel process per tenant (separate IMConsole instances, separate PCs or VMs, true isolation), or one shared kernel with strict gateway-side gid filtering and a hard rule that nothing in the tenant-facing path ever calls /config/user/switch.

Watch out

  • This is the trap the surface catalogue does not carry: no endpoint anywhere in the nine XP docs accepts a utag or account parameter except /config/user/login, /config/user/switch and the two info calls. Every other call, from every connected client, is answered against whichever account is currently active in the one IMService.exe process. There is no way to pin a call to a specific sub-account. If tenant B's flow ever calls /config/user/switch, tenant A's in-flight jobs on shared boards start executing under B's licensing context immediately, with no request-level warning.
  • Because devices need an active license to come online, a switch is not cosmetic: boards licensed only under the account just switched away from can drop offline mid-job under the other tenant's context, surfacing as an im_log push, not as an error on the call that was actually running.
  • gid groups are not account-scoped either. They live under whichever single account is logged in, so switching utag does not hand you a second isolated group namespace to go with it; groups and accounts are two unrelated axes, and only the group axis behaves per-object rather than per-process.
  • No locking exists on /device/set. Two gateway instances (or the gateway racing a human at the console) assigning different gid values to the same device id resolve last-write-wins, with nothing to detect the collision after the fact.
  • The gateway is the entire security boundary. If it is bypassed, is compromised, or simply is not running, 9911 is still open and unauthenticated to anyone on the LAN, per-client isolation included; the trap above is a reason to avoid switch even for a well-meaning operator working the console directly while clients are connected.
  • Reusing accounts, phones, or a rented board pool to run third-party apps for multiple paying clients raises the same terms-of-service exposure already flagged for automation in general, now multiplied by however many clients' accounts pass through the same hardware; keep each client's own app accounts on their own boards via gid, and do not let one board serve two clients' logins.

Scale

Grouping and gateway filtering cost nothing extra at the kernel: they are the same GET calls this section already measured at 512 req/s across ten concurrent pollers, filtered client-side against a cached allow-list. The limiting resource is still the board-serialized lease from the scheduler card above, now partitioned per tenant instead of per job; a client's usable capacity is exactly the boards in their gid that are also state 2, bound, and mirroring, which today is at most the 2 live phones, not a share of 19. One shared kernel scales the gateway's own request handling roughly linearly with clients until the boards themselves saturate; one kernel per tenant scales instead in PCs and IMConsole logins, trading a global-switch risk of zero for a hardware cost per tenant. Given the trap above, quote capacity per client the same way the rest of this section insists on quoting it per phone class: as a live computed number from /device/group/get-dev plus /config/usb/get, never as 19 divided by client count.

Skipping straight to the vendor's own client: imouse-py

Before hand-rolling any of the HTTP or WebSocket plumbing above, read imouse-py (pip install imouse-py), the XP edition's official Python client, documented at /iphone-farm-setup/xp-api-documentation/python-library. It wraps the same path-style endpoints in two layers: a thin imouse.api(host=...) that exposes one method per call, and a recommended imouse.helper(api) that groups them the way this handoff does, a console object with device, airplay, usb, group, imconfig and user sub-objects for rack-wide operations, and a helper.device(id) object with image, keyboard, mouse and shortcut sub-objects for per-phone ones. Callbacks are handled the same way: an @event.on("im_connect")-style decorator per event name, with the payload already parsed into typed models (DeviceInfo, UsbInfo, UserData, ImServerConfigData) instead of a raw dict. Phonefarm has nothing equivalent, it ships only a loose ios_at_api.py plus a PyQt6 sample script, so this is an XP-only advantage, not a cross-edition one.

Its value here is as ground truth, not as a runtime dependency. The vendor's own mouse_click(deviceid, button, x, y) signature is a direct, code-level confirmation of the parameter order and defaults in the keyboard-and-mouse doc, positional button as an empty string defaults to left-click, matching curl .../mouse/click?id=...&x=100&y=100 with button omitted. Where this handoff has had to hedge, for example whether dev_rotate's payload sits inside data.list or at data, or whether error_push ever names the failing device, the library's typed models and its helper grouping are a second independent source to check a field name or a default against before committing it to a C# type. It will not resolve every open question: the library was not exercised against this rig any more than the WebSocket transport was, so treat it as a stronger prior, not a substitute for a live capture.

Two concrete uses follow from that. Someone building the Windows console this API implies should still read imouse-py's source, even though it is Python and the target is C#, because its class boundaries (console-level versus device-level, plus the event dispatcher) are a tested precedent for where to draw the same seams, and its method signatures are a faster way to settle a disputed parameter than re-deriving it from the doc's prose tables. Someone who only wants to prototype a job or validate an idea against the rack, rather than ship the console, can skip the transport layer entirely: pip install imouse-py, call helper.console.device.list_by_id(), helper.device(id).mouse.swipe(...) and @event.on(...) directly, and never hand-write an HTTP GET or open the WebSocket at ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api themselves. Both readers still inherit every constraint measured elsewhere in this handoff, single-id-only on /pic/* and the shortcut read-backs, one shared parameter set per comma-separated id list, no authentication on the LAN, since the library is a thinner client over the same kernel, not a different one.

MARK-LIMITS-MARK

Section 12 · Limits and risks

Hard limits, misconceptions and risks

Everything up to here described what the rack can do. This section is the boundary: the capabilities buyers assume are present and are not, the ones that exist in the product but are missing on this rig, and the ones that exist but are shaped differently from the mental model people bring to a phone farm. Every limit below is either documented in the vendor material or measured on this hardware on 10 September 2026. Where the XP edition installed here differs from the Phonefarm edition the vendor documents separately, that is called out.

Absent from the API in both editions

These two are not configuration problems or plug-in problems. No function exists, in the XP documentation set installed on this rig or in the Phonefarm document, that performs them. Both are among the first things operators assume a rack of SIM-carrying phones can do.

Sending an SMS or iMessage by API call

Not possibleRefuted

There is no messaging endpoint. The Phonefarm shortcut table lists id 12 "Send SMS" struck through, alongside struck-through id 14 "Read text aloud", and the XP edition on this rig has no messaging path at all: its shortcuts page documents 19 functions covering album, file, clipboard, open URL, restart and shutdown, brightness, torch, flight mode, cellular data, WLAN and IP, and none of them is messaging. A full-text search of all nine XP doc files for sms, iMessage and the Chinese equivalent returns no endpoint. What remains is ordinary UI automation through the visible Messages app, one thread per phone.

How

  1. shortcut#12 Send SMS no XP path — the capability people look for. Struck through by the vendor in one edition, absent from the other. Do not call it.
  2. shortcut#13 Open URL /shortcut/exec/url — nearest workaround: open the composer from an sms: URL. Endpoint verified, custom URL schemes are not (every doc example is an http domain).
  3. shortcut#10 /shortcut/clipboard/set — place a non-ASCII or long body on the pasteboard, then paste with /key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+v.
  4. send_key / click /key/sendkey?fn_key=ENTER — or /mouse/click on the send arrow. Whether Return sends in Messages or inserts a newline is an iOS behavior no doc covers.
  5. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?binary=true — confirm the bubble by mean absolute pixel difference, single id only.

Needs

  • A SIM with active SMS service in the handset. Neither XR on this rig has SIM state recorded, so even the workaround is unproven here.
  • The iMouse iOS Shortcut installed, its IP edited to 192.168.4.29, run once with every permission granted, and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key.
  • Board bound and at /config/usb/get state 2, location_crc non-empty, AssistiveTouch and Full Keyboard Access on, and IMConsole.exe running.
  • Send-arrow and QuickType coordinates measured per phone in mirror pixels (500 x 1080), not iOS points (414 x 896).

Watch out

  • No step in the workaround chain is verified on this hardware or iOS build. /shortcut/exec/url is a general-purpose Open URL action with a 15 s default outtime and no confirmation that the composer opened, so a blind ENTER or a blind tap at a guessed coordinate lands on whatever app was already frontmost.
  • /shortcut/exec/url and /mouse/click both fan out to a comma-separated id list, so one wrong URL or one wrong shared coordinate is broadcast identically to every phone in the batch.
  • Nothing reads, enumerates or exports Messages. There is no inbox endpoint and no thread list.
  • Legal exposure is the dominant risk and it is severe. Unsolicited commercial SMS to US numbers falls under the TCPA with statutory damages assessed per message, CAN-SPAM covers commercial content, and PECR plus GDPR apply in the UK and EU. Carrier acceptable-use policies prohibit bulk or automated messaging from consumer SIMs, and Apple's terms prohibit automated bulk iMessage sending. Driving the UI carries the same liability an API send would.
  • Every message is visible on the screen and persists in the thread and in carrier records.

Scale

Not applicable to the claimed capability. For the UI workaround, budget roughly 3 to 6 seconds of wall time per message per phone with everything working first try, so on the order of 600 to 1,200 messages per hour per phone as a pure rig ceiling. That number is not the real ceiling: carrier anti-spam systems, platform abuse detection and legal liability stop this design far below what the hardware could sustain. This is not a gateway.

Reading an incoming SMS, one-time code or notification text

Not possibleRefuted

No function in either edition returns the body of an SMS, a push notification or Notification Center content, and no callback fires when a message arrives. The 18 documented WebSocket callbacks are device, board, cast and license state only, so an event-driven code relay cannot be built at all. The only text-out channels are /shortcut/clipboard/get, which reads whatever is already on the pasteboard, and the OCR family, which is plug-in gated and dead on this rig. Everything real here is a per-phone UI flow with vision done on the PC.

How

  1. none no /shortcut/sms, no /device/notification — enumerated across all 60-odd XP paths. Phonefarm id 12 is outbound and struck through, and XP has no generic numbered-shortcut dispatcher to reach it.
  2. callbacks ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — 18 callbacks, none carrying message content. Detection is polling only, never an event.
  3. send_key fn_key /key/sendkey?fn_key=NoticeBar — workaround A: open Notification Center so the text is on screen, then capture the frame and run your own OCR on the PC. Documented, not exercised here.
  4. screenshot + click /pic/screenshot?rect=[l,t,r,b] then /mouse/click — workaround B: when a code arrives while a field is focused, iOS offers it in the QuickType bar. Poll a crop of that strip for a mean pixel difference above about 20 against the 0.02 idle floor, then tap it. No reading required.
  5. click time=800 + shortcut#11 /mouse/click?time=800 then /shortcut/clipboard/get — workaround C: long-press the bubble, tap Copy, read data.text back. Exact characters rather than a guess.

Needs

  • The phone must actually receive the message. Codes sent to a third-party virtual number never reach the rack.
  • Board at state 2, location_crc present, and the invisible iOS accessibility set (AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, tracking speed max, Auto-Lock Never, portrait lock).
  • Workaround C and any /shortcut/other/* path need the iMouse Shortcut provisioned, v1.3 or higher for the recognition fallbacks.
  • An OCR engine on the PC, because the kernel provides none here.

Watch out

  • fn_key=NoticeBar and the QuickType tap are documented but were not exercised in the live probe. Treat them at lower confidence than the verified mouse and screenshot mechanics.
  • The QuickType strip is not at a fixed position: keyboard height varies with input mode, third-party keyboards and per-app toolbars, so the crop box is a per-app constant you must measure, not a rig constant.
  • A notification that iOS collapses into Notification Center without a banner (Focus modes, Deliver Quietly) never appears on the mirrored screen, and that phone setting is invisible to the API.
  • Polling has a latency window that can miss a short-lived code, and the miss is silent.
  • Reading messages is only defensible on handsets and accounts the operator owns. Doing it on anyone else's raises privacy and computer-misuse exposure quite apart from platform terms, and automated handling of login codes is often prohibited by the platform's own terms even for your own account.
  • A code captured into a PC-side screenshot is a live secret on disk. Purge it rather than logging it, and remember the kernel API is unauthenticated on the LAN, so any host on the subnet can pull the same frames.

Scale

Never mirrored, because each handset's code is different. Only the normalizing Home presses and /mouse/reset can be fanned out. The polling itself is free (raw BMP frames cost 2 ms at p50 and phones are independent), but SMS delivery of 5 to 30 seconds dominates, plus seconds of UI navigation. Budget tens of seconds per code, not milliseconds.

Missing on this rig, not from the product

Trap The blocked call answers HTTP 200

A missing plug-in does not produce a transport error. GET /api/pic/ocr returns HTTP 200 with an empty result and data.code 28, message 插件未连接. A client that checks only the HTTP status, or the top-level status field, will record a success. Branch on data.code everywhere, never on message text, which is Chinese in this edition.

Server-side OCR and find-text to read the screen

Not possibleRefuted

Every "read the number, then decide" idea routes through the kernel's OCR endpoints, and on this rig they are dead. The probe on 10 September 2026 returned data.code 28, which the XP code table defines as plug-in not connected. That kills /pic/ocr, /pic/ocr-ex, /pic/find-text and /pic/find-text-ex, and with them the OCR-dependent point-capture helpers behind automatic screen connection and device restart. This is a rig fact, not a product fact: the endpoints are fully documented with defined parameters and response shapes, and installing the vendor plug-in brings them back. Note also the scope: the kernel cannot read text here, but the rack still can, client-side, and that path is the recommended one.

How

  1. ocr / ocr_ex /pic/ocr, /pic/ocr-ex — blocked. Single id, optional rect as [left, top, right, bottom], returns list of text with center and rect.
  2. none /pic/find-text, /pic/find-text-ex — blocked, XP-only endpoints on the same plug-in. These are the calls a "detect the throttle banner" flow would need.
  3. find_image / find_image_ex /pic/find-image, /pic/find-image-cv — untested, presumed blocked. Gated by opencv_num. Probe with one template crop before designing on it.
  4. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — works. Raw bottom-up BMP, 1,620,054 bytes, p50 2 ms. Feed the decoded buffer, or a rect crop, to Windows.Media.Ocr, Tesseract or PaddleOCR on the host. The frame is in the same 500 x 1080 space /mouse/click expects, so host-OCR boxes are directly tappable.
  5. send_key + shortcut#11 /key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+a, then WIN+c, then /shortcut/clipboard/get — exact strings instead of a probabilistic read, where the text is selectable.
  6. n/a /config/imserver/set?ocr_num=<n> then /imserver/restart — the real fix. The plug-in binary is not obtainable through the API, and the restart drops every mirroring session.

Needs

  • To restore the blocked calls: the vendor OCR plug-in package for the XP edition, installed and connected to IMService.exe, then ocr_num set and the kernel restarted. ocr_num above 1 only means something on the GPU build.
  • For the host-OCR path: an OCR engine on the PC and a decoder for a 54-byte-header bottom-up 500 x 1080 x 3 buffer. Reuse one buffer per poller; each 1.6 MB frame is far above the .NET Large Object Heap threshold, and without reuse the measured cost was 488 MB/s of allocation and 496 gen-2 collections per 8 s, against 2.9 MB/s with reuse.
  • For the clipboard and native-album paths: the full iMouse Shortcut prerequisite chain, plus Full Keyboard Access for the WIN+a and WIN+c combinations.

Watch out

  • The image-search verdict is inference, not measurement. Only /pic/ocr was probed. Record the real answer for /pic/find-image-cv before repeating the claim, and treat /pic/find-multi-color being plug-in-free as an argument from silence.
  • Host OCR on a lossy 500 x 1080 mirror frame is marginal for small digits: 1,234 can read as 1,284. Route anything where an exact numeric or currency value matters through the clipboard path, or through a native-resolution album capture, never through host OCR on the mirror frame alone.
  • The clipboard path only works where the text is genuinely selectable. Text baked into an image, a WebView that blocks selection, or a custom-rendered element returns empty or stale content, silently.
  • The /shortcut/other/* recognition fallbacks are named in the XP doc with no parameter table, no example and no response body. They are an unexplored lead, not a solution.
  • Every /pic/* path is single id, as are /shortcut/album/get and /shortcut/album/down, so text checks scale linearly with phones while input does not.
  • Pixel-color state checks break on dark mode, accessibility contrast settings, Night Shift and app redesigns. Pin the display settings and re-capture after any app update.
  • Installing the plug-in is rig-wide and costs a kernel restart, so every phone must re-cast. Plan a maintenance window, not a rolling upgrade.
  • The Phonefarm doc marks ocr_ex professional-version-only while XP states no edition gate. The mapping between Phonefarm professional and the installed XP International Edition is defined nowhere, so do not assume the license covers it.

Scale

The 2 ms screenshot is never the bottleneck, the recognizer is. Host OCR on a frame or crop runs roughly 50 to 300 ms per phone on CPU, so a 19-phone rack checked once a minute costs about 6 s of CPU per sweep while a per-second loop across the rack does not fit. Frame supply is genuinely parallel: two phones polled flat out gave 83 and 85 req/s, ten concurrent pollers gave 512 req/s total. The floor is the AirPlay source rate, which is per-phone: 192.168.4.68 delivers about 29 new frames per second under motion while its identical twin 192.168.4.27 delivers about 4.5, so a verification step on the slow phone waits about 220 ms per frame and must not time out on a 30 fps assumption. A still screen produces almost no new frames, so discard repeats with a same-as-previous check rather than re-running OCR.

Present, but not the shape people assume

The remaining three are the expensive misconceptions. In each case the endpoint exists, accepts the call and returns success, and the wrongness shows up later, in the posted content, in the typed field, or in a rack that has gone dark.

Per-phone parameters in one multi-id request

Not possibleRefuted

A comma-separated id list is a fan-out, not a batch. Every endpoint that accepts multiple ids carries exactly one parameter set, applied identically to every id, and there is no array-of-per-device-payloads form anywhere in the XP docs, the Phonefarm doc or the Python library. The other half of the wall is read-back: every /pic/* path and every shortcut read (clipboard/get, album/get, album/down, file/get, device/ip) is marked "Multiple is not allowed". Distinct content per phone is always N calls, and reading state back from N phones is always N calls. Read this as a throughput model, not a broken feature: the mirrored half really is O(1) requests.

How

  1. mouse_reset_pos + send_key /mouse/reset?id=<list> then /key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+h — shared baseline for the whole target set in one request. Two Home presses: the first leaves the app, the second returns to page one.
  2. shortcut#10 / #13 / #7 /shortcut/clipboard/set, /shortcut/exec/url, /shortcut/album/upload — these accept an id list, but text, url and files are single shared values. Loop one id per call whenever the payload differs.
  3. send_key / click /key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+v then /mouse/click?id=<list> — back to one request for all, provided every follower's imgw and imgh match the master.
  4. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id_k>&binary=true — verification is N requests, by documentation. Cheap, but N.
  5. set_dev / del_dev /device/set, /device/del — the one exception: these return data.list of the ids that actually succeeded. Input paths return a single data.code with data.id echoing the whole list.

Needs

  • A controller that structurally forbids combining a personalized field with a comma id list. The API will accept it and fan the same payload out to every phone.
  • A follower list filtered to matching imgw and imgh before any shared coordinate call, and built only from phones that are online, bound and on the intended screen.
  • For personalized payloads, the full Shortcut provisioning on that phone, plus iOS 15 or later for /shortcut/file/* and /shortcut/switch/device.

Watch out

  • The failure is silent and one-directional. Passing an id list with a personalized field is a valid request that applies the same text, URL or file to every phone, with no error, because input endpoints report one code for the whole list. Guard it in the controller's types, not at review time.
  • A shared coordinate sent to a phone with different imgw or imgh lands somewhere else entirely and still returns code 0. The two XRs here have different home screens, so the same coordinate is Clock on one and Reminders on the other.
  • A multi-id tap that hit the stuck-click state on one board reads as success. Send /mouse/reset to the whole set before any tap-critical sequence and verify per phone with a pointer-box pixel difference (1.4 to 9.8 for a landed pointer against a 0.02 idle floor).
  • outtime is milliseconds in XP (default 15000) and seconds in Phonefarm, and the doc's type column calls it Boolean, which is a translation artifact. sleep on /shortcut/clipboard/set is a separate parameter in seconds.
  • Unverified: whether concurrent Shortcut round trips across phones serialize inside IMService. Mouse, key and screenshot traffic were measured as independent, but a Shortcut adds a second, Wi-Fi-bound leg that was never load-tested. Treat the personalized loop as serial until measured.
  • The Phonefarm sibling looks like it has a batch form and does not: its shortcut function takes a device list but one shared parameter string, and it is professional-version-only. Moot here, since this kernel rejects every Phonefarm function name with HTTP 500.

Scale

Shared steps cost one request regardless of N, and the board walks all listed phones in parallel, so the cost is pointer-walk distance at about 0.6 ms per pixel (1,000 px measured at 592 ms), identical for one phone or nineteen. Personalized steps are N requests, each a Shortcut round trip bounded by outtime; if each fires promptly, budget 1 to 3 s per phone, and note the unhandled worst case is 19 phones at up to 15,000 ms each, about 4.75 minutes for one round. Verification runs up to 84 req/s per phone and is never the constraint. The Shortcut round trips dominate by three orders of magnitude.

Typing non-ASCII text with the keyboard endpoints

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

The direct limit is confirmed. /key/sendkey, /key/down and /key/up all document key as English, numbers and English characters only, the Phonefarm sibling states it harder as "Chinese is not supported", and there is no Unicode typing endpoint at all: the string send_text appears zero times in the XP documentation set. Emoji, CJK and accented Latin cannot be typed through the HID keyboard path. The documented route around it is two calls, clipboard then paste, and both fan out to an id list, so one shared Unicode string reaches N phones in two requests. On this rig that route is a design, not a capability: no /shortcut/* endpoint has ever been probed here, so treat non-ASCII as unavailable until a clipboard round trip returns code 0 on these phones.

How

  1. send_key key="Nouveautés" /key/sendkey?key=<text> — works for ASCII only, and neither doc defines behavior for out-of-domain bytes, so there is no error code to detect the failure.
  2. send_text no XP path — refuted for this rig. No such path, no send_text_ok callback, 9912 closed, and bare Phonefarm function names to 9911 return HTTP 500.
  3. click / send_key fn_key /mouse/click or /key/sendkey?fn_key=OPENKeyboard — focus the target field. Send /mouse/reset to the set first.
  4. shortcut#10 /shortcut/clipboard/set — place the Unicode string on the pasteboard. Send it as POST application/json in UTF-8, not as a GET query string.
  5. send_key fn_key=WIN+v /key/sendkey?id=<list>&fn_key=WIN+v — paste. Needs Full Keyboard Access on, or the combination is never interpreted.
  6. shortcut#11 /shortcut/clipboard/get — round-trip an identical string. This is the cheapest single proof that the Shortcut is installed, the hotkey binding fires and the phone can reach the kernel.

Needs

  • The iMouse Shortcut installed on every phone that needs Unicode, with the kernel IP edited inside it, run once with every prompt allowed, and Shortcuts, Advanced set to allow running scripts and sharing large amounts of data.
  • The Shortcut bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key through the console's Send Binding Key, and the board bound and at state 2, because the Shortcut is launched by a HID hotkey.
  • Full Keyboard Access on with 1 s auto-hide, phone unlocked, portrait, Auto-Lock Never.
  • Provisioning is manual and per phone. At 19 boards that is 19 GUI passes with no API to batch it, and it must be redone on every phone whenever the kernel IP changes, for example after a DHCP re-address.

Watch out

  • The single observable symptom of any missing piece in the phone-side chain is data.code 30, call timeout, after outtime. Nothing distinguishes a missing Shortcut from a denied permission dialog.
  • WIN+v pastes whatever is on the pasteboard. If clipboard/set silently failed and the paste is sent anyway, the previous string, possibly another phone's text, gets posted into a live field. Gate the paste on clipboard/set returning code 0, and treat the first production use on each phone as a dry run verified by clipboard/get.
  • Pasting destroys the previous pasteboard contents, and there is no read-modify-restore primitive beyond get then set. The text also sits on the pasteboard afterward, where any app that reads it on foreground can see it, and Apple's Universal Clipboard may propagate it to other signed-in devices. That last point is field behavior, not vendor documentation, so verify it rather than assuming it.
  • Glyph-level verification must be client-side or by eye. /pic/find-text would be the clean check and is dead here.
  • The IME-switching alternative cannot produce emoji and depends on undocumented per-phone keyboard state; picking a candidate blind needs recognition this rig does not have. The URL alternative only works for apps that honor a text parameter, which is an app fact with no vendor documentation behind it.
  • Pasting the identical string across many phones is ordinary bulk-content behavior, and platforms commonly treat identical repeated posts as spam under their terms. Whether bulk posting is permitted at all is governed by each platform's terms for the accounts involved.

Scale

ASCII is effectively free: one call carries a whole string to the whole rack. Unicode costs a Shortcut round trip, but both write calls fan out, so one shared string reaches N phones in exactly two requests, bounded by the slowest phone's round trip. Cost is per distinct string, not per character: a 3-character caption and a 2,000-character bio are the same two calls. Distinct text per phone serializes at one clipboard/set each. Verification does not fan out, and its latency is dominated by the slow phone's 4.5 fps AirPlay link rather than by request throughput.

Turning Wi-Fi off and back on as a round trip

Not possibleRefuted

Turning Wi-Fi off from the API is a one-way door. /shortcut/switch/wlan with state=0 is fully documented and takes an id list, but the iMouse Shortcut that executes it is a phone-side Shortcut that fetches its instruction from the kernel over the LAN. The USB board delivers only the trigger hotkey. The moment state=0 lands, the phone can no longer be told state=1, and the AirPlay video channel dies with it, leaving a controllable phone you cannot see and cannot instruct. Airplane mode through /shortcut/switch/flight has the same trap. The general rule for this rig: every shortcut-backed function is a LAN function, so no shortcut may be used to disable the LAN.

How

  1. get_usb_list + get_device_list /config/usb/get + /device/get — the last full snapshot you will get. Control is board state 2, video is device state non-zero with a live air_pid.
  2. shortcut id 23 /shortcut/switch/wlan?state=0 — the outbound half, which genuinely works and fans out to the whole rack in one request.
  3. dev_disconnect WS callback + /pic/screenshot — the video channel collapses, device state drops to 0, the socket to AirplayMirroring.exe on TCP 17000 tears down, and screenshots answer code 25, device offline.
  4. shortcut id 22 /shortcut/switch/wlan?state=1 — the break. The board still delivers the hotkey and iOS still launches the Shortcut, but the Shortcut's first act is to fetch its instruction from an IP it can no longer reach. The call ends in code 30 after outtime.
  5. mouse_reset + send_key + click /mouse/reset, /key/sendkey?fn_key=ControlBar, /mouse/click — blind, open-loop recovery over USB at coordinates memorized in advance. Unverified on two counts and not a fallback with known odds.
  6. none phone-side setting, no API — the supported alternative. Set IPv4 to Manual with the router and gateway field left empty, so the phone keeps LAN reachability for mirroring and shortcuts while default traffic leaves over the SIM.
  7. shortcut ids 24, 21, 20 /shortcut/device/ip, /shortcut/switch/cdpd — network QA that never surrenders the control plane: confirm LAN reachability, and cycle a stalled cellular data session with state=0 then state=1.

Needs

  • The full Shortcut prerequisite chain for any of these calls to fire at all, plus the invisible iOS accessibility settings and IMConsole.exe running.
  • A frame captured and coordinates recorded before Wi-Fi is cut, per phone, if blind recovery is to be attempted at all.
  • For the supported alternative: a SIM with an active data plan in each phone, and the manual IPv4 edit applied by hand on each phone. There is no API for that setup, so it does not scale the way the broken toggle appeared to.

Watch out

  • The outbound half works, so do not read this as "the endpoint does not exist". Only the round trip is impossible.
  • Whether the state=0 call returns code 0 or code 30 is undetermined and depends on whether the Shortcut acknowledges the kernel before the radio drops. Do not branch recovery or alerting logic on that code, because the phone goes dark either way.
  • Blind recovery rests on two untested assumptions: that /mouse/* still acts on a device whose state is 0 (code 25 exists and may gate it), and that the Control Center tile restores what the Shortcut switched off. It also assumes the AssistiveTouch and Full Keyboard Access prerequisites survived, which no software can confirm. Budget for a physical trip to the shelf with a cable.
  • There is no observation channel to close the loop on: no mirror frame, and no server-side recognition either.
  • A rack-wide state=0 is one comma-separated, unauthenticated HTTP GET away from taking every phone off-network at once. That is a self-inflicted outage needing a person at every affected phone. Keep 9911 firewalled and never put this behind an unconfirmed UI button. If it must be tested, test one expendable phone off-hours with someone at the shelf.
  • A widely reported iOS behavior is that Wi-Fi re-enabled by hand while airplane mode is on survives later airplane-mode cycles, which would make the flight toggle recoverable. That is not stated in any vendor document and was not tested here. Prove it on one expendable phone before trusting it.
  • Before assuming any shortcut call fires on this rig at all, run GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 and check it returns the same address as the device record's ip field. Phonefarm gates its whole shortcut dispatcher as professional-version-only; XP attaches no edition note, but the path was never exercised here.

Scale

Not applicable to the round trip, since it does not complete. The dispatch side is cheap, one comma-list GET for the whole rack, which is exactly what makes the failure mode dangerous rather than throttled. /shortcut/device/ip is single id, so reachability checks are one request per phone bounded by outtime; run them in parallel rather than in a loop. The supported alternative is a one-time manual setup of a few minutes per phone, after which cellular cycling is a single rack-wide call with no ongoing cost and mirroring never drops.

Open What is still unprobed on this rig

Three gaps matter more than the rest, because designs get built on them. No /shortcut/* endpoint has ever been called on these two phones, so every Shortcut-backed capability in this document is documented-but-unexercised here. The image-search plug-in was never probed, and the OCR result makes its absence likely rather than certain. And /pic/find-multi-color is presumed kernel-internal only because no doc names a plug-in for it, which is an argument from silence given that /pic/ocr turned out to be gated. Each of these is a single cheap probe. Run them before the console's feature set is promised to anyone.

Telemetry and phone-side configuration

The two requests a fleet console asks first, "how is this phone doing" and "is this phone set up correctly", are the two the API answers least. Both are documented absences, verified by reading the field tables end to end rather than by failing to find a parameter.

Phone telemetry: battery, temperature, storage, position, carrier

Not possibleRefuted

Neither edition exposes any phone telemetry. The XP device record returned by /device/get is a closed list covering network identity, model and iOS build, screen geometry, board binding and mirroring state, and nothing else. Grepping both doc sets for battery, temperature, storage, GPS, carrier and signal returns no hit outside location and location_crc, which are mouse calibration parameters. The 19-entry XP shortcut catalogue covers albums, files, clipboard, URL, restart, brightness, torch, airplane mode, cellular, Wi-Fi and IP, with no reader for power, heat, free space or position.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get — confirm the ceiling. Returns ip, mac, user_name, version (18.7.10), model (iPhone11,8), width/height (414x896), imgw/imgh (500x1080), state, air_pid, vid/pid/uid, gid/gname, location_crc, the five air_* overrides and uver. No power, thermal, storage, position or carrier field exists.
  2. get_device_list + get_usb_list + callbacks /api/device/get, /api/config/usb/get, ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — the health telemetry that does exist, split along the two channels. Video ready is state non-zero with a live air_pid (22236 here); control ready is board state 2 with the phone bound to that board's uid. Callbacks dev_connect, dev_disconnect, usb_change and error_push carry the transitions.
  3. none client-side frame-rate counter — add the measured new-frame rate as a link-quality proxy per phone. On this rig 192.168.4.68 produces about 29 new frames per second under driven motion and its identical twin 192.168.4.27 about 4.5.
  4. shortcut#15, set_airplay_mode GET /api/shortcut/switch/bril?id=<ids>&state=0.05, GET /api/device/airplay/set?id=<ids>&air_fps=<n>&air_ratio=<n> — the nearest thing to a thermal or battery control loop. Both are inputs only, with no corresponding reading.
  5. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1 — the public egress IP, single id only. state=0 returns the LAN address, which should match the ip field from /device/get, making this the cheapest end-to-end proof that the Shortcut is installed and the hotkey binding fires.

Needs

  • Nothing at all for the negative finding. /device/get with no id returns every device in one call and answers today.
  • For any /shortcut/* route, the iMouse Shortcut installed on each phone with the kernel IP (192.168.4.29) edited in, run once with every permission allowed, Shortcuts Advanced set to allow running scripts and sharing large data, and the Shortcut bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key through the console's Send Binding Key. /shortcut/file/* and /shortcut/switch/device additionally need iOS 15 or later.
  • For any screen-reading route, the vendor OCR plug-in installed and connected, which is not the case here, or your own OCR engine running on the raw BMP frames on the PC.

Watch out

  • location and location_crc are pointer calibration, not geolocation. Both XRs carry the shared-library CRC B0DBD800, byte identical to the vendor's own doc example. A dashboard that maps this field is mapping a checksum.
  • Reading battery off a Settings screenshot is not a degraded version of telemetry, it is a from-scratch vision and automation project. On this rig it is blocked end to end: /pic/ocr answers but returns data.code 28, plug-in not connected, so /pic/ocr, /pic/ocr-ex, /pic/find-text and /pic/find-text-ex are all unavailable. Label it blocked pending plug-in install, not available but slow.
  • Estimating free space by summing Photos and On My iPhone through the Shortcut is not a weak proxy, it is not a proxy at all. It excludes apps, caches and system data entirely, so the error against true free space is unbounded. Do not carry it into a capacity plan.
  • Both levers are open loop and one is disruptive. Brightness has no getter, and changing any air_* value disconnects the cast immediately and applies on the next projection.
  • Public-IP geolocation is coarse and wrong behind CGNAT or a carrier's shared egress, and every phone on one LAN reports the same address. Treat it as network egress information, never as device position, and keep it out of logs you would share.
  • A scrape built on UI navigation can appear to succeed while reading stale data for hours, because a failed tap and an unchanged screen look identical. The stuck-click state makes this concrete: /mouse/click can stop landing while /mouse/move and hardware keys still respond, and only /mouse/reset clears it.
  • A thermal shutdown presents as dev_disconnect and usb_change code 20 arriving together. A cable pull hits usb_change alone and a Wi-Fi loss hits dev_disconnect alone, so correlate the two callbacks before naming a cause.

Scale

The negative check is one request for the whole rack. The workarounds scale badly and in different ways. Every shortcut reader is single id (/shortcut/album/get, /shortcut/file/get, /shortcut/clipboard/get, /shortcut/device/ip all state "Multiple is not allowed") with a 15,000 ms default outtime, so a 19-phone sweep is 19 sequential round trips. Only the write and switch calls take a comma-separated id list and fan out in one request. A UI-navigation read costs roughly 3 to 5 seconds per phone, dominated by pointer travel at about 0.6 ms per pixel and by per-phone frame settle, which is about 35 ms on the fast XR and 220 ms or more on the slow one. That is on the order of 15 to 20 phones per hour for a one-shot manual check, far below any monitoring cadence, and it interrupts whatever the phone was doing.

Wrong "location_crc is where the phone is"

It is the CRC of an entry in the vendor's shared mouse parameter library, used to match calibration across devices of the same model. Both phones on this rig carry B0DBD800. There is no geolocation anywhere in either API edition, and the only position-adjacent value available, the public IP, describes a network, not a phone.

Auditing the phone-side accessibility settings from the PC

Not possibleRefuted

The vendor requires five phone-side settings on every slot: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity at maximum, Full Keyboard Access on with auto-hide at 1 s, Trackpad and Mouse tracking speed at maximum, Display and Brightness with Auto-Lock set to Never and View set to Standard, and a Control Center laid out with two rows of icons at the bottom, which the vendor notes affects automatic screencasting. None of the five is readable through either edition. A search for "accessibility" or "assistive" across the whole XP documentation set returns zero hits, and the consequence is the vendor's own support case: a phone can mirror perfectly, report state 1 with a live air_pid, and silently discard every input.

How

  1. get_device_list GET /api/device/get — 26 fields of geometry, network, binding and mirroring state. Not one describes an iOS setting.
  2. none GET /api/config/imserver/get — kernel-side fields only (air_play_name, lang, mdns_type, opencv_num, ocr_num, allow_ip_list, thread_mode, mouse_mode, flip_right and the rest). Phonefarm has no configuration endpoint at all.
  3. shortcut ids 1-24 the 19 documented /shortcut/* paths — every one writes or reads content. None reads a Settings toggle.
  4. mouse_reset_pos + mouse_move + get_device_screenshot GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<ids>, GET /api/mouse/move?id=<id>&x=380&y=880, GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — behavioral probe 1. Diff a roughly 40 px box around the commanded point: a landed pointer measures 1.4 to 9.8 mean absolute difference against a 0.02 idle floor.
  5. send_key GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=WIN+h — behavioral probe 2, the keyboard path. A whole-frame mean difference above 20 (142 measured) means the key was interpreted. The plain Home key needs kernel 2026.2.27 or later and iOS 26.1 or later, so on these 18.7.10 phones WIN+h is the correct choice.
  6. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&x=<x>&y=<y>&button=1 — behavioral probe 3, the one that matters. Press Home twice first to normalize, then tap a target whose position you read from that phone's own frame.
  7. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 — an indirect tell. A data.code 0 whose data.text equals the device record's ip proves part of the phone-side setup, but only the Shortcut part.

Needs

  • Mirroring live (state non-zero with a live air_pid) so the probes are optically verifiable, and the board at state 2 in /config/usb/get with non-empty vid/pid/uid in the device record.
  • A non-empty location_crc, otherwise every /mouse call returns data.code 11, no mouse parameters.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. With only IMService.exe up, this rig reported both phones at state 0 and an empty board list.
  • A client-side frame differ computing mean absolute pixel difference on the bottom-up BMP (1,620,054 bytes). Byte or MD5 comparison is useless, because encoder noise and the clock change every frame.

Watch out

  • Passing every probe is not a settings audit and must never be reported as one. A phone can land the pointer, honor WIN+h and register a tap while still having mid-range tracking sliders or a one-row Control Center, and that misconfiguration surfaces later as offset taps or a dropped mirror, not as a failed probe.
  • WIN+h succeeding proves only the keyboard path. It was measured still working on a phone whose taps were being silently discarded, so it is never a proxy for input health.
  • Auto-Lock Never, View Standard, lowest brightness and StandBy off are not testable by any probe at all.
  • The shortcut round trip is ambiguous on failure. data.code 30, call timeout, cannot distinguish Shortcut not installed from binding not configured from phone unreachable, so do not sell it as diagnostic of any single failure mode.
  • Probe 3 has a real side effect: it opens whatever is at the tapped coordinate. Run the sweep as a scheduled, bounded pass, not as a continuous background health check, or a fleet ends up in unexpected app states.
  • A failed probe must produce a work order for a person at the rack, never an automated remediation. The settings cannot be changed from the PC either, so any automatic "fix" can only be a benign retry, and a retry loop hides exactly the failure this entry is about.
  • A probe run against an unlocked phone captures whatever it is displaying into the 1.6 MB frames you diff. Treat probe frames as disposable.
  • Passing today says nothing about tomorrow. Nothing on the PC can observe a toggle being changed on the phone, so results carry a timestamp and are re-run on events: shift change, phone re-seated, iOS update.
  • Dropped from earlier drafts: the claim that reaching a phone-side collection page proves LAN connectivity. The XP docs document no such URL. The Phonefarm ?fun=collection form belongs to the other edition. Use the ip field or the shortcut round trip instead.

Scale

The audit itself is impossible at any rate. The substitute sweep is cheap: /mouse/reset, /mouse/move, /mouse/click and /key/sendkey all take a comma-separated id list, so the input half costs one request for N phones and the board walks them in parallel. Verification is single id (/pic/screenshot states "Multiple is not allowed") but phones are independent, measured at 83 and 85 req/s with two concurrent pollers and 512 req/s aggregate with ten. Budget pointer travel, not requests: a 1000 px reposition is about 592 ms. Allow at least one new frame after each action, roughly 35 ms on the fast XR and 220 ms on the slow one, never a fixed 30 fps assumption. A three-probe sweep of 19 phones lands around 20 to 40 seconds, which is affordable far more often than it is useful.

Transport and frame fidelity

Server-pushed frame streaming and a second AirPlay receiver

Not possibleRefuted

The Phonefarm doc advertises two capacity features this rig does not have. loop_device_screenshot makes the kernel push screenshots at a chosen interval as binary WebSocket frames, retunable live and stoppable with stop:true. get_airplaysrvnum and set_airplaysrvnum read and set how many AirPlay receiver services one kernel advertises, each appearing to the phones as a separate target. The installed XP kernel has neither: no loop or push endpoint, no binary WebSocket frame format, and a single receiver in /config/imserver/get with no count field. The live probe confirms it, since POST {"fun":"get_airplaysrvnum"} to 9911 returns status 500 and port 9912 is closed.

How

  1. loop_device_screenshot none — do not design around a pushed stream. Every one of XP's documented callbacks is a JSON envelope; there is no binary opcode, no frame header and no interval parameter anywhere in the XP doc set.
  2. get_device_screenshot (binary, ws-only in Phonefarm) GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<one id>&binary=true — the substitute. One poller per phone at a fixed period, 33 to 50 ms for a live view and 100 to 500 ms for wall tiles. XP states plainly that with binary true the JSON is not returned and raw image data comes back directly, so HTTP binary works here where Phonefarm forbids it.
  3. none client-side buffer reuse and SameAsPrevious — reuse one 1.62 MB buffer per poller and discard frames whose mean absolute difference from the previous frame is under 1.
  4. get_device_screenshot isjpg / gzip /api/pic/screenshot jpg=true — never on loopback. The kernel re-encodes at 40.5 ms p50 with a hard cap near 21 req/s. Reserve it for a remote client that cannot afford 1.6 MB per frame. XP has no gzip and no original flag.
  5. get_airplaysrvnum / set_airplaysrvnum none — no receiver count exists. The nearest call, /config/imserver/set with air_play_name or air_play_port, renames or moves the one receiver and needs /imserver/restart, which drops every mirroring session.
  6. get_airplaysrvnum → data.ver WS callback im_connect → data.ver — the kernel version comes from the WebSocket on connect, not from any HTTP path. Features are gated on it, and the two editions use different version schemes, so do not compare them.

Needs

  • IMService.exe on TCP 9911 for both HTTP and WebSocket at /api, plus IMConsole.exe running and logged in.
  • Target phone mirroring, with an established socket on TCP 17000 from the phone's IP.
  • One poller thread and one reusable 1.62 MB buffer per phone, since /pic/screenshot is single id and every raw frame exceeds the .NET Large Object Heap threshold.
  • imgw/imgh read per device. Frames and input coordinates share that space (500 x 1080 here), not the 414 x 896 logical size.

Watch out

  • The substitute is not a literal equivalent. Phonefarm's push let the kernel pace the stream and multiplex many devices over one socket using the frame's deviceid header. On XP the client owns pacing and demultiplexing and holds N sockets, so ten tiles means ten sockets and ten times the request overhead even though wall-clock latency is fine.
  • Quote the spread, not just the median, in any capacity claim: ten concurrent pollers measured 512 req/s aggregate at p50 3 ms with a worst p95 of 142 ms, which is 47 times the median.
  • No transport beats the phone's own AirPlay production rate, measured at about 29 new frames per second on one XR and 4.5 on its identical twin on the same iOS build. That is the second phone's Wi-Fi link, and the vendor console hits the same wall.
  • Use a fixed poll period. Deriving the interval from observed frame gaps is positive feedback and was measured decaying 23 fps to 16.5 fps.
  • Only two phones are live here, so nothing establishes how many phones one PC's single receiver can actually carry. Do not extrapolate a per-PC capacity number from a two-phone test, and do not port Phonefarm's 50-to-100-phone mode table, whose measurement basis is undefined and which does not exist on XP.
  • mdns_type and allow_ip_list were not probed and the doc's wording does not clearly separate the two modes. Treat them as an untested lever, and note they gate AirPlay discovery only, never the API.
  • Any client library ported from the Phonefarm docs fails loudly but unhelpfully on every call: the XP kernel splits fun on "/" and expects at least two segments, so bare function names return status 500, "List index out of bounds (1)", rather than a clean unsupported error. Guessed paths return 404 with a Chinese "interface does not exist" message. Porting needs a full path rewrite, not a compatibility shim.

Scale

Polling scales linearly with no shared kernel bottleneck. One phone sustains 84 req/s at 2.0 ms p50; two phones flat out measured 83 and 85 req/s, identical to either alone; ten pollers reached 512 req/s aggregate. A wall A/B showed the master unaffected, 17.7 fps with the wall off against 17.6 fps with it running. Input traffic and frame polling do not interfere in either direction. Receiver count is the hard stop: one receiver per kernel, so capacity grows by adding PCs, with the per-PC ceiling unmeasured.

Pixel-exact or color-accurate assertions on mirror frames

Not possibleRefuted

/pic/screenshot returns the AirPlay decoder's frame at imgw x imgh, 500 x 1080 on these XRs, against an iOS logical size of 414 x 896 and a physical panel of 828 x 1792. It is a rescaled, lossily encoded stream whose idle frame-to-frame noise measures 0.02 to 0.03 mean absolute difference with nothing happening. One-pixel misalignment, anti-aliasing changes, sub-pixel text rendering and exact color values cannot be asserted from it, and XP's screenshot parameter table has no original flag to escape the rescale.

How

  1. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<deviceid>&binary=true — fast structural check. Raw BMP, 2 ms, 1,620,054 bytes.
  2. none none (client-side) — compare by mean absolute pixel difference. Measured on this rig: untouched phone 0.02 to 0.03, a real UI reaction 20 to 160.
  3. none GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<deviceid>&rect=[l,t,r,b]&binary=true — crop server-side to the region under test to cut both noise and payload. rect and save_path are XP-only additions.
  4. send_key fn_key GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=shift+win+3 — the exact route, per screen. The phone takes its own screenshot into Photos at the panel's native 828 x 1792.
  5. shortcut#1 GET /api/shortcut/album/get?id=<deviceid>&num=1 — list the new entry. XP has no date filter, so pick the newest by create_time or diff the listing before and after.
  6. shortcut#2 POST /api/shortcut/album/down {id, list:[{album_name:"", name:"IMG_xxxx", ext:"png"}], zip:1, outtime} — pull the PNG to <install dir>\Shortcut\Media and diff it exactly on the PC. Name and extension are separate fields on XP, unlike Phonefarm's single filename string.

Needs

  • Mirroring live for any /pic/screenshot call, and a bound, connected board plus Full Keyboard Access for the shift+win+3 hotkey.
  • For the exact route, the iMouse Shortcut installed, kernel-IP-edited, run once with all permissions allowed and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, with Shortcuts Advanced set to allow sharing large amounts of data and Photos permission granted on first run with the phone unlocked.

Watch out

  • Fixing the phone's display settings does not recover color accuracy. Brightness, True Tone, Night Shift and air_ratio all shift sampled RGB, but the deeper reason is structural: the AirPlay stream's H.264-family encoding uses 4:2:0 chroma subsampling by design and discards color detail on every frame regardless of any iOS setting.
  • Raising air_ratio is a red herring, not a fidelity fix. It changes the encoder's output resolution without touching the lossy compression or the per-phone source cadence, so it makes images larger without making them more exact, and it invalidates every template and color table built at the previous ratio.
  • The exact route is doc-derived, not measured. No /shortcut/* call has been exercised on this rig, and a missing binding fails silently for about 15 seconds before returning data.code 30. Verify it with a single dry run, send shift+win+3 then poll /shortcut/album/get, before writing it into a deliverable as supported.
  • Even the native PNG is exact to what the screen displayed, not to a render target. It is still a composite from the OS compositor and its font rendering.
  • Never assert on frame equality. A mirrored screen never repeats a frame exactly, and this project already drew a wrong conclusion once by byte-comparing frames and deciding an untouched phone had reacted.
  • Harvesting native screenshots fills the camera roll. Plan cleanup with /shortcut/album/del, and note that /shortcut/album/clear is destructive and should stay behind a human confirmation.

Scale

Mirror diffs are cheap: 2 ms per raw frame, about 84 req/s per phone, phones independent, and input traffic does not interfere. A full-fleet structural sweep of 19 phones is well under a second of API time, bounded in practice by how fast the UI under test actually changes and by new-frame availability, which is 29 per second on one phone here and 4.5 on the other. The native-PNG route is orders of magnitude slower: a hotkey, a Photos write, an album listing and a LAN transfer, four serialized single-id steps per screen per phone, estimated at 5 to 15 seconds each. Budget it for the handful of screens that genuinely need exactness.

Trap Hashing frames to detect change
