MD5 or byte equality reports "changed" on an idle, untouched phone every single time, because the clock, the AirPlay encoder's noise and wallpaper parallax move pixels on every frame. Any change detection must threshold a mean absolute pixel difference, ideally against an idle control. The measured floor on this rig is 0.02 to 0.03; a real reaction measures 20 to 160; a landed pointer, visible only in a small box around the commanded coordinate, measures 1.4 to 9.8.

App state, traffic and builds

Structured app state: DOM, accessibility tree, element list, logs

Not possibleRefuted

There is no "get elements" call in either edition. Neither API exposes the iOS accessibility tree, a view hierarchy, a web DOM, app variables, console output, crash logs or anything inside an app sandbox. The only observable state is pixels, colors within those pixels, plug-in recognition results on those pixels, and whatever the iOS Shortcut can put on or read from the clipboard and the Files app. This single fact makes the whole automation model on this rack coordinate-and-vision based, so every use case elsewhere in this document that assumes element-level targeting inherits the same limitation and needs its own per-app, per-iOS-version coordinate baseline.

How

  1. none none — the capability itself. The full XP endpoint set and the Phonefarm function list were searched; nothing returns element structure, and guessed paths return HTTP 404.
  2. click + send_key + shortcut#11 GET /api/mouse/click?id=<id>&x=&y=&time=600, then /api/key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+a, then fn_key=WIN+c, then GET /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<one id> — the strongest substitute for text. time is the delay between press and release, so 600 ms is a long press that raises the Select All menu where WIN+a is not honored. Returns exact Unicode with zero structure.
  3. find_image / find_image_ex GET /api/pic/find-image or /api/pic/find-image-cv — element positions by template. Returns data.list[{index, centre, rect, code}] in mirror pixels, so centre feeds /mouse/click directly. Plug-in gated.
  4. ocr / ocr_ex GET /api/pic/ocr, /api/pic/ocr-ex, /api/pic/find-text, /api/pic/find-text-ex — labels and on-screen strings as a flat list of strings with boxes. Unavailable here: /pic/ocr returns data.code 28.
  5. find_multi_color POST /api/pic/find-multi-color with list:[{first_color:"x|y|RRGGBB-tolerance,...", rect, similarity}] — an "is the UI in state X" check. No plug-in is named for it in either doc, which makes it the most likely recognition function to work on this rig, but that is an inference from the docs and not a measurement: it has not been probed, and a data.code 28 would prove it gated after all.
  6. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<one id>&binary=true — the fallback that always works. Run your own OCR or template matching on the PC, budgeting 100 to 300 ms of client-side recognition against 2 ms of capture.
  7. mouse_reset_pos GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<id1,id2,...> — before any tap-critical vision flow. A flow that clicks a correctly located center and sees nothing happen is usually the stuck-click state, not a bad match.

Needs

  • For the clipboard route, the iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited and bound on each phone (unverified here), Full Keyboard Access on so iOS honors WIN+a and WIN+c, and a view whose content is genuinely selectable text. Native table cells, images and canvas content are not.
  • For the template and OCR routes, the corresponding vendor plug-in installed and connected via opencv_num or ocr_num with a kernel restart, which is not the case here.
  • For any vision flow, a per-app, per-iOS-version coordinate and template baseline, re-measured whenever the app or iOS updates.

Watch out

  • Every substitute returns flat data: a string, a center point, a match or no match. Never hierarchy, role, enabled state or identity.
  • The clipboard route is asymmetric in cost. WIN+a and WIN+c fan out to N phones in one /key/sendkey call, but /shortcut/clipboard/get is single id and each round trip costs roughly a second over Wi-Fi.
  • Apps can remove Select All from the callout menu entirely, common in banking and DRM-protected reading apps, and the automation cannot distinguish that from an empty field: both produce no meaningful clipboard change. Run a positive control against a known-good selectable field alongside the target to confirm the mechanism is even active for that app.
  • The clipboard is a single shared slot. A scrape overwrites whatever a paste step was about to use, so sequence them deliberately.
  • Correction to a common overstatement: the Files app and the photo albums are listable and downloadable through the Shortcut on iOS 15 or later. What is unreachable is another app's private container, which is where app state, databases and logs live.
  • The two phones here already have different home screens and wallpapers, so the same coordinate hits a different app on each. Normalize with two Home presses before reusing any coordinate across phones, and do not assume identical layouts.
  • Lifting screen content or clipboard text from apps holding other people's data is personal-data processing the moment it lands in a PC-side log, and the frames capture notifications and account names incidentally. Restrict scrapes to accounts you own or have written authorization for, keep derived fields rather than whole frames, and set a retention limit. Automated extraction from third-party apps and sites is also typically a Terms of Service breach regardless of technique.

Scale

Raw frame capture is 2 ms per phone with phones independent, so vision input is effectively unbounded. Client-side recognition adds 100 to 300 ms per frame and is bounded by PC CPU, not the kernel. The clipboard scrape is the bottleneck at roughly 1 to 2 seconds per phone, because /shortcut/clipboard/get is a single-id Shortcut round trip with a 15 s default timeout. Once the long-press selection step, the positive control and the per-app copy-availability check are included, call it a few hundred reliable text lifts per hour per phone for real content. Every recognition endpoint, /pic/find-image, /pic/find-image-cv, /pic/ocr and /pic/find-multi-color, is explicitly single id, so recognition never batches across phones either.

Capturing the phone's network traffic, ad requests or push payloads

Not possibleRefuted

Neither edition exposes a proxy, packet capture, HAR export or any traffic hook. A grep of the whole XP doc set returns no endpoint that reads a request, a response body or a push payload. The only network-adjacent calls are the Shortcut IP lookup and the connectivity toggles /shortcut/switch/flight, /cdpd and /wlan. What the rack can observe is what renders on screen, so an ad-verification or attribution deliverable can only be "the rendered creative, the timestamp, the phone identity and the egress IP", never the request and its response.

How

  1. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<deviceid>&binary=true — pull a raw mirror frame of the rendered creative or banner. Pixels only; no network metadata accompanies a frame.
  2. send_key fn_key + ocr GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<ids>&fn_key=NoticeBar, then GET /api/pic/ocr?id=<deviceid> — open Notification Center and read the banner text. NoticeBar is in the XP hotkey table and absent from Phonefarm's. This reads rendered text, never an APNs payload.
  3. find_image / find_image_ex POST /api/pic/find-image-cv {id, img_list, rect:[l,t,r,b], similarity, all, same} — identify the creative by template instead of by request body. Plug-in gated on opencv_num, unprobed here.
  4. none GET /api/device/get → ip — the LAN address for phone-to-request correlation on the local segment, with no Shortcut needed.
  5. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<deviceid>&state=1 — the extranet address, only needed if requests leave via NAT with a different apparent IP per phone, which is network-dependent and unverified here.

Needs

  • Mirroring live for any frame- or recognition-based observation.
  • The OCR plug-in connected for /pic/ocr and /pic/find-text, which is not the case here, and opencv_num at 1 or more for /pic/find-image-cv, unprobed.
  • The iMouse Shortcut installed, kernel-IP-edited and hotkey-bound for /shortcut/device/ip.

Watch out

  • The notification fallback is doubly blocked here, not singly. Even with the OCR plug-in connected, opening Notification Center surfaces a push banner only if the phone is unlocked and the app has not suppressed banners.
  • Mirror frames carry no timestamp or provenance of their own, so an evidence package must record the request you sent, the id, the coordinates and the wall-clock time alongside the frame.
  • XP's rect is a flat [left, top, right, bottom] array. The Phonefarm four-corner-point form does not apply here.
  • The nearest real workaround, an HTTP interception proxy set by hand in each phone's Wi-Fi settings, sits entirely outside this API and cannot be scripted through the kernel at all. It is a footnote, not a chain step. Certificate pinning in most SDKs defeats it anyway, installing a CA profile weakens that phone's TLS trust until it is removed, and it must be confined to apps and accounts you own, since intercepting other people's traffic engages wiretap and computer-misuse law as well as those apps' terms.
  • A static-IP-without-gateway Wi-Fi arrangement means cellular traffic never crosses a LAN proxy at all.

Scale

Zero for the capability itself. For the observation fallback, raw frames are 2 ms p50 at about 84 req/s per phone with phones independent, and /pic/screenshot is single id so capture is one request each. The useful evidence rate is bounded by the phone's AirPlay source rate, 29 new frames per second on one XR and 4.5 on its twin. Because OCR is non-functional here, the effective rate of verified text extractions today is zero per hour per phone.

Installing builds, reading device internals, driving the app by element ID

Not possibleRefuted

There is no endpoint in either edition to install an IPA or TestFlight build, to read battery, CPU, memory, thermal state or console logs, to report an app's version, or to query a UI element tree the way XCUITest does. A grep across the XP doc set for battery, install, log, element and crash returns only kernel-side logs (airplay_connect_log, restart_log, im_log, error_push) and the account pages. Every CI pipeline assumes install the build, drive by element ID, collect logs; on this rack each of those three is absent or a weaker, pixel-based substitute.

How

  1. shortcut#13 GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<ids>&url=<https or itms-beta URL> — open the store or TestFlight page. This opens a URL, it does not install anything. Accepts a comma-separated id list.
  2. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=<px>&y=<px>&button=1 — tap Install, Update or Open by coordinate. XP's button is numeric 1 to 8, where Phonefarm used the strings "left" and "right". Send /mouse/reset to the target set first.
  3. ocr / find_image_ex GET /api/pic/ocr, POST /api/pic/find-text, /api/pic/find-image-cv — verify the installed version by reading the app's own About screen. All plug-in gated, so on this rig the check must be done client-side on a raw BMP.
  4. shortcut#11 GET /api/shortcut/clipboard/get?id=<deviceid>&outtime=<ms> — the only documented value channel back from the phone. It returns whatever is on the clipboard and cannot itself obtain battery, CPU or memory.
  5. shortcut#4 / shortcut#5 GET /api/shortcut/file/get?id=<deviceid>&path=<path>, then POST /api/shortcut/file/down — retrieve only files the app itself writes into the Files app, iOS 15 or later, both single id, landing in <install dir>\Shortcut\File. Crash .ips files and os_log are not exposed to Shortcuts.
  6. find_image_ex / ocr / find_multi_color /api/pic/find-image-cv, /api/pic/find-text, /api/pic/find-multi-color — navigation is coordinate, template, text or color based. All single id.

Needs

  • The iMouse Shortcut installed, kernel-IP-edited, run once with all permissions allowed and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, for every /shortcut/* step, plus iOS 15 or later for the file endpoints.
  • The board bound (vid and pid set together through /device/set) and connected at board state 2, plus the iOS accessibility prerequisites, for any tap-based flow.
  • App Store or TestFlight access on each test Apple ID, already signed in, with the phone unlocked so store and trust prompts can be answered by a person.

Watch out

  • Triggering a user-authored Shortcut from the PC to report battery is not a supported capability and should not appear in any deliverable that claims it. XP's fn_key vocabulary is a fixed enumerated table (WIN+h, Home, TAB+b, TAB+l, AppSwitch, ControlBar, NoticeBar, OPENKeyboard, shift+win+3 and +4, the clipboard chords, IME and volume keys), with no entry for an arbitrary user Shortcut.
  • /pic/find-multi-color is the one recognition endpoint with no documented plug-in dependency, which makes it plausibly available here, but that is an inference and not a probe. Carry the same hedge it gets elsewhere: assume gated until a call returns data.code 0.
  • Never script an Apple ID sign-in through these endpoints. The API is unauthenticated and speaks plain HTTP, so anything typed through /key is visible to any host on the subnet. Hand account sign-in to a person at the rack.
  • The phone's single wired port is occupied by the control board, so USB-side tooling cannot share the device. Crash-log extraction with a desktop utility is a manual, one-phone-at-a-time cable swap, which is throughput zero for unattended automation. Unplugging also drops that phone's control channel from board state 2 back to 1 and requires re-binding, and the vendor states the board works only with its supplied cable.
  • The fan-out claim holds only for phones with identical layouts. Taps are in mirror pixels and the two XRs here have different home screens, so a coordinate that hits Install on one does not necessarily hit it on the other. Per-phone calibration is required and was not verified.
  • There is no rollback. An install driven by taps cannot be uninstalled by any API function either.
  • Repeated installs across many devices under one Apple ID can trip App Store limits and TestFlight tester counts. Use accounts you own and stay inside their terms. Enterprise or ad-hoc distribution profiles change a phone's trust posture and should be a deliberate, documented decision.

Scale

Install by UI is roughly five taps plus download time per phone. Navigation calls fan out in one request where layouts match, but every verification step is single id and must be looped, and pointer travel adds about 0.6 ms per pixel regardless of fleet size. Serialized behind download completion that is on the order of 1 to 3 attempts per minute per phone under ideal conditions, lower in practice because store-side throttling of many downloads from one LAN applies and because OCR verification is unavailable here, forcing slower client-side inspection. Device internals and element-ID driving are zero: no endpoint exists, and any number quoted for them describes a manual screen-reading workflow, not an API capability.

The input surface

Pinch, rotate, two-finger and pressure gestures

Not possibleRefuted

The control board is a single-pointer HID mouse and keyboard bridge. Every input endpoint, /mouse/click, /mouse/down, /mouse/move, /mouse/up, /mouse/swipe and /mouse/wheel, commands one pointer position, and button 1 to 8 selects a mouse button, not a finger. There is no second-pointer call, no touch-count parameter and no pressure parameter anywhere in either edition, so pinch-to-zoom, two-finger rotate, multi-finger swipes and pressure gestures cannot be emitted. "Swipe" in this API means a one-finger drag, not gestures in general.

How

  1. click / mouse_down / mouse_move / mouse_up / swipe / mouse_wheel that is the complete mouse surface — establish the limit from the endpoint set itself. /mouse/move takes only id, x, y: one position. /mouse/swipe takes one start and one end.
  2. click x2 at the same coordinate GET /api/mouse/click?id=<ids>&x=250&y=540 twice in quick succession — workaround A, app-native double-tap zoom. Do not move between the taps: the board walks the pointer at about 0.6 ms per pixel, so any repositioning breaks the interval.
  3. mouse_wheel GET /api/mouse/wheel?id=<ids>&direction=up|down|left|right&len=30&number=1 — workaround B, where content scrolls rather than zooms. len is 1 to 127 and XP adds the horizontal pair Phonefarm lacked. Wheel scrolling avoids the pointer-walk cost entirely.
  4. click /api/mouse/click on the app's own +/- buttons or zoom slider — workaround C, the only one that is parameterizable, repeatable and verifiable. If the app under test is yours, a debug zoom control costs less than any of the above and gives an exact factor instead of an opaque gesture.
  5. get_device_screenshot GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true before and after — verify by mean absolute pixel difference, in a box around the expected content region rather than whole-frame.

Needs

  • Board bound and connected plus the full iOS accessibility checklist, none of it queryable over the API.
  • Coordinates in mirror pixels read per device from /device/get, never iOS points.
  • Two Home presses to normalize before mirroring any coordinate across phones.

Watch out

  • This is a hardware and protocol limit, not a configuration gap. The board presents a 9-byte vendor HID output report as a mouse and keyboard bridge, and the kernel exposes exactly one pointer. No plug-in, license tier or iOS setting adds a second contact point, and iOS treats a Lightning-connected pointer accessory as one AssistiveTouch cursor in any case.
  • The double-tap workaround is inferred from a timing budget, not observed. iOS's recognition window is roughly 300 to 500 ms in practice and Apple does not publish the figure; what is measured here is only that the input channel is fast enough to fire both taps inside it. Confirm with a before and after diff showing an actual scale change before relying on it. Apps that do not implement double-tap zoom simply get two taps.
  • Ctrl plus wheel is not expressible: /key/down accepts single keys and documented fn_key combinations, and a bare CTRL is not in that vocabulary.
  • Replaying a recorded AssistiveTouch custom gesture is an iOS feature, not an API feature, and it is location-locked: apps that zoom about the pinch center will zoom about the point where the gesture was recorded, and the replay cannot be parameterized per call. It also requires re-enabling the floating AssistiveTouch menu against the vendor's prescribed configuration, which puts a permanent button in every frame and invalidates templates and pixel-diff baselines captured without it. Worst of all, the drift is undetectable through the API, since no gesture-list endpoint exists, so a silently wrong replay looks identical to a correct one in logs.
  • A whole-frame diff cannot distinguish a successful zoom from an accidental app switch or a keyboard appearing: all three land in the 20 to 160 range. Box-diff the content region.
  • None of the recognition-based verification paths are available on this rig, so success or failure has to be judged by client-side pixel diffing of raw BMP frames.
  • Pressure and haptics are unobservable regardless: the mirror carries pixels only, so even a pressure gesture, if it could be emitted, could not be verified.

Scale

Irrelevant to the limit itself. Of the substitutes, double-tap and wheel scroll fan out to the whole rack in one request each, since both take comma-separated id lists and the board walks every listed phone in parallel at the cost of one. Verification is single id but phones are independent, so a before and after pair costs roughly 5 to 15 ms per phone and a 19-phone sweep stays well under a second. The real gate is the app's own animation settle, roughly 300 to 600 ms, which puts a fully confirmed action at single digits per minute per phone and an unconfirmed, pipelined one in the thousands per hour.

Walls the API cannot cross

Apple Pay, Face ID and side-button confirmations

Not possibleRefuted

The rack cannot cross the Apple Pay sheet, a Face ID prompt, or any step that needs a physical button press. The control board is a HID pointer and keyboard bridge, and the XP /key/sendkey hotkey table, read in full in both places it appears, contains no side button, no power button and no biometric action. The nearest entries are TAB+l (lock) and CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r (restart). The furthest the API reaches is tapping the control that raises the sheet, then screenshotting the result.

How

  1. click, swipe /api/mouse/click, /api/mouse/swipe drive the cart and checkout up to the payment sheet. XP button is numeric (1 left, 2 right); len is a fraction, 0.9 meaning 10% to 90%. Coordinates are mirror pixels, 500 x 1080 here.
  2. click /api/mouse/click taps the Apple Pay or Confirm control. This is the last action the API can take in the flow.
  3. get_device_screenshot /api/pic/screenshot?id=…&binary=true captures the sheet as evidence of where the flow stopped. Raw BMP is 2 ms and 1,620,054 bytes on this rig, and the call can be repeated to watch the sheet time out or be cancelled, so the API is not blind after the tap, only unable to act.
  4. send_key /api/key/sendkey?id=…&fn_key=… confirms the absence: the XP hotkey enumeration is closed, and the Phonefarm list is a strict subset of it.
  5. No API call. Auto-Lock set to Never on each phone, in Display & Brightness, keeps the lock gate out of the run. This is per-phone iOS configuration and invisible to the API.
  6. No API call. A merchant sandbox with a stored non-biometric method is the only route that lets a checkout flow complete unattended, and it must be a genuine test environment.

Needs

  • Board bound and connected, valid mouse parameters, and the iOS accessibility settings, for the taps that reach the sheet at all.
  • Auto-Lock set to Never on each phone so the lock gate does not appear mid-run.
  • A merchant test or sandbox environment if the flow has to finish without a person present.

Watch out

  • This is a platform boundary, not a rig limitation. No plug-in, professional edition, Shortcut or firmware version in either document changes it.
  • Never push payment credentials or device passcodes through /key/sendkey or /shortcut/clipboard/set. The API is unauthenticated and reachable by any host on the LAN, and it would breach payment-network and platform rules in any case.
  • A restart by any route, /device/restart, /shortcut/switch/device state=1 or fn_key=CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r, leaves the phone at the passcode screen. Mirroring drops too, so air_pid goes empty and state returns 0. An automation loop must detect that and route to a human queue rather than keep tapping a dead mirror.
  • The two XRs here have different home screens and app layouts, so fanning a checkout tap out to a comma-separated id list risks hitting a different control on each phone. In a live payment flow that is a real charge, not a cosmetic error.
  • /pic/screenshot is single-id, so evidence capture is one request per phone even though the taps that got there fan out.

Scale

Not improved by batching. Driving N phones to the sheet costs one comma-separated tap sequence and well under a second of board time regardless of N, so arrivals at the sheet are as cheap as the browse flow allows. Completions are zero per hour by platform design, at any fleet size, because every arrival then queues on a person. Plan the rack around queueing sheets for a human, or around a sandbox that avoids the sheet entirely.

No outbound events, no caller authentication

Kernel-originated webhooks or outbound event calls

Not possibleRefuted

Neither edition can be told to POST an event, such as device offline, board unplugged or cast finished, to a URL you own. The kernel's entire event surface is a set of JSON callbacks broadcast to clients that have already connected to its own WebSocket, ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api on XP and ws://host:9911/clinet on Phonefarm. The XP configuration endpoint exposes 19 fields and not one is a URL, endpoint, notification or webhook field. The only way an event leaves the rack is a bridge process you run, holding a persistent socket, making the outbound call itself with its own authentication.

How

  1. none (Phonefarm has no kernel-configuration function beyond airplay server count and restart) /api/config/imserver/get confirms the absence: air_play_name, lang, mdns_type, connect_failed_retry, air_play_ratio, opencv_num, ocr_num, allow_ip_list, air_play_fps, air_play_img_fps, air_play_refresh_rate, air_play_port, air_play_audio, auto_connect, auto_updata, thread_mode, mouse_mode, flip_right, plus enable_hardware_acceleration on /set. No callback address anywhere.
  2. ws://host:9911/clinet (the vendor's own spelling) ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api opens the only event channel, and the client opens it. XP serves HTTP and WebSocket on the same port. On connect the kernel sends im_connect with data.ver, the only place the XP kernel version is exposed.
  3. dev_connect, usb_change, collection, binary loop-screenshot frames im_connect, dev_connect, dev_disconnect, dev_rotate, dev_change, dev_delete, group_change, group_delete, usb_change, collection_mouse, airplay_connect_log, restart_log, user_info, im_log, error_push, im_config_change, logout, dev_sort_change: all 18 XP callbacks are verified in the callback page. The envelope is {fun, status:200, message, msgid:0, data:{list, code, id, message}}, with device records inside data.list. usb_change carries data.code 19 (board to PC), 20 (board off PC), 12 (board to phone).
  4. none none: debouncing and the outbound call with your own credentials is entirely your code.
  5. none user_info callback plus a periodic GET /api/device/get monitors the bridge itself. user_info is pushed at login and every 30 s, so it doubles as a socket heartbeat, but only while the kernel is logged in. The periodic /device/get is the transport-independent liveness check.

Needs

  • A bridge host, which can be the rig itself, with outbound network access to wherever the events are going.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. With only IMService.exe up, the live probe showed both phones at state 0 and an empty board list, so no meaningful events would ever fire.
  • Kernel reachable on TCP 9911, restricted at the Windows firewall rather than trusted to be reached only by the bridge.
  • A WebSocket client library, and reconnect logic, because /imserver/restart drops every socket.

Watch out

  • There is no HTTP long-poll, no server-sent-events endpoint and no queue to drain. Anything broadcast while the bridge was down is lost, so reconcile with /api/device/get and /api/config/usb/get on every reconnect.
  • XP has no server-push frame stream at all, so job-finished signals derived from the screen must be polled with /pic/screenshot, never awaited as an event.
  • error_push is the only asynchronous failure signal, and it does not cover this rig's most consequential failure mode. A stuck click returns data.code 0 while taps are not landing, measured at 0.09 against 141.96 mean pixel difference. Nothing in the source material says a stuck click raises error_push, so treat that as no rather than as an open question. The only working detector is a pointer-box pixel diff on the AirPlay frame, which lives on the video channel, not the event channel.
  • Any outward alert claiming action X succeeded on phone Y must be backed by a screen diff, not by the absence of an error callback.
  • Multiple clients each receive every broadcast, so a second subscribed bridge is legitimate redundancy. It also means a rogue LAN client can read every broadcast, including device names, ip, mac and user_name, with no way for your bridge to know it is not alone.

Scale

Callback volume is negligible and does not grow with phone count: connect and disconnect events, board plug events, config changes, and a user_info heartbeat every 30 s, all on one shared socket. One WebSocket client comfortably serves the whole 19-board rack, and extra clients cost the kernel almost nothing. Frame data never travels on this channel; video is polled per phone at 2 ms and 1.62 MB a frame, single id, with phones independent at 83 to 85 req/s each.

Authenticating API callers: the XP kernel is open to anything on the LAN

Not possibleRefuted

Neither edition has any concept of a client credential. The two settings integrators mistake for access control do something else. /config/user/login licenses the kernel to the vendor account and returns total_license, overdue_time and user_state; mdns_type and allow_ip_list are documented as screencast discovery rules, governing which phones may find the AirPlay receiver. No XP endpoint takes a token, key or session, and every vendor example calls a remote host with no credential. Any host that can reach TCP 9911 can enumerate devices, poll frames, inject taps and text, rewrite kernel config, and call /imserver/restart, which takes no parameters at all.

How

  1. get_device_list GET http://<rig ip>:9911/api/device/get returns the full device list with no challenge. The equipment doc's own examples are remote-host calls to 192.168.9.9:9911 with no credential of any kind. On this rig the same call returns both XRs with ip, mac, user_name, model and board binding.
  2. none /api/config/user/login, /info, /logout, /switch confirms the login endpoint is licensing, not caller auth: the response is entirely licence state. After logout the kernel refuses devices but the HTTP and WebSocket API keep answering.
  3. none /api/config/imserver/get | /set confirms mdns_type (0 allows all, 1 specifies the IP, 2 the IP in the list) and allow_ip_list ("It only takes effect when the rule is 1") gate AirPlay discovery only. Setting mdns_type=1 narrows who can find the advertised receiver name, not who can call port 9911.
  4. restart /api/imserver/restart shows the blast radius: its parameter table is fun only, no id and no credential. Stated for threat modeling, not as a procedure to run against a rig you do not own.
  5. none none: the only real fix is outside the API. A Windows Firewall inbound rule scoping TCP 9911 to the controller hosts, TCP 17000 and UDP 5353 scoped to the phone VLAN or SSID, optionally a reverse proxy or gateway in front of 9911 that adds a token, rate limits and an audit ledger, and an ACL on C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json.

Needs

  • Nothing. The exposure is the default state and cannot be turned off from inside the API.
  • To mitigate: administrator rights on the kernel PC's firewall, and control of the switch or AP to put phones on their own VLAN or SSID.

Watch out

  • There is no documented token, key, session, per-endpoint permission, caller allow-list or audit log in either edition. The XP error table, codes 0 to 41, contains no unauthorized code, which is itself evidence that callers are never checked.
  • The absence is documented by omission plus the vendor's own remote-host examples, and corroborated by the live probe here: unauthenticated GETs to /api/device/get, /api/config/usb/get and /api/device/group/get all answered.
  • A reverse proxy helps only if 9911 itself is firewalled to localhost or the proxy. Otherwise callers simply bypass it.
  • C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json stores the vendor account password as trivially reversible hex obfuscation, so file access to the PC is a live credential regardless of network rules. Firewalling 9911 does nothing about that.
  • The kernel keeps no caller log, so a firewall rule applied to the wrong interface or VLAN is undetectable from inside the product. Catching it needs an external port scan or a deliberate read-only probe from a second host you own.
  • Describing the exposure is not permission to reach a rig you do not own. Probing or driving someone else's kernel over a network is unauthorized access.

Scale

Not throughput-bound. This is a binary exposure, and one firewall rule covers an entire rack regardless of phone count. In a multi-kernel deployment each additional PC is an additional open surface needing its own rule, because there is no central policy point inside the vendor stack; a shared gateway in front of them is the only place a token, rate limit or audit trail can exist. The exploit is cheap: a raw BMP frame costs an uninvited caller 2 ms and 1.62 MB per phone per call, and ten concurrent pollers sustained 512 req/s against this kernel with no degradation, so continuous video exfiltration of the whole rack is trivial once a host is on the LAN.

Wrong allow_ip_list is not an API access control

It is a screencast discovery rule, and by its own description it applies only when mdns_type is 1. Setting it changes which phones can find the AirPlay receiver. It changes nothing about who can call /api. Every mitigation for caller access lives at the network layer or on the host.

Input primitives and their ceilings

Keyboard: ASCII only, one key per down or up, no cadence or repeat control

PartialWith caveats

/key/sendkey types a string of "English, numbers and English characters" or fires one hotkey from a closed vendor list. /key/down and /key/up take a single key each; /key/down additionally accepts fn_key for a combination, but /key/up has no fn_key parameter, so /key/upall is the only documented way to clear a held chord. None of the four keyboard endpoints has a parameter for inter-key delay, key repeat, typing speed or maximum length, and non-ASCII text is not supported at all. The documented XP route for Unicode is the clipboard plus WIN+v.

How

  1. send_key /api/key/sendkey?id=…&key=user123 types an ASCII string in one call. The XP parameter table is exactly fun, id, key, fn_key. id takes a comma list, so one request types the same string on N phones. Send text as POST JSON in UTF-8 so punctuation is not mangled in a query string.
  2. send_key, one call per character or chunk /api/key/sendkey, one call per character or chunk is the only cadence lever. Whatever timing happens inside a single string is the kernel's and is undocumented.
  3. key_down, key_up, key_release_all /api/key/down (key, or fn_key for a combination), then /api/key/sendkey, then /api/key/up (key only), then /api/key/upall holds a modifier or chord.
  4. send_key with fn_key /api/key/sendkey?id=…&fn_key=… fires a documented hotkey. The XP list is closed: WIN+h, Home, TAB+b, AppSwitch, ControlBar, NoticeBar, TAB+l, OPENKeyboard, shift+win+3, shift+win+4, CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r, CTRL+ALT+WIN+p, WIN+c, WIN+v, WIN+a, WIN+x, SwitchIme, BACKSPACE, a bare space, TAB, ENTER, the four arrows, MuteSoundSwitch, VolumeUp, VolumeDown, Play/Pause.
  5. send_text (not accepted by the XP kernel) /api/shortcut/clipboard/set?id=…&text=…&sleep=…&outtime=… then /api/key/sendkey?id=…&fn_key=WIN+v enters Chinese, emoji or any non-ASCII text. sleep is in seconds because "on some mobile phones it may take a while for the paste to be effective"; outtime is milliseconds, default 15 s. Round-trip proof is /shortcut/clipboard/get, single id, returning the identical string.

Needs

  • Full Keyboard Access on with auto-hide 1 s on every phone, or hotkeys and typed characters are not interpreted.
  • AssistiveTouch on, the phone bound to its board with vid and pid set together, and that board at state 2 in /config/usb/get.
  • A focused text field. No endpoint checks focus, and a send into an unfocused screen silently does nothing.
  • For the Unicode route only: iMouse Shortcut installed with the kernel IP edited in, run once with every prompt allowed, and bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key. Not verified on this rig.

Watch out

  • No delay, repeat-rate, speed or length parameter exists on any of the four endpoints. This was checked field by field against the XP tables.
  • XP's key-name vocabulary is narrower than Phonefarm's. SHIFT, CTRL, ALT, ESC, PAGEUP, PAGEDOWN, F1 to F12 and FN are Phonefarm-only names and are unverified on this kernel; XP's documented route for a combination is fn_key on /key/down. An interrupted chord leaves a modifier held, and the next plain type is silently corrupted until /key/upall.
  • Verify with a box diff cropped to the caret or field region, not a whole-frame threshold. The 20-and-above reacted threshold used elsewhere in this handoff was calibrated on full-icon taps (141.96 and 162.66 against an idle floor of 0.02 to 0.03); a single character in a small field can sit close to that floor and read as a false negative.
  • A silent no-op and a slow-AirPlay false negative look identical. On phone .27, at roughly 4.5 new frames per second, a real reaction can take 200 ms to appear at all, so poll 2 to 3 frame intervals, 400 to 700 ms, before concluding a keypress failed.
  • Nothing on this rig proves the correct characters landed. Frame diff proves the screen changed, and the clipboard round trip proves the clipboard holds string X; /pic/ocr answers data.code 28, so confirming typed text needs a human or a vision model reading the raw BMP.
  • Pair /mouse/reset with the focus-a-field-then-type pattern this use case depends on, not just once at session start. The measured stuck-click state is cleared by reset and not by /mouse/up.
  • The fn_key=Home variant needs kernel 2026.2.27 or later. The iOS build on these phones, 18.7.10, is an independent fact and does not tell you the kernel build, which has not been checked here. WIN+h is the safe default.

Scale

The send side is fleet-wide and cheap: every keyboard endpoint accepts a comma-separated id list, so typing to all 19 phones costs the same round trip as one phone, with no pointer-walk cost. There is no measured latency for /key/sendkey specifically; /mouse/move's p50 of 0.5 to 11.7 ms is a plausible floor for a similar payload, so budget tens of milliseconds per call when splitting a long string. Verification is the real ceiling and is per phone: at 2 to 3 confirming frames per action, a .68-class phone (about 29 new frames/s) supports roughly 3,000 to 8,000 verified actions per hour, and a .27-class phone (about 4.5 new frames/s) roughly 1,000 to 1,500.

Scroll wheel: capped at 127 per event, with no pixel or position semantics

PartialWith caveats

/mouse/wheel takes len 1 to 127, documented only as "Scroll length 1-127" with no unit, times number events, in direction up, down, left or right. XP adds the horizontal pair that Phonefarm lacks. Nothing states how len maps to pixels, nothing reports the current scroll offset, and there is no scroll-to-position or scroll-to-element call among the seven mouse endpoints. "Scroll exactly 300 px" is not expressible, so the robust pattern is scroll then look, at one screenshot per iteration per phone.

How

  1. mouse_wheel /api/mouse/wheel?id=…&direction=down&len=40&number=3 scrolls. Phonefarm documents up and down only and calls the field length. Wheel costs no pointer travel, unlike a swipe of the same distance. Position the pointer over the view you intend to scroll with /mouse/move first.
  2. get_device_screenshot /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single id>&binary=true grabs a frame. binary=true returns raw bytes and no JSON, p50 2 ms and 1,620,054 bytes, bottom-up BMP; jpg=true costs 40 ms and caps near 21 req/s; the default base64 JSON form is 26 ms. rect crops server-side, save_path writes to disk.
  3. find_multi_color, find_image, ocr /api/pic/find-multi-color, or client-side matching on the raw BMP looks for the target. XP's colour format is absolute points, x|y|RRGGBB-tolerance, inside a list of configs, returning data.list[{index, centre}].
  4. Same calls in a client loop, with a hard iteration cap. Budget the wait per iteration from the phone's own AirPlay source rate, not your poll rate: roughly 220 ms per genuinely new frame on the slow XR.
  5. Compare consecutive frames to detect the end of the list. Threshold the mean absolute pixel difference: the idle floor measured 0.02 to 0.03 on a 0 to 255 scale and a real reaction 20 to 160, so anything under about 1 after a scroll means nothing moved. Never compare hashes; MD5 reports changed on an untouched phone because of clock, encoder noise and wallpaper parallax.
  6. swipe /api/mouse/swipe with sx, sy, ex, ey is the fallback when positional control matters, at the cost of the roughly 0.6 ms per pixel pointer walk. Two documentation traps: the XP table labels sx, sy, ex and ey all as "y coordinate", and the JSON examples spell the parameter steping while the table says stepping.

Needs

  • Board bound with vid and pid set together, showing state 2 in /config/usb/get.
  • location_crc non-empty on the device record, or every mouse call returns data.code 11, no mouse parameters.
  • Coordinates in that device's imgw x imgh mirror space, 500 x 1080 here, never the 414 x 896 logical points.
  • Trackpad & Mouse tracking speed at maximum on every phone, since the setting is part of the wheel-to-scroll mapping and a mirrored wheel call only lines up if the phones share it.

Watch out

  • The 127 ceiling is per event. Larger movement comes only from raising number, which issues more discrete events rather than one bigger one.
  • len has no documented unit and no documented mapping to pixels or rows in either edition. Treat identical values in different apps, or on different phones, as producing different amounts of scroll until measured.
  • No endpoint reports a scroll offset and none accepts a target, so every loop must be bounded by an iteration cap plus a frame check rather than by arithmetic.
  • A wheel event delivered while the pointer sits over the wrong view scrolls the wrong thing with no error. data.code 0 means the board accepted the event, not that anything scrolled.
  • All six /pic/* endpoints are single-id, so the scroll fans out and the verification does not. OCR is unavailable here (data.code 28) and the image-search plug-in status is unverified, so client-side matching on the raw BMP is the only channel known to work today.
  • If taps stop registering mid-loop while moves still work, send /mouse/reset to the whole target set.

Scale

One /mouse/wheel call drives every listed phone. Verification is one 2 ms raw-BMP request per phone per iteration, and pollers are independent: two phones flat out measured 83 and 85 req/s at p50 3 ms each, and ten concurrent pollers 512 req/s in total. Nineteen phones at five iterations is negligible against the phones' own frame production, which is the real ceiling at about 29 fps on the good XR and 4.5 on its twin. Wheel is the only scroll primitive whose cost does not grow with the distance travelled.

Pointer-walk speed caps swipes: velocity-dependent flicks are out of reach

PartialWith caveats

The board walks the pointer to its destination at a measured 0.6 ms per pixel, so a full-height 1080 px swipe takes roughly 580 ms of travel and iOS reads it as a slow drag rather than a flick. Neither /mouse/swipe nor /mouse/move exposes a duration or velocity parameter. The only levers are distance, the stepping and step_sleep loop, and brake. Momentum fling scrolling, fast card-swipe UIs, velocity-thresholded swipe-to-dismiss and many game gestures cannot be produced directly.

How

  1. mouse_move twice /api/mouse/move?id=…&x=20&y=540 then x=480 measures the floor. Measured ladder: 2 px 1.0 ms, 100 px 78 ms, 400 px 250 ms, 1000 px 592 ms. Latency is a function of distance, not jitter, so never read a 264 ms move as noise.
  2. swipe /api/mouse/swipe?id=…&direction=left&len=0.8 prefers the short axis. Read the mapping carefully: 0.9 slides from 10% to 90% and 0.8 from 20% to 80%, so len is the far edge and the span is twice len minus one. On the 500 px width, len 0.8 gives a 300 px stroke, about 180 ms, and len 0.6 gives only 100 px. The 1080 px height is the expensive axis.
  3. swipe with explicit coordinates /api/mouse/swipe with sx, sy, ex, ey in mirror pixels finds each app's page-turn threshold empirically. A 150 to 200 px stroke is usually enough. XP adds stepping (loop count), step_sleep (ms between steps) and brake (stop immediately after sliding); Phonefarm's equivalent is the single for loop count.
  4. mouse_wheel /api/mouse/wheel?id=…&direction=down&len=127&number=k substitutes for momentum scrolling. It buys distance, not velocity.
  5. click with button:'right' or time:700 /api/mouse/click?id=…&button=2 or &time=700 substitutes a long press or secondary click for a fast reveal swipe. Swipe-to-delete rows usually have an equivalent context menu behind a long press.
  6. mouse_up, mouse_reset_pos /api/mouse/up?id=…&button=1, /api/mouse/reset?id=… recovers after any composed gesture. A real drag is down, streamed moves, then up; an interrupted one leaves the button held.

Needs

  • Board bound and at state 2, location_crc non-empty, or mouse calls return data.code 11.
  • All coordinates in the device's imgw x imgh mirror space, 500 x 1080 on these XRs.
  • Per-phone iOS accessibility settings: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity at maximum, Trackpad & Mouse tracking speed at maximum, portrait lock, Auto-Lock never. None of these is queryable over the API.
  • Optional: /config/imserver/set mouse_mode=true, documented as "use fast and accurate mouse movement" and applying without a kernel restart. Whether it changes the walk rate is unverified here.

Watch out

  • This is a hardware floor, not a missing parameter. No duration, velocity or speed argument exists in either edition, so a genuine high-velocity flick is not achievable.
  • The substitutes are not equivalent: the wheel gives distance without momentum, and a long press opens a menu rather than performing the swipe the UI expected.
  • A stroke slow enough to read as a drag can pick up and move an icon or reorder a list instead of scrolling.
  • brake and step_sleep get one line each with no timing semantics. Measure their effect per app.
  • Phonefarm documents that percentage-mode swipes randomly vary their start and end coordinates, and does not say whether that still applies with explicit coordinates. XP documents no randomization at all, so verify stroke geometry from the frame on either edition.
  • data.code 0 means the board accepted the call. Follow every composed drag with /mouse/up and confirm with a frame diff.

Scale

Walking the pointer on N phones in parallel costs the same as one, because every mouse endpoint takes a comma id list and the board drives the listed phones together: a 300 px stroke on 19 phones is still about 180 ms of wall time. The binding constraint is per-gesture latency, not throughput. Input traffic was measured not to slow frame polling, 98.8 req/s while streaming moves against 78.7 with no input, so verification can run concurrently. Exclude from any mirrored gesture a phone whose imgw or imgh differs from the master, since the same coordinate is a different place on a different-sized mirror.

Rotation: dev_rotate is the only signal, and the landscape mapping is undocumented

PartialWith caveats

Rotation is detectable, not controllable, and not documented. XP exposes rotate (0 vertical, 1 horizontal) in every device record and broadcasts dev_rotate with the full record in data.list. There is no endpoint to rotate a phone, lock orientation or read the lock state; that is a Control Centre setting. What neither document states is how imgw, imgh and the coordinate origin behave when rotate flips to 1, so any landscape transform must be measured on the rig before it is trusted. XP's only landscape knob is the kernel-wide Boolean flip_right, documented by name alone.

How

  1. none (phone-side setup) none: lock portrait on every phone, close StandBy, and give Control Centre two rows of icons, which the vendor says "affects automatic screencasting". No API in either edition sets or reads orientation lock, verified by absence across all nine XP doc pages.
  2. get_device_list /api/device/get reads rotate and the mirror geometry per phone. imgw and imgh are the actual image size and the input coordinate space; width and height are logical points, 414 x 896 here, and are not. Live: both XRs rotate 0, 500 x 1080.
  3. callback dev_rotate dev_rotate on ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api subscribes to rotation events. The record is inside data.list, not data, and the XP socket path is /api, not Phonefarm's /clinet.
  4. mouse_move plus get_device_screenshot /api/mouse/move then /api/pic/screenshot?id=…&binary=true measures the landscape mapping instead of assuming one. Rotate a phone by hand, reset, move to three known points, and mean-abs-diff a 40 px box at each commanded point: a landed pointer measured 1.4 to 9.8 against an idle floor of 0.02.
  5. none /api/config/imserver/set flip_right sets the landscape handling mode if the measurement calls for it. It is in the no-restart list, and other connected clients receive im_config_change. Its actual effect on frame or coordinate orientation is described nowhere, so treat it as an experiment.
  6. click, swipe, mouse_move /api/mouse/click, /api/mouse/swipe, /api/mouse/move, /api/mouse/reset: partition every mirrored id list by rotate and by imgw and imgh before sending input. One bad member sends the whole batch to the wrong place.
  7. send_key fn_key=WIN+h /api/key/sendkey?id=…&fn_key=WIN+h, twice returns a phone to a known portrait state. Measured working on this rig even while the pointer was in the stuck-click state. Two presses are needed, the first to leave the app and the second to return to page one.

Needs

  • Orientation lock on and StandBy off on every phone, plus the two-row Control Centre layout, before any calibration or auto-cast.
  • A WebSocket client on ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api to receive dev_rotate. Polling /device/get is the fallback and adds latency.
  • A measured, per-model coordinate set for landscape. There is no documented transform to derive one.
  • Board bound and mouse parameters present, or /mouse/* returns code 2, 3 or 11 regardless of orientation.

Watch out

  • XP code 15 is "No coordinates", not "Must be in portrait orientation". The portrait error text exists only in the Phonefarm table and does not apply to this kernel.
  • No document in either edition says imgw and imgh swap on rotation, and this rig has never run a phone in landscape. The XP dev_rotate example itself shows rotate 0 with the geometry unchanged. Treat the swap as an untested hypothesis, and treat any x-to-y transform as something to measure, not a recipe.
  • Whether the shared-library calibration, location_crc B0DBD800, stays accurate in landscape is unstated in both docs and untested here.
  • With OCR returning code 28 and the image-search plug-in presumed absent, there is no server-side way to re-find an element after an unexpected rotation. Recovery is Home-press normalization plus re-measurement, or client-side matching on raw BMP frames.
  • /pic/find-multi-color tables are absolute pixel coordinates and are therefore orientation-specific too. A portrait table will not match a rotated frame.
  • Because the API is unauthenticated, another LAN client can flip flip_right underneath you. Watch im_config_change.

Scale

Rotation state is per phone, so a mirrored id list must be partitioned by rotate value and by mirror size. Detection costs nothing: dev_rotate is pushed to every connected client, and frame polling is per-phone independent at 83 and 85 req/s with two pollers, 512 req/s across ten, p50 3 ms. Re-measuring a landscape map costs three /mouse/move round trips plus three raw BMP grabs per model, with pointer travel dominating at 0.6 ms per pixel.

Trap An unnoticed rotation mirrors taps into the wrong place on every phone at once

Every mouse and key endpoint takes a comma-separated id list, and one phone that rotated mid-batch relocates every coordinate in that list. Guard each batch with a rotate check and a /mouse/reset when the target set changes, and drop any phone whose rotate, imgw or imgh differs from the master. In a real app, and not a test screen, that misdirected tap can be destructive.

Licensing, boards and calibration

Edition gating is a Phonefarm concept; XP licenses per device

PartialWith caveats

The Phonefarm doc marks the whole shortcut dispatcher and ocr_ex "professional version only". The XP docs gate no endpoint by edition at all. XP licenses through a vendor account instead, whose payload carries pass, user_state (1 is formal authorization, anything else is test), total_license, local_total_license, dev_num, dev_online_num and overdue_time, pushed unsolicited as user_info every 30 seconds. There is no documented mapping between the two schemes, so the correct stance here is to assume nothing about /shortcut/* or /pic/ocr-ex until a round trip has returned data.code 0.

How

  1. none /api/config/user/info reads licence and account state. Not probed on this rig: the 10 September probe used /user/get, which 404s. The field table lists dev_num twice with conflicting glosses; read it as the device count and dev_online_num as the online count.
  2. none user_info and im_log WebSocket callbacks keep watching without polling. im_log carries notices such as the vendor's own example, not logged in so going online is not allowed.
  3. shortcut#24 /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<one id>&state=0 proves the shortcut channel with the cheapest round trip. state 0 is LAN and 1 extranet; id is single only; outtime is milliseconds with a 15000 default, where Phonefarm's was seconds. Pass condition is data.code 0 and data.text equal to the ip field from /device/get. That one call proves the Shortcut is installed, the AssistiveTouch binding fires, and the phone can reach the kernel.
  4. shortcut#10 and #11 /api/shortcut/clipboard/set then /api/shortcut/clipboard/get proves the write and read pair before relying on Unicode text entry.
  5. ocr_ex /api/pic/ocr-ex is worth probing only after the plug-in exists. XP names it in prose under /pic/ocr with no parameter table of its own, and /pic/ocr answers data.code 28 here.
  6. click, swipe, send_key /api/mouse/click, /api/mouse/swipe, /api/key/sendkey is the fallback where the shortcut layer is unavailable: slow, screen-dependent, and with every step verified by pixel diff on raw BMP frames.
  7. none none (IMConsole.exe, outside the API): measured, with IMService.exe up but the console not running, /device/get showed both phones state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list. The API cannot bring the rack up on its own.

Needs

  • A vendor account logged in by the operator, through the console, with enough device authorizations for the phones brought online.
  • iMouse Shortcut installed per phone with the kernel IP edited in, run once with every permission allowed, bound to an AssistiveTouch custom key, plus the Shortcuts advanced allowances for running scripts, sharing large data and deleting without confirmation.
  • Board bound and connected, since the shortcut is launched by a HID hotkey, and the phone reachable on the LAN, since the shortcut answers the kernel over Wi-Fi.
  • OCR plug-in installed and connected for /pic/ocr and /pic/ocr-ex, with ocr_num set and a kernel restart. iOS 15 or later for the file shortcuts and /shortcut/switch/device, Shortcut 1.3 or later for the /shortcut/other/* fallbacks.

Watch out

  • "Professional version only" exists solely in the Phonefarm document. Nothing maps it onto the XP licence model, so do not code against a professional flag on this kernel.
  • No /shortcut/* endpoint has been proven on this rig, and the phone-side install state is unknown. A first call may legitimately time out with data.code 30 after 15 seconds without anything being broken in software, which is hard to tell from a network fault at a glance.
  • The vendor's own example shows total_license 0 alongside local_total_license 100 and user_state 2. The relationship between the counters on trial versus formal accounts is undocumented, so do not compute capacity from one alone.
  • XP status semantics differ from Phonefarm's entirely. Top-level status 200 means the request was accepted; the outcome is data.code against XP's own 0 to 41 table, where 28 is plug-in not connected, 29 plug-in call timeout, 30 call timeout, 36 parameter error, 37 login failed, 41 incompatible commands. Reusing Phonefarm's 1 to 32 codes mis-reads every result.
  • Messages are Chinese on this build. Branch on data.code, never on message text.
  • Exceeding authorization surfaces as an im_log notice, not a call failure, so an over-provisioned rack fails quietly at the point where phones try to come online.

Scale

The licence count caps the rack independently of hardware: 19 populated boards are useless beyond the account's authorization, and dev_online_num against total_license, or local_total_license on a trial, is the live headroom reading, refreshed free every 30 s. Shortcut calls are the slow path at a 15 s default timeout, and the read-shaped ones (album get and down, file get and down, clipboard get, device ip) are single-id, so a rack-wide probe is N sequential round trips. The write-shaped ones (clipboard set, exec url, the switches, album upload, delete and clear, file upload and delete) take a comma id list and fan out in one request.

One board per phone, single-id capture, and a 19-slot rack

Native APIWith caveats

Control is addressed one board per phone. Each board enumerates as VID 720A with a unique PID and a uid of PID plus a four-character suffix, and /device/set makes the binding with vid and pid set together, one device at a time. Input mirrors to N phones in one request, because every /mouse/* and /key/* endpoint takes a comma-separated id and the board walks the listed phones in parallel. Capture does not: every /pic/* endpoint is marked "Multiple is not allowed". This rack has 19 boards across three seven-port hubs, 21 slots, and two phones mirroring today.

How

  1. get_usb_list /api/config/usb/get inventories the control channel, returning data.list[{vid,pid,uid,ver,state}]. state appears in the example but not the field table; its meaning comes from the usb_change code table plus measurement here: 1 is a board on the PC with no phone, 2 a board with a phone attached.
  2. get_device_list /api/device/get inventories the video channel. state 0 is not online, non-zero is online, and air_pid is the AirplayMirroring process id and the live proof of mirroring. Control-ready and video-ready are independent readings and must be reported separately.
  3. set_dev /api/device/set?id=…&vid=720A&pid=… binds a phone to its board. The response is the list of ids successfully set, not the full record, so re-read /device/get to confirm. To learn which uid a slot is, replug the phone cable and watch usb_change code 12.
  4. set_dev with a new pid /api/device/set with the new vid and pid moves a phone to a different board. No unbind endpoint is documented in either edition. /device/del removes records entirely, refuses online devices with code 7, and broadcasts dev_delete.
  5. restart_usb /api/device/usb/restart?id=720A|C241 resets a wedged board without touching the phone or the kernel. XP addresses boards, not phones, so an unbound board can be reset too. Expect usb_change 20, then 19, then 12 when the phone re-attaches.
  6. callback usb_change usb_change tracks hardware changes without polling, with the event type in data.code.
  7. set_group, set_dev name /api/device/group/set, /api/device/set name+gid, /api/device/group/get-dev labels the rack. PIDs are opaque, so hub and port is the stable physical label, and it comes from Windows PnP rather than the API.

Needs

  • Connection order enforced by the hardware: board to PC (state 1), then phone to board with the vendor cable (state 2), then mirroring, then bind the uid.
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in, or the board list comes back empty and every phone reads state 0.
  • A device authorization per phone. Board count is not the only ceiling.
  • Hub and port topology recorded out of band, so an unresponsive board can be found physically.

Watch out

  • One board per phone is a vendor product-page statement, not an API guarantee. The API simply offers no way to share a board.
  • Neither doc states a maximum device count for the kernel. Nineteen is this rack's physical fact, not an API limit.
  • Cable substitution leaves a board at state 1 with a phone visibly plugged in, a silent control-channel failure no API field explains. Surface the vendor-cable requirement in diagnostics.
  • A wrong pid in /device/set binds a phone to another slot, and every tap then lands on a different handset with no error. Never route or display by ver or uver, which are mojibake on this build.
  • Phonefarm's per-device auto-cast switch has no XP equivalent; XP's auto_connect is a single global flag, so "this phone re-casts itself" is not expressible per slot. Phonefarm's three airplay presets and their bandwidth guidance do not exist in XP either, so any per-phone bandwidth budget must be measured, not quoted.
  • /device/airplay/set disconnects the current cast immediately and applies on the next cast. Never call it mid-run on a working phone.
  • There is no supported path to drive the boards directly: the nine-byte vendor HID report layout on usage page 0xFF00 is undocumented, so IMService stays a hard dependency.

Scale

Control scales linearly and cheaply: a comma id list on click, move, swipe, reset, sendkey, up, upall, airplay connect and disconnect, collection and usb restart drives N phones in one request, and a move of a given distance costs the same wall clock for one phone as for two. Video does not scale that way: one AirPlay session per phone, one screenshot request per phone, measured 83 and 85 req/s with two pollers and 512 req/s across ten, raw BMP at 2 ms and 1.62 MB against JPEG at 40 ms and about 21 req/s. Source frame rate is the real limit and is per phone: 28.9 new frames per second on 192.168.4.68 against 4.5 on its identical twin at .27, a Wi-Fi and AirPlay property the vendor console hits too.

Device floor and calibration coupling: iOS 15, and a parameter record per model and iOS version

PartialWith caveats

Supported hardware is iPhone 6s and later. The vendor settings page says iOS 13.4 and above, the product page says 15 and above, and the XP doc independently requires 15 or later for the file shortcuts and /shortcut/switch/device, so design to 15. Pointer accuracy depends on a mouse-parameter record: /device/get exposes location and location_crc, and with neither present every mouse call fails with code 11. Both XRs here carry an empty location and location_crc B0DBD800, a shared library profile byte-identical to the vendor doc's own example.

How

  1. get_devicemodel_list /api/config/devicemodel/get checks the model and parameter library. The endpoint exists and returns data.list, but the XP doc elides the payload entirely, so the record shape is undocumented on this edition. Probe it before depending on it. /device/model/get is not the path and 404s.
  2. get_device_list /api/device/get?id=… checks each phone actually has parameters. Live: B0DBD800 on both XRs, location empty, which is a library match rather than a per-device measurement.
  3. mouse_collection_open plus mouse_collection_cfg /api/device/collection/mouse?id=…&cmd=1 starts a collection when no record matches. cmd 0 queries, 1 starts, 2 stops, one endpoint replacing Phonefarm's three. Progress arrives on the collection_mouse callback: 0 success, 4 failed, 5 a device is collecting, 8 scan code opened, 9 entered the collection page, 14 start working, 21 at work.
  4. Collection page opened full-screen from a Home Screen icon none (undocumented) is the phone-side step. XP gives no phone-side collection URL; the console presents a QR code, and codes 8 then 9 are the only signals. The console route is right-click the mirrored phone, Set Mouse Parameters, profile 1 for iOS 14.2 and above.
  5. save_dev_location /api/device/collection/mouse/save?id=…&describe=XR-18.7.10 publishes to the shared library, single id plus free text, then stop with cmd=2.
  6. set_dev location_crc /api/device/set?id=a,b,c&location_crc=… copies the calibration to same-model phones. Here id does take a comma list; only vid plus pid binding is single-device.
  7. mouse_reset_pos, mouse_move, get_device_screenshot /api/mouse/reset, then moves to (20,20), (480,1060), (250,540), each followed by a binary screenshot probes accuracy after any iOS update or settings change. Find the pointer by mean-abs diff in a 40 px box: measured 1.4 to 9.8 against an idle floor of 0.02, with a commanded (380,880) landing at (377,875). Error growing toward the far corner means the per-pixel scale is wrong.

Needs

  • Automatic iOS updates disabled on every phone. Phone-side, with no API to read or set it.
  • Tracking Speed and AssistiveTouch tracking sensitivity at the same settings the library record was collected with. Both invisible to the API.
  • Board bound and connected, or codes 2, 3 and 13 appear, with the phone online and in portrait.
  • Only one device collecting at a time, and the vendor console available for the QR step.

Watch out

  • The XP doc never says library records are keyed by model plus iOS version; that is Phonefarm's statement and matches observed behavior. Treat it as behavioral, not contractual. The corollary, that an iOS update silently loses the match, has not been observed here: these XRs are on 18.7.10 and still match B0DBD800.
  • XP documents no way to delete a record from the library, so a bad describe or a bad CRC is permanent on this edition.
  • The collection endpoint's parameter table advertises a comma id list while code 5 forbids concurrent collection. Follow the code, not the table.
  • Never invent or guess a location_crc. Only a collected or library value belongs there, and a wrong one mis-positions every tap with no error.
  • Calibration accuracy cannot be confirmed by OCR or template matching on this rig, so verification is pointer-box and whole-frame pixel diffs on raw BMP frames. Never MD5-compare frames; an untouched mirrored screen never repeats byte for byte.
  • Send /mouse/reset before any accuracy probe. The stuck-click state otherwise makes a correctly calibrated phone look mis-calibrated.
  • A heterogeneous rack still needs mirrored coordinate lists split by imgw and imgh regardless of calibration, and the two XRs here have different home screens, so a shared coordinate is only fair after two WIN+h presses normalize the state.
  • Because the API is unauthenticated, another LAN client can overwrite location_crc on any device. Watch dev_change.

Scale

One successful collection per model plus iOS version serves the whole rack: the resulting CRC is distributed to every same-model phone in a single /device/set with a comma id list, and same-model phones auto-match from the library on connect. Collection itself is serialized and drives real UI, so a mixed rack costs one manual console session per model and iOS combination. The accuracy probe is cheap and fully parallel: three moves plus three 2 ms raw BMP grabs per phone, with phones polling independently at 83 to 85 req/s each.

Vision on this rig

Vision plug-ins absent: OCR and image search answer code 28

Needs plug-inWith caveats

On this rig /api/pic/ocr answers HTTP 200 with data.code 28, plug-in not connected. The image-search pair, /pic/find-image and /pic/find-image-cv, is backed by the same plug-in architecture, since the kernel config exposes opencv_num and ocr_num as instance counts, so assume both are absent until probed. /pic/find-text and /pic/find-text-ex sit on the OCR plug-in and go with it. Every "locate the element, then tap its centre" design therefore moves client-side, or waits on the vendor plug-in.

How

  1. ocr /api/pic/ocr baselines the gate. Verified live on 10 September 2026: status 200, data.code 28. The XP code table reads 28 plug-in not connected, 29 plug-in call timed out, 31 OCR did not recognize the text, 32 no text found. The success shape is data.list[{text, centre, rect, similarity}].
  2. find_image /api/pic/find-image (DM-compatible) and /api/pic/find-image-cv (OpenCV) probes the image-search gate, which has not yet been done here. Both take a single id and img_list as base64 strings or local PC paths, returning data.list[{index, centre, rect, code}].
  3. No Phonefarm equivalent /api/pic/find-text and /api/pic/find-text-ex: an XP-only convenience that OCRs then matches strings. Same plug-in, therefore unavailable here.
  4. get_device_screenshot /api/pic/screenshot?id=…&binary=true is substitute 1, client-side vision on raw frames. Measured p50 2.0 ms, 84 req/s flat out, 1,620,054 bytes of bottom-up BMP, which is 500 x 1080 x 3 plus a 54-byte header. Decode, then run an OCR or template stack on the PC at roughly 50 to 300 ms per full frame, an order of magnitude less on a cropped rect. Coordinates come out already in the space /mouse/click wants.
  5. find_multi_color /api/pic/find-multi-color is substitute 2, colour-table matching, gate unknown. XP's table is a comma-separated list of absolute points, x|y|RRGGBB-tolerance, not Phonefarm's anchor-plus-offset form. The doc offers /shortcut/other/find-multi-color as a fallback in exactly the phrasing it uses for the plug-in functions, so do not assume it is kernel-internal.
  6. shortcut dispatcher /api/shortcut/other/screenshot, find-image, find-image-cv, ocr, ocr-ex, find-text, find-text-ex, find-multi-color is substitute 3, on-phone recognition. Named once each in the picture-recognition page, with no parameter tables at all, and requiring the full Shortcut prerequisite chain. It trades a plug-in dependency for a phone-side dependency, not for no dependency.
  7. none /api/config/imserver/set opencv_num, ocr_num, then /api/imserver/restart applies if the plug-ins are bought. Neither field is in the no-restart list, so a kernel restart is required, which drops every mirroring session. ocr_num is annotated "Only the GPU version is effective".
  8. restart_device /api/device/restart, or /api/shortcut/switch/device state=1, or /api/key/sendkey fn_key=CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r shows that a driven restart has two OCR-free routes. The hotkey needs no vision at all, only Full Keyboard Access and a bound board, and is the route to prefer here. The shortcut route also covers shutdown, which Phonefarm has no equivalent for.

Needs

  • To restore server-side vision: the vendor OCR and OpenCV plug-in packages for the XP edition, installed so the kernel stops returning code 28, and a GPU build if ocr_num above 1 is to mean anything.
  • To use the client-side substitute: a PC-side OCR and template stack consuming raw bottom-up BMP frames, with one reusable buffer per poller. Each 1.6 MB frame exceeds the .NET Large Object Heap threshold, and without reuse the measured cost was 488 MB/s of allocation and 496 gen-2 collections in 8 s.
  • To use the /shortcut/other/* fallbacks: iMouse Shortcut 1.3 or later installed per phone, kernel IP edited in, run once with permissions granted, bound to an AssistiveTouch key, plus a working board.
  • Templates and colour tables built from the same phone at the same air_play_ratio. They are specific to the 500 x 1080 stream.

Watch out

  • OCR is confirmed unavailable; image search is presumed unavailable but has not been probed. Say unknown, not absent, until /pic/find-image-cv has actually been called.
  • Every recognition endpoint is single-id, so recognition never fans out the way /mouse/click does.
  • XP rect is a flat [left x, top y, right x, bottom y] array everywhere. Phonefarm's four-corner-point form will not parse here.
  • Changing air_play_ratio globally, or air_ratio per device, invalidates every template and colour table at once, and the per-device change disconnects the cast and applies only on the next connect.
  • Designing a flow around /pic/ocr here produces code 28 at runtime, not at build time, because the endpoint answers HTTP 200 and looks healthy. Guessed paths return 404 and Phonefarm-style bare function names return HTTP 500, so a client that checks only HTTP status will misreport all three failure modes.
  • Exact-colour matching with zero tolerance produces intermittent false negatives because of AirPlay encoder noise. Match on data.code, never on the Chinese data.message strings.

Scale

Client-side vision is bounded by PC cores, not by the kernel. Frame fetch is 2 ms and phones are independent, two pollers at 83 plus 85 req/s and ten at 512 req/s in total, but 19 phones at four full-frame OCR passes per second at about 100 ms each is roughly eight cores of work. Cropping to a rect before recognizing is the single biggest lever, with small-region template matching about ten times cheaper than a full frame. Server-side plug-ins would not parallelize better, since their endpoints are single-id and concurrency is a config knob rather than a per-request property. A still screen produces almost no new frames, so discard near-identical polls with a mean-pixel-difference test and never with MD5.

Tip Restarting a phone does not need vision

Phonefarm's restart_device depends on save_restart_point, which needs the OCR and image-search plug-ins. XP has two routes that need neither: fn_key=CTRL+ALT+SHIFT+WIN+r on /key/sendkey, which needs only Full Keyboard Access and a bound board, and /shortcut/switch/device with state=1 on iOS 15 or later, which also covers shutdown at state=0. Both leave the phone at the passcode screen with mirroring dropped, so pair either with a check for state 0 and a human queue.

The phone itself is a limit: locks, prompts and reboots

The rack drives a mirror and a HID board. It does not drive iOS. Anything iOS puts in front of the app, a lock screen, an Apple ID prompt, a software update, is a wall the API has no call to pass.

Phones must stay unlocked: nothing in the API unlocks a screen or answers a system prompt

PartialWith caveats

Across the whole XP surface, /device/*, /mouse/*, /key/*, /pic/*, /shortcut/*, /config/* and /imserver/*, there is no unlock function and no channel that reports "locked" as distinct from "offline". After a lock, a reboot, a battery event or iOS re-authenticating on its own, the phone sits on a screen the rack cannot pass, and a passcode, Face ID, Apple ID, 2FA, software update, Screen Time or "Trust This Computer" prompt stops it just as hard. What you do get is prevention, which is phone-side, detection, and recovery of the mirror once a human has unlocked.

How

  1. (none) none — prevention is phone-side and invisible to the API: Auto-Lock Never, StandBy off, portrait lock on, applied at commissioning and re-checked after every iOS update
  2. send_key /key/sendkey fn_key=TAB+l — the documented lock hotkey. Never script it. There is no unlock counterpart anywhere in the hotkey table
  3. get_device_list /device/get — state 0 means not online, non-zero means online; air_pid is the live AirplayMirroring.exe process id, 22236 for both XRs here
  4. callback dev_disconnect ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — the mirror dropping arrives as a broadcast with the full record at state 0, instead of a polling loop
  5. get_device_screenshot + ocr /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true — lock-screen detection has to be client-side matching here, because /pic/find-text and /pic/ocr return data.code 28
  6. auto_connect_screen /device/airplay/connect — re-cast after a human unlock; /device/airplay/connect/all takes no parameters, and the global auto_connect flag applies without a kernel restart
  7. restart_device /device/restart — expect a lock screen after every reboot, roughly 60 to 90 seconds, tracked on the restart_log callback rather than by screenshot, because there is no mirror during the reboot

Needs

  • Dedicated phones with Auto-Lock Never, StandBy off and portrait lock, none of which is queryable over 9911
  • A stored per-phone lock-screen reference at the current air_play_ratio. The two XRs here have different wallpapers, so one reference cannot serve both
  • A WebSocket client for dev_disconnect and airplay_connect_log
  • A named human escalation path per physical slot, because an unlock cannot be automated

Watch out

  • state 0 conflates locked, Wi-Fi dropped, AirPlay session died and phone off. The board channel (/config/usb/get state 2) is the only independent second signal, and it says nothing about the screen
  • A retry loop against a locked phone never succeeds and buries the real cause in airplay_connect_log noise. connect_failed_retry=0 means infinite retries and makes this worse
  • auto_connect is a global kernel flag on XP. There is no per-device cast-on-connect flag as in the Phonefarm edition
  • Hardware-keyboard passcode entry at the lock screen is undocumented and untested. Do not build on it. Repeated wrong entries hit iOS lockout timers that no API call can clear, and entering a passcode on a device you are not authorized to access is a computer-misuse offence (CFAA in the US, the Computer Misuse Act in the UK) however the keystrokes are delivered
  • Scripting TAB+l against a comma-separated id list can lock the entire rack in one request with no scripted way back

Scale

Detection parallelizes perfectly: /device/get returns the fleet in one call, dev_disconnect is broadcast, and pollers are independent (two at 83 and 85 req/s, ten at 512 req/s aggregate). Recovery partly parallelizes. The unlock is the one rack operation that does not parallelize at all: an iOS update or a power blip locks all 19 phones at once and each needs an individual human touch, so rack-wide recovery time is linear in phone count.

Exposure you cannot configure away

What the rack inherently exposes: shared egress, simultaneous input, pointer-type taps, hardware-keyboard text

PartialWith caveats

Two properties of this stack are not configurable. Network identity: each phone reaches the internet through whatever egress its Wi-Fi gives it, and the only API readout is /shortcut/device/ip, useful for geo and ad verification and for confirming a test device egresses where you expect. Input identity: /mouse/* and /key/* deliver HID mouse and hardware-keyboard events through the board, not synthesized finger touches, /key/sendkey is ASCII-only, and AssistiveTouch, which the rack requires, is a runtime accessibility state. A third property is timing: every input endpoint takes a comma-separated id list, so a mirrored action lands on N phones inside one request.

How

  1. shortcut#24 /shortcut/device/ip — state 0 gives the LAN address, state 1 the extranet address; single id, default outtime 15000 ms. XP adds the LAN readout Phonefarm lacked, and comparing state 0 against the ip field from /device/get is the cheapest end-to-end proof the Shortcut chain works
  2. shortcut#18-#23 /shortcut/switch/wlan, /flight, /cdpd — a factual constraint, not a technique: turning Wi-Fi or flight mode on kills the AirPlay video channel while USB control survives. The vendor's static-IP-without-gateway setup exists so a phone stays on the LAN for mirroring while cellular carries its internet traffic
  3. click / swipe / mouse_move / send_key /mouse/*, /key/* with "Separate multiple devices with commas" — the board walks all listed phones in parallel and a move to N phones costs the same as to one, about 0.6 ms per pixel either way
  4. click /mouse/click — button is numeric on XP ("1" left, "2" right, up to "8"), x and y are mirror pixels, time is press-to-release in milliseconds
