  5. send_key /key/sendkey key=<ASCII> — both XP key pages say "Only English, numbers and English characters are supported". For anything else, /shortcut/clipboard/set then fn_key=WIN+v is the documented Unicode path
  6. swipe /mouse/swipe — for a repeatable stroke supply explicit sx/sy/ex/ey, or build it from /mouse/down, /mouse/move, /mouse/up. The Phonefarm doc says percentage mode varies start and end coordinates; the XP doc documents no such variation
  7. (none) none — there is no rate limiter in either edition. Backing off on a platform rate-limit response is entirely the client's job

Needs

  • The iMouse Shortcut installed, permissioned and bound to an AssistiveTouch key for every /shortcut/* call, including the IP readout
  • Full Keyboard Access on and AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity at maximum, or neither hotkeys nor coordinates work
  • Written authorization for every account and service the rack touches
  • A client-side scheduler that can stop a phone's queue, because the API provides none

Watch out

  • /shortcut/device/ip and /shortcut/clipboard/get are single-id only; the switch and clipboard-set endpoints take comma lists
  • Toggling wlan or flight drops the video channel and the Shortcut's own LAN return path, so the call may time out with code 30 and the phone will need re-casting
  • Nothing in this API exposes a knob for what iOS reports about the device, the input type or the accessibility state
  • Automation, multi-accounting and device farms breach the terms of service of every major platform (Meta, TikTok, X, Google, Apple). Enforcement is account termination and, for commercial operators, civil action. That is a property of the use, and the mitigation is authorization and rate discipline, not concealment
  • A rig that delivers pointer-type touches and hardware-keyboard text cannot faithfully reproduce a real finger or the on-screen keyboard, so any test depending on touch semantics or IME behavior needs a human
  • The pointer-type and accessibility-flag observations are iOS behavior and appear in none of the reference documents. Treat them as context, not as verified API facts

Scale

The comma-separated id list is the throughput story: one request drives every listed board in parallel and measured input latency is unchanged between one phone and two. Input traffic and frame polling do not interfere, 98.8 req/s of screenshots with input streaming versus 78.7 without. The ceilings are elsewhere: the 0.6 ms/px pointer walk (a 1000 px move is 592 ms), the per-phone AirPlay source rate, and the 15 s default outtime that makes Shortcut-mediated operations roughly two orders of magnitude slower than a mouse call.

Legal and platform exposure is a property of the use: no audit log, no consent store, no rate limiter

PartialWith caveats

The kernel sends a mirrored tap to every id in the list without regard for what the tap does. The exposure lives in the use: unsolicited commercial SMS or iMessage (TCPA, PECR), commercial email or DM without opt-out (CAN-SPAM), processing other people's personal data harvested from screens or clipboards (GDPR, CCPA), access without authorization (CFAA, Computer Misuse Act), and breach of platform terms, which is civil rather than criminal but ends accounts. What the API contributes is metadata only: groups, custom names, per-phone identity and frame evidence on disk.

How

  1. set_group /device/group/set?id=0&name=ClientA — id "0" creates a group, any other id renames it; broadcast to every client as group_change. On this rig the group list is empty and both XRs sit in the default ungrouped bucket
  2. set_dev /device/set?id=<ids>&gid=<gid>&name=A-slot-01 — comma list for name and gid; returns only the ids that succeeded. Names and groups persist in DeviceList.json, the only operational metadata the kernel keeps
  3. get_device_list /device/get — deviceid, mac, ip, user_name, version, model, state, air_pid, imgw, imgh, gid, vid, pid, uid. It does not include the board's hub and port, which comes from Windows PnP
  4. shortcut#24 /shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=1 — record the egress actually used, and re-take it after any radio change rather than caching it
  5. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&save_path=D:\evidence\ — XP-only: the kernel writes the file and returns its path in data.image. Default BMP is about 1.6 MB per frame, jpg=true is about 96 KB at a 40 ms encode
  6. (none) none — cap actions per phone per hour in your own scheduler before calling /mouse/click, /key/sendkey or /shortcut/exec/url
  7. (none) /config/imserver/set allow_ip_list — see the trap below. The only real access control is a Windows Firewall rule on TCP 9911 and 17000
  8. (none) ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — dev_change, dev_delete, group_change, group_delete, im_config_change, dev_sort_change, error_push, im_log, user_info (every 30 s). Live broadcasts, not a log

Needs

  • Written authorization for every account, device and system the rack touches. The tool cannot distinguish an account you own from one you do not
  • A consent and opt-out record for any outbound messaging, maintained outside the kernel
  • A lawful basis and a retention policy for stored screen captures and clipboard content, both of which routinely contain other people's personal data
  • A firewall rule limiting 9911 and 17000 to the controller host, and a client that holds the WebSocket open if any audit trail is required

Watch out

  • There is no field for purpose, client, consent, operator or authorization. Everything substantive lives in your own store
  • /device/group/del returns code 34 ("Please remove the device in the group first") and /device/del returns code 7 for an online device, so the metadata layer resists tidy-up while the rack is running
  • C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json holds the vendor account password as reversible hex obfuscation. Any tool that reads it holds a live credential and must never print or commit it
  • The callbacks identify no caller and persist nothing, so there is no server-side record of who drove the rack or on whose authority

Scale

Compliance work scales with phones, accounts and messages, not with API calls. Labelling 19 phones is two calls. Evidence capture does not fan out: /pic/screenshot is single-id, cheap in kernel terms but about 30 MB per rack-wide BMP snapshot. /shortcut/device/ip is the slow link at a 15 s default timeout per phone.

Trap allow_ip_list is not access control

It is documented under "Screencast Discovery Rules" and only takes effect when the rule is 1. It gates which phones may discover the AirPlay receiver, not who may call the HTTP or WebSocket API. Verified live: the API on 9911 accepts unauthenticated calls from any LAN host, and the vendor's own examples call it from a remote 192.168.9.9.

Physical limits: radio, heat and battery

Wi-Fi is the AirPlay bottleneck: per-phone frame rates differ sixfold

PartialWith caveats

Video is one-way, iPhone to Wi-Fi to AirplayMirroring.exe on TCP 17000, one session per phone. Nothing in the XP API touches the radio. Measured here: two identical iPhone XRs on the same iOS build and the same AP deliver 28.9 and 4.5 new frames per second under continuous driven motion, alone or together, so the slow one is its own link rather than kernel contention. The only documented levers are per-device /device/airplay/set, the global air_play_* block, and network design outside the API.

How

  1. get_device_list /api/device/get — state, air_pid, imgw/imgh, srv_name, ip and the per-device air_* overrides (0 means use global). Verified: two iPhone11,8 on iOS 18.7.10, state 1, air_pid 22236, imgw 500 by imgh 1080, logical size 414 by 896
  2. (none) /api/config/imserver/get — read the global casting configuration before changing it. Documented but not probed here. The guessed path /config/get returns 404
  3. swipe + get_device_screenshot /api/mouse/swipe driving motion, /api/pic/screenshot?binary=true polled per phone — measure the real source rate by counting frames whose mean absolute pixel difference from the previous frame exceeds about 1
  4. set_airplay_mode /api/device/airplay/set?air_ratio=720&air_fps=15&air_audio=1 — air_ratio is one of 0/720/1080/1400/1920/2650, air_refresh 0 to 60, air_fps and air_img_fps 0 to 30, air_audio 0 global / 1 off / 2 on. The change disconnects the current cast and applies on the next one
  5. (none) /api/config/imserver/set air_play_ratio=720&air_play_fps=15 then /api/imserver/restart — the global air_play_audio is Boolean, while the per-device air_audio is Integer 0/1/2. Every air_play_* field needs the restart
  6. (none) /api/imserver/regmdns — XP-only: re-advertise the receiver (mDNSResponder.exe, "iMouseXP-5429" on UDP 5353) instead of restarting the kernel again
  7. auto_connect_screen /api/device/airplay/connect — confirm recovery with state non-zero, a live air_pid, an ESTABLISHED socket on 17000 from that phone's IP, and a frame that changes under motion. XP has no force flag, so disconnect first

Needs

  • Phones and PC on the same LAN segment with mDNS (UDP 5353) allowed, and the receiver name matching air_play_name
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. With only IMService.exe up, /device/get showed both phones at state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list
  • A client that decodes the 1,620,054-byte bottom-up BMP and computes mean absolute pixel difference, because there is no server-side frame comparison

Watch out

  • The Phonefarm three-mode bandwidth table (about 5, 10 and 20 Mbps, "about 100 or 50 phones") does not exist on XP, is described there as being for one landscape game with no stated measurement method, and the derived "19 phones is about 190 Mbps" is an extrapolation, not a measurement
  • Only two phones have ever been measured here. Whether 19 concurrent sessions starve each other on one AP is untested: plausible physics, not an observed result
  • That lowering air_ratio changes imgw/imgh, and so invalidates stored coordinates and templates, is a reasonable inference from the parameter descriptions but is neither documented nor measured. Re-read imgw/imgh from /device/get after any ratio change
  • /pic/screenshot accepts one id only, unlike every /mouse/* and /key/* endpoint, so frame measurement is N concurrent requests
  • A still screen produces almost no new frames, so any fps measurement without driven motion measures nothing. Do not derive the poll interval from observed frame gaps: doing so decayed a 23 fps stream to 16.5 fps through positive feedback. Use a fixed period
  • XP has no multi-receiver concept. Phonefarm's get_airplaysrvnum and set_airplaysrvnum have no XP equivalent, so spreading load across several named receivers on one PC is not available
  • Losing Wi-Fi kills only video. A phone stays fully controllable over USB while blind, so a health model must report control-ready and video-ready separately or a radio problem will be misdiagnosed as a dead board

Scale

The kernel is demonstrably not the constraint: raw BMP p50 2.0 ms when paced at 50 ms, 84 req/s flat out at p50 12.7 ms; two phones concurrently gave 83 and 85 req/s at p50 3 ms each; ten pollers gave 512 req/s total. JPEG costs p50 40.5 ms and caps at about 21 req/s because the kernel re-encodes, so choose it only where 1.6 MB per frame is unaffordable, never on loopback. The real ceiling is per-phone production, 28.9 fps on 192.168.4.68 and 4.5 fps on 192.168.4.27. Budget 1.6 MB per poll with a reused buffer: without reuse, 488 MB/s of allocation and 496 gen-2 collections per 8 s; with reuse, 2.9 MB/s and zero to one.

No thermal or battery telemetry exists: heat management is open-loop

PartialWith caveats

Rack phones run with the screen permanently on, the board charging them continuously and the SoC encoding an H.264 stream around the clock. Nothing in the XP API reports temperature, battery level, charge state or thermal throttling. The /device/get record carries air_handle, air_pid, rotate, state, imgw/imgh, gid, the air_* overrides, name, srv_name, width/height, ip, mac, user_name, version, model, deviceid, device_name, location, location_crc, vid, pid, uid, gname, uver, and nothing else. No /shortcut/* path reports battery either.

How

  1. shortcut#15 /api/shortcut/switch/bril?id=<comma list>&state=0.05&outtime=15000 — comma list confirmed; state is a float documented as greater than 0 and less than 1; outtime is milliseconds on XP and seconds on Phonefarm
  2. set_airplay_mode /api/device/airplay/set?air_ratio=720&air_fps=10&air_audio=1 — cut encode and radio load per phone. The Phonefarm energy-saving preset does not exist on XP; these explicit knobs replace it
  3. discon_airplay / auto_connect_screen /api/device/airplay/disconnect then /api/device/airplay/connect — a rest phase stops the encoder while USB control stays alive. Both take comma id lists
  4. find_multi_color / get_device_screenshot /api/pic/find-multi-color, or safer here /api/pic/screenshot?binary=true analysed client-side — detect the iOS thermal warning screen. XP encodes absolute anchors as "x|y|RRGGBB-tolerance,..." inside a list of configs, not Phonefarm's first_color plus offset form
  5. get_device_list /api/device/get, then rebuild the comma id list — there is no API-level exclude flag; the target set is whatever list your client sends

Needs

  • The Shortcut chain for /shortcut/switch/bril, which is not verified on this rig. Without it the only brightness lever is manual, per phone, and the API cannot read brightness back
  • A captured reference of the actual iOS thermal warning screen on this model, which is itself a hardware-stress exercise to produce
  • Acceptance that rest phases blind the phone: no screenshots, no find-image, no OCR while disconnected

Watch out

  • A thermally throttled phone answers every call with data.code 0 while the iOS temperature screen blocks all UI, so mirrored taps land on nothing. It looks identical to the silent stuck-click state: use the pixel oracle, not return codes
  • Airplane mode as a cooling measure is a trap. /shortcut/switch/flight?state=1 kills Wi-Fi, which kills both the video channel and the Shortcut's own return path, and the reverse call has to travel that same dead path. The same applies to /shortcut/switch/wlan?state=0. Never wire either to an automated thermal response
  • The claim that iOS pauses charging above about 40 C, visible on the lock screen, is outside every reference file and is not checkable here. With Auto-Lock set to Never there is no lock screen in the mirror to read, so it is not an observation channel
  • A swelling battery lifts the display and can stress or short the board's cable. There is no software signal at all; the first symptom is physical, so inspect on a schedule
  • The vendor setup page warns that inserting the control board in the wrong orientation can cause a short-circuit burnout at your own risk, and that no cable end or metal part may touch the yellow PCBA area

Scale

Brightness, cast settings and disconnect/connect all take comma id lists, so a 19-phone adjustment is one request each. Detection is the only per-phone cost: a once-a-minute thermal check across 19 phones is roughly 30 MB/min of loopback traffic and a few tens of milliseconds of kernel time. Rested phones consume no AirPlay bandwidth, which also relieves shared-AP pressure. Shortcut calls round-trip over each phone's Wi-Fi, so a rack-wide brightness change is bounded by the slowest link.

The limits of what a response tells you

A code 0 response only means the board accepted the report: the frame is the only oracle

Native APIVerified

Status 200 means the request was accepted and data.code 0 means the kernel executed it. Neither says iOS acted. Measured on this rack on 10 September 2026: a phone entered a state where /mouse/move visibly moved the pointer and fn_key=Home still worked (whole-frame mean difference 142.15), while every /mouse/click returned code 0 and produced 0.09 against an idle floor of 0.02 to 0.03. /mouse/up did not clear it. /mouse/reset did, and it stayed cleared: the same click then measured 141.96. The same false-success shape covers a mis-calibrated pointer, a banner over the target, a locked phone and the thermal screen.

How

  1. mouse_reset_pos /api/mouse/reset?id=<comma list> — the only call measured to clear the silent stuck-click state, and the clearing persists. Send it before any tap-critical sequence and whenever the target set changes
  2. get_device_screenshot /api/pic/screenshot?id=<single id>&binary=true — capture the reference frame. Raw bytes, no JSON wrapper; unlike the Phonefarm sibling, binary works over plain HTTP here
  3. mouse_move /api/mouse/move?x=380&y=880 then a re-capture — prove the control channel by diffing a small box around the commanded point. A move to 380,880 put the pointer at 377,875 in the captured frame
  4. click /api/mouse/click?x=<x>&y=<y>[&button=1][&time=<ms>] — require a whole-frame mean difference above about 20. A real reaction measures 20 to 160 (162.66 and 141.96 observed); under 1 is nothing happened
  5. (none) ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api callback error_push — data.call_fun and data.message, the vendor example being "/mouse/down" with "Hardware not working (unknown error)". The only asynchronous signal that an input call failed at the board, and it arrives after the synchronous code 0
  6. send_key fn_key WIN+h /api/key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+h (twice) — normalize the screen before a shared-coordinate probe. The first press leaves the app, the second returns to page one

Needs

  • A per-phone idle control frame and threshold, captured while nothing is driving that phone
  • imgw/imgh per device from /device/get. Coordinates are mirror pixels, 500 by 1080 here, not iOS logical points at 414 by 896
  • A WebSocket client for error_push, dev_disconnect and usb_change. HTTP alone cannot see them
  • Client-side BMP decoding and mean-absolute-difference arithmetic. The API offers no frame comparison of any kind

Watch out

  • Never MD5-compare frames. The clock, encoder noise and wallpaper parallax change every frame, so byte equality reports "reacted" for an untouched phone. An earlier diagnostic in this project drew a wrong conclusion exactly that way
  • A probe tap on a shared coordinate is only fair if the phones have the same element there. The two XRs here have different home screens, so the same coordinate is Clock on one and Reminders on the other. Prefer a move-only probe with a pointer-box diff, which is state-independent
  • A phone at 4.5 new frames per second needs about 220 ms before the post-action frame can differ. Wait for a genuinely new frame, not a fixed short delay
  • The pointer renders as a small low-contrast grey dot that a whole-frame diff cannot see. A 40 px box around the commanded point measured 1.4 to 9.8 against a 0.02 idle floor
  • /mouse/reset is confirmed only to clear the stuck-click state. Whether it corrects a drifted pointer is unverified; an offset pointer is a calibration problem and needs /device/collection/mouse
  • error_push has no per-request correlation id, only call_fun and message, so matching it to a specific in-flight request is the client's problem

Scale

/mouse/reset fans out to the whole target set in one request, so a 19-phone reset is one call. The probe screenshots are the per-phone cost at about 2 ms each, so a 19-phone control check is well under 100 ms of kernel time plus one source-frame interval per phone, which is the real wait: about 35 ms on a healthy link and about 220 ms on the slow XR. Move latency scales at 0.6 ms/px identically for one phone or many, so a long probe move is hundreds of milliseconds of board time, not jitter.

Tip Reset is free, detection is not

Sending /mouse/reset costs one request and has no downside, so send it whenever the target set changes rather than trying to detect the stuck state first. Diagnosing that state as a mirroring fault and restarting the cast wastes the session and does not clear it.

The limits of reach: files, audio and events

File access stops at Photos and the Files "On My iPhone" tree

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

The entire on-device file surface is the Shortcut layer: /shortcut/album/{get,upload,down,del,clear} for the Photos library and /shortcut/file/{get,upload,down,del} for the Files app tree on iOS 15 and later. That is the whole list. Nothing in either edition reads another app's documents, caches, databases, logs or keychain, installs apps or configuration profiles, or pulls a device backup. Anything an app does not surface through Photos or Files is reachable only as pixels, and only pushed in through that app's own import UI driven by taps.

How

  1. shortcut#7 POST /api/shortcut/album/upload — id comma list, files as an array of PC paths the kernel can read, blank album_name means Recents, zip 0/1, outtime in milliseconds. The response returns the 10 newest album records
  2. shortcut#8 POST /api/shortcut/file/upload — iOS 15 and above, id comma list, path defaults to the My iPhone root. Code 27 is "Path does not exist", so create the directory first
  3. shortcut#1 / #4 GET /api/shortcut/album/get, /api/shortcut/file/get — both single id only. XP filters albums by album_name and num and has no date filter. An empty ext denotes a directory; code 35 means the list is empty
  4. shortcut#2 / #5 POST /api/shortcut/album/down, /api/shortcut/file/down — single id only, and list entries split name and extension into separate fields. Files land in the install directory under \Shortcut\Media and \Shortcut\File
  5. click / swipe /api/mouse/click, /api/mouse/swipe — handing a seeded file to a specific app is UI automation in mirror pixels, verified only by frame differencing
  6. shortcut#3 / #6 POST /api/shortcut/album/del, /api/shortcut/file/del, GET /api/shortcut/album/clear — the del calls take comma id lists and return the 10 newest remaining records. Clear wipes an entire album
  7. shortcut#24 GET /api/shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 — the cheapest proof the whole channel works before building on it. A 15 s wait ending in code 30 means the hotkey did not launch the shortcut

Needs

  • The iMouse Shortcut installed with the kernel IP edited in, run once with every permission allowed, and Shortcuts > Advanced set to allow running scripts, sharing large amounts of data, deleting without confirmation and deleting large amounts of data
  • The shortcut bound to an AssistiveTouch key, with the board connected and the phone on the LAN. The trigger travels over USB while the payload travels over Wi-Fi, so both channels must be up
  • iOS 15 or later for every /shortcut/file/* path; the XRs here are on 18.7.10
  • Target directories that already exist, and outtime raised well above the 15000 ms default for large transfers

Watch out

  • None of this is verified on this rig. The Shortcut install state was never probed, /api/pic/ocr answering code 28 shows the plug-in layer is incomplete, and the guessed path /shortcut/get returned 404. Run the IP probe before designing around any of it
  • Asymmetric multi-device support: upload and delete accept comma lists, but album/get, album/down, file/get, file/down, clipboard/get and device/ip are all single-id, so a rack-wide harvest is N requests
  • Download calls return only a status code. The bytes land on the kernel PC's disk, so a client on another machine gets no file back from the API
  • Deletion permissions are granted once on the phone and then apply to every later call. A wrong name in a del list, or a stray album/clear, destroys user data with no undo and no prompt
  • Uploads read PC paths with the kernel process's privileges, and the API on 9911 is unauthenticated, so any LAN host can push files into every phone's Photos library or pull them off
  • The "path must start and end with /" rule comes from the Phonefarm doc and is not stated in the XP parameter table. Only the millisecond outtime unit is confirmed for XP

Scale

Seeding is one request for the rack, but the transfer crosses each phone's own Wi-Fi link, so wall time is bounded by the slowest radio. Harvesting is strictly one request per phone. Use zip=1 for many small files. Shortcut transfers share the LAN with AirPlay, so a large push further depresses the frame rate of an already-slow phone: schedule bulk transfers outside verification windows. A 50 MB video to 19 phones on a contended AP is minutes, and the default timeout fires long before that.

Text-to-speech is withdrawn in both editions; a user-authored Shortcut is the only substitute

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Phonefarm shortcut sub-function 14, "Read text aloud", is struck through in the vendor table, and the XP shortcut page has no TTS function at all. Neither edition has any audio-output or audio-capture endpoint; air_audio only decides whether the AirPlay stream carries the phone's sound to the PC receiver. The feature can be rebuilt on the phone: put the words on the clipboard, then launch a user-authored "Get Clipboard, Speak Text" Shortcut by URL scheme. Nothing reports back that anything was spoken.

How

  1. n/a (phone-side) none — author a Shortcut named for example "Speak Clip" on each phone. There is no API to install, list or trigger Shortcuts by name
  2. shortcut id 10 /shortcut/clipboard/set — id comma list, text, sleep in seconds, outtime in milliseconds. Unicode-safe, so non-ASCII works where /key/sendkey cannot. Returns data.code 0 with no payload
  3. shortcut id 13 /shortcut/exec/url — id comma list, url, outtime. Passing shortcuts://run-shortcut?name=Speak%20Clip is documented iOS behavior but undocumented vendor behavior, so probe it on one phone. It briefly foregrounds the Shortcuts app
  4. send_key fn_key /key/sendkey fn_key — refuted as an alternative trigger: the XP fn_key vocabulary is a closed set and a custom combination cannot be defined through the API
  5. set_airplay_mode /device/airplay/set air_audio — receive-side only. It governs whether the mirrored stream carries audio to the PC, not whether the phone's own speaker sounds

Needs

  • The iMouse Shortcut installed and permissioned, plus a second hand-authored Shortcut on each phone
  • The phone reachable from the kernel on the LAN and cabled to a bound board at state 2, so both the trigger and the callback path work
  • IMConsole.exe running and logged in. XP paths on 127.0.0.1:9911 only; Phonefarm function names return HTTP 500 here and 9912 is closed

Watch out

  • The vendor TTS function itself is not achievable in either edition. Only the home-made substitute works
  • No completion signal. XP has no send_text_ok equivalent, so code 0 means accepted, not spoken
  • With air_audio set to on, the sound is carried to the PC receiver, which can make an ear test misleading about where playback happened. Changing air_audio also drops the current cast
  • A Shortcuts permission prompt left untapped blocks every later triggered Shortcut on that phone, and shows up in the mirror as a dialog
  • Unverified on this rig: no /shortcut/* endpoint has ever been called here. Prove the channel with the IP probe first

Scale

Clipboard-set and exec-url both take comma id lists, so making the whole rack speak the same line is two requests. Different text per phone is one clipboard call each, bounded by outtime, so 19 distinct lines is roughly 20 s serial or a few seconds concurrent. Playback is local to each speaker with no mixing or sequencing control, so simultaneous speech on a rack is unintelligible by design, and genuinely a noise problem in a shared room.

No push, badge or background-event listener exists; only what is drawn on the mirror can be polled

PartialWith caveats

Nothing in either edition subscribes to APNs, badge counts or app events. The XP callback page has 19 sections and every one is about the rig itself. The only substitute is pixels: poll a cropped band of the mirror, threshold a mean absolute difference, then open Notification Centre and read the text with client-side OCR, because the kernel OCR plug-in is not connected here.

How

  1. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot with rect=[0,0,500,120] — id single only, binary true for raw bytes, jpg false is the XP default, plus save_path. Crop to the banner band; read imgw/imgh per phone first
  2. n/a (client-side) none — threshold a mean absolute pixel difference: 0.02 to 0.03 on an untouched phone, 20 to 160 for a real reaction. There is no server-side change detector
  3. send_key fn_key /key/sendkey fn_key=NoticeBar — open Notification Centre for the full text instead of the truncated banner. Related entries: ControlBar, AppSwitch, WIN+h
  4. ocr / ocr_ex /pic/ocr, /pic/ocr-ex, /pic/find-text, /pic/find-text-ex, or the plug-in-free /shortcut/other/* equivalents — all single id. On this rig /api/pic/ocr answers data.code 28, so OCR must run client-side or the Shortcut route must be stood up
  5. click /mouse/click, preceded by /mouse/reset — act on the notification in mirror pixels, then dismiss with two presses of WIN+h
  6. shortcut id 13 /shortcut/exec/url — where the app allows it, deep-link to the inbox and poll that screen instead of waiting for a banner
  7. (none) ws://127.0.0.1:9911/api — the real event bus covers the rig only: im_connect, dev_connect, dev_disconnect, dev_rotate, dev_change, dev_delete, group_change, group_delete, usb_change, collection_mouse, airplay_connect_log, restart_log, user_info, im_log, error_push, im_config_change, logout, dev_sort_change

Needs

  • The phone mirroring and unlocked with Auto-Lock Never, and notifications set to show as banners for the apps of interest, none of which is queryable through the API
  • Client-side OCR or per-app pixel templates on the PC
  • Per-phone imgw/imgh read before any rect or click coordinate is computed, and the board at state 2 if the flow acts on what it finds

Watch out

  • Subscribing to push notifications, badge counts or background app events is not achievable. Only visible pixels can be polled, and only while the phone is awake and mirroring
  • Detection latency is bounded by the phone, not the kernel. A banner shown for 3 s can be missed on the 4.5 fps XR
  • Opening Notification Centre covers the screen, invalidates any coordinate the flow was about to use, and must be dismissed before the next action
  • A banner covers the top of the mirror and can swallow a tap that a mirrored click intended for a different phone. Exclude any phone whose imgw/imgh differs from the master
  • The rect and binary combination is documented as two independent parameters but has not been measured here; the 2 ms and 1.62 MB figures are for the uncropped frame
  • Reading notification content from accounts that are not yours is personal-data processing subject to privacy law, and this rig's API is unauthenticated on all interfaces, so any LAN host can pull the same frames. Automating replies to other people's messages may also breach the messaging platform's terms

Scale

Capture is per-phone independent and nearly free: two pollers at 83 and 85 req/s, ten at 512 req/s total, with input traffic and polling measurably not interfering. So 19 phones at 4 polls per second is trivial, and a 120-row crop is a fraction of the 1.6 MB full frame. Reuse buffers, since each full frame exceeds the .NET Large Object Heap threshold. Use a fixed poll period. The binding constraints are per-phone source rate and, for client-side OCR, PC CPU per frame.

Also worth knowing

Audio: real at the receiver, narrower than "no audio capture"

Wrong "The API has no audio capture" overstates the limit

Two cards elsewhere in this handoff, the VoiceOver audit in the QA section and the text-to-speech entry in this section, state flatly that the API has no audio capture. That is true of the HTTP surface: no endpoint hands back audio bytes the way /pic/screenshot hands back image bytes. It is not true of the rack. air_play_audio in /config/imserver/set and the per-device air_audio override in /device/airplay/set exist to route each phone's sound into the PC's AirPlay receiver, and that receiver is an ordinary Windows process, AirplayMirroring.exe, whose output is capturable like any other Windows audio session. The correct claim is narrower: no call returns a WAV. The audio exists at the receiver and is capturable host-side, and a second, independent route captures sound at the phone itself. That reopens playback QA, ad-audio verification, alarm and notification-sound checks, and, directly against the QA-part2 claim, VoiceOver auditing, since spoken accessibility output leaves the phone through the same audio path as any other app sound.

Capturing a phone's AirPlay audio as a file, host-side

Plus external toolingWith caveats

Whatever a phone plays through its own speaker, an ad's soundtrack, a podcast, a VoiceOver announcement, an alarm, is mirrored to the PC over the same AirPlay session that carries the picture. air_play_audio is the global switch and air_audio (0 use global, 1 off, 2 on) is the per-device override, both documented with a boolean and an integer enum respectively, nothing more exotic. The API never returns the samples; a Windows-side loopback recorder does. This is the missing half of the bandwidth story: air_audio was already known here as a knob for shrinking mirroring traffic, and it is that, but it is also the thing that decides whether there is anything to record.

How

  1. get_im_config /config/imserver/get — read air_play_audio first. Not queried on this rig; the vendor's own example response ships it true, but that is the doc default, not a measurement here.
  2. set_im_config /config/imserver/set?air_play_audio=true — global enable if it reads false. Not on the no-restart list the doc publishes, so this one requires a kernel restart and drops every mirroring session, exactly like the OCR fix earlier in this section.
  3. set_dev_airplay /device/airplay/set?id=<id>&air_audio=2 — force one phone's audio on, or air_audio=1 to force a phone's audio off. The doc states that setting these per-device overrides disconnects that phone's cast immediately and the new value applies on the next mirroring connection; not exercised live here, so budget a reconnect, not an instant switch.
  4. send_key /key/sendkey?fn_key=Play/Pause — start the media under test without touching the mirror-image coordinates, useful before a capture window opens.
  5. none Windows process loopback capture, e.g. via NAudio, against AirplayMirroring.exe's PID — no XP path; this is the external tool. Read the target PID from the device record's air_pid field so the capture always points at the process actually holding that phone's session, not a hardcoded PID.
  6. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?binary=true — a timestamped frame alongside the audio buffer, so a review can confirm which visible moment produced which sound.
  7. send_key /key/sendkey?fn_key=MuteSoundSwitch or VolumeUp/VolumeDown — normalize the phone's own volume before capture, or mute it afterward, without the reconnect cost of touching air_audio again.

Needs

  • A confirmed air_play_audio read and, if it was off, one kernel restart accepted as a maintenance window, the same cost already paid for the OCR plug-in fix.
  • A Windows audio capture library that supports per-process loopback (the Windows process-loopback capture API, available since Windows 10 2004, exposed by NAudio and similar libraries). Nothing in the iMouse product supplies this.
  • The device record's live air_pid polled before each capture, since a phone that reconnects gets served by whichever AirplayMirroring.exe instance answers next.

Watch out

  • Measured on this rig on 10 September 2026: both XRs showed air_pid 22236, the identical AirplayMirroring.exe process, while both were mirroring. A process-scoped loopback capture on that PID captures every phone routed through it mixed together, not one phone. Whether air_audio=1 on the phones you are not testing actually removes their contribution to that shared mix, or only stops their video-adjacent overhead while the mixed audio session includes them regardless, is undocumented and unmeasured here.
  • The practical isolation method is therefore one of two disruptive options: set air_audio=1 on every phone except the target before each capture and accept a reconnect on all of them, or use /device/airplay/disconnect to take every other phone off mirroring for the duration of the test. Neither is a background operation; both interrupt phones that are not under test.
  • The Phonefarm sibling's set_airplaysrvnum can run multiple AirPlay receiver instances, which would give a real per-receiver isolation boundary. XP has no receiver-count concept, only the single air_play_name in /config/imserver/get, so that isolation path does not exist on this edition.
  • Whether the hardware volume keys (VolumeUp, VolumeDown, MuteSoundSwitch) act on the same audio session AirPlay mirrors, versus a separate ringer or call-volume path, is an iOS behavior no vendor doc covers. Verify with a capture before trusting a mute.
  • A restart to flip the global switch invalidates every live capture and every bound coordinate sequence that assumes the phone is still mirroring; sequence it like the OCR fix, as a planned window, not a per-test toggle.

Scale

The global switch and the screenshot calls are cheap and already fan out or run at the rig's usual per-id rates. Isolation is what does not scale: proving a clean single-phone recording costs one reconnect cycle per phone you silence, so testing all 19 boards one at a time against a shared receiver is 18 mute-and-reconnect operations per test round, not a parallel sweep. Treat this as a one-phone-at-a-time QA lane, not a rack-wide audio pipeline, until the mixing question above is measured.

Recording a phone's microphone through a self-authored Shortcut

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

This is a second, unrelated audio route: not the phone's outgoing sound, its incoming microphone. iOS Shortcuts ships a general-purpose Record Audio action that saves a clip to Files or the Shortcut's own output. Nothing in the iMouse documentation names it; it is a capability of Apple's Shortcuts app that a rack operator would have to build themselves, on top of the one fixed iMouse Shortcut this handoff documents elsewhere.

How

  1. none no XP path — build a distinctly named Shortcut by hand on the phone: Record Audio, a fixed duration, then Save File to Files or iCloud Drive. Run it once locally so the microphone permission prompt is already answered; a remote trigger cannot see or dismiss that dialog.
  2. shortcut#13 /shortcut/exec/url?url=shortcuts://run-shortcut?name=<name> — trigger it remotely. /shortcut/exec/url is a general Open URL action, and every example in the XP, equipment and shortcuts docs uses an http or https domain; a shortcuts:// scheme reaching this endpoint is inferred from Apple's own URL scheme, not demonstrated anywhere in the vendor material.
  3. shortcut#6 /shortcut/file/get?id=<id> — poll for the new file by name and timestamp once the recording should be done. There is no completion callback; exec/url returning code 0 only means the OS accepted the URL, not that the Shortcut finished.
  4. shortcut#7 /shortcut/file/down?id=<id>&list=[{name,ext}] — pull the audio file back to the PC. Single id, like every other /shortcut/* read path.

Needs

  • iOS's own microphone permission granted by hand, once, per phone. No endpoint grants it remotely.
  • The same invisible iOS accessibility baseline the rest of this document assumes: unlocked screen, IMConsole.exe running, board at state 2. iOS 15 or later for the /shortcut/file/* family.
  • A distinct, identically spelled Shortcut authored and saved on every phone that needs this, by hand, with no API to push or template it, the same manual-per-phone cost already described for the Unicode Shortcut in this section.

Watch out

  • No /shortcut/* endpoint of any kind has been exercised on this rig. This route inherits that at full force, on top of an untested URL scheme.
  • The microphone hears whatever is acoustically present, the phone's own speaker if something is playing, room noise, or, depending on iOS version and the calling app, audio from an active call. Call and FaceTime audio capture through this route is a guess about iOS behavior, not a documented one, and should be tested on an expendable line before being relied on.
  • This captures a live voice, not a UI state. Two-party consent recording statutes in a number of US states, and wiretap and interception law generally, apply to recorded calls regardless of what the platform's own terms say. Room or ambient recording without the knowledge of the people present raises the same exposure. Confirm consent and jurisdiction before pointing this at anything but test content the operator controls end to end.

Scale

One phone at a time in practice: a personalized shortcuts:// URL only reaches every phone in an id list if every phone carries a Shortcut of that exact name, and even then each phone's recording, poll and download are three separate single-id calls. Budget a Shortcut round trip per phone plus the recording's own duration, the same order of magnitude as the Unicode clipboard round trip elsewhere in this document, not the sub-millisecond fan-out of a shared mouse or key call.

Automating apps that refuse simulators, emulators and jailbroken devices

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

Banking and fintech apps, government e-ID and passport apps, insurance and healthcare portals, and DRM-gated media apps commonly run their own root, jailbreak and emulator checks and refuse to load, or drop to a degraded mode, on an Android emulator, an iOS simulator or a jailbroken phone. A device cloud built on cloud-hosted emulator VMs is exactly what those checks exist to catch. This rack is 19 stock iPhone XRs with no jailbreak and no app installed on the handset, driven through a USB HID accessory board and mirrored over AirPlay, so an app running on it sees genuine consumer hardware and a stock OS, the same as it would from the owner's hand. That is the rack's strongest point of difference against a simulator farm for this exact class of app, and it is worth stating plainly rather than leaving it implicit.

How

  1. click / send_key /mouse/click, /key/sendkey — log in and navigate the app's screens. Board HID, no phone-side Shortcut needed, and both fan out to a comma id list in one request.
  2. get_device_screenshot /pic/screenshot?id=<id>&save_path=<dir> — capture evidence of screen state (a balance, a claim status, a verification screen) as a file on the PC. Single id, as documented.
  3. shortcut#10 / #11 /shortcut/clipboard/set then WIN+a, WIN+c, /shortcut/clipboard/get — where an exact string matters more than a screenshot (an account number, a policy ID, a confirmation code), select and copy, then read data.text back. Needs the full iMouse Shortcut chain on that phone.
  4. get_user_info /config/user/info — check dev_num and dev_online_num before committing a regulated-app workflow to the whole rack, since it says how many devices the license actually covers.

Needs

  • Accounts the operator owns, or is specifically authorized by the account holder or the platform to test with. Nothing here changes what the app's own terms of service permit.
  • For the clipboard steps, the same iMouse Shortcut prerequisite chain documented elsewhere in this section: Shortcut installed and IP-configured on the phone, AssistiveTouch and Full Keyboard Access on, board at state 2.
  • Coordinates and timing measured per app screen, the same as any other UI-automation flow on this rig.

Watch out

  • Face ID, Touch ID, Apple Pay, Secure Enclave-backed key confirmation, and a physical side-button double-press all stop the rack cold. No function in the API can satisfy a biometric prompt or a Secure Enclave confirmation, so a KYC selfie liveness step or a payment confirmation step is the one part of these flows that cannot be automated end to end. Everything up to that gate can be driven; the gate itself cannot.
  • Frames and clipboard reads captured from these apps carry regulated data by construction: account numbers, health information, ID document images, policy details. /pic/screenshot?save_path writes that data unencrypted to local disk in plain BMP or JPG with no retention control of its own, and port 9911 has no authentication, so any other host on the LAN can request the same screenshot or the same clipboard read while the workflow runs. Purge captured frames rather than archiving them, and keep 9911 off any network you do not control.
  • Being real hardware defeats false positives from an emulator check, not the anti-fraud or anti-abuse logic behind it. This is a statement about what the app's device check sees, not a way to get past controls it is not designed to catch.
  • Scope every use of this to apps and accounts the operator owns or is authorized to test. Running it against an account that is not the operator's, or against a platform whose terms forbid automated interaction, carries its own legal exposure under computer-misuse, banking, health-privacy or platform-terms law well before the technical wall above is reached.

Scale

Navigation is cheap and shared: /mouse/click and /key/sendkey take a comma id list, so stepping the whole rack through an identical login or menu sequence is one request regardless of phone count. Verification is not: /pic/screenshot and /shortcut/clipboard/get are single id, so confirming the result on each phone is always N requests, one per phone, the same throughput ceiling documented for the rest of the rig. Check dev_num and dev_online_num from /config/user/info before scaling a regulated-app workflow past what the license and the online fleet actually support.

The one avenue that could move the walls: talking to the boards directly

Every limit above is a limit of the documented HTTP API sitting on top of IMService.exe. Underneath it there is a second, undocumented surface: each board enumerates as a USB HID device, vendor ID 720A, on a vendor-defined usage page (0xFF00, usage 0x00) that Windows cannot decode from the descriptor alone. What is measured is only the shape of the channel: a 9-byte output report (1 report ID plus an 8-byte payload) carries PC-to-board commands, and a 17-byte input report (1 report ID plus 16 bytes) carries board-to-PC replies. The content of those bytes is unread. analysis/HARDWARE.md names the fix as its own second recommended next step: run the original vendor software, capture its USB traffic with USBPcap or Wireshark while triggering known actions such as Home, a single tap and a swipe, and diff the reports to recover the command layout. That work has not been started, and it has not appeared anywhere else in this handoff as a project option.

It matters because it is the only lever in sight against three things this document otherwise treats as fixed. First, the 0.6 ms-per-pixel pointer walk: /mouse/move /mouse/move measured at 592 ms for a 1,000-pixel jump, and /mouse/swipe /mouse/swipe rides the same walk underneath its steping, step_sleep and brake parameters, which govern how many loop iterations a slide takes and the pause between them, not how fast the board itself moves the cursor. A 1,080-pixel swipe still takes about 580 ms of travel regardless of how those three parameters are set, which is why velocity-dependent flicks do not fire. Whether that pacing is a firmware limit of the board or an artifact of how IMService.exe frames each move as a step sequence is exactly the question a decoded report would answer; today there is no way to tell the two apart. Second, the comma-list fan-out: the "one parameter set for every id" constraint is a property of the HTTP layer, where a single call carries one shared payload to a list of ids. Each board is a separate USB device with its own PID, so writing distinct 9-byte reports to distinct device handles is a structurally different operation from a shared HTTP parameter, and might allow real per-phone payloads in one coordinated pass instead of one HTTP call per phone. Third, total dependence on the vendor kernel: /config/usb/get /config/usb/get is the only window onto board attach state (vid, pid, uid, ver, state), and /device/usb/restart /device/usb/restart is the only reset path, and both exist only because IMService.exe is running and licensed. Direct HID access would let a console enumerate and drive boards through the Windows HID APIs with no kernel process, and no license, in the loop at all.

None of that is close to free. It needs a capture rig: a machine running the original iMouse software, USBPcap or Wireshark recording the USB traffic, and one board set aside that can be sacrificed if a command byte is guessed wrong. It needs protocol work with no starting point better than diff-and-guess, first the 8-byte command space, then the meaning of the 16-byte reply, with nothing in any vendor document to check the guesses against. It costs the vendor relationship: no more firmware updates, no more support, and whatever validation IMService.exe currently does on a report before it reaches the board has to be rediscovered or done without. And it carries a real risk of bricking a board, because a malformed report sent straight to unknown firmware has no documented safe-failure behavior, unlike an HTTP call that answers a clean status 500 or a data.code the docs define.

Nothing here depends on which edition's kernel is installed; the boards and their HID bridge sit underneath both, and the capture-and-diff evidence for the report sizes was gathered against this XP rig. Treat this as a parallel investigation, run against a spare board once the documented-API console is otherwise working, never as a prerequisite for it. Everything else in this handoff already ships on /config/usb/get, /device/usb/restart and the rest of the documented surface; this is the one place where a locked door is at least a door, not a wall.

The Apple-ecosystem checklist

Ten features a buyer will ask about by name before asking about anything below this line. None of the underlying vendor terms (Bluetooth, NFC, Wallet, Siri, eSIM, Guided Access, Screen Time, Find My, Family Sharing, iCloud) appears anywhere in the nine XP doc files or the Phonefarm doc: a full-text search across all ten returns zero hits. That absence cuts two ways. Where the feature needs a radio or a physical button the API does not expose, it is a hard wall, not a gap to work around. Where the feature is just another app on the home screen, it is ordinary UI automation, no different from anything else in this document, and in three cases it is a better answer to a real operator problem than anything already covered.

FeatureFeasibilityVerdictMechanism, and why
Apple Watch and wearable pairing Not possible Refuted No endpoint. Pairing is a Bluetooth handshake plus a confirmation tap on both the phone and the watch, and neither edition documents a single Bluetooth call of any kind, not a scan, not a connect, not a state read. There is no channel to start this, driven or otherwise.
AirPods and audio routing Not possible Refuted Same wall. Even switching output among AirPods already paired by hand would mean a blind /mouse/click on the Control Center audio card, a coordinate never measured on this rig and not worth designing on when the API cannot see or set the Bluetooth state behind it.
CarPlay Not possible Refuted CarPlay needs a wired or Bluetooth session with a head unit that does not exist in a rack, and no function in either doc names it. Not a rig limitation, a category mismatch.
NFC and Wallet Not possible Refuted A Wallet tap-to-pay or transit pass is triggered by a physical double-click of the side button. The /key/sendkey hotkey table (WIN+h, ControlBar, NoticeBar, TAB+l, and the rest) opens every other hardware-button surface but has no side-button entry at all, and there is no software trigger for the NFC radio either.
Find My Partial, UI only With caveats Opening the app is ordinary automation: /key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+h to a known home screen, then /mouse/click on the icon. Nothing reads a location back through the API, only through the mirrored screen, so this is a screenshot-and-look tool, not a query. Still genuinely useful here: 19 owned handsets on a shelf is exactly the loss and theft scenario Find My is for, and it costs nothing beyond one Apple ID sign-in per phone.
Family Sharing Partial, UI only With caveats Reachable the same way as any Settings screen, /mouse/click through Settings, the account banner, then Family Sharing. Little reason to use it on a rack of independent farm phones, and any per-account change it makes is one phone at a time: the shortcut fan-out endpoints (/shortcut/exec/url and the rest) share one payload across an id list, but Family Sharing has no shortcut path at all, so there is no batch form to fall back on.
Screen Time and Guided Access Partial (Screen Time) / Not possible (Guided Access trigger) With caveats Screen Time app limits are a one-time /mouse/click walk through Settings per phone, and once set they enforce themselves with no further API calls, which is a real guardrail against an automation that drifts into the wrong app. Guided Access does the same job more tightly, pinning the screen to one app, but its standard trigger is a physical triple-click of the side button, again absent from the /key/sendkey hotkey table, so nothing here can turn it on or off once configured.
iCloud backup and restore Partial, UI only With caveats Settings > [name] > iCloud > iCloud Backup is reachable by /mouse/click, and restoring a fresh phone from an existing backup is the fastest route to identical home screens across the rack, faster than laying out icons by hand on each one. The wall shows up at sign-in: a new Apple ID on a phone needs two-factor approval, a code delivered by SMS or push that this rig cannot read (see the messaging entries above), so this only scales across phones that already share one signed-in account.
eSIM Partial, UI only With caveats The Settings walk to Cellular, Add eSIM is ordinary automation, and an activation code supplied as text rather than a QR image can be typed in with the documented Unicode route, /shortcut/clipboard/set then /key/sendkey?fn_key=WIN+v. Carrier activation by QR code cannot be automated at all: that flow points the phone's camera at a printed or displayed code, and nothing in the API can present an image to the camera or trigger the scan. Treat provisioning as a manual, per-phone task like the rest of the one-time setup chain.
Siri and dictation Not possible (Siri) / Partial (dictation) Refuted (Siri) / With caveats (dictation) Siri has no software trigger in either edition: it is invoked by a side-button long-press or by "Hey Siri," and neither is a key the hotkey table defines. Keyboard dictation is only the microphone glyph on the on-screen keyboard opened with fn_key=OPENKeyboard, tappable like any other icon, but there is no endpoint that returns what it transcribes; the result still has to leave the phone through the clipboard round trip documented for Unicode text.

Tip Three of these are worth building, not just noting

Find My, Screen Time app limits and iCloud backup or restore all clear the same bar as everything else marked "with caveats" in this document: reachable by /mouse/click and /key/sendkey through the visible UI, verifiable by screenshot, and each solving a real problem for a rack of owned handsets rather than a workaround for a missing feature. None of the three has been exercised on this hardware; treat the coordinates and timings as unmeasured until probed here, the same caveat that applies to every UI-automation entry in this handoff.

Trap The pattern behind six refusals is one missing radio and one missing button

Apple Watch pairing, AirPods, CarPlay, NFC and Wallet, and Siri's own trigger all fail for one of two reasons: the API defines no Bluetooth function anywhere, in either edition, and the /key/sendkey hotkey table has no entry for the side button, single-click, double-click or long-press. Any future vendor firmware or edition that adds either one would reopen this whole list at once, so it is worth re-checking both facts, not just re-testing each feature individually, before assuming they are still closed.

Trap Regulated data has no separate lane on this rack

GDPR and CCPA are not the only regimes this rig can walk into, and nothing in the kernel treats regulated data differently from any other pixel. The facts are scattered across this document; here they are in one place. /pic/screenshot with save_path set writes a full, unencrypted BMP or JPG of whatever the phone was displaying to a plain filesystem path on the kernel PC, no encryption parameter exists. /shortcut/clipboard/get returns data.text for whatever is on the pasteboard, which on a banking, health or support app is routinely a password, a one-time code or a card number, in plaintext, in the HTTP response. Every saved frame accumulates in that same folder with no expiry, no size cap and no delete-by-age call anywhere in the XP or Phonefarm docs, so save_path is an unbounded archive of everything ever shown on screen. C:\iMouseXP\IMService.json holds the vendor account password behind /config/user/login as reversible hex obfuscation, recoverable from that file alone, and because /config/user/switch moves between the ten utag sub-accounts without asking for the password again, that one recoverable string is a skeleton key to all ten. And allow_ip_list and mdns_type under /config/imserver/set gate AirPlay discovery only; the HTTP and WebSocket API on port 9911 authenticates no one, so any host on the LAN reaches all of the above. None of this is a bug. It is the documented shape of the product. It becomes a compliance problem the moment the screen being mirrored belongs to a banking, health, government or customer-support workflow, several of which this document proposes elsewhere.

RegimeWhat triggers it on this rigControl to add, since the API has none
GDPR / CCPAAny frame from /pic/screenshot or clipboard text from /shortcut/clipboard/get that identifies an EU, UK or California resident becomes personal data the instant it lands on disk or in a response body.A lawful basis and a written retention limit for the save_path folder, enforced by your own scheduler, since no kernel call deletes or ages out a saved frame.
HIPAAA frame or clipboard read taken while a patient portal, telehealth or pharmacy app is on screen is electronic protected health information the moment it is captured, whether or not anyone reads it.Never capture the full frame near such an app: use /pic/screenshot's rect to crop to only the field needed, encrypt the volume the archive lives on, and treat the operator as a business associate needing a signed agreement with whoever owns the data.
PCI-DSSA card number or CVV copied inside a payment app and read back with /shortcut/clipboard/get, or a card-entry screen caught by an unscoped /pic/screenshot, puts the rack in scope as a system that can see cardholder data.Never persist the text field from a clipboard read; verify success by length or hash, not by logging the value. Crop screenshots away from card-entry fields entirely rather than after the fact.
KYCWhere a utag sub-account under /config/user/login represents a verified identity, for example an exchange or bank account, the phone screens driving its onboarding are the KYC evidence trail, and the single recoverable password in IMService.json is the key to every one of that login's ten sub-accounts at once.One phone number and password per regulated program, never shared across utag slots with unrelated workloads, so a leaked IMService.json exposes one program instead of ten.

Trap allow_ip_list will not do the job people assign it

Operators reach for /config/imserver/set's allow_ip_list and mdns_type as if they were the access control for regulated workloads. They are not: they are documented as screencast discovery rules, and take effect only when mdns_type is 1. The HTTP and WebSocket API on 9911 has no authentication in either edition and accepts calls from any LAN host regardless of these settings. The only real boundary is a Windows Firewall rule scoping TCP 9911 and 17000 to the controller host, applied outside the API, before any regulated data touches this rack.

Wrong The SMS refutation covers the vendor endpoints, not the rack

The verdict above is correct as written for what it measures. Phonefarm's shortcut id 12, Send SMS, is struck through in the vendor's own function table, and no XP path replaces it. A full-text search of all nine XP doc files finds nothing. That part of the entry should stand.

But it is a claim about two vendor endpoints, not about the rack. The custom-Shortcut channel this document already builds elsewhere is ordinary Apple Shortcuts automation, and Shortcuts ships a native Send Message action that composes and sends an iMessage or SMS itself, with no on-screen tap and no Messages UI involved. That action is not an iMouseXP function, but the rack already has two ways to reach it. /key/sendkey?fn_key= fires the AssistiveTouch key bound to the phone's provisioned Shortcut, and /shortcut/clipboard/set already lands a recipient and body on that phone's pasteboard in one fanned-out call, so a Send Message step added to that Shortcut, reading its inputs from the clipboard, turns an existing text-delivery mechanism into a real send. /shortcut/exec/url is a second, unverified path to the same result: iOS's shortcuts://run-shortcut URL scheme can launch a named Shortcut with an input string directly, which would let one Open URL call pass the message text without a clipboard round trip, but every documented example of this endpoint is an http domain, so treat that shortcuts:// route as presumed rather than confirmed until it is probed on this rig.

None of this is a case for unsolicited or bulk sending. Confine it to messages the recipient has already agreed to receive, an operator-owned second number or an account that opted in, the same population the rest of this section assumes. The channel is still outbound only: no function in either edition returns a message body, and none of the 18 WebSocket callbacks fires on receipt, so there is no way to read a reply and no two-way flow to build on top of this. What actually constrains the capability is carrier acceptable-use terms on the sending SIM, Apple's terms for Shortcuts-driven Messages automation, and the consent and anti-spam law already named for the UI workaround: TCPA, CAN-SPAM, PECR and GDPR. That is a legal and contractual limit, not a technical one.

Re-test before this gets promised to anyone: add the Send Message step to the provisioned Shortcut, fire it through both trigger paths, and record whether a blocked permission or bad recipient comes back as anything other than the same data.code 30 timeout every other missing-Shortcut symptom produces. Until that probe runs, this entry should read Needs Shortcut, With caveats, not Not possible, Refuted.

MARK-SETUP-MARK

Section 13 · Prerequisites and setup checklist

Prerequisites and setup checklist

Every capability in this document rests on a stack of things the API cannot see: iOS accessibility toggles, a bound board, a calibrated pointer, a running console, and on two functions, a plug-in that is not installed on this rig. This section lists what each capability class needs, how to prove it is actually working rather than merely configured, and the order to bring a new phone onto the rack.

Global one-time setup (per rig, not per phone)

  • Install the VC runtime and add the iMouseXP install/download folder to Windows Security or 360 exclusions; several install prompts must be allowed or the kernel service and AirPlay receiver never register.
  • Plug boards into the PC before cabling phones. Order is enforced by the hardware: a board reaches /config/usb/get state 1 first, state 2 only once a phone is cabled to it.
  • Start IMConsole.exe and log in. On this rig, with only IMService.exe running, both phones read state 0 in /device/get and the board list in /config/usb/get was empty. The API alone does not bring the rack up.
  • Set air_play_name, air_play_port, air_play_ratio/fps/refresh_rate, and the plug-in counts opencv_num / ocr_num in /config/imserver/set, then call /imserver/restart once (most of these fields need a restart; lang, mdns_type, connect_failed_retry, allow_ip_list, auto_connect, auto_updata, thread_mode, mouse_mode and flip_right apply live).
  • Open the firewall for TCP 9911 (API), TCP 17000 (AirPlay) and UDP 5353 (mDNS) on the phones’ LAN segment, and restrict who else can reach them: the API on this kernel has no authentication.

Trap Two editions, one kernel, wrong function names fail silently-ish

This rig runs the XP kernel on port 9911 with path-style endpoints (/api/mouse/click?id=...). Sending a Phonefarm-style function call such as {"fun":"get_device_list"} to this kernel returns HTTP 500 “List index out of bounds”, not a normal JSON error. Port 9912, which the Phonefarm doc uses, is closed here. Confirm the edition before trusting any function name from the Phonefarm doc: check the response shape of a known-good XP path first.

New-phone bring-up order

Steps in the order the hardware and software enforce them. Each has an immediate check; do not skip ahead on a step that has not passed its check.

  1. Board to PC. Plug the board into a free hub port. Check: /config/usb/get lists its vid/pid at state 1.
  2. Cable to phone. Use the vendor-supplied Lightning or USB-C cable only; a substitute cable is a real failure mode. Check: the same board entry moves to state 2.
  3. Phone-side accessibility settings. On the phone: AssistiveTouch on with tracking sensitivity at maximum and “Always Show Menu” off; Full Keyboard Access on with 1 s auto-hide; Trackpad & Mouse tracking speed at maximum (this menu only appears while the board is attached — its absence is itself a diagnostic); Auto-Lock Never; portrait orientation locked; StandBy off; Control Center with two rows of icons at the bottom. None of this is queryable over the API. Check: only by driving input in a later step.
  4. Mirror the phone. Control Center > Screen Mirroring > select the receiver named in air_play_name (this PC advertises as iMouseXP-5429). Check: /device/get shows a non-zero state and a non-zero air_pid, and imgw/imgh are populated (500×1080 on this rig’s XRs).
  5. Bind the board to the device record. /device/set?id=<deviceid>&vid=720A&pid=<pid> (vid and pid must be set together; binding is single-device). If unsure which physical board is which, unplug and replug the phone cable and watch which uid changes state. Console equivalent: right-click the phone > Bind hardware. Check: /device/get shows the vid/pid/uid populated.
  6. Calibrate (mouse parameters). Check /device/get for a non-empty location_crc first — the shared library (this rig’s value: B0DBD800) may already cover the model and iOS version. If empty, run /device/collection/mouse?id=<id>&cmd=1, complete the collection page on the phone’s home-screen icon, then cmd=2 to stop and /device/collection/mouse/save to publish it. Check: the corner-accuracy probe below.
  7. Install and bind the iMouse Shortcut (only if you need clipboard/Unicode text, album, files, device switches, or the shortcut OCR/image-search fallbacks). Turn on the four Shortcuts > Advanced permissions, scan the console’s QR code, edit the IP inside the shortcut to the kernel PC’s LAN address, run it once and allow every prompt, then bind the launch hotkey under AssistiveTouch > Devices > Customise More Buttons and click “Send Binding Key” in the console. Check: /shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 returns code 0 with the phone’s known LAN IP.
  8. Plug-ins (only if OCR or image-template search is needed). Install the vendor OCR and image-search plug-ins alongside the kernel, set ocr_num / opencv_num, restart the kernel. Check: /pic/ocr?id=<id> returns code 0 instead of 28. On this rig it currently returns 28 — treat OCR and template search as unavailable until this changes.

Verification recipes reused across capability classes

Most of the checks above reduce to a handful of repeatable measurements. Use these instead of ad hoc checks; two of the alternatives below are documented traps.

  • Board and binding: /config/usb/get state 2 means a board is enumerated and a phone is cabled to it; it says nothing about video. /device/get vid/pid/uid non-empty means that device record is bound to that board.
  • Mirroring: /device/get state non-zero and air_pid non-zero together are the live proof; air_pid is the PID of the running AirplayMirroring.exe.
  • Mouse parameters: /device/get location_crc (or location) non-empty; empty means every mouse call returns code 11.
  • Did an input actually land: take the mean absolute pixel difference of a raw BMP frame (/pic/screenshot?binary=true) in a roughly 40 px box around the target coordinate, before and after the action. An idle phone reads 0.02–0.03; a landed tap or move reads 1.4 and up; a keypress that changes the whole screen reads 20 and up. Never compare frames byte-for-byte or by hash: the AirPlay encoder never reproduces a frame exactly, so a hash comparison reports every idle phone as “reacted”.
  • Stuck taps: if /mouse/move and hardware keys work but /mouse/click reads at the idle floor, send /mouse/reset to the affected id and retry before concluding the phone is unresponsive. Do this for the whole target set whenever the mirrored group changes, before any tap-critical sequence.
  • Corner accuracy after calibration: move to three points spanning the frame (e.g. a near corner, the far corner, the centre) and box-diff each; error that grows toward the far corner means the per-device scale is wrong and needs a fresh collection rather than the shared library.
  • Cross-phone actions: press Home twice before mirroring one coordinate to several phones. The two XRs on this rig have different home screens, so an unnormalised coordinate lands on a different app on each.
