Tip Start every session with three calls

/config/imserver/get (kernel alive and configured), /config/usb/get (board count and states), /device/get (mirroring state and air_pid per phone). If IMConsole has not been started since boot, the second and third will read empty or state 0; start it before running anything else.

Also worth knowing

Phone provisioning as an automatable job

Jumping into Settings by URL scheme, then searching inside Settings itself

Needs ShortcutWith caveats

The five phone-side prerequisites this section already calls unreadable and "Not possible" (AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, tracking speed, Auto-Lock, Control Center rows) all live inside Settings, and today reaching them means tapping the Settings icon by hand on every phone. /shortcut/exec/url already opens "any app via its URL scheme or universal link" per its own doc entry; the same call fired at an iOS Settings URL such as prefs:root=General or App-Prefs:root=General lands directly on a Settings pane without ever touching the home screen. Once inside Settings, its own search field is fixed native chrome, not a user-arranged icon, so it is legal to target with one blind coordinate across every phone on the same iOS build, unlike the home screen this document already flags as non-uniform.

How

  1. mouse_reset_pos, send_key GET /api/mouse/reset?id=<a,b,c> then GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<a,b,c>&fn_key=WIN+h (twice) — clear stuck clicks and normalize to home page one, same as the existing Spotlight recipe.
  2. shortcut#13 / /shortcut/exec/url GET /api/shortcut/exec/url?id=<a,b,c>&url=App-Prefs:root=General — one call, comma-fanned to the whole target set, opens Settings directly on every listed phone.
  3. click GET /api/mouse/click?id=<a,b,c>&x=&y= — tap the visible search field near the top of the Settings root list (a fixed OS-chrome coordinate, not a user-arranged one).
  4. send_key (key) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<a,b,c>&key=assistivetouch — type the pane's name (ASCII only) instead of guessing which nested menu it lives in.
  5. send_key (fn_key) GET /api/key/sendkey?id=<a,b,c>&fn_key=ENTER — open the top search hit, then proceed with clicks local to that pane.

Needs

  • iMouse Shortcut installed, IP-edited, run once, and bound to an AssistiveTouch key (bring-up step 7); verify first with /shortcut/device/ip?id=<id>&state=0 before designing around this call, exactly as the existing Spotlight card already recommends.
  • Full Keyboard Access on, for the typed pane name to register.

Watch out

  • Neither vendor doc names prefs: or App-Prefs: specifically; the doc's grant is the general "any URL scheme" claim on shortcut#13, not a tested Settings deep link. Confirm the exact root anchor and any sub-pane fragment on one phone before fleet-wide use; Apple has narrowed what these schemes can open in past iOS releases without notice.
  • A root anchor (prefs:root=General) is far more likely to keep working than a deep sub-pane fragment for something like Accessibility > Touch > AssistiveTouch, which is why the in-Settings search step exists: it reaches a specific pane without needing a guessed or brittle deep-link string.
  • /key/sendkey is ASCII-only in both editions; a pane name is fine, but do not expect this route to help with non-Latin text anywhere else in Settings.
  • /key/sendkey also documents an OPENKeyboard fn_key ("open the on-screen keyboard") in the XP hotkey table; it is not verified here beyond that one-line description, and it does not appear to be a substitute for tapping the search field first, only a possible way to force a keyboard to appear once a field already has focus.
  • Without OCR, there is no server-side confirmation the search actually landed on the intended pane rather than a similarly named one; corroborate with the colour test below when the destination is a toggle.

Scale

/shortcut/exec/url, /mouse/click and /key/sendkey all accept comma-separated id lists, so this whole chain runs once against all 19 boards rather than once per phone, the same fan-out already used elsewhere in this document.

Reading a toggle's on/off state from its pixels

Native APIWith caveats

None of the five accessibility prerequisites expose a queryable state anywhere in either doc; the only way to know AssistiveTouch or Full Keyboard Access is actually on is to look at the switch. With the OCR and image-search plug-ins gated (code 28 on this rig), a colour test on the switch's green fill is the one audit path that does not depend on either plug-in, because the toggle is visible in the mirror stream regardless of plug-in state. This turns setup verification from "assume it's configured" into "read it back," even on this rig today.

How

  1. pic/screenshot (rect) GET /api/pic/screenshot?id=<id>&binary=true&rect=x0,y0,x1,y1 — grab a raw BMP crop tight around the switch's known coordinate; this is the same rect-crop mechanism the setup section already uses for the mean-pixel-difference input check, just decoded for colour instead of difference.
  2. pic/find-multi-color POST /api {"fun":"/pic/find-multi-color","data":{"id":"<id>","list":[{"first_color":"x|y|34C759-202020","similarity":0.85,"rect":[x0,y0,x1,y1]}],"same":false,"all":false}} — kernel-side alternative: ask directly whether the anchor pixel matches iOS system green within tolerance, without pulling the frame client-side at all.
  3. Compare the sampled or matched colour against a green/gray pair captured once on this rig with the toggle in each known state, rather than trusting a textbook hex value.
  4. On a mismatch, mouse/click the same coordinate and re-run the read to confirm the flip actually landed, rather than trusting the click alone.

Needs

  • The toggle already on screen at a known coordinate — this pairs with the URL-scheme-plus-search recipe above (or, until layouts are standardized, a per-phone coordinate) to get there deterministically.
  • Fixed brightness and True Tone off, per this section's existing prerequisite table for multi-colour search, so the sampled RGB does not drift between phones or over the course of a day.
  • Mirroring only for the read; the board is needed only for the corrective click, not for the check itself.

Watch out

  • /pic/find-multi-color is not named as needing a plug-in in either doc, unlike OCR and image search, but it has not been exercised on this rig — run one call against a known-on and known-off toggle before trusting it in a loop.
  • iOS system green is commonly cited near #34C759, but that is a starting anchor, not a measured value from these XRs; calibrate similarity the same empirical way the mean-pixel-difference thresholds elsewhere in this section were calibrated (idle floor vs. landed action), not from the doc's own example similarity of 0.85, which was chosen for a much larger multi-pixel colour table.
  • A colour match at one coordinate only proves that coordinate is green; it says nothing about which setting the switch belongs to. It is only meaningful once the on-screen pane is already known, which is why this card is paired with, not a substitute for, deterministic navigation.
  • Both /pic/screenshot and /pic/find-multi-color take one device id per call ("multiple is not allowed"), unlike /mouse/click and /key/sendkey; a fleet-wide audit is one request per phone, not one request for the fleet.

Scale

The read itself is one call per phone regardless of fleet size, so a 19-board audit is 19 requests either way; the corrective click and re-check that follow a mismatch are the more expensive part per phone, but they only run for the phones that failed the read, not the whole rack.

Standardizing the home screen so one coordinate is legal fleet-wide

Plus external toolingWith caveats

This section already measures the consequence of skipping this step: two identical XRs on this rig have different home screens, so an unnormalized coordinate lands on a different app on each. Restoring every phone from one reference backup, or manually matching layouts by hand, removes that variable at setup time instead of working around it in every later recipe. Neither path runs through the iMouse API; the API's role is limited to confirming and recording which phones have actually been normalized.

How

  1. (External) Restore each phone from one reference backup, via Finder or Apple Configurator over the same cable already used for board control, or from a single iCloud backup taken on a template phone — so wallpaper, page count, folder structure and icon order match across the fleet. Nothing in either vendor doc exposes this; it is standard Apple device management running alongside, not through, the kernel.
  2. (External, only for a handful of phones) Absent a reference backup, manually drag icons into a matching layout once per phone, using the phone's own touch or a board-driven drag (mouse/down at the icon, mouse/move to the target slot, mouse/up) — labor that does not amortize past a few units.
  3. device/set (name) GET /api/device/set?id=<id>&name=XR-18.7-layoutA — once a phone's layout is confirmed to match the reference, tag its device record so later fleet-wide blind clicks can filter get_device_list on that label before firing. This changes nothing on the phone; it is a queryable marker for "trust one coordinate here," on the same terms this document already uses the device name elsewhere: a convenience label, not a source of truth the kernel checks.

Needs

  • A reference phone or backup image, and Finder, Apple Configurator, or iCloud — none of which the iMouse API touches.
  • The accessibility bring-up in this section's new-phone order (step 3) completed and captured in that same reference backup, not before it.

Watch out

  • A restore also resets AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, tracking speed, Auto-Lock and Control Center layout to whatever the backup captured. If the reference backup predates the accessibility bring-up, restoring it undoes that bring-up, and the phone re-enters exactly the "looks fine, ignores input" state this section warns about, until bring-up is repeated.
  • A restore does not require re-collecting mouse parameters, since the shared library keys on model and iOS version rather than a specific phone, but re-check location_crc via /device/get afterward rather than assuming it survived.
  • iCloud or Finder restores need bandwidth and an Apple ID per phone; 19 phones restoring in parallel are bounded by the office uplink, a different ceiling from the 21 req/s screenshot cap or the 0.6 ms/px pointer-walk cost measured elsewhere in this document, and worth planning around separately.
  • /device/set name is unvalidated free text with no schema; a layout-version convention is a discipline the operator enforces, the kernel does not check it.

Scale

This converts the home-screen coordinate problem from a per-action risk, remembering which phones are safe to target blindly, into a one-time per-phone setup cost paid once at bring-up and repaid only after a restore, the same amortization this section already applies to board binding and mouse-parameter calibration.

Network prerequisites for the video channel

Opening TCP 9911, TCP 17000 and UDP 5353 on the firewall gets packets through the host; it does not get the phone onto a network where those packets can find the PC. mDNS is link-local multicast, and most of the ways "the receiver does not appear in Screen Mirroring" actually happens live below the firewall, on switch and AP configuration the API cannot see or fix. The table below lists the conditions in the order worth checking, and what /imserver/regmdns can and cannot do about each.

ConditionEffect on mirroringFix within this APINote
Phones and the rack PC on the same layer-2 broadcast domainUDP 5353 mDNS is link-local; it does not cross a router or a VLAN boundary. A phone on a guest VLAN or a separate subnet from the PC will never see air_play_name in Screen Mirroring, no matter how long you wait.None. /imserver/regmdns re-sends the advertisement on the interface the kernel is already bound to; it cannot make that advertisement reach a different broadcast domain. This is a switch/AP-configuration fix (same VLAN, same subnet), not an API call.Same on both editions; mDNS behavior is OS/network-stack level, not kernel-specific.
Access-point client isolationClient isolation (the default on most guest and many corporate SSIDs) blocks device-to-device traffic between Wi-Fi clients on the same AP, even on the same subnet. The receiver is silently invisible; no error appears anywhere in the API.None from the kernel side. /imserver/regmdns re-broadcasts into a network where isolated clients still cannot receive it. Disable client isolation for the SSID the phones use, or put the rack on a dedicated SSID/VLAN without it.Same on both editions. Worth checking first since it produces the exact symptom this section is written for and leaves no trace in /config/imserver/get or any callback.
Multicast filtering and mDNS proxies on enterprise APs/switchesEnterprise gear commonly drops multicast by default, rate-limits it, or requires IGMP snooping with a working querier; some only forward mDNS across APs/VLANs when an explicit mDNS reflector or Bonjour-gateway service is turned on. Symptoms are intermittent: a phone sees the receiver right after /imserver/regmdns, then loses it after roaming to another AP.None. allow_ip_list and mdns_type (0 = advertise to everyone, 1 = restrict to allow_ip_list) control who the kernel is willing to advertise to, not whether the advertisement is allowed to travel through the network fabric. Re-running /imserver/regmdns after an AP-side change is a reasonable retest, not a fix on its own.Same on both editions; this is infrastructure the rack owner does not control if the network is managed by IT.
2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz airtime for N simultaneous mirrorsOnce connected, each AirPlay mirror is a sustained unicast TCP stream on port 17000, so N phones mirroring at once is N concurrent video streams contending for the same radio. 2.4 GHz has less usable bandwidth and far more contention from neighboring networks; this rig already shows a large frame-rate gap between its two XRs (about 29 vs about 4.5 new frames/s under motion, per HARDWARE.md) attributable to per-phone link quality, not the kernel.None directly; air_play_ratio, air_play_fps and the per-device /device/airplay/set overrides trade image quality for bandwidth, but they cannot fix a contended radio. Put the phones on 5 GHz where the hardware supports it, and keep the rack off a busy shared 2.4 GHz SSID.Same on both editions; scales worse the more phones mirror at once, independent of any plug-in or licence.
DHCP reservation for the rack PCThe iMouse Shortcut on every phone has the kernel's LAN IP typed into it by hand during setup. If the PC's DHCP lease changes, or the PC reboots and is handed a different address, every shortcut-based function (clipboard paste, Unicode text entry, album/file transfer, power/brightness/torch/radio switches, /shortcut/device/ip itself) breaks on every phone at once, with no warning from the kernel: the phone simply cannot reach the address baked into its shortcut.None; there is no API call that pushes a new kernel IP into an already-installed shortcut. Recovery is manual on each phone: open Shortcuts, edit the IP field, run it once, allow the prompts again. Give the rack PC's NIC a DHCP reservation (or a static IP) up front so this never has to happen.Same on both editions; this is the one item on this list that is a rack-wide manual re-provisioning event rather than a one-time network setting, so it is worth fixing before onboarding more phones, not after.

Trap /imserver/regmdns is a re-broadcast, not a network fix

Four of the five rows above are conditions that /imserver/regmdns cannot correct: a wrong VLAN, client isolation, a filtered multicast path and a stale phone-side shortcut IP all sit outside the kernel. Calling it repeatedly against one of these will not help; check the network condition first, then call it once to confirm the advertisement goes out. /device/airplay/connect/all is the right recovery call once a batch of phones can see the receiver again, so it belongs after a network fix, not instead of one.

Windows host settings that keep 19 boards enumerated

None of the following is an iMouse function. All five are Windows or filesystem settings on the host PC that sit underneath every capability class above, and none of them is queryable through /config/usb/get or /device/get, only their absence is: a board that flaps between state 2 and state 1 with no cable touched, or a rack that comes up with an empty board list, is usually one of these settings, not a bad board. Set them once per host, not per phone.

SettingWhere to change itWhy it matters on this rigHow to prove it worked
USB selective suspend, disabled globally and per hubControl Panel > Power Options > Change plan settings > Advanced > USB settings > USB selective suspend setting = Disabled, on every power plan in use; then Device Manager > each Generic USB Hub (VID_1A40&PID_0201, three of them chained, per HARDWARE.md) > Properties > Power Management > uncheck “Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power”. Repeat for every USB Root Hub above the three 7-port hubs.Windows can independently suspend an idle hub or an idle board to save power. The resume sequence is the exact usb_change pattern this rig already produces on purpose from /device/usb/restart: code 20 (hardware disconnected), then 19 (connected to computer), then 12 (connected to phone), with the board’s /config/usb/get state dropping from 2 to 1 (or briefly absent) and back to 2. A fleet watchdog built to catch usb_change flapping cannot tell a power-managed hub from a failing one; on a 19-board, three-hub chain there are 19 boards plus at least 3 hub devices that can each be suspended independently.Poll /config/usb/get every few seconds for an idle period (no calls to any device) and confirm no board changes state and no usb_change callback fires. Any flap during a period with zero API traffic is a power-management symptom, not a hardware one.
Sleep and hibernate, both set to NeverPower Options > Screen and sleep > set Sleep to Never (and Hibernate, if enabled, to Never) on both the plugged-in and, if this is a laptop, battery profile.System sleep suspends the whole USB subsystem at once, not one hub at a time: all 19 boards and both AirPlay sessions drop together. Unlike the console dependency below, a sleep/resume cycle is not something the vendor docs describe recovering from automatically, and this project has not tested it; treat every board and every phone as needing to be re-verified after any resume, the same way they are re-verified after a fresh boot./device/get for every phone shows a live, non-zero air_pid and /config/usb/get lists all 19 boards at their prior states, with no manual re-cast or rebind required.
Fast Startup, disabledControl Panel > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do > Change settings that are currently unavailable > uncheck “Turn on fast startup”.Fast Startup hibernates the kernel session instead of fully shutting it down, so a “shutdown” does not reinitialize the USB controllers the way a cold boot does. On a chain of three 7-port hubs with 19 of 21 ports populated, that raises the odds of boards re-enumerating with different PIDs or not all coming back, which matters because this rig addresses boards by PID (vid|pid in /device/usb/restart), not by physical port. This is standard Windows/USB behavior, not something either API doc documents, so verify it on this host rather than assuming it.After a full shutdown and cold power-on, /config/usb/get lists the same 19 uid values as before shutdown, at hub/port positions matching the recorded topology.
IMConsole.exe running at every boot, with a restart-on-exit ruleTask Scheduler: a task triggered “At log on” (or “At startup” if the host auto-logs in), action = launch IMConsole.exe, with an action to relaunch it if the process exits. This is not the same as a Windows service Recovery tab: IMConsole.exe is the console GUI, not the IMService.exe kernel service, so native service recovery only covers the kernel half.Directly measured on this rig: with only IMService.exe running, /device/get read state 0 for both phones and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list; once IMConsole.exe was started and logged in, both phones showed state 1 and all 19 boards listed. The API alone does not bring the rack up after a reboot./config/usb/get returns 19 boards and /device/get shows non-zero state for every phone that was mirroring before reboot, within a few minutes of the host coming up unattended, with nobody at the keyboard.

Open Headless console launch is untested

Every observation of the console bringing the rack up on this rig happened with an interactive, logged-in desktop session. Task Scheduler can launch IMConsole.exe without anyone logged in (“Run whether user is logged in or not”), but a GUI app started that way may not get a renderable window, and it is not verified here whether the rack still comes up in that mode. Test it once on this host: reboot with no one logged in, wait, then poll /config/usb/get and /device/get remotely. If the board list stays empty, fall back to auto-login plus an on-screen launch.

Disk budget and rotation for a frame archive

/pic/screenshot with binary=true returns the raw BMP the decoder already holds: measured 1,620,054 bytes per frame on this rig’s 500×1080 stream (500 × 1080 × 3 bytes plus a 54-byte header), call it 1.6 MB. With save_path set, the kernel writes that BMP to disk and returns the path instead of the bytes; the documented response is code, id, image (the path) and message, nothing about free space, retention or overwriting. A frame archive that polls all 19 boards will fill a disk unless something outside the API manages it.

Capture cadence, per phoneAggregate rate, 19 phonesPer hourPer day
1 frame / s (continuous)~30.4 MB/s~109 GB~2.6 TB
1 frame / 10 s~3.0 MB/s~11 GB~263 GB
1 frame / 60 s (health-check only)~0.5 MB/s~1.8 GB~44 GB

The JPEG variant (binary=true&jpg=true) shrinks each frame to roughly 96 KB but costs a kernel-side re-encode measured at 40 ms and a hard ceiling around 21 requests per second on this host; that ceiling is a property of the kernel doing the re-encoding, so budget archival JPEG capture across all 19 phones against one shared ceiling, not 21 per phone. Raw BMP has no such cap and is the right default for an archive; reserve JPEG for a slow or remote link.

Trap save_path has no rotation, and the filename is not one either

Left alone, save_path writes one file per call forever; nothing in either API doc deletes, caps or ages out old frames. The filename the kernel generates (for example 1128935437.bmp in the vendor’s own example) is an opaque kernel-assigned number, not a timestamp or sequence you can sort or expire by. Build retention outside the API: a scheduled task that deletes files older than a fixed window, or a watchdog that stops capture below a free-space threshold, keyed off your own capture-time filename rather than the one the kernel hands back.

Clock sync for evidence timestamps

Neither /pic/screenshot nor /config/usb/get nor /device/get nor the usb_change callback carries a server-side timestamp field; every one of the response bodies checked in these docs is limited to status, code, id and the payload itself. The only time base for an archived frame or a logged board flap is the host clock at the moment your own code made the call. If that clock drifts, or resets on a sleep/resume or a Fast-Startup hybrid boot, an evidence trail built from this archive cannot be lined up against another system’s logs, or even against itself across a restart.

  • Enable the Windows Time service (w32tm) against a reliable NTP source and confirm it is running, rather than the default best-effort domain/workgroup sync.
  • Stamp every archived frame and every logged callback with your own capture-side timestamp at the moment of the call; do not depend on file creation time alone, since a restore, copy or antivirus scan can rewrite it.
  • Re-check sync after any change to the sleep/hibernate/Fast Startup settings above: a resume from sleep or hibernate is a common source of a clock jump on hosts that were not already NTP-disciplined.

A. Error codes (data.code)

Every XP call answers HTTP status 200 once the kernel accepts the request; the real result is data.code below, with data.message carrying a Chinese string that should never be pattern-matched. A bare Phonefarm-style function name (no leading slash, two segments) never reaches this table at all: it fails one level up with HTTP status 500, "List index out of bounds," which is a routing rejection, not a code 41.

CodeMeaningUsual cause or remedy
0success—
1id does not existCheck the id against /device/get; typo, or the device never appeared.
2device not bound to hardwareRun /device/set with vid and pid, or bind it from the vendor console.
3hardware not connectedBoard not seen on the USB bus. Check /config/usb/get state, the cable, the hub port.
4collection failedRetry mouse-parameter collection; confirm board and phone are both connected.
5a device is already collectingOnly one device can run /device/collection/mouse at a time. Wait or stop it (cmd=2).
6device is not collecting mouseStart collection with cmd=1 before sending cmd=2 or a status query.
7device id does not exist, or device is online/device/del and /device/group/del refuse an online device; disconnect it first.
8scan code opened successfullyCalibration progress notice, not an error.
9entered the collection pageCalibration progress notice, not an error.
10hardware id is emptyThe id parameter is missing from the request.
11no mouse parametersDevice has no calibration. Set a location_crc from the library, or run a collection.
12hardware and phone connectingProgress notice; also the usb_change event code for "phone attached to board."
13hardware not connected to phoneBoard is on the PC (state 1) but no phone is cabled to it (not state 2).
14start workingCalibration progress notice, not an error.
15no coordinatesA call that needed a screen position received none.
16hardware not working, unknown errorBoard-level fault. Power-cycle the board, reseat the cable, or try /device/usb/restart.
17retry on failureCalibration is retrying automatically.
18failure stopCalibration gave up after retries.
19hardware and computer connectingProgress notice; also the usb_change event code for "board connected to PC."
20hardware disconnected from computerBoard dropped off the USB bus. Check the hub and cable.
21at workCalibration in progress.
22device onlineThe operation needs the device offline first (for example, delete).
23hardware unbound deviceThe board has no device record bound to it.
24hardware not turned onBoard did not complete its handshake with the kernel.
25device is offlineNot mirroring. Screenshot, OCR and input calls fail until it reconnects.
26screenshot failedDevice dropped mid-capture; retry.
27path does not existsave_path, or a file path inside a Shortcut call, is invalid.
28plugin not connectedOCR or image-search plug-in not installed. This is the code every /pic/ocr call returns on this rig.
29plugin interface call timed outThe plug-in is overloaded or hung.
30call timeoutThe outtime budget elapsed before a phone-side Shortcut replied.
31OCR did not recognize the textNo text in the search region met the similarity threshold.
32no text found/pic/find-text found no match.
33failGeneric failure with no more specific code.
34remove the device from the group first/device/group/del refuses a non-empty group.
35file list empty, or none of the files existA Shortcut file or album transfer was given a bad path or filename.
36parameter errorA required field is missing or malformed.
37login failed/config/user/login credentials rejected.
38registration failedAccount registration rejected.
39password reset failedAccount password reset rejected.
40failed to send verification codeAccount verification-code request rejected.
41incompatible commandsThe path is not valid for this call or this kernel build. Not the same failure as the HTTP 500 a bare Phonefarm function name gets; that is rejected before it reaches this table.

XP also exposes two Shortcut paths with no Phonefarm id at all: /shortcut/album/clear (empty an album) and /shortcut/switch/device (state 0 shuts the phone down, state 1 restarts it, iOS 15+).

C. Phonefarm to XP function mapping

Every Phonefarm function name and its XP path equivalent, grouped by area. "None" means XP has no equivalent call; "partial" means the XP path covers only part of what the Phonefarm function did.

Device and group management

D. Named keys and hotkey combos (send_key)

/key/sendkey takes either key (ASCII text to type, or a single named key) or fn_key (a combination hotkey) in one call, never both; leave the other field blank. Both are ASCII only, no Chinese or other Unicode; for non-ASCII text use /shortcut/clipboard/set followed by fn_key=WIN+v to paste.

Named single keys (key parameter, and /key/up, /key/down)

  • BACKSPACE, SPACE (a blank single space), TAB, ENTER, UpArrow, DownArrow, LeftArrow, RightArrow, plus any single ASCII letter, digit or punctuation character.

E. Supported iPhone models and mirror geometry

Confirmed on this rig: two iPhone XR, internal model iPhone11,8, iOS 18.7.10, logical width x height 414 x 896 points, mirror imgw x imgh 500 x 1080 pixels on both phones, air_pid 22236, location_crc B0DBD800 (a shared-library calibration record, not a per-device one).

The full model and calibration library is served by get_devicemodel_list (Phonefarm) and /config/devicemodel/get (XP); the XP doc elides its own response as "too many to list," so the table below is what the reference docs actually show plus the logical sizes their examples span, not a live probe of this kernel's library.

Logical width x height (points)Doc example device(s)Note

Trap imgw x imgh is not a per-model constant

The equipment-related XP doc's own two worked examples show the identical iPhone 6s logical size, 375 x 667, captured at imgw/imgh 750 x 1334 in one record and 460 x 818 in another. The mirror-pixel size is a property of the live AirPlay stream and its cast settings (air_ratio, air_fps, and so on at connect time), not of the phone model. Always read imgw/imgh from /device/get for the specific device record being addressed, never assume it from the model name or the logical size above. Every /mouse/click, /mouse/move and /pic/screenshot coordinate is in this mirror-pixel space, not the logical points space.

F. Ports and processes on the PC

Port / transportProcessPurposeStatus on this rig
9911 TCPIMService.exeHTTP + WebSocket XP API, both under /apiOpen. The only API surface this rig answers on.
3362 UDPIMService.exeInternal kernel trafficOpen
17000 TCPAirplayMirroring.exeAirPlay mirroring session dataOpen. 4 established sockets from the 2 phones, measured 10 Sep 2026.
47010 TCPAirplayMirroring.exeAirPlay mirroring, secondaryOpen
5353 UDPmDNSResponder.exeBonjour; advertises the PC as AirPlay receiver "iMouseXP-5429"Open
5356 UDPmDNSResponder.exeBonjourOpen
18082mDNSResponder.exeBonjourOpen
9912 TCP—The Phonefarm-edition HTTP API port; not used by the XP kernel installed on this rigClosed, nothing listening

Processes. IMService.exe is the kernel; it must be running for the API to answer at all. IMConsole.exe is the vendor console UI; on this rig, with it not running, /device/get reported both phones state 0 and /config/usb/get returned an empty board list even though IMService.exe was up, so the console has to be started for mirroring and board enumeration to come up. AirplayMirroring.exe mirrors the AirPlay video; its PID (22236, live on this rig) is what /device/get's air_pid field echoes as proof a phone is actually mirroring, not just bound.

Trap no authentication on 9911

Any host on the LAN can call http://<pc>:9911/api with no credential of any kind. Firewall 9911 and 17000 to trusted hosts; do not expose this PC to an untrusted network, and never add a bearer token or API key expecting the kernel to check it.
